* Another student: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿In a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shuʿarā' 195].
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down (193) upon your heart, that you may be among the warners (194) in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shuʿarā' 193–195]. And these letters, by the requirement of the Arabic tongue, have no meaning; they are merely letters of the alphabet. On this basis, if we take that the Qur'an was revealed in a clear Arabic tongue, it becomes clear that these letters have no meaning in themselves. If an objector raises the point and says: if you say they have no meaning in themselves, then they are meaningless (*laghw*), so what is the answer?
* A student: The answer to that is to say: they have a meaning in something else, they have a meaning..
* The Shaykh: They have a purpose. What is it?
* A student: It is the challenge.
* The Shaykh: The completeness of the challenge, in that it is said: O Arabs, you compose your speech from these letters.
* A student: And you are not able to produce the like of this Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you. Is there any indication of what has been mentioned, that they are letters intended to show the completeness of the challenge to these Arabs?
* A student: Yes indeed, because most of the surahs that begin with these letters are followed by the word "the Qur'an."
* The Shaykh: Well done. Because mention of the Qur'an comes after them, indicating that the Qur'an is made of these letters, and yet you were unable to produce it.

His words: ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (2). A Book whose verses are detailed﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 2, 3]. Parse the sentence (*iʿrāb*).
* A student: ﴿Tanzīl﴾ allows two possibilities: that it is a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*) and ﴿kitāb﴾ is a delayed subject (*mubtada' mu'akhkhar*); and it allows that ﴿tanzīl﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*) and ﴿kitāb﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*), and this is the preferred view.
* The Shaykh: And which did the author follow?
* A student: The first, which the author followed: that ﴿tanzīl﴾ is a fronted predicate and ﴿kitāb﴾ is a delayed subject.
* The Shaykh: Yes, go on.
* Another student: On the contrary, the author mentioned that ﴿tanzīl﴾.
* The Shaykh: On the contrary, the author mentioned that ﴿tanzīl﴾.
* A student: Is a delayed subject, and ﴿kitāb﴾ is the predicate.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well done.

His words: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. He said: (it is a *ḥāl* from ﴿kitāb﴾ by its description). What is the meaning of this?
* A student: That in a *ḥāl* it is not permissible for it to be a non-derived noun (...) the derived noun, so he answered that it is a *ḥāl* by its description.
* The Shaykh: Well done, that is complete. There is also another possibility: that it is a *ḥāl* from ﴿kitāb﴾ by its description, by the description of the Book, and it is also an answer to an implied question, which is: how is it correct for a *ḥāl* to come from an indefinite noun? So he said: it is described, ﴿a Book whose verses are detailed﴾, and when an indefinite noun is described, a *ḥāl* may come from it, as is well known in the books of grammar.

His words: ﴿bashīran wa nadhīran fa-aʿraḍa aktharuhum﴾. ﴿Bashīran﴾ ("bringing good news"), (﴿li-qawmin yaʿlamūn﴾ "for a people who know," meaning they understand this, and they are the Arabs). That is, Allah made it an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know it and understand it, and they have no excuse for opposing it and disbelieving in it, because they know it, as He said in another verse: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3]; that is, you may understand its meaning, since it came in the language of the Arabs.

﴿Bashīran wa nadhīran﴾ ("﴿bashīran﴾ is an attribute of ﴿Qur'ānan﴾"), meaning: We made it an Arabic Qur'an, ﴿a Book whose verses are detailed, an Arabic Qur'an, bringing good news and warning﴾. Bringing good news to whom? Bringing good news to those who believe in it, as He said: ﴿And guidance and good news for the Muslims﴾ [al-Naḥl 102], and warning to those who disbelieve in it. If you wish, say: it is a warner to all the worlds, as He said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that it may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqān 1].

The point is that the good news is specific, and the warning is general, and sometimes it is specific, as He said: ﴿And that you may warn with it a stubborn people﴾ [Maryam 97], meaning those who disbelieved in it, so take heed. Thus *bashīr* is specific to those who believe, and *nadhīr* can be general and can be specific. What is a *bashīr*? The *bashīr* is one who informs of what gladdens, and his report is called *bishārah* (good news) because its effect appears on the skin (*bashrah*) of a person; that is why the lines of his face shine with joy. ﴿Nadhīran﴾: the warning (*indhār*) is notification accompanied by frightening.

﴿Fa-aʿraḍa aktharuhum fa-hum lā yasmaʿūn﴾. ﴿Fa-aʿraḍa aktharuhum﴾: the *fa* is conjunctive, and "turned away" (*aʿraḍa*) is conjoined to ﴿fuṣṣilat﴾, meaning: a Book whose verses are detailed, yet most of them turned away. It is also possible that the *fa* is for resumption (*istiʾnāf*), that is, "so they turned away," meaning it is a resumed sentence not conjoined to what precedes it.

"Most of them turned away," that is, most of those to whom it reached, ﴿so they do not hear﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 4], hearing with acceptance. This is the result of turning away, that they came to not hear, and the negation of hearing from them is because its benefit, which is admonition and acceptance, is absent.

Know that hearing is negated sometimes because its root is absent, and sometimes because its fruit is absent. His words: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml 80] is a negation of its root, since the dead do not hear. And His words: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfāl 21] are for the absence of its fruit, since hearing without fruit is like non-existence.

﴿Wa qālū﴾ ("and they said") is conjoined to ﴿fa-aʿraḍa﴾.

("﴿Wa qālū﴾" to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Our hearts are under coverings﴾ ("coverings," *aknnah*, plural of *kinn*, meaning what one is covered by)) ﴿from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier, so act, for we are acting﴾. This, may Allah protect us, is from the intensity of their obstinacy and disbelief. They said to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was calling them: ﴿Our hearts are under coverings from what you call us to﴾, like their saying: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised"﴾ [al-Baqarah 88]. The word *akinnah* is the plural of *kinn*, which is that by which one is covered.

His words: ﴿from what you call us to﴾, that is, from monotheism, obedience, and testifying to Allah's oneness and to His Messenger's prophethood. They mentioned the hearts and began with them because they are the seat of understanding.

(﴿And in our ears is deafness﴾, "heaviness") meaning: we do not hear, that is, we listen to you with aversion and hatred, as if there were heaviness of hearing in our ears. ﴿And between us and you is a barrier﴾, that is, a partition between us and you, so that we do not see you. Thus they covered all the avenues of perception: the first avenue is the heart, the second is hearing, and the third is sight. The negation of sight from them is by His words: ﴿and between us and you is a barrier﴾. Allah, the Exalted, has combined these three in His words: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 36].

And consider their saying: ﴿And between us and you there is a barrier﴾. They did not say "and between us and you a barrier," which would indicate that this barrier extends from our side to you. Accordingly, the further we move away from you, the thicker this barrier becomes, because if its beginning is from their side toward the Messenger, then as the distance increases, its thickness increases. This is because *min* (from) here indicates the starting point, so it conveys that this barrier runs directly from them to the Messenger (ﷺ). But if they had said, "and between us and you is a barrier," it would have been possible for the barrier to be in the middle, even if there were a distance between it and them. This indicates the thickness of what lies between them and the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and his remoteness from them.

﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾. This, God forbid, is a challenge to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, as it appears, and it is not a matter of permission but of challenge (﴿So act﴾ according to your religion, ﴿indeed we are acting﴾ according to our religion). It may also mean: act for your struggle, for we are acting for our struggle against you. Which of these is more eloquent: what the author (al-Mu'allif) stated, or this view? The second is more eloquent, because it is as if they are saying: act, and we too will act, and let us see which of us prevails.

Among the benefits of these verses:

* The revelation of the Qur'an is from God; this is shown by His saying: ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

* Among its benefits: the sending down of the Qur'an is one of the effects of God's mercy, as He said: ﴿from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of two of God's names, *al-Rahman* and *al-Rahim*.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the attribute of mercy indicated by these two names. We have mentioned during the tafsir that the people of ta'til (denial of divine attributes) denied that God has mercy. Did we not mention this? We said that they interpret mercy either as beneficence and reward, which is separate from Him, or as the will to bestow beneficence and reward, because they acknowledged the will. We clarified the falsehood of this view, and that the correct position is that mercy is one of the attributes of God, Mighty and Majestic, but it is not like the mercy of the created beings.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the Qur'an's verses have been detailed (*fussilat*). The detailing, as we said, is of two kinds: verbal and meaningful. Verbal detailing is by what? By the separations between the verses. Meaningful detailing is in the meaning: when God mentions a command, He mentions a prohibition; when He mentions a reward, He mentions a punishment; when He mentions the people of goodness, He mentions the people of evil, and so on; it is *mathani* (paired, repeated).

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: every verse of the Qur'an is considered a sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Its verses have been detailed﴾, and ﴿its verses﴾ is a plural that encompasses each individual one separately and also the whole collectively.

* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language. Therefore there is an honour for the Arabs, because this Qur'an was revealed in their language. It also means the preservation of the Arabic language, because this Qur'an will remain until God permits the destruction of the world. It is known that when it remains in the Arabic tongue, the Arabic language will be kept alive and will endure. This is one of the effects of the Qur'an, as he says. What did you say?

* Student: I said: in this there is that the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and that this shows the Qur'an will remain until God permits the destruction of the world, and this is evidence that the Arabic language will remain alive.

* The Shaykh: Is this what you said?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: No, this is not the meaning. We mentioned that this is an honour for the Arabs, is it not so? Since it was revealed in their language, and that in it is the preservation and perpetuation of the Arabic language, because it was revealed in it, and it will remain until God permits the destruction of the world.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: this Qur'an is not understood, even if it is in the Arabic language, except by those who have knowledge; this is shown by His saying: ﴿for a people who know﴾. As for one who is not fit for knowledge, he will gain nothing from this Book, because he is unlettered (*ummi*), and whoever recites the Qur'an without understanding its meaning is unlettered even if he recites it; this is due to the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book, except wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah 78]. So the one who knows the Qur'an only in recitation is like the one who does not recite it, and there is no difference.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the Qur'an contains good tidings and warning: a bringer of good news and a warner. But is this distributed, or can ﴿a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ be in one and the same time? It can be both. As for the first, that it is a bringer of good news and a warner, we find among its verses what is good news for the believers, and we find among its verses what is a warning. As for the second, that a single verse may benefit some people and harm others, read: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say: "Which of you has had this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has increased them in defilement to their defilement, and they died while they were disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah 124–125]. Do not be surprised that one thing may be harmful from one aspect and beneficial from another aspect: the Qur'an is beneficial to the believers and harmful to non-believers. Do not be surprised at this. I will give you a tangible example: dates, sweet in taste, a fruit, nourishment, a staple food; one person eats it and is harmed by it, and another eats it and grows by it, though it is one thing. Likewise is the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: despite the Qur'an being described with this sublime description (the detailing of its verses, that it is in the Arabic language, and that it is a bringer of good news and a warner), it has not been spared opposition and turning away; this is shown by His saying: ﴿But most of them turned away﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verses: the permissibility of negating hearing from one who does not benefit from it; this is shown by His saying: ﴿so they do not hear﴾. Similarly, it is said regarding the rest of the senses for one who does not benefit from them: we say that their existence is like non-existence. So whoever does not benefit from what he sees, we say: this one does not see, even if he has two eyes.

* Among the noble benefits of the verses: the intensity of the polytheists' hatred for the truth that was revealed. The evidence? 

* Student: That they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier, so act, indeed we are acting﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾, is that correct?
So, * among its benefits: the intensity of the polytheists' obstinacy and opposition to these attributes which the brother mentioned.

* Among the noble benefits of these verses: the challenge of these falsifiers to their falsehood.

* Derived from this: among the people of falsehood are those who challenge the people of truth until our day, until our day. But the people of truth must seek God's help, Mighty and Majestic, in confronting them, and know that a word of truth overcomes a thousand words of falsehood. But the sword depends on its wielder; a sword may be in the hand of a coward, and when he sees the enemy approaching, the sword falls from his hand. Does he benefit from the sword? No. But in the hand of a brave man, even if his sword is blunt, he would strike the heads of the enemies with it. The truth is that the sword depends on its wielder. How many a person carries many things of the Sharia but benefits neither himself nor others; and how many a person far less than that, yet God benefits through him, because he is a striver who struggles against the people of falsehood with the truth he possesses.

The student: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ha Mim. A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A Book whose verses have been detailed, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know, bearing good news and warning, yet most of them turn away, so they do not hear.﴾ [Fussilat 1-4].

The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Before we begin today's lesson, let us return to the previous lesson so that we complete the benefits. We had reached: Then He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. The basmalah has been discussed at length, and we explained that it is a verse of the Book of Allah. However, it is not a verse belonging to the surah that follows it or the one that precedes it. Rather, it is a verse recited at the beginning of the surahs, except Surah al-Bara'ah (at-Tawbah). As for its meaning, the person says: "I begin with every name of Allah." We said "every name of Allah" because "ism" (name) is a singular noun in the construct state, and a singular noun in the construct state conveys generality. Every singular noun that is added to a definite noun conveys generality. Have you not considered the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [An-Nahl 18]? ﴿The favour of Allah﴾: if we looked at its wording we would say it is singular, yet it is many and cannot be counted. So this singular noun that is added becomes general. This is the rule: "Every singular noun added to a definite noun conveys generality." Therefore we say: "with every name of Allah."

"Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim" are two adjectives of the Name Allah. However, the first takes into account the attribute, and the second takes into account the act, which is the conveying of mercy. As for the object of this prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur), it is omitted and is supplied as a delayed verb suited to the context. So if you intend to recite and say, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," supply: "I recite." This is chosen; that is, it is chosen to be a verb, because the basic principle in governing is verbs. For this reason a verb governs without condition, whereas nouns that work like verbs require conditions, as is known in the science of grammar (nahw). We chose that it be delayed for two benefits: The first benefit: seeking blessing by mentioning the name of Allah. The second benefit: to convey restriction (hasr), because when the governing element is delayed, that is a restriction. If you say: "Zayda, honour!" the meaning is: do not honour anyone else. But if you say: "Honour Zayd," it is not excluded that you may honour someone else. So we delayed it for two benefits: the first, seeking blessing by mentioning the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and the second, conveying restriction. We supplied it as suitable to the context, because it is clearer regarding the intended meaning.

If someone said: "In the name of Allah I begin," we would say: correct, but it does not make clear the intended meaning as "In the name of Allah I recite" does; that is because beginning can be for reciting and for other than reciting. Therefore it was chosen to be suited to the context. The summary now: Where is the object of the prepositional phrase? We say: it is omitted, a delayed verb suited to the context.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Ha Mim﴾. The commentator said: "Allah knows best what He means by it." This is the etiquette with the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, that whoever does not know its meaning should say: "Allah knows best what He means by it," due to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart, about all those one will be questioned﴾ [Al-Isra 36].

But someone may say: We know that these letters of the alphabet that occur in many surahs have no meaning; we know this from the Qur'an's own indication, for Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 193-195]. The Arabic tongue does not use expression with letters like these as having meaning in themselves. If you say: "A, B, J, H, Kh," they have no meaning. So if they have no meaning according to the Arabic tongue, we say: His saying ﴿Ha Mim﴾, ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [Al-Baqarah 1], ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾ [Yunus 1] and what resembles them have no meaning in themselves. An objection to this: if they have no meaning, they become meaningless, and the speech of Allah contains nothing meaningless. It is said: they are not meaningless; rather the purpose is to establish proof against those polytheists, since they were unable to bring something like the Qur'an, not even a single verse. Did the Qur'an come with letters they do not know, so that they could excuse themselves and say: "It came with letters unknown to us"? The answer: No, the Qur'an came with letters they know.

Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: For this reason you hardly see a surah beginning with these letters without the mention of the Qur'an after them. Begin from the start of al-Baqarah until you reach the end of the surahs beginning with these letters, and you will find that after them is mention of the Qur'an, as an indication that this Qur'an that rendered you incapable, O Arabs, is made of these letters from which you form your speech. This is what Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, held, and it is very clear. As for the view that they have no meaning, it was said by Mujahid ibn Jabr, the most knowledgeable of the Successors in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

He said: ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A Book whose verses have been detailed﴾ [Fussilat 2-3]. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, the commentator, said: "﴿Tanzil﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿Kitab﴾ is its predicate (khabar)." If it were said the other way around, it would be clearer: "A Book whose verses have been detailed, a revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," because one informs about the meaning concerning the essence, and does not inform about the essence concerning the meaning. This is the principle: you say "Zayd is standing." ("standing") is the predicate, and you do not say "Zayd" is the predicate. But what the author went to in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis) has a valid basis; that is, it is not false. However, if it were said that ﴿Tanzil﴾ is the predicate, placed first, and ﴿Kitab﴾ is the delayed subject, it would be clearer and more evident.

﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Who is meant? It means the Lord, Mighty and Majestic; that is: a revelation from Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. But He mentioned these two noble names as an indication that the Qur'an is mercy, because its sending down is a requirement of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Is it not possible to say "a revelation from Allah," as in another verse? However, He said ﴿from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, indicating that this Qur'an was sent down by the requirement of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that Allah showed mercy to the servants through it. "Ar-Rahman" and "ar-Rahim" are two names of Allah, among the most noble names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They come together, and they come separately from each other. If they are separated, each one includes the meaning of the other. His saying ﴿The Most Gracious, established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 5] is separated from ﴿ar-Rahim﴾, so it includes the attribute and the act; that is, Allah the Exalted is described with vast mercy, and He, glorified and exalted, shows mercy by this mercy to whomever He wills of His servants.

In His saying ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ [Yunus 107] too we say: "ar-Rahim" here includes both the attribute and the act, because it is separated from "ar-Rahman." As for when "ar-Rahman" and "ar-Rahim" come together, "ar-Rahman" is for the attribute and "ar-Rahim" is for the act. This is why "ar-Rahman" is in the pattern (fa'lan), and this pattern in the Arabic language indicates fullness and the completeness of the attribute that is intended. For example, "ghadban" is said of one who is filled with anger, and "ghadib" is said of one whose anger is light; similarly "sakran" for one filled with intoxication. So all this pattern indicates fullness and vastness. As for "ar-Rahim," the aspect of the act is predominant in it, that is: conveying mercy to the one shown mercy. For this reason it came in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿And He has always been Merciful to the believers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 43]; that is, His mercy has reached the believers in an absolute manner, while as for non-believers, He shows mercy to them in the general sense.

The summary of what we said regarding ﴿ar-Rahman ar-Rahim﴾: either "ar-Rahman" is mentioned with "ar-Rahim," or one of them is mentioned separately from the other. If one is mentioned separately from the other, the second includes it. If both are mentioned together, the aspect of attribute predominates in "ar-Rahman," and the aspect of act predominates in "ar-Rahim."

Know that these two noble names indicate that Allah, the Exalted, is described with mercy, as He said: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, possessor of mercy﴾ [Al-Kahf 58], ﴿And your Lord is the Rich, possessor of mercy﴾ [Al-An'am 133]. So mercy is His attribute, and "ar-Rahim" is His name. Is this name transitive, or is it of the intransitive verbal nouns? It is transitive, due to His saying: ﴿And He punishes whom He wills and shows mercy to whom He wills﴾ [Al-Ankabut 21].

The rule in creed is that if the name is intransitive, it includes two matters: affirmation of the name and affirmation of the attribute. If it is transitive, it includes three things: affirmation of the name, affirmation of the attribute, and affirmation of the act. So the word "al-'Azim" (the Mighty) is a name of Allah: is it intransitive or transitive? Intransitive; for this reason one says "'azuma," meaning it became great. Belief in it includes belief in "al-'Azim" as a name of Allah, and it also includes affirmation of greatness for Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

"Ar-Rahman" includes three things: "ar-Rahman" is a name of Allah; mercy is one of His attributes; and the act, that is, He shows mercy to whom He wills. On this basis, measure the rest. As for belief in the names: if a name is transitive, it is necessary to believe in the name, the attribute and the act; if it is intransitive, it is necessary to believe in the name and the attribute.

﴿A Book whose verses have been detailed﴾. "Kitab" is on the pattern "fi'al" meaning "maf'ul" (written). Written in what? We say: written in the Preserved Tablet, written in the scrolls in the hands of the angels, written in the scrolls in our hands. As for the first, its evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet﴾ [Al-Buruj 21-22]. As for the second, its evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever wills may remember it, in honoured scrolls, exalted and purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ [Abasa 12-16]. As for the third, it is clear. So every mention of "kitab" includes these three meanings: a kitab, that is, written in what? In the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels, in the scrolls in our hands.

(﴿Whose verses have been detailed﴾: the rulings, the narratives and the admonitions have been made clear.) Tafsil is the opposite of ijmal (summarization/generality). That is, the verses of the Qur'an are detailed, but they sometimes come in general terms and sometimes in detail; and when the general is detailed, everything becomes detailed.

His saying ﴿ayatuh﴾ is the plural of "ayah." An ayah in the Qur'an is whatever is separated from what precedes it and what follows it by a pause. For this reason you hear the scholars say: "fawasil al-ayat," meaning the places where an ayah is separated from what comes before and after it. Among these noble verses there is the long, the short and the medium. The longest verse in the Book of Allah is the verse of debt: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾ [Al-Baqarah 282]. The shortest verse is ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ [Ta-Ha 1]; but this is among the letters that have no meaning, as we established.

Let us see: ﴿Thumma nazar﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 21] and ﴿Mudhammatan﴾ [Ar-Rahman 64], which of them has more letters? ﴿Thumma nazar﴾ has six letters; the doubled Mim against two ﴿mudhammatan﴾...?

Students: Eight, Shaykh.

Other students: Nine.

The Shaykh: So which is more? Six or eight? Then ﴿Thumma nazar﴾ is the shortest verse in the Book of Allah, and the rest are medium, some leaning toward length and some toward brevity. The sunnah regarding verses is that you recite them according to how they are divided. This is the sunnah. So recite ﴿Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2] ... ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger or of those who are astray﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2-7]. How many verses? Seven verses; you recite them separately. If you run them together, there is no harm, since no prohibition of that has come; but it is not appropriate for a person to rush through the Qur'an in such a way that letters are lost. Indeed, it may be forbidden if some letters must be lost. As for rushing in which a person completes the letters, there is no harm, but it is better to pause at each verse. Here we ask the brother: do you pause at the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [Al-Ma'un 4]? Is it not a verse?

Student: But it is not a pausal point (wasl).

The Shaykh: Why? Did we not say it is better to pause at each verse?

Student: (...) "those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer."

The Shaykh: But if you pause?

Student: The meaning changes (...) the warning is for all who pray.

The Shaykh: What do you all say? Does one pause or not?

Students: One pauses.

The Shaykh: One pauses, brothers, one pauses, because it is a verse; because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the One who sent it down, and made this a verse separated from the other. Perhaps in pausing at the verse there is a driving of a wedge into the heart, so that the listener is astonished: how is there woe for those who pray? Then he awaits eagerly the meaning that clarifies this. Then comes ﴿Who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [Al-Ma'un 5], as though it were rain upon barren land, is it not so? So we pause at this, and there is no objection. As for ﴿Do not approach prayer﴾ [An-Nisa 43], we do not pause there, because it is not the head of a verse; rather we say: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾.

So ﴿whose verses have been detailed﴾ includes both verbal and meaningful detail. Verbal detail: Allah made each verse independent of the other, each separated from the other. Meaningful detail: clarification and explanation of what was general. For this reason the author, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed only to the meaningful detail, saying: "made clear by the rulings, the narratives and the admonitions." But it should be said that it has been detailed in two respects, verbal and meaningful: the verbal, that each verse is detailed from the other; and the meaningful, that it is made clear and what was general in it is clarified, whether rulings or other matters. ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is? Then what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾ [Al-Infitar 17-18] is general; it is detailed by His saying: ﴿The Day when no soul will possess anything for another, and the command that Day belongs to Allah﴾ [Al-Infitar 19]. ﴿The Striking Calamity. What is the Striking Calamity? And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [Al-Qari'ah 1-3] is general; it is detailed by His saying: ﴿The Day when people will be like scattered moths﴾ [Al-Qari'ah 4]. So the detail here, that is, the meaningful detail, means the clarification of the Qur'an: that it is explained and made evident, even if it comes in general terms, it must be clarified.

﴿A Qur'an, Arabic﴾ is a hal (circumstantial accusative) from ﴿Kitab﴾ by its attribute. The commentator of the Jalalayn, may Allah have mercy on him, is very good: he said: "﴿Qur'anan﴾ is a hal." It is as if someone objected to him: how do you say it is a hal, when a hal is a description, and "Qur'an" is not a description? He answered: by its attribute, where is its attribute? ﴿'Arabiyyan﴾. If the noble verse were only ﴿Qur'anan﴾, it would not be valid for it to be a hal, because a hal must be a derived noun: an active participle, a passive participle, or something similar. "Qur'an" is it derived or not? Not derived; for this reason he said it is "a hal from ﴿Kitab﴾ by its attribute." So "by its attribute" refers to "Qur'an," as if he said: it is valid for it to be a hal because it is described.

If someone says: how do you make it a hal from ﴿Kitab﴾, when ﴿Kitab﴾ is indefinite, and the one a hal refers to must be definite?

We said: this indefinite noun (*nakirah*) in His words ﴿a Book whose verses are detailed﴾ has been specified by its descriptive clause, and an indefinite noun that has been specified becomes close to a definite one. Therefore it is permissible for a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, a description of the state of the subject at the time of the action) to come from it.

So now we have two problems.

The first problem: how did the *ḥāl* come from ﴿kitāb﴾ (a Book), which is indefinite? Its answer: the indefinite noun *kitāb* was described by His words ﴿whose verses are detailed﴾, and when an indefinite noun is described, a *ḥāl* may come from it.

The second problem: if we parse ﴿Qur'ānan﴾ as a *ḥāl*, how can it be a *ḥāl* when it is not a derived noun (*mushtaq*)? Its answer: it is a noun described by a derived noun, and therefore a *ḥāl* may come from it.

﴿Qur'ānan ʿArabiyyan﴾. As for the meaning of its being *ʿArabī* (Arabic), first: *Qur'ān*, the word *Qur'ān* is on the pattern *fuʿlān*, like *shukrān* (gratitude) and *ghufrān* (forgiveness), and similar words. Is it in the sense of *qāri'* (reciter, active participle) or in the sense of *maqrū'* (recited, passive participle)? It was said: it is in the sense of *maqrū'*. Is *maqrū'* from gathering (*jam'*) or from recitation (*tilāwah*)? It was said: it is from *qarā yaqrī*, meaning "to gather," and from it comes the name *qaryah* (village), because it gathers people. And it was said: it is from *qara'a*, meaning "to recite." The correct view is that it is permissible for it to be from both: since the word is capable of both meanings and there is no contradiction between them, it is understood as having both meanings together. This is if we say that ﴿Qur'ān﴾ means *maqrū'*. It is also permissible that it means the active participle *qāri'*, so *Qur'ān* in the sense of *qāri'* means: one that gathers the rulings, the affirmation of Tawhid, and other things. As for ﴿ʿArabiyyan﴾, it is a relative adjective referring to the Arabs, because it came in their language. And Allah knows best.

* A student: May Allah reward you (...). From Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you recite ﴿Al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn﴾, then recite ﴿Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm﴾ (...)."
* The Shaykh: This is not authentic; this hadith is not authentic. What proves that is the authentic hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the Sahih that Allah, the Exalted, said: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves" — meaning al-Fatihah — "when he says: ﴿Al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn﴾, He says: My servant has praised Me." [Narrated by Muslim (395/38) from Abu Hurayrah.] Until the end of the hadith, and it began with His words: ﴿Al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn﴾.

Second: the Messenger (ﷺ) did not vocalize it (*yajhar bihā*) in the audibly recited prayers, according to the preferred view. Had it been part of al-Fatihah, he would have vocalized it as he vocalized the rest of the verses.

Third: the Basmalah is not part of the rest of the surahs of the Qur'an, so we need strong evidence showing that it is part of al-Fatihah.

Fourth: His words, "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves," are halves in terms of the wording and halves in terms of meaning, and this does not hold if we make the Basmalah part of it. Listen: ﴿Al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn﴾ is for Allah; ﴿al-Raḥmāni l-Raḥīm (3), Māliki yawmi d-dīn﴾ is for Allah. Three verses. ﴿Ihdina ṣ-ṣirāṭa l-mustaqīm﴾ is for the servant; ﴿ṣirāṭa lladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim﴾ is for the servant; ﴿ghayri l-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa la ḍ-ḍāllīn﴾ is for the servant. So: three and three, and ﴿Iyyāka naʿbudu wa iyyāka nastaʿīn﴾ is divided between them, as the hadith states: "This is between Me and My servant in two halves." So there are three verses and a half for Allah, and three verses and a half for the servant. If we said the Basmalah is part of it, this division would not hold.

Fifth: if you make the Basmalah part of al-Fatihah, the last verse becomes long and does not fit with what precedes it, because the last verse would be ﴿ṣirāṭa lladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim ghayri l-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa la ḍ-ḍāllīn﴾, and this does not match His words ﴿Iyyāka naʿbudu wa iyyāka nastaʿīn﴾ or ﴿Ihdina ṣ-ṣirāṭa l-mustaqīm﴾. This is contrary to eloquence (*balāghah*). So we have four aspects, all of which indicate that the Basmalah is not part of al-Fatihah.

* A student: O Shaykh! May Allah bless you. Regarding the mention of past nations: when we pass by a specific person among those destroyed, is it good for a person to attach a curse (*sabb*) to him, just as we attach mercy or supplication to those among the righteous whom we mention?
* The Shaykh: There is no harm if we are certain, for example you say: "Pharaoh, may Allah curse him." There is no objection.
* A student: Is there no objection, or is it recommended?
* The Shaykh: No. As for it being recommended, I hold back from that, because of the Messenger's saying: "Do not revile the dead, for they have gone forward to what they have sent ahead."  [Narrated by al-Bukhari (1393) from ʿĀ'ishah.]
* A student: So the preferable path, based on "The believer is not one who curses much (*laʿʿān*)," should be left, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No. Cursing (*liʿān*) is for the living. As for this, we curse him because Allah cursed him.
* A student: ﴿al-Raḥmāni l-Raḥīm﴾. Some exegetes mentioned that *al-Raḥmān* is more general than *al-Raḥīm*: it includes the disbelievers, whereas *al-Raḥīm* is specific to the believers. Is this correct?
* The Shaykh: Yes, some of them said this. They said: *al-Raḥmān* is general and *al-Raḥīm* is specific. But what we have mentioned is better, and Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, drew attention to it; I think it is in *Badā'i' al-Fawā'id*.
* A student: If we say that the Qur'an means *qāri'* (an active participle), do both meanings apply to it, meaning in the sense of gathering and in the sense of recitation, as if it recounts to us the news of those who came before (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, no. They mentioned that *qāri'* means only *jāmi'* (gathering), because in reality the Qur'an does not speak and recite itself, but it is recited (*maqrū'*) in terms of recitation.
* A student: The verses that occur in the Qur'an, for example: ﴿Such days We alternate among people﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 140]. Is it correct that the use of them has been forbidden outside their proper place?
* The Shaykh: No, citing them is not objectionable.
* A student: (...) outside their proper place.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. But making the Qur'an a replacement for ordinary speech is forbidden. For this reason the author of *Jawāhir al-Adab* mentioned a story under the heading: "One who speaks with the Noble Qur'an instead of ordinary speech." He brought the story of a woman who addressed her children with the Qur'an. If she said "You are going out in the morning," she said: ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾ [al-Kahf 62], and if she ordered them to buy something from the market she said: ﴿Send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾ [al-Kahf 19], and similar things.
Then at the end of the story he said: "This woman, for so many years, speaks with the Qur'an, fearing that she might slip and the Merciful be angry with her." In reality she slipped completely; she makes the verses of the Noble Qur'an descend upon her own specific purposes. This is not permissible. But citing the Qur'an, such as when you see a man captivated by the world, and you say: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 46], this is not objectionable. It has also come in a hadith that when the Messenger (ﷺ) saw al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn stumbling in their new garments, he came down, took them, and said: "Allah has spoken the truth": ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghābun 15]. [Narrated by Abu Dawud (1109), al-Tirmidhi (3774), al-Nasa'i (1413), and Ibn Majah (3600) from Buraydah ibn al-Ḥuṣayb.]
* * *
* The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful: ﴿Ḥā Mīm (1). A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (2). A Book whose verses are detailed, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know (3), a bringer of good news and a warner, but most of them turn away, so they do not hear (4). And they say: "Our hearts are under coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier; so act, for we are acting."﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 1–5].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. What is meant by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾?
* A student: This is from the inimitability (*iʿjāz*) which none knows except Allah.
* The Shaykh: There is another opinion. What is it?
* The student: Some scholars explained it, saying: it is from the inimitability (...) these letters are from the Arabic language.
* The Shaykh: That it has no meaning in itself, is that so? But it has a purpose (*maghzā*).
* A student: It has two purposes, and that it is a challenge to the Arabs.
* The Shaykh: From the completeness of the challenge, since the speech of the Arabs is composed of these letters, and yet they were unable to produce the like of the Qur'an. Which of the two do you prefer?
* A student: Both are valid.
* The Shaykh: Not both are valid; they are contradictory.
* A student: I prefer that it is a challenge to the Arabs, an inimitability.
* The Shaykh: That in itself it has no meaning, is that right?
* A student: It has a meaning, but..
* The Shaykh: No, how can it have a meaning?
* A student: It has a meaning (...).
* The Shaykh: So you have preferred the first.
* A student: The second.
* The Shaykh: What is the second?
* A student: The second, I mean.
* The Shaykh: What is the second? Because this is a mix-up of the wheat and the chaff. What?
* A student: The second: that they are letters, that is, Arabic letters. Allah, glorified and exalted, sent them down..
* The Shaykh: They have no meaning in themselves. This is the important point, everyone. What is the evidence that they have no meaning in themselves?
* A student: Because their meaning is not known.
* The Shaykh: Glory be to Allah! So it has a meaning but it is not known. You have retracted your statement.
* A student: That these letters, the Arabs, that is, know them, and they have no meanings (...).
* Another student: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿In a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shuʿarā' 195].
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down (193) upon your heart, that you may be among the warners (194) in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shuʿarā' 193–195]. And these letters, by the requirement of the Arabic tongue, have no meaning; they are merely letters of the alphabet. On this basis, if we take that the Qur'an was revealed in a clear Arabic tongue, it becomes clear that these letters have no meaning in themselves. If an objector raises the point and says: if you say they have no meaning in themselves, then they are meaningless (*laghw*), so what is the answer?
* A student: The answer to that is to say: they have a meaning in something else, they have a meaning..
* The Shaykh: They have a purpose. What is it?
* A student: It is the challenge.
* The Shaykh: The completeness of the challenge, in that it is said: O Arabs, you compose your speech from these letters.
* A student: And you are not able to produce the like of this Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you. Is there any indication of what has been mentioned, that they are letters intended to show the completeness of the challenge to these Arabs?
* A student: Yes indeed, because most of the surahs that begin with these letters are followed by the word "the Qur'an."
* The Shaykh: Well done. Because mention of the Qur'an comes after them, indicating that the Qur'an is made of these letters, and yet you were unable to produce it.

His words: ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (2). A Book whose verses are detailed﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 2, 3]. Parse the sentence (*iʿrāb*).
* A student: ﴿Tanzīl﴾ allows two possibilities: that it is a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*) and ﴿kitāb﴾ is a delayed subject (*mubtada' mu'akhkhar*); and it allows that ﴿tanzīl﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*) and ﴿kitāb﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*), and this is the preferred view.
* The Shaykh: And which did the author follow?
* A student: The first, which the author followed: that ﴿tanzīl﴾ is a fronted predicate and ﴿kitāb﴾ is a delayed subject.
* The Shaykh: Yes, go on.
* Another student: On the contrary, the author mentioned that ﴿tanzīl﴾.
* The Shaykh: On the contrary, the author mentioned that ﴿tanzīl﴾.
* A student: Is a delayed subject, and ﴿kitāb﴾ is the predicate.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well done.

His words: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. He said: (it is a *ḥāl* from ﴿kitāb﴾ by its description). What is the meaning of this?
* A student: That in a *ḥāl* it is not permissible for it to be a non-derived noun (...) the derived noun, so he answered that it is a *ḥāl* by its description.
* The Shaykh: Well done, that is complete. There is also another possibility: that it is a *ḥāl* from ﴿kitāb﴾ by its description, by the description of the Book, and it is also an answer to an implied question, which is: how is it correct for a *ḥāl* to come from an indefinite noun? So he said: it is described, ﴿a Book whose verses are detailed﴾, and when an indefinite noun is described, a *ḥāl* may come from it, as is well known in the books of grammar.

His words: ﴿bashīran wa nadhīran fa-aʿraḍa aktharuhum﴾. ﴿Bashīran﴾ ("bringing good news"), (﴿li-qawmin yaʿlamūn﴾ "for a people who know," meaning they understand this, and they are the Arabs). That is, Allah made it an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know it and understand it, and they have no excuse for opposing it and disbelieving in it, because they know it, as He said in another verse: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3]; that is, you may understand its meaning, since it came in the language of the Arabs.

﴿Bashīran wa nadhīran﴾ ("﴿bashīran﴾ is an attribute of ﴿Qur'ānan﴾"), meaning: We made it an Arabic Qur'an, ﴿a Book whose verses are detailed, an Arabic Qur'an, bringing good news and warning﴾. Bringing good news to whom? Bringing good news to those who believe in it, as He said: ﴿And guidance and good news for the Muslims﴾ [al-Naḥl 102], and warning to those who disbelieve in it. If you wish, say: it is a warner to all the worlds, as He said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that it may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqān 1].

The point is that the good news is specific, and the warning is general, and sometimes it is specific, as He said: ﴿And that you may warn with it a stubborn people﴾ [Maryam 97], meaning those who disbelieved in it, so take heed. Thus *bashīr* is specific to those who believe, and *nadhīr* can be general and can be specific. What is a *bashīr*? The *bashīr* is one who informs of what gladdens, and his report is called *bishārah* (good news) because its effect appears on the skin (*bashrah*) of a person; that is why the lines of his face shine with joy. ﴿Nadhīran﴾: the warning (*indhār*) is notification accompanied by frightening.

﴿Fa-aʿraḍa aktharuhum fa-hum lā yasmaʿūn﴾. ﴿Fa-aʿraḍa aktharuhum﴾: the *fa* is conjunctive, and "turned away" (*aʿraḍa*) is conjoined to ﴿fuṣṣilat﴾, meaning: a Book whose verses are detailed, yet most of them turned away. It is also possible that the *fa* is for resumption (*istiʾnāf*), that is, "so they turned away," meaning it is a resumed sentence not conjoined to what precedes it.

"Most of them turned away," that is, most of those to whom it reached, ﴿so they do not hear﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 4], hearing with acceptance. This is the result of turning away, that they came to not hear, and the negation of hearing from them is because its benefit, which is admonition and acceptance, is absent.

Know that hearing is negated sometimes because its root is absent, and sometimes because its fruit is absent. His words: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml 80] is a negation of its root, since the dead do not hear. And His words: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfāl 21] are for the absence of its fruit, since hearing without fruit is like non-existence.

﴿Wa qālū﴾ ("and they said") is conjoined to ﴿fa-aʿraḍa﴾.

("﴿Wa qālū﴾" to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Our hearts are under coverings﴾ ("coverings," *aknnah*, plural of *kinn*, meaning what one is covered by)) ﴿from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier, so act, for we are acting﴾. This, may Allah protect us, is from the intensity of their obstinacy and disbelief. They said to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was calling them: ﴿Our hearts are under coverings from what you call us to﴾, like their saying: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised"﴾ [al-Baqarah 88]. The word *akinnah* is the plural of *kinn*, which is that by which one is covered.

His words: ﴿from what you call us to﴾, that is, from monotheism, obedience, and testifying to Allah's oneness and to His Messenger's prophethood. They mentioned the hearts and began with them because they are the seat of understanding.

(﴿And in our ears is deafness﴾, "heaviness") meaning: we do not hear, that is, we listen to you with aversion and hatred, as if there were heaviness of hearing in our ears. ﴿And between us and you is a barrier﴾, that is, a partition between us and you, so that we do not see you. Thus they covered all the avenues of perception: the first avenue is the heart, the second is hearing, and the third is sight. The negation of sight from them is by His words: ﴿and between us and you is a barrier﴾. Allah, the Exalted, has combined these three in His words: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 36].

And consider their saying: ﴿And between us and you there is a barrier﴾. They did not say "and between us and you a barrier," which would indicate that this barrier extends from our side to you. Accordingly, the further we move away from you, the thicker this barrier becomes, because if its beginning is from their side toward the Messenger, then as the distance increases, its thickness increases. This is because *min* (from) here indicates the starting point, so it conveys that this barrier runs directly from them to the Messenger (ﷺ). But if they had said, "and between us and you is a barrier," it would have been possible for the barrier to be in the middle, even if there were a distance between it and them. This indicates the thickness of what lies between them and the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and his remoteness from them.

﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾. This, God forbid, is a challenge to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, as it appears, and it is not a matter of permission but of challenge (﴿So act﴾ according to your religion, ﴿indeed we are acting﴾ according to our religion). It may also mean: act for your struggle, for we are acting for our struggle against you. Which of these is more eloquent: what the author (al-Mu'allif) stated, or this view? The second is more eloquent, because it is as if they are saying: act, and we too will act, and let us see which of us prevails.

Among the benefits of these verses:

* The revelation of the Qur'an is from God; this is shown by His saying: ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

* Among its benefits: the sending down of the Qur'an is one of the effects of God's mercy, as He said: ﴿from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of two of God's names, *al-Rahman* and *al-Rahim*.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the attribute of mercy indicated by these two names. We have mentioned during the tafsir that the people of ta'til (denial of divine attributes) denied that God has mercy. Did we not mention this? We said that they interpret mercy either as beneficence and reward, which is separate from Him, or as the will to bestow beneficence and reward, because they acknowledged the will. We clarified the falsehood of this view, and that the correct position is that mercy is one of the attributes of God, Mighty and Majestic, but it is not like the mercy of the created beings.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the Qur'an's verses have been detailed (*fussilat*). The detailing, as we said, is of two kinds: verbal and meaningful. Verbal detailing is by what? By the separations between the verses. Meaningful detailing is in the meaning: when God mentions a command, He mentions a prohibition; when He mentions a reward, He mentions a punishment; when He mentions the people of goodness, He mentions the people of evil, and so on; it is *mathani* (paired, repeated).

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: every verse of the Qur'an is considered a sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Its verses have been detailed﴾, and ﴿its verses﴾ is a plural that encompasses each individual one separately and also the whole collectively.

* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language. Therefore there is an honour for the Arabs, because this Qur'an was revealed in their language. It also means the preservation of the Arabic language, because this Qur'an will remain until God permits the destruction of the world. It is known that when it remains in the Arabic tongue, the Arabic language will be kept alive and will endure. This is one of the effects of the Qur'an, as he says. What did you say?

* Student: I said: in this there is that the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and that this shows the Qur'an will remain until God permits the destruction of the world, and this is evidence that the Arabic language will remain alive.

* The Shaykh: Is this what you said?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: No, this is not the meaning. We mentioned that this is an honour for the Arabs, is it not so? Since it was revealed in their language, and that in it is the preservation and perpetuation of the Arabic language, because it was revealed in it, and it will remain until God permits the destruction of the world.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: this Qur'an is not understood, even if it is in the Arabic language, except by those who have knowledge; this is shown by His saying: ﴿for a people who know﴾. As for one who is not fit for knowledge, he will gain nothing from this Book, because he is unlettered (*ummi*), and whoever recites the Qur'an without understanding its meaning is unlettered even if he recites it; this is due to the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book, except wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah 78]. So the one who knows the Qur'an only in recitation is like the one who does not recite it, and there is no difference.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the Qur'an contains good tidings and warning: a bringer of good news and a warner. But is this distributed, or can ﴿a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ be in one and the same time? It can be both. As for the first, that it is a bringer of good news and a warner, we find among its verses what is good news for the believers, and we find among its verses what is a warning. As for the second, that a single verse may benefit some people and harm others, read: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say: "Which of you has had this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has increased them in defilement to their defilement, and they died while they were disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah 124–125]. Do not be surprised that one thing may be harmful from one aspect and beneficial from another aspect: the Qur'an is beneficial to the believers and harmful to non-believers. Do not be surprised at this. I will give you a tangible example: dates, sweet in taste, a fruit, nourishment, a staple food; one person eats it and is harmed by it, and another eats it and grows by it, though it is one thing. Likewise is the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: despite the Qur'an being described with this sublime description (the detailing of its verses, that it is in the Arabic language, and that it is a bringer of good news and a warner), it has not been spared opposition and turning away; this is shown by His saying: ﴿But most of them turned away﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verses: the permissibility of negating hearing from one who does not benefit from it; this is shown by His saying: ﴿so they do not hear﴾. Similarly, it is said regarding the rest of the senses for one who does not benefit from them: we say that their existence is like non-existence. So whoever does not benefit from what he sees, we say: this one does not see, even if he has two eyes.

* Among the noble benefits of the verses: the intensity of the polytheists' hatred for the truth that was revealed. The evidence? 

* Student: That they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier, so act, indeed we are acting﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾, is that correct?
So, * among its benefits: the intensity of the polytheists' obstinacy and opposition to these attributes which the brother mentioned.

* Among the noble benefits of these verses: the challenge of these falsifiers to their falsehood.

* Derived from this: among the people of falsehood are those who challenge the people of truth until our day, until our day. But the people of truth must seek God's help, Mighty and Majestic, in confronting them, and know that a word of truth overcomes a thousand words of falsehood. But the sword depends on its wielder; a sword may be in the hand of a coward, and when he sees the enemy approaching, the sword falls from his hand. Does he benefit from the sword? No. But in the hand of a brave man, even if his sword is blunt, he would strike the heads of the enemies with it. The truth is that the sword depends on its wielder. How many a person carries many things of the Sharia but benefits neither himself nor others; and how many a person far less than that, yet God benefits through him, because he is a striver who struggles against the people of falsehood with the truth he possesses.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verses 6–7 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you"﴾. That is, I am not a stranger to you. Why do you disbelieve in me when I am a human being like you? I am not a jinn that you should shun me, nor an angel that you should shun me. I am only a human being like you. The *bashar* (human beings) are the children of Adam, and they were named *bashar* because their skin (*bashara*) is visible, as their bodies appear uncovered. This is one of the blessings of Allah the Mighty and Majestic upon us and of His mercy. Allah made the human being bare, except for clothing, so that he would remember that he is bare of faith, except for a garment. What is the garment of faith? It is piety (*taqwa*), as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the garment of piety, that is best﴾ [al-A'raf 26]. Allah made us need physical covering so that we would know that we also need the covering of the inner self. So you are bare of faith unless you wear the garment of piety.

So who are the *bashar*? They are the children of Adam. They were named so because their skin is visible and has no covering over it, unlike other animals, which are covered either by wool, fur, hair, feathers, or other things. He says: ﴿I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed﴾. The phrase ﴿like you﴾ is an emphasis of the meaning of humanity. Otherwise, if he had said only ﴿I am only a human being﴾, would that imply that he is like us or different from us? But he emphasized this meaning with His words ﴿like you﴾, yet he is distinguished by ﴿to whom it is revealed that your God is one God﴾, and so on. This is the distinction and the difference: Muhammad (ﷺ) is a human being to whom revelation is sent.

The one who reveals (*yuha*) is Allah, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Quran so that you may warn the mother of cities and those around it﴾ [al-Shura 7]. So the one who reveals is Allah, and the agent is omitted because it is known. It may be said that it is omitted both because it is known and for generality, since Allah the Exalted may reveal to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) through Jibril, and He may reveal to him without an intermediary. *Al-Iha'* (revelation) is informing quickly and secretly. This informing, done quickly and secretly, is called *iha'*. For this reason, if someone is beside you and you want to ask him while the class is crowded with students, and you fear being overheard, you say: "What? Did you hear now or not?" in a low voice and quickly, so that no one notices you. So every informing done quickly and secretly is called *wahy* (revelation). It is so because the Prophet (ﷺ) receives revelation while people are sitting around him and do not know what the Messenger said.

﴿to whom it is revealed that your God is one God﴾: this clause is in the position of a deputy subject (*na'ib al-fa'il*) of the verb. That is: this news is revealed to me, ﴿that your God is one God﴾. ﴿Innama﴾ is a particle of restriction (*hasr*). On this basis, the sentence contains both negation and affirmation, because restriction is the affirmation of the ruling for what is mentioned and the negation of it for anything else.

Now we will address the ways of restriction, or some of them:
From the ways of restriction: ﴿innama﴾ or ﴿anama﴾, which are one and the same.
The second: negation and affirmation, such as "There is no one standing except Muhammad."
The third: placing before what should be after, such as: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 284].
The fourth: the insertion of a separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*), such as your saying: "Zayd is the excellent one." The separating pronoun gives the meaning of restriction. These are four ways, and they are the most frequently used.

﴿So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness, and woe to the polytheists﴾. "Be upright toward Him" means: aim toward Him. For this reason He did not say "be upright for Him" but said ﴿toward Him﴾, so the verb "be upright" includes the meaning of "aim toward," and so it is more eloquent than "be upright for Him," because one who is upright for a thing may be upright for it while staying in his place without striving toward it. But when it is said "be upright toward Him," it indicates striving toward Allah the Mighty and Majestic and intending Him. Therefore it takes the preposition "toward" (*ila*). Here, is one letter standing in for another, or is the letter kept in its meaning while the verb is given a meaning that suits the letter?

There are two opinions: one view is that the figurative usage is in the particle, and another view is that it is in the verb or the complement. Is my speech now Arabic or non-Arabic? It is Arabic. ﴿A spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan 6]. ﴿from which they drink﴾: does a person drink from a spring? Does he drink from it? That is, can you take the river, for example, in your hand like this and raise it to your mouth as if it were a vessel? You say "I drank with the vessel," which is clear. ﴿A spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾: can the spring be lifted by the hand and drunk from? No. So what should we say?

On this, the scholars have two opinions:
One of them: the figurative usage is in the particle, meaning that the *ba'* (with) means *min* (from), so the servants of Allah drink from it. Is the spring drunk from or not? It is drunk from by hand, or by a vessel, or by any means.
The second opinion: the figurative usage is in the verb, meaning that "drink" has been given a meaning that suits the *ba'*. What suits the *ba'* here? ("quench"). "The servants of Allah quench themselves with it," meaning that it is a spring that quenches. So which of these is better? Which of them is better? I do not say which is easier?
* A student: The second.
* The Shaykh: Have you changed your opinion or are you still with it? There is no vote now, go with what you see. As for if we say the *ba'* means *min*, it is easy, because you can supply any suitable particle and the matter ends. But if we say the *ba'* keeps its own meaning and the verb has been given a meaning that fits it, then it may be difficult for a person to determine the suitable verb. But we say that giving the verb a meaning suitable to the particle is preferable.
Let me explain this to you. If we say ﴿the servants of Allah drink from it﴾ and that the *ba'* means *min*, have we gained a benefit by using *ba'* instead of *min*? We have not gained anything. So bringing this particle causes some confusion, and we have harmed the meaning as well as gaining nothing, because placing one particle in place of another without a reason causes confusion and ambiguity. But if we give the verb a meaning that suits the particle, we gain more benefit, because your estimate, "quench with it," includes the drinking that was mentioned and includes the quenching, so we gain a benefit. This opinion, namely that the verb is given a meaning that suits the particle, is the one held by the Basran grammarians, and I think it is the view chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, because of this benefit we mentioned.
I always hope that students will understand these subtle distinctions, because they sharpen the mind in one respect and open wide horizons for understanding meanings and increasing benefit. Pay attention to them.
* A student: If we say the particle means the other particle, we have gained nothing. Yet in other places in some verses, such as His saying ﴿And I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha 71], we said it means *'ala* (on) and did not give the verb another meaning.
* The Shaykh: No, that is necessary: *fi* means *'ala*, but even so there is a benefit in using *fi* where *'ala* would be expected. I do not know whether I have pointed this out to you or not. We say: if He had said "I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees" with *'ala*, the crucifixion might be a mere hanging with loose rope, but with ﴿in the trunks﴾ it is as if He tied them very tightly, so that these crucified people seem to be inside them, and so we gain a benefit.
* A student: The question is not part of the lesson.
* The Shaykh: Not part of the lesson?
* A student: It is about grammar. How do we expand in grammar (...)?
* The Shaykh: In reality grammar is not difficult except for someone who imagines it is difficult. Otherwise it is one of the easiest sciences. But if you intend to enter grammar while believing it is difficult, be sure it will be closed to you. Do you understand? That is why it is said that it is a palace of reeds with an iron door. Break this door and nothing will remain before you. So do not make it difficult. If I say to you "Zayd stood" (*qama Zaydun*), what do you say about Zayd? Subject (*fa'il*).
And if I say "Zayd was struck" (*duriba Zaydun*)?
* A student: Object.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not the object. "Zayd was struck": linguistically it is correct to say *maf'ul* (the thing done to), since he is struck. But technically we say *na'ib al-fa'il* (deputy subject). Why? Because the subject is a pillar of the sentence. Either it exists, or its deputy exists. Do you understand? In any case, God willing, it is easy, and God willing we will now focus on grammar for you.
* A student: ﴿Bearer of good news and warner﴾. We said that *bushra* (good news) is specific, and that *nudhara* (warning) is sometimes general and sometimes specific. Is it permissible for *bushra* to be general too?
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: Because He gave the disbelievers good news of punishment.
* The Shaykh: ﴿So give them good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 21]. They said this is sarcasm toward them, like when you mock a person by saying "Rejoice in the whip on your back," mocking him.
* A student: May Allah be good to you. Here Allah said ﴿A Book whose verses are explained in detail﴾, and in another verse: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeated (*mathani*)﴾ [al-Zumar 23]. How do we reconcile these verses?
* The Shaykh: There is no contradiction, because His saying ﴿mathani﴾ means ﴿fussilat﴾ (explained in detail), since its meanings are repeated (*tuthana*): good is mentioned and then evil, the people of good and the people of evil, paradise and hellfire, and similar things.
* A student: This is what is meant (...).
* The Shaykh: This is what is meant by His saying ﴿mathani﴾. As for what is meant by His saying ﴿mutashabihan﴾ (consistent), its meaning is that some of it resembles other parts in perfection, beauty, and excellence. I thought you would ask: how do we reconcile Allah's praise of the Quran as "consistent" with His saying ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book, in it are verses that are clear (*muhkamat*), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (*mutashabihat*). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾ [Al 'Imran 7]? The reconciliation is that it is consistent in excellence, with parts resembling one another. As for *muhkamat* and *mutashabihat*: the *muhkamat* are those whose meaning is clear, and the *mutashabihat* are those whose meaning is hidden.
* * *
* The student: ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to the polytheists (6) Who do not give zakat and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers (7). Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that is never cut off (8). Say, "Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days and attribute to Him equals? That is the Lord of the worlds" (9). And He placed on the earth firmly set mountains from above it and blessed it and determined therein its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask (10). Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or by compulsion." They said, "We come willingly" (11). So He completed them as seven heavens in two days and inspired in each heaven its command. And We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and as protection. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing (12). But if they turn away, say, "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud"﴾ [Fussilat 6–13].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed. Earlier we discussed the saying of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us"﴾ [Fussilat 5], and so on, and we mentioned that the faculties of perception are...
* A student: Perception by the heart, perception by hearing, and perception by sight.
* The Shaykh: Does this verse include the blocking of these faculties in them?
* The student: Yes, the verse includes it.
* The Shaykh: How?
* A student: His saying ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us"﴾: this is the blocking of the heart's perception (...). The second perception, by hearing, is ﴿and in our ears is deafness﴾, and the third perception, by sight, is ﴿and between us and you is a barrier﴾.
* The Shaykh: Well done. What is the difference between the two expressions, ﴿and between us and you is a barrier﴾ and ﴿between us and you is a barrier﴾?
* A student: ﴿And between us and you is a barrier﴾ is more intense than "between us and you is a barrier"...
* The Shaykh: More intense than "between us and you is a barrier"? How so?
* A student: Because when there is a barrier from between us and you, the barrier between them becomes stronger the farther they move from it.
* The Shaykh: So this barrier extends from them to the Messenger, even if the distance is great? And in the second case?
* A student: In the second case the barrier is between them without extending from them to the Messenger.
* The Shaykh: The barrier exists with the smallest thing, even if the distance between them is great.
His saying ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾: what is meant by it?
* A student: A challenge.
* The Shaykh: A challenge, as if we are saying: we do not care about you. Act, and we will act. Is that right?
What did the Prophet (ﷺ) establish regarding these people's denial? That is, did he say that he was of another kind, like the angels and the jinn, or what? What did the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, establish regarding the denial of these people? Did he say that he was of a different kind, like the angels and jinn, or something else?
* A student: They denied that he could be a human being like them who calls them.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: He established that he is of their kind.
* The Shaykh: He established that he is of their kind, a human being, but he is distinguished by being revealed to. What was revealed to the Messenger (ﷺ)?
* A student: Monotheism: ﴿that your God is one God﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is monotheism. Is this what all the messengers brought?
* The student: Yes, without doubt.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence that all messengers called to monotheism?
* The student: The evidence is His saying in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity but Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya 25].
* The Shaykh: This is in Surat al-Nahl?!
* The student: No, it is in a different surah, not in Surat al-Nahl, but there is a verse in Surat al-Nahl that I forgot.
* The Shaykh: You do not have to specify the verse's location. ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity but Me, so worship Me﴾. What you want in Surat al-Nahl is His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid Taghut"﴾ [al-Nahl 36].
Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said: ﴿That your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness﴾ [Fussilat 6]. ﴿So be upright toward Him﴾: it appears that this is part of the words of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, that he was commanded to say. The meaning of "be upright toward Him" is: be upright in His religion, intending Him. So it indicates sincerity in action.
﴿And seek His forgiveness﴾: ask Him for forgiveness. Forgiveness includes two things: covering the sin and pardoning it, because it is derived from *al-mighfar*, which is what a fighter wears on his head to protect himself from weapons. The *mighfar* includes protection and covering. On this basis, whenever you ask for forgiveness, remember that you want Allah the Mighty and Majestic to overlook you, so that He does not punish you and conceals your sin.
("Seek His forgiveness"): that is, ask Him for forgiveness, which is covering the sin and overlooking it.
(﴿And woe﴾ is a word of punishment.) The commentator says: ﴿to the polytheists﴾. ("Woe") here is a subject (*mubtada'*), and the fact that it is indefinite is permitted because it is for threat. It is a word of warning and threat. It has been said that it is a valley in Hellfire, but the more correct view is the first: it is a word of threat and warning for everyone who opposes.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 41, verses 6–7 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ means: for those who associate partners with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Their association may be in worship ('ibadah), in divinity (uluhiyyah), or in the Names and Attributes. Whoever claims that there is a creator with Allah, or a helper, or an independent agent who creates some things, is a mushrik (one who commits shirk, associating partners with Allah). Whoever worships another alongside Allah, or shows off in his worship to someone other than Allah, is a mushrik. Whoever claims that the Attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, resemble the attributes of the created beings is a mushrik. Know that shirk is divided into two kinds: minor (asghar) and major (akbar). It is also divided, from another angle, into hidden (khafi) and manifest (jali). All of this is well known in the books of tawhid (the science of Divine Oneness) and 'aqidah (creed).

﴿الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ [Fussilat 7]. This is a description of the mushrikin. ﴿الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْتُونَ﴾ means: they do not give the zakat. The word zakat here may mean the purification of the soul (zakat al-nafs), and it may mean the zakat on wealth (zakat al-mal). If it means zakat on wealth, there is a difficulty, because its apparent meaning requires that the disbelievers are obligated to pay zakat. It is well known that a person is not required to pay zakat until he becomes Muslim, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Mu'adh: "You are going to a people of the Book, so let the first thing you call them to be the Oneness of Allah. Then call them to prayer. Then call them to zakat." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1395) and Muslim (19/31), from Ibn 'Abbas.]

This indicates that a person is not addressed with zakat, meaning its payment, until he embraces Islam. As for if we say that the intended meaning of zakat is the purification of the soul, then this objection does not arise. But another difficulty arises from the wording, which is His saying ﴿لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾. Is the purification of the soul something that can be given? This is a matter for consideration. For this reason, the verse presents a difficulty whichever of these two interpretations you adopt. When a verse has a difficulty between two meanings, we seek the preponderant (al-murajjih) one.
