The preponderant view is that the intended meaning is the purification of the soul, and the meaning is: they do not give their souls their purification. And in the hadith: "Give your soul its piety, and purify it; You are the best one to purify it." [Narrated by Muslim (2722/72), from Zayd ibn Arqam.]

So, on this basis, we prefer that the intended meaning of zakat is the purification of the soul, and the meaning is: they do not give their souls their purification, rather they neglect it and are heedless of it. ﴿وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ كَافِرُونَ﴾. ﴿وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ﴾: ﴿بِالْآخِرَةِ﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur) related to ﴿كَافِرُونَ﴾, and (هم) is a subject (mubtada'), and the second ﴿هُمْ﴾ ... The mufassir says: "(تأكيد)" [emphasis]. Emphasis of what? It is a verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi) of the first (هم). Verbal emphasis is when the word is repeated in its own form, as Ibn Malik said:

*"Of emphasis, the verbal kind comes repeated, like your saying: 'Proceed, proceed.'"*

﴿وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ كَافِرُونَ﴾ means: they deny it and do not believe in it. They say: ﴿مَا هِيَ إِلَّا حَيَاتُنَا الدُّنْيَا نَمُوتُ وَنَحْيَا وَمَا يُهْلِكُنَا إِلَّا الدَّهْرُ﴾ [al-Jathiyah 24], meaning: some people die and others live, and only time destroys us, and there is no resurrection and no reckoning.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the obligation for the Prophet ﷺ to inform his ummah that he is a human being like them, based on His saying: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ﴾ [Say: I am only a human being like you].

* Among its benefits: the emphasis of this announcement, since the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey it in a special way. The whole Qur'an was something the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to convey: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67]. But at times verses pass by you in which the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to convey them specifically, and this is evidence of their importance and significance. This is frequent, such as His saying: ﴿قُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ﴾ [al-Nur 30], and ﴿وَقُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنَاتِ يَغْضُضْنَ مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِنَّ﴾ [al-Nur 31], and what is similar to that. So there is in this a specific instruction to convey it, and it indicates care for it and attention to it. Are you understanding this or not? The whole Qur'an the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey, the evidence being: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾.

In some verses the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to convey them in a specific way, saying: "Say such-and-such." This indicates care for them, attention to them, and that they have a special importance. Here He said: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾, and he was commanded to convey and proclaim that he is a human being like us.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of those who say that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was created from light, based on His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who say he was light and had no shadow, walking in the sun without a shadow. The reason for this: affirming his humanity through similarity: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾. So any hadiths that bring such matters, which would take the Prophet ﷺ outside the bounds of humanity, are fabricated and false, because he is a human being like us.

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ experiences heat and cold, hunger and thirst, fear and safety, and other requirements of humanity, based on the general wording of His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾. Look at how humanity is affirmed through similarity, so that no one says that this is figurative. So He emphasized this humanity with similarity.

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ does not know the unseen except what is revealed to him, because we do not know the unseen, and he is a human being like us.

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ does not possess benefit or harm for himself or for others. The reason: he is like us, and if we do not possess benefit or harm for ourselves or for others, then neither does the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family.

* Among its benefits: the death of the Prophet ﷺ is a real death, and with his death his deeds ended, except for what reaches him of the rewards of his ummah's good deeds, based on His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾. Similarity requires equality in every respect, except what the evidence has specified. By this, the hope of everyone who asks the Messenger ﷺ to intercede for him is cut off, such as one who stands at his grave and says: "O Messenger of Allah, intercede for me." This is not permissible, because it is transgression in supplication, where a person asks for what is not his due. And the Messenger cannot do it, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, because he has died. When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off, neither by supplication nor by anything else.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Prophet ﷺ may forget, because this is required by humanity, as he affirmed in his saying: "I am only a human being like you; I forget as you forget." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (401), Muslim (572/89), from Ibn Mas'ud.]

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ exercises ijtihad (independent reasoning), and may err in his ijtihad, because this is required by humanity. This actually occurs, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْكَ لِمَ أَذِنْتَ لَهُمْ حَتَّى يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكَ الَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا وَتَعْلَمَ الْكَاذِبِينَ﴾ [al-Tawbah 43], and in His saying: ﴿عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّى (١) أَنْ جَاءَهُ الْأَعْمَى (٢) وَمَا يُدْرِيكَ لَعَلَّهُ يَزَّكَّى (٣) أَوْ يَذَّكَّرُ فَتَنْفَعَهُ الذِّكْرَى (٤) أَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَى (٥) فَأَنْتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّى (٦) وَمَا عَلَيْكَ أَلَّا يَزَّكَّى (٧) وَأَمَّا مَنْ جَاءَكَ يَسْعَى (٨) وَهُوَ يَخْشَى (٩) فَأَنْتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّى﴾ [‘Abasa 1–10].

But he, ﷺ, is distinguished from others in that he is never left to persist in an error, even one made through ijtihad. Others may not be reminded, and may not remember when they forget, and may not be taught when they are ignorant. That is, our errors may persist without our being alerted to them or noticing them. But the Messenger ﷺ cannot be left to persist in an error, and cannot be left in forgetting what is obligatory. Rather, he must either notice it or be alerted to it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the prophethood of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family. It is derived from His saying: ﴿يُوحَى إِلَيَّ﴾ [It is revealed to me], because revelation (wahy) is only for a prophet.

If someone says: How can you say that revelation is only for a prophet, when Allah the Exalted revealed to other than humans? He said: ﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا﴾ [al-Nahl 68], and He said, concerning non-prophets: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ فَإِذَا خِفْتِ عَلَيْهِ فَأَلْقِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ﴾?

We say: This objection arises only for one who does not distinguish between the meanings of revelation. As for one who distinguishes between them and says: revelation is either through a law (shar') or through something other than law. If it is through law, then it is only for Messengers or Prophets. If it is through something other than law, it is of the category of inspiration (ilham). So the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾ means: He inspired it to take houses from the mountains, and so on. Likewise ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى﴾ means revelation of inspiration. With this, the difficulty is removed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the importance of tawhid, since He restricted revelation to tawhid: ﴿يُوحَى إِلَيَّ أَنَّمَا إِلَهُكُمْ﴾ [Fussilat 6]. Although other things were revealed to him, such as prayer, zakat, and other things, nevertheless, because the most important thing he brought was tawhid, revelation was restricted to it: ﴿أَنَّمَا إِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾ [Your God is only one God].

I say to you: whenever a person realizes tawhid, he must establish the laws of Islam. Do you understand? Because if he has made Allah One through his intention and made it his life, then he must turn toward Him, and in what does he turn toward Him? Through the path He legislated, which leads to Him. For this reason we say: the hadith of 'Itban: "Allah has forbidden the Fire to whoever says: 'There is no god but Allah,' seeking by that the Face of Allah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (425), Muslim (33/263), from 'Itban ibn Malik] is on its apparent meaning. Whoever says: "There is no god but Allah," seeking by it the Face of Allah, is forbidden from the Fire. And the requirement of his being forbidden from the Fire is that he does not do a major sin that makes him deserve the Fire or requires his entry into it. Everyone who says "There is no god but Allah," seeking the Face of Allah, will not do what angers Allah. How can you seek His Face and then do what angers Him? Does doing what angers Him prevent you from reaching His Face or not? Yes, it prevents you. If it prevents you while you seek His Face, then you must turn away from it, either by abstaining from it entirely, or by repenting from it if you have fallen into it. Pay attention to this point, because some people say to us: "You declare the one who abandons prayer a disbeliever, yet the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah has forbidden the Fire to whoever says: There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah,' and he did not mention prayer." We say to him: On the contrary, he mentioned prayer and mentioned what is less than prayer too, in what? In his saying: "seeking by that the Face of Allah."

We say: It is impossible in any circumstance for a man who says "There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah" to persist in abandoning prayer. Whoever tries to combine that with abandoning prayer has tried to combine water and fire. This is an obvious matter. Now, with Allah's highest example, I will give you an example. If you wanted to reach a person and were striving by every means to reach him, would you do what prevents you from reaching him, by disobeying him? Never. Rather, you would look at what he loves and do it, in order to reach him, and so that he would welcome you.

But if you say: "By Allah, I love so-and-so, and I want to reach him," and so-and-so says: "Do not walk this path," and you say: "By Allah, I love this man," and then you walk the opposing path, while he says to you, for example: "If you want to come to me, come by the right path," and you say: "By Allah, I love so-and-so and love reaching him. In the name of Allah," but with which path? With the left path, and you are walking the left path while saying: "By Allah, I love this man and glorify him, and he is dearer to me than myself." Is this true or false? It is clearly false. So everyone who says "There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah" will shun sins, even minor ones. For this reason the restriction of revelation in this verse is to what? To tawhid: ﴿يُوحَى إِلَيَّ أَنَّمَا إِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾ [Fussilat 6], and He is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of sincerity (ikhlas) to Allah and steadfastness (istiqamah) in His religion...

* A student: Sincerity is from His saying: ﴿إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾, and steadfastness from ﴿فَاسْتَقِيمُوا﴾.

* The Shaykh: No.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿اسْتَقِيمُوا إِلَيْهِ﴾. ﴿اسْتَقِيمُوا﴾ is the action, and ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾ is sincerity.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to the mushrikin, based on His saying: ﴿وَوَيْلٌ لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [Fussilat 6]. This type of warning may apply to what is shirk and may apply to what is less than that. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ (١) الَّذِينَ إِذَا اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 1–2], and these are not mushrikin; meaning, their act does not lead to shirk. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Woe to the one who speaks and lies in order to make the people laugh; woe to him, then woe to him." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (4990) and al-Tirmidhi (2315), from Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah.] This too is not shirk. So it cannot be said that every threat expressed with this word indicates that the act is shirk; rather it may be shirk or what is less than it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that tawhid is a purification of the soul, based on His saying: ﴿الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ [Fussilat 7]. There is no doubt that tawhid is a purification of the soul, because you cut off attachments to other than Allah, except for what Allah loves. The one who truly is united in heart is always with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always turning in His decree of destiny (qada' kawni), content with it, just as he turns in His legislative decree (qada' shar'i), content with it. For this reason, if you find that when prosperity reaches him he thanks Allah and does not become arrogant, and when adversity reaches him he is patient and does not become resentful, he is always with Allah. He says to himself: "I am a servant of Allah; He does with me what He wills. I am a servant of Allah. If He afflicts me with prosperity, I give thanks, and that is better for me. If He afflicts me with adversity, I am patient, and that is better for me. I am a servant of Allah and cannot oppose Allah's decree. If He decrees joy for me today, I rejoice, and if He decrees evil for me tomorrow, I am displeased," and he walks with Allah along with His decree and destiny. This is the one who finds complete ease. For this reason, among the fruits of faith in destiny (qadar) is that a person is always at peace, with no anxiety or sadness. Even if a person may feel sorrow at the first shock, by consoling himself and contemplating the decree, the matter becomes easy for him. Otherwise, it is well known that a person is not made of iron or stone and is affected, but when he consoles himself and steels himself, he becomes patient and reassured. So the point is that tawhid is entirely good, and all of it is zakat, a purification and cleansing of the soul.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the mushrikin do not believe in the Hereafter. For this reason, when they are told: "Affirm the Oneness of Allah and you will be saved from His punishment," they say: "There is no punishment." They deny the Hereafter.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that belief in the Hereafter calls to tawhid and its realization. This is a truth and a reality. Every person who believes that he will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in a level plain, in which he sees neither crookedness nor elevation, and that he will be recompensed for his deeds, every sensible person will prepare for that day. For this reason, it is befitting for us, while our hearts are with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to remember the Hour and the standing of people. Is there between a person and this state a specified, known time?

Ibn ʿUthaymin's commentary on Surah 41, verses 6–7 (part 3 of 3):

No, never. One reaches this only when he dies, and when does he die? No one knows. A person may leave his house and never return to it; he may sleep on his bed and be carried away dead; he may get into his car and never get out of it. So, my brother, when heedlessness takes hold of your heart, remember this day on which you and all of creation will be gathered barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, with no wealth, no children, and no one to protect you. Remember this, and when you remember it, you will work for this day.

Your brothers, your children, your fathers, your mothers, those you have lost in this life: when will you be gathered with them? On this day. There is no gathering except on this day. So prepare yourself for this day, do righteous deeds, do not let the caravan pass you by, be at its forefront, and make the world a follower of yours, not make yourself a follower of it, so that you may be saved. Every person who believes in the Hereafter, when he remembers it, will work for it, because of Allah's words: ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾ [al-Saffat 61]. I ask Allah, exalted is He, to make me and you among the God-fearing who believe in the Hereafter and work for it.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, we said: (...) the Prophet ﷺ (...), and that he does not possess benefit or harm (...). Some people go to the grave of the Prophet ﷺ, call upon Allah there, and cite the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa 64]. They say: this verse is not restricted to that specific time; they say: what is the fault of those who come after him, that he does not seek forgiveness for them when they come to the Prophet ﷺ?
* Shaykh: This, may Allah bless you, falls under the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ [Ali ʿImran 7]. The one who said to him: ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves﴾ [an-Nisa 64] speaks of specific people, as evidenced by His words: ﴿when they had wronged themselves﴾. Is "idh" [when] referring to the past or the future? To the past. ﴿They had come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾ [an-Nisa 64], meaning: you had asked forgiveness for them. But the noun is stated explicitly in a position where a pronoun would be expected, to magnify the status of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and to show that he is closer to them in responding: ﴿they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa 64]. ﴿So no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves﴾ [an-Nisa 64–65], and so on to its end. He did not say: "if they, when they wrong themselves," for if He had said "if they wrong," we would say: this applies to them and to others. Rather He said: ﴿when they had wronged themselves﴾. Furthermore, the Messenger's seeking forgiveness after his death is impossible, because seeking forgiveness is an action, and action has ceased with his death. Moreover, these people are not more knowledgeable about the Book of Allah, nor more aware of the state of the Messenger of Allah, than the Companions. Did any of them come to the Messenger's grave and say: "O Messenger of Allah, ask forgiveness for me"? Never. Rather, when they were struck by drought, they did not say: "O Messenger of Allah, our wealth has perished and the roads have been cut off, so supplicate to Allah that He send us relief," even though they were beside him. Rather, they sought relief and called upon Allah themselves, and ʿUmar asked al-ʿAbbas to supplicate to Allah, exalted is He. But every person of falsehood must find some doubt in the Book and the Sunnah, and this is from the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, and His trial and testing. As Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book Dar' Taʿarud al-ʿAql wa'l-Naql and in his fatawa as well: every person who uses a sound proof from the Book or the Sunnah for falsehood, that proof is in fact a proof for refuting his falsehood, not for establishing it. The evidence is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Falsehood does not approach it from before it or behind it; it is a revelation from One Wise and Praiseworthy﴾ [Fussilat 42].
* Student: Shaykh, in the definition of a prophet: one to whom revelation is sent but who is not commanded to convey it. If someone says: how, when we are (...) the nation of the Prophet ﷺ, and it was not conveyed to them, yet they were commanded to convey it?
* Shaykh: This question is built upon a disagreement among the scholars: who is the prophet and who is the messenger? The majority of scholars hold that the messenger is one who is sent, to whom the law is revealed, and who is sent with it and commanded to convey it. As for the prophet, he is one who is given news (nubbiʾa), i.e., informed, and informing does not necessarily entail the obligation to convey. So he is one to whom a law is revealed but who is not commanded to convey it, rather he is commanded to act upon it himself. This news is then either a renewal of an earlier message or the establishment of a law that did not previously exist. This view held by the majority is the correct one, because if we said that the prophet is one who renews an earlier law and is commanded to convey it to the people and to awaken them, then the prophethood of Adam would become problematic, for Adam was a prophet who was addressed directly, and yet no messenger preceded him.
If someone asks: then what is the benefit?
We say: the benefit, first: the interest of this prophet is himself, that a law was revealed to him.
Second: if he is within an earlier law, then it is a renewal of that law; and if he is not within an earlier law, as with Adam, then people in his time were primitive, not numerous, did not differ, and the world had not been opened to them, so they would look at what their father did and imitate it, without need for a messenger to be sent to them. Hence Allah said: ﴿Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners﴾, meaning: then they differed, ﴿so Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news﴾ ﴿and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. So the view of the majority of scholars is the one that appears preponderant to me: the prophet is one to whom a law is revealed but who is not commanded to convey it. As for us, since there is no prophet after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we have become commanded to convey his message; so we are, in reality, messengers of the Messenger of Allah. This is why the hadith states: «Indeed, the scholars are the heirs of the prophets»[[Related by Abu Dawud (3641), al-Tirmidhi (2682), and Ibn Majah (223) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda.]].
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾ [Fussilat 6]. We parsed "woe" (wayl) as a subject (mubtada'). Could it be correct that it is a verbal noun (masdar) for an obligatorily omitted verb?
* Shaykh: A verbal noun for an obligatorily omitted verb! First, does it have a verb from its own root?
* Student: That is, in the sense of their saying: "sat the crouching squatter..."
* Shaykh: Does "wayl" have a verb from its root?
* Student: It has no verb.
* Shaykh: Then how can it be a verbal noun?
The second point: a verbal noun for an omitted verb is in the accusative.
* Student: By way of substitution for the verb, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: That does not work; even if it substitutes for the verb, it would be in the accusative. There is no difficulty with it except what I have told you: that it is introduced with it while it is indefinite, so we say that what specified it is the threat (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verses 6–7 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you"﴾. That is, I am not a stranger to you. Why do you disbelieve in me when I am a human being like you? I am not a jinn that you should shun me, nor an angel that you should shun me. I am only a human being like you. The *bashar* (human beings) are the children of Adam, and they were named *bashar* because their skin (*bashara*) is visible, as their bodies appear uncovered. This is one of the blessings of Allah the Mighty and Majestic upon us and of His mercy. Allah made the human being bare, except for clothing, so that he would remember that he is bare of faith, except for a garment. What is the garment of faith? It is piety (*taqwa*), as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the garment of piety, that is best﴾ [al-A'raf 26]. Allah made us need physical covering so that we would know that we also need the covering of the inner self. So you are bare of faith unless you wear the garment of piety.

So who are the *bashar*? They are the children of Adam. They were named so because their skin is visible and has no covering over it, unlike other animals, which are covered either by wool, fur, hair, feathers, or other things. He says: ﴿I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed﴾. The phrase ﴿like you﴾ is an emphasis of the meaning of humanity. Otherwise, if he had said only ﴿I am only a human being﴾, would that imply that he is like us or different from us? But he emphasized this meaning with His words ﴿like you﴾, yet he is distinguished by ﴿to whom it is revealed that your God is one God﴾, and so on. This is the distinction and the difference: Muhammad (ﷺ) is a human being to whom revelation is sent.

The one who reveals (*yuha*) is Allah, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Quran so that you may warn the mother of cities and those around it﴾ [al-Shura 7]. So the one who reveals is Allah, and the agent is omitted because it is known. It may be said that it is omitted both because it is known and for generality, since Allah the Exalted may reveal to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) through Jibril, and He may reveal to him without an intermediary. *Al-Iha'* (revelation) is informing quickly and secretly. This informing, done quickly and secretly, is called *iha'*. For this reason, if someone is beside you and you want to ask him while the class is crowded with students, and you fear being overheard, you say: "What? Did you hear now or not?" in a low voice and quickly, so that no one notices you. So every informing done quickly and secretly is called *wahy* (revelation). It is so because the Prophet (ﷺ) receives revelation while people are sitting around him and do not know what the Messenger said.

﴿to whom it is revealed that your God is one God﴾: this clause is in the position of a deputy subject (*na'ib al-fa'il*) of the verb. That is: this news is revealed to me, ﴿that your God is one God﴾. ﴿Innama﴾ is a particle of restriction (*hasr*). On this basis, the sentence contains both negation and affirmation, because restriction is the affirmation of the ruling for what is mentioned and the negation of it for anything else.

Now we will address the ways of restriction, or some of them:
From the ways of restriction: ﴿innama﴾ or ﴿anama﴾, which are one and the same.
The second: negation and affirmation, such as "There is no one standing except Muhammad."
The third: placing before what should be after, such as: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 284].
The fourth: the insertion of a separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*), such as your saying: "Zayd is the excellent one." The separating pronoun gives the meaning of restriction. These are four ways, and they are the most frequently used.

﴿So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness, and woe to the polytheists﴾. "Be upright toward Him" means: aim toward Him. For this reason He did not say "be upright for Him" but said ﴿toward Him﴾, so the verb "be upright" includes the meaning of "aim toward," and so it is more eloquent than "be upright for Him," because one who is upright for a thing may be upright for it while staying in his place without striving toward it. But when it is said "be upright toward Him," it indicates striving toward Allah the Mighty and Majestic and intending Him. Therefore it takes the preposition "toward" (*ila*). Here, is one letter standing in for another, or is the letter kept in its meaning while the verb is given a meaning that suits the letter?

There are two opinions: one view is that the figurative usage is in the particle, and another view is that it is in the verb or the complement. Is my speech now Arabic or non-Arabic? It is Arabic. ﴿A spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan 6]. ﴿from which they drink﴾: does a person drink from a spring? Does he drink from it? That is, can you take the river, for example, in your hand like this and raise it to your mouth as if it were a vessel? You say "I drank with the vessel," which is clear. ﴿A spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾: can the spring be lifted by the hand and drunk from? No. So what should we say?

On this, the scholars have two opinions:
One of them: the figurative usage is in the particle, meaning that the *ba'* (with) means *min* (from), so the servants of Allah drink from it. Is the spring drunk from or not? It is drunk from by hand, or by a vessel, or by any means.
The second opinion: the figurative usage is in the verb, meaning that "drink" has been given a meaning that suits the *ba'*. What suits the *ba'* here? ("quench"). "The servants of Allah quench themselves with it," meaning that it is a spring that quenches. So which of these is better? Which of them is better? I do not say which is easier?
* A student: The second.
* The Shaykh: Have you changed your opinion or are you still with it? There is no vote now, go with what you see. As for if we say the *ba'* means *min*, it is easy, because you can supply any suitable particle and the matter ends. But if we say the *ba'* keeps its own meaning and the verb has been given a meaning that fits it, then it may be difficult for a person to determine the suitable verb. But we say that giving the verb a meaning suitable to the particle is preferable.
Let me explain this to you. If we say ﴿the servants of Allah drink from it﴾ and that the *ba'* means *min*, have we gained a benefit by using *ba'* instead of *min*? We have not gained anything. So bringing this particle causes some confusion, and we have harmed the meaning as well as gaining nothing, because placing one particle in place of another without a reason causes confusion and ambiguity. But if we give the verb a meaning that suits the particle, we gain more benefit, because your estimate, "quench with it," includes the drinking that was mentioned and includes the quenching, so we gain a benefit. This opinion, namely that the verb is given a meaning that suits the particle, is the one held by the Basran grammarians, and I think it is the view chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, because of this benefit we mentioned.
I always hope that students will understand these subtle distinctions, because they sharpen the mind in one respect and open wide horizons for understanding meanings and increasing benefit. Pay attention to them.
* A student: If we say the particle means the other particle, we have gained nothing. Yet in other places in some verses, such as His saying ﴿And I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha 71], we said it means *'ala* (on) and did not give the verb another meaning.
* The Shaykh: No, that is necessary: *fi* means *'ala*, but even so there is a benefit in using *fi* where *'ala* would be expected. I do not know whether I have pointed this out to you or not. We say: if He had said "I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees" with *'ala*, the crucifixion might be a mere hanging with loose rope, but with ﴿in the trunks﴾ it is as if He tied them very tightly, so that these crucified people seem to be inside them, and so we gain a benefit.
* A student: The question is not part of the lesson.
* The Shaykh: Not part of the lesson?
* A student: It is about grammar. How do we expand in grammar (...)?
* The Shaykh: In reality grammar is not difficult except for someone who imagines it is difficult. Otherwise it is one of the easiest sciences. But if you intend to enter grammar while believing it is difficult, be sure it will be closed to you. Do you understand? That is why it is said that it is a palace of reeds with an iron door. Break this door and nothing will remain before you. So do not make it difficult. If I say to you "Zayd stood" (*qama Zaydun*), what do you say about Zayd? Subject (*fa'il*).
And if I say "Zayd was struck" (*duriba Zaydun*)?
* A student: Object.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not the object. "Zayd was struck": linguistically it is correct to say *maf'ul* (the thing done to), since he is struck. But technically we say *na'ib al-fa'il* (deputy subject). Why? Because the subject is a pillar of the sentence. Either it exists, or its deputy exists. Do you understand? In any case, God willing, it is easy, and God willing we will now focus on grammar for you.
* A student: ﴿Bearer of good news and warner﴾. We said that *bushra* (good news) is specific, and that *nudhara* (warning) is sometimes general and sometimes specific. Is it permissible for *bushra* to be general too?
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: Because He gave the disbelievers good news of punishment.
* The Shaykh: ﴿So give them good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 21]. They said this is sarcasm toward them, like when you mock a person by saying "Rejoice in the whip on your back," mocking him.
* A student: May Allah be good to you. Here Allah said ﴿A Book whose verses are explained in detail﴾, and in another verse: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeated (*mathani*)﴾ [al-Zumar 23]. How do we reconcile these verses?
* The Shaykh: There is no contradiction, because His saying ﴿mathani﴾ means ﴿fussilat﴾ (explained in detail), since its meanings are repeated (*tuthana*): good is mentioned and then evil, the people of good and the people of evil, paradise and hellfire, and similar things.
* A student: This is what is meant (...).
* The Shaykh: This is what is meant by His saying ﴿mathani﴾. As for what is meant by His saying ﴿mutashabihan﴾ (consistent), its meaning is that some of it resembles other parts in perfection, beauty, and excellence. I thought you would ask: how do we reconcile Allah's praise of the Quran as "consistent" with His saying ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book, in it are verses that are clear (*muhkamat*), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (*mutashabihat*). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾ [Al 'Imran 7]? The reconciliation is that it is consistent in excellence, with parts resembling one another. As for *muhkamat* and *mutashabihat*: the *muhkamat* are those whose meaning is clear, and the *mutashabihat* are those whose meaning is hidden.
* * *
* The student: ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to the polytheists (6) Who do not give zakat and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers (7). Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that is never cut off (8). Say, "Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days and attribute to Him equals? That is the Lord of the worlds" (9). And He placed on the earth firmly set mountains from above it and blessed it and determined therein its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask (10). Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or by compulsion." They said, "We come willingly" (11). So He completed them as seven heavens in two days and inspired in each heaven its command. And We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and as protection. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing (12). But if they turn away, say, "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud"﴾ [Fussilat 6–13].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed. Earlier we discussed the saying of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us"﴾ [Fussilat 5], and so on, and we mentioned that the faculties of perception are...
* A student: Perception by the heart, perception by hearing, and perception by sight.
* The Shaykh: Does this verse include the blocking of these faculties in them?
* The student: Yes, the verse includes it.
* The Shaykh: How?
* A student: His saying ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us"﴾: this is the blocking of the heart's perception (...). The second perception, by hearing, is ﴿and in our ears is deafness﴾, and the third perception, by sight, is ﴿and between us and you is a barrier﴾.
* The Shaykh: Well done. What is the difference between the two expressions, ﴿and between us and you is a barrier﴾ and ﴿between us and you is a barrier﴾?
* A student: ﴿And between us and you is a barrier﴾ is more intense than "between us and you is a barrier"...
* The Shaykh: More intense than "between us and you is a barrier"? How so?
* A student: Because when there is a barrier from between us and you, the barrier between them becomes stronger the farther they move from it.
* The Shaykh: So this barrier extends from them to the Messenger, even if the distance is great? And in the second case?
* A student: In the second case the barrier is between them without extending from them to the Messenger.
* The Shaykh: The barrier exists with the smallest thing, even if the distance between them is great.
His saying ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾: what is meant by it?
* A student: A challenge.
* The Shaykh: A challenge, as if we are saying: we do not care about you. Act, and we will act. Is that right?
What did the Prophet (ﷺ) establish regarding these people's denial? That is, did he say that he was of another kind, like the angels and the jinn, or what? What did the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, establish regarding the denial of these people? Did he say that he was of a different kind, like the angels and jinn, or something else?
* A student: They denied that he could be a human being like them who calls them.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: He established that he is of their kind.
* The Shaykh: He established that he is of their kind, a human being, but he is distinguished by being revealed to. What was revealed to the Messenger (ﷺ)?
* A student: Monotheism: ﴿that your God is one God﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is monotheism. Is this what all the messengers brought?
* The student: Yes, without doubt.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence that all messengers called to monotheism?
* The student: The evidence is His saying in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity but Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya 25].
* The Shaykh: This is in Surat al-Nahl?!
* The student: No, it is in a different surah, not in Surat al-Nahl, but there is a verse in Surat al-Nahl that I forgot.
* The Shaykh: You do not have to specify the verse's location. ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity but Me, so worship Me﴾. What you want in Surat al-Nahl is His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid Taghut"﴾ [al-Nahl 36].
Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said: ﴿That your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness﴾ [Fussilat 6]. ﴿So be upright toward Him﴾: it appears that this is part of the words of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, that he was commanded to say. The meaning of "be upright toward Him" is: be upright in His religion, intending Him. So it indicates sincerity in action.
﴿And seek His forgiveness﴾: ask Him for forgiveness. Forgiveness includes two things: covering the sin and pardoning it, because it is derived from *al-mighfar*, which is what a fighter wears on his head to protect himself from weapons. The *mighfar* includes protection and covering. On this basis, whenever you ask for forgiveness, remember that you want Allah the Mighty and Majestic to overlook you, so that He does not punish you and conceals your sin.
("Seek His forgiveness"): that is, ask Him for forgiveness, which is covering the sin and overlooking it.
(﴿And woe﴾ is a word of punishment.) The commentator says: ﴿to the polytheists﴾. ("Woe") here is a subject (*mubtada'*), and the fact that it is indefinite is permitted because it is for threat. It is a word of warning and threat. It has been said that it is a valley in Hellfire, but the more correct view is the first: it is a word of threat and warning for everyone who opposes.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 41, verses 6–7 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ means: for those who associate partners with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Their association may be in worship ('ibadah), in divinity (uluhiyyah), or in the Names and Attributes. Whoever claims that there is a creator with Allah, or a helper, or an independent agent who creates some things, is a mushrik (one who commits shirk, associating partners with Allah). Whoever worships another alongside Allah, or shows off in his worship to someone other than Allah, is a mushrik. Whoever claims that the Attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, resemble the attributes of the created beings is a mushrik. Know that shirk is divided into two kinds: minor (asghar) and major (akbar). It is also divided, from another angle, into hidden (khafi) and manifest (jali). All of this is well known in the books of tawhid (the science of Divine Oneness) and 'aqidah (creed).

﴿الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ [Fussilat 7]. This is a description of the mushrikin. ﴿الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْتُونَ﴾ means: they do not give the zakat. The word zakat here may mean the purification of the soul (zakat al-nafs), and it may mean the zakat on wealth (zakat al-mal). If it means zakat on wealth, there is a difficulty, because its apparent meaning requires that the disbelievers are obligated to pay zakat. It is well known that a person is not required to pay zakat until he becomes Muslim, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Mu'adh: "You are going to a people of the Book, so let the first thing you call them to be the Oneness of Allah. Then call them to prayer. Then call them to zakat." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1395) and Muslim (19/31), from Ibn 'Abbas.]

This indicates that a person is not addressed with zakat, meaning its payment, until he embraces Islam. As for if we say that the intended meaning of zakat is the purification of the soul, then this objection does not arise. But another difficulty arises from the wording, which is His saying ﴿لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾. Is the purification of the soul something that can be given? This is a matter for consideration. For this reason, the verse presents a difficulty whichever of these two interpretations you adopt. When a verse has a difficulty between two meanings, we seek the preponderant (al-murajjih) one. The preponderant view is that the intended meaning is the purification of the soul, and the meaning is: they do not give their souls their purification. And in the hadith: "Give your soul its piety, and purify it; You are the best one to purify it." [Narrated by Muslim (2722/72), from Zayd ibn Arqam.]

So, on this basis, we prefer that the intended meaning of zakat is the purification of the soul, and the meaning is: they do not give their souls their purification, rather they neglect it and are heedless of it. ﴿وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ كَافِرُونَ﴾. ﴿وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ﴾: ﴿بِالْآخِرَةِ﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur) related to ﴿كَافِرُونَ﴾, and (هم) is a subject (mubtada'), and the second ﴿هُمْ﴾ ... The mufassir says: "(تأكيد)" [emphasis]. Emphasis of what? It is a verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi) of the first (هم). Verbal emphasis is when the word is repeated in its own form, as Ibn Malik said:

*"Of emphasis, the verbal kind comes repeated, like your saying: 'Proceed, proceed.'"*

﴿وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ كَافِرُونَ﴾ means: they deny it and do not believe in it. They say: ﴿مَا هِيَ إِلَّا حَيَاتُنَا الدُّنْيَا نَمُوتُ وَنَحْيَا وَمَا يُهْلِكُنَا إِلَّا الدَّهْرُ﴾ [al-Jathiyah 24], meaning: some people die and others live, and only time destroys us, and there is no resurrection and no reckoning.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the obligation for the Prophet ﷺ to inform his ummah that he is a human being like them, based on His saying: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ﴾ [Say: I am only a human being like you].

* Among its benefits: the emphasis of this announcement, since the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey it in a special way. The whole Qur'an was something the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to convey: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67]. But at times verses pass by you in which the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to convey them specifically, and this is evidence of their importance and significance. This is frequent, such as His saying: ﴿قُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ﴾ [al-Nur 30], and ﴿وَقُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنَاتِ يَغْضُضْنَ مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِنَّ﴾ [al-Nur 31], and what is similar to that. So there is in this a specific instruction to convey it, and it indicates care for it and attention to it. Are you understanding this or not? The whole Qur'an the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey, the evidence being: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾.

In some verses the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to convey them in a specific way, saying: "Say such-and-such." This indicates care for them, attention to them, and that they have a special importance. Here He said: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾, and he was commanded to convey and proclaim that he is a human being like us.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of those who say that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was created from light, based on His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who say he was light and had no shadow, walking in the sun without a shadow. The reason for this: affirming his humanity through similarity: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾. So any hadiths that bring such matters, which would take the Prophet ﷺ outside the bounds of humanity, are fabricated and false, because he is a human being like us.

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ experiences heat and cold, hunger and thirst, fear and safety, and other requirements of humanity, based on the general wording of His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾. Look at how humanity is affirmed through similarity, so that no one says that this is figurative. So He emphasized this humanity with similarity.

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ does not know the unseen except what is revealed to him, because we do not know the unseen, and he is a human being like us.

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ does not possess benefit or harm for himself or for others. The reason: he is like us, and if we do not possess benefit or harm for ourselves or for others, then neither does the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family.

* Among its benefits: the death of the Prophet ﷺ is a real death, and with his death his deeds ended, except for what reaches him of the rewards of his ummah's good deeds, based on His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾. Similarity requires equality in every respect, except what the evidence has specified. By this, the hope of everyone who asks the Messenger ﷺ to intercede for him is cut off, such as one who stands at his grave and says: "O Messenger of Allah, intercede for me." This is not permissible, because it is transgression in supplication, where a person asks for what is not his due. And the Messenger cannot do it, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, because he has died. When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off, neither by supplication nor by anything else.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Prophet ﷺ may forget, because this is required by humanity, as he affirmed in his saying: "I am only a human being like you; I forget as you forget." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (401), Muslim (572/89), from Ibn Mas'ud.]

* Among its benefits: the Prophet ﷺ exercises ijtihad (independent reasoning), and may err in his ijtihad, because this is required by humanity. This actually occurs, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْكَ لِمَ أَذِنْتَ لَهُمْ حَتَّى يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكَ الَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا وَتَعْلَمَ الْكَاذِبِينَ﴾ [al-Tawbah 43], and in His saying: ﴿عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّى (١) أَنْ جَاءَهُ الْأَعْمَى (٢) وَمَا يُدْرِيكَ لَعَلَّهُ يَزَّكَّى (٣) أَوْ يَذَّكَّرُ فَتَنْفَعَهُ الذِّكْرَى (٤) أَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَى (٥) فَأَنْتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّى (٦) وَمَا عَلَيْكَ أَلَّا يَزَّكَّى (٧) وَأَمَّا مَنْ جَاءَكَ يَسْعَى (٨) وَهُوَ يَخْشَى (٩) فَأَنْتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّى﴾ [‘Abasa 1–10].

But he, ﷺ, is distinguished from others in that he is never left to persist in an error, even one made through ijtihad. Others may not be reminded, and may not remember when they forget, and may not be taught when they are ignorant. That is, our errors may persist without our being alerted to them or noticing them. But the Messenger ﷺ cannot be left to persist in an error, and cannot be left in forgetting what is obligatory. Rather, he must either notice it or be alerted to it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the prophethood of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family. It is derived from His saying: ﴿يُوحَى إِلَيَّ﴾ [It is revealed to me], because revelation (wahy) is only for a prophet.

If someone says: How can you say that revelation is only for a prophet, when Allah the Exalted revealed to other than humans? He said: ﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا﴾ [al-Nahl 68], and He said, concerning non-prophets: ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ فَإِذَا خِفْتِ عَلَيْهِ فَأَلْقِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ﴾?

We say: This objection arises only for one who does not distinguish between the meanings of revelation. As for one who distinguishes between them and says: revelation is either through a law (shar') or through something other than law. If it is through law, then it is only for Messengers or Prophets. If it is through something other than law, it is of the category of inspiration (ilham). So the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾ means: He inspired it to take houses from the mountains, and so on. Likewise ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَى أُمِّ مُوسَى﴾ means revelation of inspiration. With this, the difficulty is removed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the importance of tawhid, since He restricted revelation to tawhid: ﴿يُوحَى إِلَيَّ أَنَّمَا إِلَهُكُمْ﴾ [Fussilat 6]. Although other things were revealed to him, such as prayer, zakat, and other things, nevertheless, because the most important thing he brought was tawhid, revelation was restricted to it: ﴿أَنَّمَا إِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾ [Your God is only one God].

I say to you: whenever a person realizes tawhid, he must establish the laws of Islam. Do you understand? Because if he has made Allah One through his intention and made it his life, then he must turn toward Him, and in what does he turn toward Him? Through the path He legislated, which leads to Him. For this reason we say: the hadith of 'Itban: "Allah has forbidden the Fire to whoever says: 'There is no god but Allah,' seeking by that the Face of Allah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (425), Muslim (33/263), from 'Itban ibn Malik] is on its apparent meaning. Whoever says: "There is no god but Allah," seeking by it the Face of Allah, is forbidden from the Fire. And the requirement of his being forbidden from the Fire is that he does not do a major sin that makes him deserve the Fire or requires his entry into it. Everyone who says "There is no god but Allah," seeking the Face of Allah, will not do what angers Allah. How can you seek His Face and then do what angers Him? Does doing what angers Him prevent you from reaching His Face or not? Yes, it prevents you. If it prevents you while you seek His Face, then you must turn away from it, either by abstaining from it entirely, or by repenting from it if you have fallen into it. Pay attention to this point, because some people say to us: "You declare the one who abandons prayer a disbeliever, yet the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah has forbidden the Fire to whoever says: There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah,' and he did not mention prayer." We say to him: On the contrary, he mentioned prayer and mentioned what is less than prayer too, in what? In his saying: "seeking by that the Face of Allah."

We say: It is impossible in any circumstance for a man who says "There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah" to persist in abandoning prayer. Whoever tries to combine that with abandoning prayer has tried to combine water and fire. This is an obvious matter. Now, with Allah's highest example, I will give you an example. If you wanted to reach a person and were striving by every means to reach him, would you do what prevents you from reaching him, by disobeying him? Never. Rather, you would look at what he loves and do it, in order to reach him, and so that he would welcome you.

But if you say: "By Allah, I love so-and-so, and I want to reach him," and so-and-so says: "Do not walk this path," and you say: "By Allah, I love this man," and then you walk the opposing path, while he says to you, for example: "If you want to come to me, come by the right path," and you say: "By Allah, I love so-and-so and love reaching him. In the name of Allah," but with which path? With the left path, and you are walking the left path while saying: "By Allah, I love this man and glorify him, and he is dearer to me than myself." Is this true or false? It is clearly false. So everyone who says "There is no god but Allah, seeking by that the Face of Allah" will shun sins, even minor ones. For this reason the restriction of revelation in this verse is to what? To tawhid: ﴿يُوحَى إِلَيَّ أَنَّمَا إِلَهُكُمْ إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾ [Fussilat 6], and He is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of sincerity (ikhlas) to Allah and steadfastness (istiqamah) in His religion...

* A student: Sincerity is from His saying: ﴿إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾, and steadfastness from ﴿فَاسْتَقِيمُوا﴾.

* The Shaykh: No.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿اسْتَقِيمُوا إِلَيْهِ﴾. ﴿اسْتَقِيمُوا﴾ is the action, and ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾ is sincerity.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to the mushrikin, based on His saying: ﴿وَوَيْلٌ لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [Fussilat 6]. This type of warning may apply to what is shirk and may apply to what is less than that. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ (١) الَّذِينَ إِذَا اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 1–2], and these are not mushrikin; meaning, their act does not lead to shirk. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Woe to the one who speaks and lies in order to make the people laugh; woe to him, then woe to him." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (4990) and al-Tirmidhi (2315), from Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah.] This too is not shirk. So it cannot be said that every threat expressed with this word indicates that the act is shirk; rather it may be shirk or what is less than it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that tawhid is a purification of the soul, based on His saying: ﴿الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ [Fussilat 7]. There is no doubt that tawhid is a purification of the soul, because you cut off attachments to other than Allah, except for what Allah loves. The one who truly is united in heart is always with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always turning in His decree of destiny (qada' kawni), content with it, just as he turns in His legislative decree (qada' shar'i), content with it. For this reason, if you find that when prosperity reaches him he thanks Allah and does not become arrogant, and when adversity reaches him he is patient and does not become resentful, he is always with Allah. He says to himself: "I am a servant of Allah; He does with me what He wills. I am a servant of Allah. If He afflicts me with prosperity, I give thanks, and that is better for me. If He afflicts me with adversity, I am patient, and that is better for me. I am a servant of Allah and cannot oppose Allah's decree. If He decrees joy for me today, I rejoice, and if He decrees evil for me tomorrow, I am displeased," and he walks with Allah along with His decree and destiny. This is the one who finds complete ease. For this reason, among the fruits of faith in destiny (qadar) is that a person is always at peace, with no anxiety or sadness. Even if a person may feel sorrow at the first shock, by consoling himself and contemplating the decree, the matter becomes easy for him. Otherwise, it is well known that a person is not made of iron or stone and is affected, but when he consoles himself and steels himself, he becomes patient and reassured. So the point is that tawhid is entirely good, and all of it is zakat, a purification and cleansing of the soul.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the mushrikin do not believe in the Hereafter. For this reason, when they are told: "Affirm the Oneness of Allah and you will be saved from His punishment," they say: "There is no punishment." They deny the Hereafter.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that belief in the Hereafter calls to tawhid and its realization. This is a truth and a reality. Every person who believes that he will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in a level plain, in which he sees neither crookedness nor elevation, and that he will be recompensed for his deeds, every sensible person will prepare for that day. For this reason, it is befitting for us, while our hearts are with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to remember the Hour and the standing of people. Is there between a person and this state a specified, known time?

Ibn ʿUthaymin's commentary on Surah 41, verses 6–7 (part 3 of 3):

No, never. One reaches this only when he dies, and when does he die? No one knows. A person may leave his house and never return to it; he may sleep on his bed and be carried away dead; he may get into his car and never get out of it. So, my brother, when heedlessness takes hold of your heart, remember this day on which you and all of creation will be gathered barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, with no wealth, no children, and no one to protect you. Remember this, and when you remember it, you will work for this day.

Your brothers, your children, your fathers, your mothers, those you have lost in this life: when will you be gathered with them? On this day. There is no gathering except on this day. So prepare yourself for this day, do righteous deeds, do not let the caravan pass you by, be at its forefront, and make the world a follower of yours, not make yourself a follower of it, so that you may be saved. Every person who believes in the Hereafter, when he remembers it, will work for it, because of Allah's words: ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾ [al-Saffat 61]. I ask Allah, exalted is He, to make me and you among the God-fearing who believe in the Hereafter and work for it.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, we said: (...) the Prophet ﷺ (...), and that he does not possess benefit or harm (...). Some people go to the grave of the Prophet ﷺ, call upon Allah there, and cite the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa 64]. They say: this verse is not restricted to that specific time; they say: what is the fault of those who come after him, that he does not seek forgiveness for them when they come to the Prophet ﷺ?
* Shaykh: This, may Allah bless you, falls under the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ [Ali ʿImran 7]. The one who said to him: ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves﴾ [an-Nisa 64] speaks of specific people, as evidenced by His words: ﴿when they had wronged themselves﴾. Is "idh" [when] referring to the past or the future? To the past. ﴿They had come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾ [an-Nisa 64], meaning: you had asked forgiveness for them. But the noun is stated explicitly in a position where a pronoun would be expected, to magnify the status of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and to show that he is closer to them in responding: ﴿they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa 64]. ﴿So no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves﴾ [an-Nisa 64–65], and so on to its end. He did not say: "if they, when they wrong themselves," for if He had said "if they wrong," we would say: this applies to them and to others. Rather He said: ﴿when they had wronged themselves﴾. Furthermore, the Messenger's seeking forgiveness after his death is impossible, because seeking forgiveness is an action, and action has ceased with his death. Moreover, these people are not more knowledgeable about the Book of Allah, nor more aware of the state of the Messenger of Allah, than the Companions. Did any of them come to the Messenger's grave and say: "O Messenger of Allah, ask forgiveness for me"? Never. Rather, when they were struck by drought, they did not say: "O Messenger of Allah, our wealth has perished and the roads have been cut off, so supplicate to Allah that He send us relief," even though they were beside him. Rather, they sought relief and called upon Allah themselves, and ʿUmar asked al-ʿAbbas to supplicate to Allah, exalted is He. But every person of falsehood must find some doubt in the Book and the Sunnah, and this is from the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, and His trial and testing. As Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book Dar' Taʿarud al-ʿAql wa'l-Naql and in his fatawa as well: every person who uses a sound proof from the Book or the Sunnah for falsehood, that proof is in fact a proof for refuting his falsehood, not for establishing it. The evidence is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Falsehood does not approach it from before it or behind it; it is a revelation from One Wise and Praiseworthy﴾ [Fussilat 42].
* Student: Shaykh, in the definition of a prophet: one to whom revelation is sent but who is not commanded to convey it. If someone says: how, when we are (...) the nation of the Prophet ﷺ, and it was not conveyed to them, yet they were commanded to convey it?
* Shaykh: This question is built upon a disagreement among the scholars: who is the prophet and who is the messenger? The majority of scholars hold that the messenger is one who is sent, to whom the law is revealed, and who is sent with it and commanded to convey it. As for the prophet, he is one who is given news (nubbiʾa), i.e., informed, and informing does not necessarily entail the obligation to convey. So he is one to whom a law is revealed but who is not commanded to convey it, rather he is commanded to act upon it himself. This news is then either a renewal of an earlier message or the establishment of a law that did not previously exist. This view held by the majority is the correct one, because if we said that the prophet is one who renews an earlier law and is commanded to convey it to the people and to awaken them, then the prophethood of Adam would become problematic, for Adam was a prophet who was addressed directly, and yet no messenger preceded him.
If someone asks: then what is the benefit?
We say: the benefit, first: the interest of this prophet is himself, that a law was revealed to him.
Second: if he is within an earlier law, then it is a renewal of that law; and if he is not within an earlier law, as with Adam, then people in his time were primitive, not numerous, did not differ, and the world had not been opened to them, so they would look at what their father did and imitate it, without need for a messenger to be sent to them. Hence Allah said: ﴿Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners﴾, meaning: then they differed, ﴿so Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news﴾ ﴿and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. So the view of the majority of scholars is the one that appears preponderant to me: the prophet is one to whom a law is revealed but who is not commanded to convey it. As for us, since there is no prophet after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we have become commanded to convey his message; so we are, in reality, messengers of the Messenger of Allah. This is why the hadith states: «Indeed, the scholars are the heirs of the prophets»[[Related by Abu Dawud (3641), al-Tirmidhi (2682), and Ibn Majah (223) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda.]].
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾ [Fussilat 6]. We parsed "woe" (wayl) as a subject (mubtada'). Could it be correct that it is a verbal noun (masdar) for an obligatorily omitted verb?
* Shaykh: A verbal noun for an obligatorily omitted verb! First, does it have a verb from its own root?
* Student: That is, in the sense of their saying: "sat the crouching squatter..."
* Shaykh: Does "wayl" have a verb from its root?
* Student: It has no verb.
* Shaykh: Then how can it be a verbal noun?
The second point: a verbal noun for an omitted verb is in the accusative.
* Student: By way of substitution for the verb, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: That does not work; even if it substitutes for the verb, it would be in the accusative. There is no difficulty with it except what I have told you: that it is introduced with it while it is indefinite, so we say that what specified it is the threat (...).

Student: "Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask. Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly. So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as protection. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing." [Fussilat 9–12].

Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward never to be cut off" [Fussilat 8]. When He mentioned the punishment of the polytheists, He explained the reward of the believers; because Allah Most High revealed this Book as oft-repeated (mathani), and the matter is so in order that a person may proceed toward his Lord between fear and hope. When he hears the punishment of the deniers, he fears, and when he hears the reward of the believers, he hopes. Likewise, a person should proceed toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic, between fear and hope, as He, the Exalted, said: "Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear" [al-Anbiya' 90]. But at some times it may be beneficial to give precedence to hope, and at other times it may be beneficial to give precedence to fear. So when a person's desire for sin becomes strong, he should give precedence to the side of fear until he refrains from it. And when a person performs an act of worship, he should give precedence to the side of hope, which is Allah, blessed and exalted, accepting it. Likewise, in a state of illness he should also return to Allah, glorified and exalted, and think well of Him, as came in the hadith: "None of you should die except while thinking well of his Lord"[[Recorded by Muslim (2877/81) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]], blessed and exalted.

He says: "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds" — Allah Most High combined creed and action, faith and Islam. "Believe" refers to creed, "do righteous deeds" refers to Islam. As you see, this occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Faith alone is not sufficient; rather, righteous deeds are necessary for the reward to be obtained. Whenever "those who believe" appears, what is meant is belief in what must be believed of the six fundamentals that the Messenger (ﷺ) explained to Gabriel when he said: "Iman is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and that you believe in divine decree (qadar), its good and its evil"[[Recorded by Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]]. This is because the general faith in the Qur'an is explained, or its explanation is detailed by the Sunnah, for no one knows the Book of Allah better than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for His saying "do righteous deeds": it is known that "righteous" (al-salihat) is an adjective of a noun that is omitted; the implied meaning is "the righteous deeds." So what are the righteous deeds? Righteous deeds are those that combine two conditions: first, sincerity to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; second, following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So every deed that contains shirk is not righteous, and it is rejected upon its doer, based on the words of Allah in the sacred hadith: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners from partnership; whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his partner"[[Recorded by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Likewise, following the Messenger is necessary; an innovated deed is not accepted even if the person is sincere in it, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]. Therefore, righteous deeds must include two things: sincerity to Allah and following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

"For them is a reward never to be cut off" [Fussilat 8]. This sentence is the predicate of "inna." Some say that the fronting of the prepositional phrase "lahum" indicates restriction, meaning: for them, not for others among the deniers or the wicked. "Ajr" means reward; "ghayr mamnun" means not cut off. The commentator says: "not cut off" — rather it is everlasting, as Allah said: "And for them is their provision therein morning and evening" [Maryam 62]. It was also said: "ghayr mamnun" means not given with a favor (mannah), i.e., they are given it without reproach; this is also a possibility. And when it is a possibility that does not contradict the first meaning, both meanings are intended by the verse. We have an important principle in tafsir, as well as in hadith: if a text can bear two meanings that do not contradict each other, the text is understood as both together, because Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows what His speech can bear, and so does His Messenger (ﷺ). Since neither of the two possibilities is specified, the text must include both. But if one of them is stronger than the other, the stronger one is followed. For this reason we say: the apparent meaning of the text takes precedence over ta'wil, and ta'wil, as you know, is following the less probable meaning.

So "for them is a reward never to be cut off" means: a reward not cut off, and a reward not given with reproach.

Then He, the Exalted, said: "Say: Do you indeed disbelieve" [Fussilat 9]. "Say" — i.e., O Muhammad, to these deniers: "Do you indeed disbelieve." This sentence is an interrogative with the meaning of affirmation, i.e., "Indeed you disbelieve." "Inna" is for emphasis and "latakfuruna" is also for emphasis; this is because the lam that falls in the predicate of "inna" or its delayed subject is for emphasis.

"Qul a-innakum": grammatically, "inna" puts the subject in the accusative and raises the predicate; the "ka" is its noun, and the clause "latakfuruna" is its predicate. As for the readings, listen: it is said: (with the second hamza realized fully and with its facilitation). Realizing it is that you say "a-innakum"; facilitating it is that you say "a-innakum" passing over it quickly. (And inserting an alif between them in both forms, and between the two and the first.) "Both forms" — what are the two forms? Realization and facilitation. Insert an alif between them on both readings, and the readings become four: inserting the alif, you say "aa-innakum" in realization, and "aa-innakum" in facilitation. So: realization and facilitation, with an alif and without it, two times two, four readings.

"Latakfuruna bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn": "takfuruna" means you deny Him and refuse to worship Him in arrogance, because all disbelief revolves around two things; pay attention to them: disbelief revolves around two things, either denial (jahd) or arrogance (istikbar). For example, Satan disbelieved by what? By arrogance; otherwise he acknowledged Allah and His might and His power, but he was arrogant. And the people of Pharaoh and those like them disbelieved by what? By denial. So the basis of all disbelief rests on these two matters: denial or arrogance. Therefore His saying "latakfuruna" includes both meanings, since they denied the Tawhid of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and were arrogant toward His worship.

"Bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn": He did not say "by Allah," but mentioned one of His acts, Glorified and Exalted, an act these idols cannot do. Mentioning an act that these idols cannot do is at the same time an establishment of proof: that is, you disbelieve in this while your idols do not do it.

"Latakfuruna bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn." The commentator said: "The Sunday and Monday," because the first day on which Allah began creation was Sunday.

"Wa taj'aluna lahu andadan": the waw is a conjunctive particle, and "taj'aluna" is coordinated with "takfuruna," not with the relative clause, i.e., not with "khalaqa."

("Andadan" — partners.) "Andadan" is the plural of "nidd," and "nidd" originally means an equal or a peer; it is said: "This is the nidd of that," i.e., its equal and counterpart. The intended meaning here is the partners whom they worship as they worship Allah. What is astonishing is that these polytheists, out of their foolishness, say: "We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah." You worship them alongside Allah and say they bring you near to Allah? Allah is free of need of this, and this only increases you in distance from Him.

"Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin": "dhalika" uses the demonstrative rather than the pronoun, and then made it a demonstrative of distance for glorification, magnification and exaltation, because distance here indicates a lofty place. "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin" — if he had said "He is the Lord of the worlds," the sentence would have been correct, but the glorification indicated by the demonstrative and the elevation indicated by the form of distance would not have been achieved. A parallel to this is "Alif-lam-mim. That is the Book" [al-Baqarah 1–2]; he did not say "it is the Book" nor "this is the Book," pointing to what we have mentioned. "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin" — the commentator said: "the Owner" (malik). In this explanation there is deficiency; rather we say: Creator, Owner and Administrator, because lordship (rububiyyah) is creation, dominion and management. So if we say "Owner," there is a deficiency in it.

"Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin" means: their Creator, their Owner, and the Manager of their affairs.

"Al-'alamin" is the plural of "'alam," which is everything other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Everything other than Allah is an "'alam," and it is called "'alam" because it is a sign ('alam) pointing to its Creator, Exalted and Majestic, for everything contains a sign indicating the oneness of Allah, His power, His wisdom, His might, and other things. The commentator said: "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin, the plural of 'alam, which is everything other than Allah, and it was pluralized because of the diversity of its kinds." That is: he did not say "al-'alam," but used "al-'alamin" because of the diversity of its kinds, with the ya' and nun ending as a predominance for rational beings.

If someone says: are rational beings more numerous, or non-rational beings?

Students: The second — rational beings.

Shaykh: We now have two opinions: rational beings are more numerous, and non-rational beings are more numerous. Is there no opinion of suspension?

Students: (...).

Shaykh: Yes? I'm saying, is there no suspension?

Student: No one can be certain.

Shaykh: So say: "I am undecided." If you cannot be certain, say "undecided," until there is a third opinion? It is said: if it is said that rational beings are more numerous, that requires evidence, and perhaps its evidence is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The heaven creaks, and it has a right to creak; there is not a space of four fingers in it except that there is an angel standing before Allah, or bowing, or prostrating"[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2312) and Ibn Majah (4190) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]. The heaven is vast and great; each heaven is wider than what is beneath it. Who can count these? This is a great matter. The House that is frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) in the seventh heaven: every day seventy thousand angels enter it, and they never return to it. Who can count the days? And every day it is visited by seventy thousand angels. So when we look at this, we say: rational beings are more numerous; who can count them? But if we look at what is on the earth, we say: non-rational beings?

Students: More numerous.

Shaykh: More numerous. So on this assumption, if we mean, for example, "those on the earth," we say: rational beings are predominant because of their nobility. The point is that if rational beings are more numerous, they are predominant because of what?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, indeed, because of their multitude. And if we say non-rational beings are more numerous, then rational beings are predominant...

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Non-rational... predominate over whom who is not discerning?

Student: Honor.

Shaykh: Because of their nobility, correct. In any case, the predominance of rational beings now: if rational beings are more numerous, it is because of their multitude; if non-rational beings are more numerous, it is because of the nobility of rational beings. "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin."

He says: "And He placed in it firm mountains" ("ja'ala" is a new clause), meaning: it is not coordinated with "khalaqa." What is astonishing is that he says: (It is not permissible to coordinate it with the relative clause because of the intervening foreign element). This is what the author held: that his saying "wa ja'ala" is a new clause. Undoubtedly, if we make it a new clause, the speech would not be coherent. The correct view is contrary to what the author said: that "ja'ala" is coordinated with "khalaqa," i.e., "bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn," and "wa ja'ala fiha rawasiya." The intervening foreign element here does no harm, either because it does no harm at all, as some have held, or because it does no harm since it is within the meaning of the speech and the speech is one. So the correct view is that "wa ja'ala" is coordinated with "khalaqa."
