The first view: the spreading is not the creation; it is something else, which God explained by His saying: ﴿He brought out from it its water and its pasture﴾ [al-Nazi'at 31]. This is the spreading, and bringing out water and pasture is something additional to creation and formation.

The second aspect: the "after" here is a sequence of mention, what the grammarians call the *tartib dhikri* (sequence of mention, as opposed to chronological sequence). Among its examples is the poet's saying:

"Indeed, the man who became a master, then his father became a master, then after that his grandfather became a master."

You see now that the order is not chronological, but this is called a sequence of mention. It allows two interpretations, but the first interpretation is more appropriate to say: the spreading out (*dahw*) of the earth is not the creation. Creating and forming is one thing, and spreading out is another. The evidence is that Allah, the Exalted, explained the spreading out when He said: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾. Have you understood now?

So there is no contradiction between the two verses, and each one is to be read in a way that does not contradict the other. Know that when a person sees two verses whose apparent meaning is contradictory, he should not hasten to judge that there is a contradiction, because two verses cannot contradict each other in every respect, as we mentioned in the principles of *tafsir* (the principles of Qur'anic exegesis). Rather, he should be patient, reflect and think. If he realizes there is no contradiction, this is what is sought. If not, he must ask the people of knowledge. If the matter still is not clear to him, he must withhold judgment, and these become among the ambiguous verses about which one must say: ﴿We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7]. We have already mentioned to you that some scholars wrote works on the verses whose apparent meaning is contradictory and reconciled between them, and I mentioned to you that among the best I have seen is what was written by Shaykh al-Shinqiti, may Allah have mercy on him, *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Inconsistency from the Verses of the Book).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the kind of disbelief that these addressees committed was *shirk* (associating partners with Allah). This is shown by His saying: ﴿and you set up rivals to Him﴾ [Fussilat 9]. Setting up rivals to Him takes many forms. One may set up a rival in His essence, saying that Allah has a like, as the Christians did when they said that Allah is the third of three, and as the *mumaththila* (those who likened Allah to His creation) did when they described Allah's attributes by the attributes of His creatures. This is *shirk*. A rival may also be in worship: a person worships something while not believing it is like Allah, but he worships it and claims he worships it only to draw near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. A rival may also be in love: a person loves a thing as he loves Allah. It is strange that Satan flows through the son of Adam like blood, so he loves a person and becomes greatly attached to him, saying, "I love him for the sake of Allah," while in reality he loves him alongside Allah and not for Allah. The one who loves a person for Allah's sake has his original love directed to whom?

* A student: To Allah.

* The Shaykh: The love of Allah. This one he loves because he loves Allah. But the one whose heart is turned toward this beloved, who thinks of nothing but him, sleeps only remembering him and wakes only remembering him, has not loved him for Allah. Rather, he loved him alongside Allah, and this is *shirk*, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among mankind are those who take, besides Allah, rivals whom they love as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 165]. Likewise, among setting up rivals is that a person's heart becomes attached to a created being through fear and hope, not love: fear and hope, such that he relies on it to obtain his livelihood or to repel harm from himself. This happens often, especially since the opening of hospitals. Most people's hearts become attached to the hospital. You find that when he falls ill he says, "I'll go and take a pill or two," and he does not say, "O Lord, grant me well-being," or turn to Allah at once. Just a pill, or two, or three, even though this doctor on whom he relies and whom he hopes in may be a disbeliever and an atheist. This too is taking a rival to Allah. For this reason, the harm of hospitals now, despite the great benefit and good they contain, and praise be to Allah, is great harm, because people now hang their hopes on hospitals and seek relief from their pains there. Never, if a person is pricked by a thorn, does he say, "Let's go to the hospital," rather than removing it with his fingernail or with tweezers. If a woman's labor pains come and she is having ordinary contractions, what does she do? The hospital. And what does the hospital say? "By Allah, this is a serious matter; there must be a Caesarean section." This Caesarean cuts the abdomen, and then she is left with ten scars on her belly, and if she gives birth to ten children, this belly can no longer bear any pregnancy; if she becomes pregnant, it bursts. All this is a kind of *shirk*. Do not turn to the hospital except in extreme necessity. Keep your hope always hung on Allah, and say: "The One who created me and brought me into existence the first time is able to remove whatever illness has befallen me, is it not so? And He is more able than anyone. He, the Mighty and Majestic, removes it without any operation, without pills, without water and without injections."

In sum, taking rivals is not specific to a particular thing; it occurs in many things. So beware of having a rival. Indeed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wretched is the slave of the dinar, wretched is the slave of the dirham, wretched is the slave of the velvet cloak, wretched is the slave of the woven garment." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (2886) from Abu Hurayrah.] Who is worshipped here? Does a person place a dinar above himself and prostrate to it and bow to it? No, nor the dirham, nor the cloak, nor the garment. But because his heart is attached to this thing, if he is given he is content, and if he is not given he is angry, he becomes its slave. We ask Allah to protect us and you from that.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration that setting up a rival to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is impossible, as shown by His saying: ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Fussilat 9]. The reason it is impossible: He is the Lord of the worlds, and what rival could be the Lord of the worlds? What do you say? Answer me. What is it? Where have you gone?

* A student: No, no, I hear...

* The Shaykh: You hear but you do not comprehend, because the heart is not present, is it not so?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, or no?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Apparently the one who admits his sin is pardoned. I say concerning His saying ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds﴾ that it is evidence that no one can be a rival to Allah. Why? In other words, who could be said to be the Lord of the worlds? No one can. He is the Lord, and everything else is one who is lordship-ed. Therefore, whatever else exists cannot rightly be a rival to Him.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the all-encompassing lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, over the whole world, as shown by His saying ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds﴾.

* Among its benefits: the obligation to submit to Him in the Sharia, just as we submit to Him in destiny (*qadar*), because this is what lordship requires. You must submit to this Lord in the Sharia just as you are submissive to Him in destiny. Everything is submissive to Allah in destiny: ﴿To Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [al-Ra'd 15]. What is this prostration? The destined prostration. So you must submit to Him in the Sharia, and humble yourself before Him, being humble before Him as you have been humble before Him in His decree.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the favor of Allah, glorified and exalted, upon His servants, in that He placed in the earth firm mountains (*rawasi*), meaning fixed things. What is the wisdom? The wisdom is mentioned by Allah in His saying: ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl 15]. Were it not for these mountains, the earth would shake with us.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the earth revolves, as shown by His saying ﴿lest it shake with you﴾, because negating shaking is evidence of the existence of the basic motion, since He did not say "lest it move with you". Negating the more specific entails the existence of the more general, as we said regarding Allah's saying: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am 103], which is evidence that Allah can be seen but not perceived in a complete way. For if He could not be seen at all, it would have to say "vision does not see Him." Since He negated the more specific, this became evidence for the existence of the more general.

Some scholars established this and said that the verse is evidence that the earth revolves, because Allah placed these mountains so that its rotation would be balanced and would not become unsteady and throw people about. But although this is strong from the standpoint of reasoning, it is not definitive, since the meaning could be that it shakes with you, that is, it trembles even if it is standing still. A ship on the water, for example, sways even when it is stationary. So the meaning would be: ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl 15], meaning lest it sway with you, whether it revolves or does not revolve. For this reason, the verse gives no definitive proof that the earth revolves.

If someone says: "You say it is possible that it indicates the earth revolves. What is your answer regarding many verses that show the sun runs, rises, sets, turns aside, hides and goes? All these actions are attributed to the sun, and the basic principle is that when an action is attributed to a thing, it is performed by that thing. So the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that the sun is what revolves around the earth: ﴿And you see the sun when it rises﴾ [al-Kahf 17]. So its meaning is that it was hidden and then rose upon us. Those who say the earth revolves would have the meaning: ﴿when it rises﴾ as 'when we rise upon it', because it is we who come to it, whereas it is stationary and fixed, I mean the sun."

We say: it is permissible that the earth revolves and the sun also revolves, and if the rotations are in opposite directions, then clearly the night and day alternate. For example, if the earth revolved toward the east and the sun revolved toward the west, this is possible with complete ease. If both revolve in one direction, then if one is faster than the other, the alternation of night and day is achieved. Whoever says that we cannot say the sun runs unless we say the earth is stationary and does not revolve, and that establishing the earth's revolution along with the sun's revolution is impossible, his statement is not correct.

What is possible is possible, even if we say both revolve. But what we currently believe is that the alternation of night and day occurs through the sun's passing over the spherical earth, not through the sphere's passing over the sun. This is what we believe until now, because this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an came from the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, who knows best what He created.

We cannot deviate from this by a hair's breadth as long as no perceptible matter has appeared to us that cannot be denied. Some of them (i.e., some of those who say the earth revolves) say: "We have a definitive matter, by the evidence of intercontinental missiles, which are calculated with a specific measure so that they match the earth's rotation and hit the target. Otherwise this would not be possible."

In any case, I wanted to speak about this to some extent, because at one time it was a subject of dispute among people, among students of knowledge, among common people, and among those who did not attain much knowledge. So we say: first, deep investigation into this and dispute over it is something that is not appropriate and has no benefit.

Second: when we want to examine the matter scientifically and theoretically, we look at the verses. If the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl 15] requires that it revolves, we say so, with no harm. There is no objection to saying it revolves, and likewise the sun, with no objection. Thus we have taken the apparent meaning of the Qur'an regarding the sun, and the apparent meaning of ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ regarding the earth. And if His saying ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ does not necessarily mean that it moves, but that it may tremble while still and fixed, then no evidence remains in the verse that the earth revolves.

* A student: (...) I acknowledge that they cannot be left to their claim (...) the sun (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. We say: we do not concede that the alternation of night and day is due to the earth's rotation; rather, we say it is due to the sun's rising over the earth.

* The student: And it does not prevent that the Lawgiver (...) the earth?

* The Shaykh: It does not prevent it. But if it were assumed that a perceptible, tangible proof came to us that the alternation of night and day is caused by the earth's rotation, we would say so, and these attributions of actions to the sun would then be understood according to the observer's perception of it.

* The student: They claim the sun is fixed...

* The Shaykh: No, I say: no. They say: does the sun revolve in the atmosphere, or does it revolve around itself?

* A student: The sun's rotation (...) an annual rotation (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. In any case, that is not our concern. The discussion is about what the Qur'an says. Now, if we read: ﴿And you see the sun when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets, passing them on the left﴾ [al-Kahf 17], there are four verbs here, all attributed to the sun. The basic principle is that actions attributed to a thing are performed by it. So the sun is what rises. They say: no, the sun does not rise upon us; rather we rise upon it because of the earth's rotation. For example, now, the lamp above me, say like the back of my hand facing it, the sun is up, then you say: this is how the sun sets. That is, we have set away from the sun, and we have risen upon it. We say: if this is established with certainty, beyond doubt, then the Qur'an never contradicts the senses, and the verbs attributed to the sun are interpreted according to the observer's perception.

* A student: How can the obedience of a disbeliever be a destined obedience?

* The Shaykh: Does Allah not command him to be sick, and he becomes sick? And to be healthy, and he becomes healthy? And to die, and he dies?

* The student: Yes.

* Another student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿They said: We come willingly﴾ [Fussilat 11]. Does this indicate that inanimate things have will and speak?

* The Shaykh: We have not reached this yet, may Allah bless you.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Does his statement not support this claim: "We are the ones who rise upon the sun"? His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he followed a way, until when he reached the setting place of the sun, he found it setting in a muddy spring﴾ [al-Kahf 85-86]. The verb was attributed to the sun, and the scholars explained that it is in the eye of the observer...

* The Shaykh: ﴿he found it setting﴾.

* The student: ﴿setting in a muddy spring﴾ ﴿he found it setting﴾ ﴿setting﴾: the verb is attributed to the sun. The scholars said it is in the eye of the observer, and it does not set; it only sets (...).

* The Shaykh: It disappears from him.

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, fine.

* The student: Does it set in a muddy spring?

* The Shaykh: How? It disappears from him into the sea, but it is not in the middle of the sea, of course. That is why He said: ﴿he found it setting﴾.

* A student: Shaykh, we learned that the earth was created before the sun, so what is the wisdom?

* The Shaykh: The earth before the sun?

* The student: The earth was created before the sun.

* The Shaykh: We did not know this. Before the heaven.

* The student: What is the wisdom in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioning the heaven and the earth (...) the heaven?

* The Shaykh: We have not reached this. The wisdom is that Allah, the Exalted, mentions the higher before the lower. As for speaking of the creation of the heavens, Allah the Exalted has made clear that the lower is created before the higher, like a building now: when you want to build something, do you build the roof before the column? So in mention and discourse, the more noble and higher is put first, and in formation and construction, one begins with the lower, because it is the foundation. (...)

* * *

* The student: ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and behind them, saying: Worship none but Allah. They said: If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels; so we disbelieve in what you have been sent with. As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the earth without right and said: Who is mightier than us in strength? Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs. So We sent upon them a furious wind during days of misfortune, to make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world; and the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgraceful, and they will not be helped. As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they used to earn. And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾ [Fussilat 14-18].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We were speaking about the benefits of the previous verses, from His saying: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days﴾ [Fussilat 9]. We took several benefits from it. How many?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Three?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Up to?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: We have not reached it.

* The student: The favor of Allah the Exalted upon His servants, in that He placed in the earth firm, fixed mountains (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verses 8–12 (part 6 of 6):

* The Shaykh: And among the benefits of these verses: Allah, exalted is He, placed the firm mountains above the earth because of the benefits in that and the averting of harms, which we pointed to in the course of the tafsir.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: Allah, exalted is He, blessed the earth, and the aspect of its blessing is evident, for it carries the living and the dead, and it carries animals whose kinds are unknown, let alone their species, and let alone their individuals, except to Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: Allah decreed the sustenance of the earth within it, meaning He made it measured by a known measure. Among that measuring is that He placed in some regions of the earth provisions that are not in other regions, so that people exchange these provisions and commerce is set in motion, along with other benefits. Perhaps the saying of the Blessed and Exalted Allah points to this: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾, meaning the rain, ﴿that they may remember﴾ [al-Furqan 50].

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the creation of the earth was completed in four days, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿in four days, equal [for those who ask]﴾ [Fussilat 10].

* Among its benefits: Allah, Blessed and Exalted, answers the questioners' questions, whether they ask with the tongue of circumstance (lisan al-hal) or with the tongue of speech (lisan al-maqal). A person may be eager to know a matter without speaking with his tongue; it is said that he is asking with the tongue of circumstance, while the person who speaks with the tongue is asking with the tongue of speech. The question about the creation of the heavens and the earth and how it happened is posed both ways.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the heaven was smoke before it was created, then Allah transformed this smoke into heavens, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke﴾ [Fussilat 11].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation (uluww), according to one of the two opinions in the interpretation of ﴿istawa﴾ (turned/rose), and the two are: what? "Intended" (qasada) or "rose up" (irtafa'a).

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: everything is receptive to being addressed by Allah, mighty and majestic, meaning it is capable of Allah addressing it; for Allah addressed the heaven and the earth while they are inanimate objects. He said: ﴿Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾. However, if we addressed an inanimate object, that would be considered foolishness and a kind of madness; but the Lord, mighty and majestic, addresses whomever He wills of His servants, rational and otherwise, and inanimate and otherwise, because whoever Allah addresses understands Allah's address.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: everything is subservient to Allah, mighty and majestic, whether it is unwilling or willing, due to His saying: ﴿Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾ [Fussilat 11].

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the complete submission of the heavens and the earth to Allah, mighty and majestic, as they said: ﴿We came, obedient﴾.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: it is valid to express about the non-rational what is expressed about the rational when the non-rational is treated as if it were rational, due to His saying: ﴿obedient﴾ [Fussilat 11]. This plural, the sound masculine plural (jam' al-mudhakkar al-salim), is only issued by a rational being, and for non-rational things one says ṭā'iʿāt and similar forms; but when the non-rational is treated in address as rational, it is valid to deal with it in the manner of the rational.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the affirmation of obedience and unwillingness for the non-rational, due to His saying: ﴿Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾. Does this mean that the non-rational has a will? The answer: yes, because the obedient one has a will, and one who is conceived as being compelled also has a will, and the will of each thing is according to its nature. It has already passed for us that pebbles glorified in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ), and there is no glorification except after a will. And it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said about Uhud: "It loves us and we love it" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4083) and Muslim (1393/504), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik]. Love is more specific than will. On this basis, these inanimate objects whose glorification we do not comprehend have a will, and they glorify Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the period of the creation of the heavens was shorter than the period of the creation of the earth, although the heavens are greater. But since the earth was placed for the creatures, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the earth He laid down for the creatures﴾ [al-Rahman 10], its creation took a longer period, to show Allah's care for this earth which He placed for the creatures, and so that the creatures on the earth may know that the consideration is in perfection, not in speed.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: Allah completed the creation of the heavens when He revealed in each heaven its command, and arranged them in a firm and perfected order.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: Allah, exalted is He, created these stars for two benefits. The first benefit: the adornment of the sky. The second benefit: the protection of the heavens from the devils; they protect the heavens from the devils and are likewise an adornment of the sky. There is a third benefit that Allah mentioned in Surat al-Nahl in His saying: ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾ [al-Nahl 16]. Therefore Qatadah, who is among the great Successors (a'immat al-tabi'in), said: Allah created these stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the sky, as missiles against the devils, and as landmarks by which one is guided [Narrated by al-Bukhari in suspended form (4/107)].

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the perfection of Allah, mighty and majestic, in His creation, due to His saying: ﴿That is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ [Fussilat 12]. This decree is undoubtedly a decree that is firm and perfected in every respect.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of two of Allah's names: al-'Aziz (the Mighty) and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing). These two names include two attributes: might ('izzah) and knowledge ('ilm). Here we ask: does al-'Aziz include what is called a judgment (hukm) or an effect (athar)? The answer: yes, based on the view that its meaning includes the might of dominance (izzat al-qahr), and the dominant must have a thing dominated so that dominance is accomplished through it. Accordingly, belief in these two names includes three matters:
First: belief in the name as a name of Allah.
Second: belief in the attribute.
Third: belief in the effect, or if you wish, say: in the judgment (hukm).

Student: "Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask. Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly. So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as protection. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing." [Fussilat 9–12].

Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward never to be cut off" [Fussilat 8]. When He mentioned the punishment of the polytheists, He explained the reward of the believers; because Allah Most High revealed this Book as oft-repeated (mathani), and the matter is so in order that a person may proceed toward his Lord between fear and hope. When he hears the punishment of the deniers, he fears, and when he hears the reward of the believers, he hopes. Likewise, a person should proceed toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic, between fear and hope, as He, the Exalted, said: "Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear" [al-Anbiya' 90]. But at some times it may be beneficial to give precedence to hope, and at other times it may be beneficial to give precedence to fear. So when a person's desire for sin becomes strong, he should give precedence to the side of fear until he refrains from it. And when a person performs an act of worship, he should give precedence to the side of hope, which is Allah, blessed and exalted, accepting it. Likewise, in a state of illness he should also return to Allah, glorified and exalted, and think well of Him, as came in the hadith: "None of you should die except while thinking well of his Lord"[[Recorded by Muslim (2877/81) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]], blessed and exalted.

He says: "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds" — Allah Most High combined creed and action, faith and Islam. "Believe" refers to creed, "do righteous deeds" refers to Islam. As you see, this occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Faith alone is not sufficient; rather, righteous deeds are necessary for the reward to be obtained. Whenever "those who believe" appears, what is meant is belief in what must be believed of the six fundamentals that the Messenger (ﷺ) explained to Gabriel when he said: "Iman is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and that you believe in divine decree (qadar), its good and its evil"[[Recorded by Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]]. This is because the general faith in the Qur'an is explained, or its explanation is detailed by the Sunnah, for no one knows the Book of Allah better than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for His saying "do righteous deeds": it is known that "righteous" (al-salihat) is an adjective of a noun that is omitted; the implied meaning is "the righteous deeds." So what are the righteous deeds? Righteous deeds are those that combine two conditions: first, sincerity to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; second, following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So every deed that contains shirk is not righteous, and it is rejected upon its doer, based on the words of Allah in the sacred hadith: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners from partnership; whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his partner"[[Recorded by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Likewise, following the Messenger is necessary; an innovated deed is not accepted even if the person is sincere in it, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]. Therefore, righteous deeds must include two things: sincerity to Allah and following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

"For them is a reward never to be cut off" [Fussilat 8]. This sentence is the predicate of "inna." Some say that the fronting of the prepositional phrase "lahum" indicates restriction, meaning: for them, not for others among the deniers or the wicked. "Ajr" means reward; "ghayr mamnun" means not cut off. The commentator says: "not cut off" — rather it is everlasting, as Allah said: "And for them is their provision therein morning and evening" [Maryam 62]. It was also said: "ghayr mamnun" means not given with a favor (mannah), i.e., they are given it without reproach; this is also a possibility. And when it is a possibility that does not contradict the first meaning, both meanings are intended by the verse. We have an important principle in tafsir, as well as in hadith: if a text can bear two meanings that do not contradict each other, the text is understood as both together, because Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows what His speech can bear, and so does His Messenger (ﷺ). Since neither of the two possibilities is specified, the text must include both. But if one of them is stronger than the other, the stronger one is followed. For this reason we say: the apparent meaning of the text takes precedence over ta'wil, and ta'wil, as you know, is following the less probable meaning.

So "for them is a reward never to be cut off" means: a reward not cut off, and a reward not given with reproach.

Then He, the Exalted, said: "Say: Do you indeed disbelieve" [Fussilat 9]. "Say" — i.e., O Muhammad, to these deniers: "Do you indeed disbelieve." This sentence is an interrogative with the meaning of affirmation, i.e., "Indeed you disbelieve." "Inna" is for emphasis and "latakfuruna" is also for emphasis; this is because the lam that falls in the predicate of "inna" or its delayed subject is for emphasis.

"Qul a-innakum": grammatically, "inna" puts the subject in the accusative and raises the predicate; the "ka" is its noun, and the clause "latakfuruna" is its predicate. As for the readings, listen: it is said: (with the second hamza realized fully and with its facilitation). Realizing it is that you say "a-innakum"; facilitating it is that you say "a-innakum" passing over it quickly. (And inserting an alif between them in both forms, and between the two and the first.) "Both forms" — what are the two forms? Realization and facilitation. Insert an alif between them on both readings, and the readings become four: inserting the alif, you say "aa-innakum" in realization, and "aa-innakum" in facilitation. So: realization and facilitation, with an alif and without it, two times two, four readings.

"Latakfuruna bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn": "takfuruna" means you deny Him and refuse to worship Him in arrogance, because all disbelief revolves around two things; pay attention to them: disbelief revolves around two things, either denial (jahd) or arrogance (istikbar). For example, Satan disbelieved by what? By arrogance; otherwise he acknowledged Allah and His might and His power, but he was arrogant. And the people of Pharaoh and those like them disbelieved by what? By denial. So the basis of all disbelief rests on these two matters: denial or arrogance. Therefore His saying "latakfuruna" includes both meanings, since they denied the Tawhid of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and were arrogant toward His worship.

"Bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn": He did not say "by Allah," but mentioned one of His acts, Glorified and Exalted, an act these idols cannot do. Mentioning an act that these idols cannot do is at the same time an establishment of proof: that is, you disbelieve in this while your idols do not do it.

"Latakfuruna bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn." The commentator said: "The Sunday and Monday," because the first day on which Allah began creation was Sunday.

"Wa taj'aluna lahu andadan": the waw is a conjunctive particle, and "taj'aluna" is coordinated with "takfuruna," not with the relative clause, i.e., not with "khalaqa."

("Andadan" — partners.) "Andadan" is the plural of "nidd," and "nidd" originally means an equal or a peer; it is said: "This is the nidd of that," i.e., its equal and counterpart. The intended meaning here is the partners whom they worship as they worship Allah. What is astonishing is that these polytheists, out of their foolishness, say: "We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah." You worship them alongside Allah and say they bring you near to Allah? Allah is free of need of this, and this only increases you in distance from Him.

"Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin": "dhalika" uses the demonstrative rather than the pronoun, and then made it a demonstrative of distance for glorification, magnification and exaltation, because distance here indicates a lofty place. "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin" — if he had said "He is the Lord of the worlds," the sentence would have been correct, but the glorification indicated by the demonstrative and the elevation indicated by the form of distance would not have been achieved. A parallel to this is "Alif-lam-mim. That is the Book" [al-Baqarah 1–2]; he did not say "it is the Book" nor "this is the Book," pointing to what we have mentioned. "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin" — the commentator said: "the Owner" (malik). In this explanation there is deficiency; rather we say: Creator, Owner and Administrator, because lordship (rububiyyah) is creation, dominion and management. So if we say "Owner," there is a deficiency in it.

"Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin" means: their Creator, their Owner, and the Manager of their affairs.

"Al-'alamin" is the plural of "'alam," which is everything other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Everything other than Allah is an "'alam," and it is called "'alam" because it is a sign ('alam) pointing to its Creator, Exalted and Majestic, for everything contains a sign indicating the oneness of Allah, His power, His wisdom, His might, and other things. The commentator said: "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin, the plural of 'alam, which is everything other than Allah, and it was pluralized because of the diversity of its kinds." That is: he did not say "al-'alam," but used "al-'alamin" because of the diversity of its kinds, with the ya' and nun ending as a predominance for rational beings.

If someone says: are rational beings more numerous, or non-rational beings?

Students: The second — rational beings.

Shaykh: We now have two opinions: rational beings are more numerous, and non-rational beings are more numerous. Is there no opinion of suspension?

Students: (...).

Shaykh: Yes? I'm saying, is there no suspension?

Student: No one can be certain.

Shaykh: So say: "I am undecided." If you cannot be certain, say "undecided," until there is a third opinion? It is said: if it is said that rational beings are more numerous, that requires evidence, and perhaps its evidence is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The heaven creaks, and it has a right to creak; there is not a space of four fingers in it except that there is an angel standing before Allah, or bowing, or prostrating"[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2312) and Ibn Majah (4190) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]. The heaven is vast and great; each heaven is wider than what is beneath it. Who can count these? This is a great matter. The House that is frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) in the seventh heaven: every day seventy thousand angels enter it, and they never return to it. Who can count the days? And every day it is visited by seventy thousand angels. So when we look at this, we say: rational beings are more numerous; who can count them? But if we look at what is on the earth, we say: non-rational beings?

Students: More numerous.

Shaykh: More numerous. So on this assumption, if we mean, for example, "those on the earth," we say: rational beings are predominant because of their nobility. The point is that if rational beings are more numerous, they are predominant because of what?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, indeed, because of their multitude. And if we say non-rational beings are more numerous, then rational beings are predominant...

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Non-rational... predominate over whom who is not discerning?

Student: Honor.

Shaykh: Because of their nobility, correct. In any case, the predominance of rational beings now: if rational beings are more numerous, it is because of their multitude; if non-rational beings are more numerous, it is because of the nobility of rational beings. "Dhalika Rabbu al-'alamin."

He says: "And He placed in it firm mountains" ("ja'ala" is a new clause), meaning: it is not coordinated with "khalaqa." What is astonishing is that he says: (It is not permissible to coordinate it with the relative clause because of the intervening foreign element). This is what the author held: that his saying "wa ja'ala" is a new clause. Undoubtedly, if we make it a new clause, the speech would not be coherent. The correct view is contrary to what the author said: that "ja'ala" is coordinated with "khalaqa," i.e., "bi'l-ladhi khalaqa al-ardha fi yawmayn," and "wa ja'ala fiha rawasiya." The intervening foreign element here does no harm, either because it does no harm at all, as some have held, or because it does no harm since it is within the meaning of the speech and the speech is one. So the correct view is that "wa ja'ala" is coordinated with "khalaqa."

("Wa ja'ala fiha rawasiya" — mountains that are fixed.) First: is "ja'ala" here one of the verbs of transformation or of bringing into existence?

Students: Bringing into existence.

Shaykh: It may mean: "and He brought into existence in it firm mountains," and it may be one of the verbs of transformation, i.e., "He made in it firm mountains." The meaning does not differ, but the grammar does. If we say it is a verb of transformation, it takes two objects; if we say it is a verb of bringing into existence, it takes one object. The author's saying "mountains that are fixed" informs us, may Allah have mercy on him, that "rawasi" is an adjective of an omitted noun; the implied meaning is "mountains, firm," and "rawasi" means "fixed."

"Wa ja'ala fiha rawasiya": may the noun being described be omitted? Yes, and it is very common.

"And of the described and the describing, understood, / it is permitted to omit the described, and in the describing it is frequent." That is: omitting the described is frequent. "A ni'mal sabighat" [Saba' 11] means: coats of mail that are full-length — the point is that it is frequent.

"Amilu al-salihat," as we have passed, omission of the described is common, because the intended thing is the attribute, and the attribute is in the adjective form, which is present.

"Min fawqiha": these firm mountains are from above.

Student: Is the parsing of "ja'ala" in the sense of "sayyara" (made)?

Shaykh: Yes, meaning: "He made in it firm mountains."

Student: The first and second objects?

Shaykh: The first object is "rawasiya," and the second is the prepositional phrase. As for his saying "min fawqiha," pay attention to this word; it has a great benefit. The firm mountains may be from below, and may be from above, is that not so? They may be from below, meaning, for example, foundations are dug into the earth so that they are firmly set and are fixed. But here he said "min fawqiha," and that is for several benefits:

The first benefit: the manifestness of these firm mountains and their clarity for people, so that they may know thereby the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and perhaps they would not be firm mountains unless they were from above, based on the fact that the earth revolves so that it maintains its... balance.

Second: when these firm mountains are from above, much benefit results in warding off storms and in shelters, as is known in caves, and as is known from the slopes, the flanks and the peaks of mountains, of plants that would not exist without these elevations.

Third: that they cause rainwater to rush down with force until it reaches lands suitable for plants, because you know that some lands are salt flats with no good in them, and some are gardens that grow. When water falls on these mountains, on their summits and their flanks, it descends to the earth with great force until it reaches what Allah wills it to reach.

Fourth: that the summits of the mountains contain better minerals than the lower earth. This is why He said: "And We sent down iron, wherein is great might" [al-Hadid 25]; We sent it down from the summits of the mountains. For this reason the scholars say that iron that comes from the summits of mountains is higher and stronger than that which comes from below. This is what we know, and what we do not know is more. The point is that the phrase "min fawqiha" has acquired a great benefit; we have mentioned four of its benefits so far.

(﴿And He placed firm mountains upon it from above it, and blessed it﴾ with abundance of water, crops and milk-giving animals (udrū')) ﴿And He blessed it﴾, meaning the earth. How great are the earth's blessings: its crops, trees, rivers, minerals and other blessings. The author's words "(al-durū')" refer to the udders of livestock, because when livestock are well fed on spring pasture their milk increases. Whoever reflects will find that the earth contains great blessings that carry the living, the dead, the wild beasts, the predators, the cattle, the insects and human beings, and it is also spacious despite all that it contains. If people were still living on the earth's surface now, you would see something terrible and difficult. But Allah made the earth ﴿a container for the living and the dead﴾ [al-Mursalat 25–26], and this is one of its blessings.

﴿And He determined within it its sustenance﴾. Regarding ﴿qaddara﴾, the author said: "divided [its sustenance] among people and livestock," and so on to the end. He determined within it the provisions. He says: qaddara comes from taqdir, which means distribution. He determined the provisions and did not place sustenance in only one part of the earth. If it were in only one part of the earth, this would be very hard on people, would it not? For example, if it were supposed that food existed only in the western side of the globe, how would the people of the east live, or conversely, how would the people of the west live? But it is determined in another way: He placed in some lands what does not grow in other lands, and vice versa. The wisdom behind this is that people exchange provisions. Those who do not have this type of food go to the lands where it is found and bring it to the land that lacks it, and vice versa. In some regions of the earth, palm trees and grapes are abundant but citrus fruits and similar things are scarce, and there are also many other things. I am not one of the people of agriculture, but there are many things that thrive in one place and not in another, so that exchange takes place among people, and so that people travel through the earth seeking provision. This is part of the wisdom in His saying: ﴿And He determined within it its sustenance﴾.

﴿In four days﴾ ((﴿in﴾ completing ﴿four days﴾, meaning the placing and what is mentioned with it occurred on Tuesday and Wednesday)). If the creation of the earth began on Sunday and Monday, then when He says ﴿in four days﴾, what remains? Tuesday and Wednesday. So the earth was created and its provisions determined ﴿in four days﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿equally, for those who ask﴾: accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar); i.e., the four days were equal, neither more nor less). By saying "equal" (istawat istiwa'an), he informs us that ﴿sawā'an﴾ is an ism maṣdar (a verbal noun that is not a full infinitive). His statement "accusative as a verbal noun" is loose, because if we say ﴿sawā'an﴾ is the maṣdar of (istawā), this does not fit the rule, since the rule is that the maṣdar matches the verb in its letters, and here (istawā) does not match ﴿sawā'an﴾. What matches is (istiwā'). So ﴿sawā'an﴾ is an ism maṣdar, like (kallama) whose maṣdar is (taklīm) and whose ism maṣdar is (kalām). Here (istawā) has the maṣdar (istiwā') and the ism maṣdar ﴿sawā'an﴾.

The main point is that His saying ﴿sawā'an﴾ means that this creation covered all four days completely. It did not happen in two or three days, but in all four days. Therefore, his statement "accusative as a verbal noun" should more correctly be stated as: it is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object), meaning the four days were equal, neither more nor less.

(﴿for those who ask﴾ about the creation of the earth and what it contains): ﴿for those who ask﴾ is not to be taken as connected to ﴿sawā'an﴾. Rather, it is the answer to an implied statement, meaning: this is an answer to those who ask, or something similar.

The main point is that His saying ﴿for those who ask﴾ indicates that what was mentioned is the answer to whoever asked about the creation of the earth and the determination of its provisions, that it was ﴿in four days equally﴾.

﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾. ﴿Then﴾ means after the creation of the earth and the determination of its provisions.

﴿He turned to the heaven﴾. The author said: "He intended toward the heaven." This is one of two views on this phrase, that it means "intended," but a complete intention. This is because istawā indicates perfection, as Allah said: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and was fully developed﴾ [al-Qasas 14]. The second view is that (istawā ilā) means (istawā 'alā), i.e., He rose over it. But the meaning chosen by the author is more correct: that He intended toward the heaven with complete and perfect will, because (ilā) indicates the end point and (ʿalā) indicates elevation. It is known that the heavens had not yet been created at that time. Furthermore, if we said that istawā means "rose," then "then He rose over the heaven" would have been true before that, when the earth was created, and He would not have been above the heaven, even though Allah's exaltedness is an attribute inseparable from His essence.

(﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke﴾: vapor rising). The phrase ﴿while it was smoke﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya), and ﴿the heaven﴾ here means the height, since it had not yet been created, but it was like smoke, i.e., rising vapor. It is said that this rising vapor ascended from the water that existed before the earth was created, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water﴾ [Hud 7]. So before the creation of the heavens and the earth there was water, above which was the Throne of the Most Merciful, the Mighty and Majestic. Then the earth was created, and from this water there emerged what? A thick rising vapor which became like smoke.

(﴿﴿So He said to it and to the earth﴾﴾ Allah said to it and to the earth: ﴿﴿Come﴾﴾ toward My purpose for you both ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾ in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning obedient or compelled; ﴿They said: We come﴾ with those within us ﴿obedient﴾﴾), and so on to the end. ﴿He said to it and to the earth: Come﴾. Is this command a creative command (amr takwīnī) or a legislative command (amr taklīfī)?

* Students: The first.

* Shaykh: If we say it is a legislative command, there is no difference whether they are obedient or compelled. That is, we said the first: is it a creative command or a legislative command? If we say it is a legislative command, it is clear, and this is why He said: ﴿willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come obedient﴾. If we say it is a creative command, it is not valid for it to be willingly or unwillingly, because a creative command is certain to take effect. So the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is a legislative command. Allah has the right to obligate whomever He wills among His servants or creatures; He may obligate whatever He wills. The rest of the discussion of these verses will come, Allah willing, in the next lesson.

* Student: The saying of Allah, glorified and exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [Fussilat 8]. Does this verse and its like serve as evidence for those who exclude righteous deeds from faith, on the basis that conjunction (ʿaṭf) implies difference?

* Shaykh: This is not valid, because the texts show that righteous deeds are part of faith. But there is no problem with one thing being divided into types. Faith includes deeds without doubt, but it has varieties: some of it is belief ('aqīda), some is verbal action, and some is physical action.

* Student: (...) Shaykh, in our discussion of rational beings: are they more numerous or are non-rational beings more numerous? Shaykh, now, we said rational beings are more numerous because of their honor, as an honoring.

* Shaykh: No, if we say it is the prevalence (taghlīb) of the majority because they are the majority.

* Student: Now, Shaykh, I did not understand. How?

* Shaykh: You did not understand?

* Student: Now, Shaykh, which is more numerous: rational beings or non-rational beings?

* Shaykh: Should I ask you?

* Student: As far as I know, we said that rational beings are more numerous due to their honor, and non-rational beings are fewer in number.

* Shaykh: No, reverse it and you will be correct. If we say rational beings are more numerous, then here He used the form for rational beings because of their majority; He gave them prevalence because of their majority. And if we say rational beings are fewer, He gave them prevalence because of their honor.

* Student: Now, Shaykh, how can we say "more numerous," when rational beings are contained within existence, and existence contains them, and everything contained is smaller than its container? If we say they are more numerous, then existence encompasses them and existence is larger.

* Shaykh: We said there is a possibility. We said: on both possibilities, this or that.

* Student: Shaykh, regarding ﴿sawā'an﴾, why do we not say that it comes from the verb (sawwā)?

* Shaykh: (sawwā)?

* Student: (sawwā).

* Shaykh: Taswiya. If we said it comes from the verb (sawwā), it would become taswiya, and that also is not suitable from (sawwā); it is valid from (istawā).

* Student: Sawā, meaning equality between two things?

* Shaykh: No. ﴿in four days sawā'an﴾ means complete and perfectly equal.

* Student: Is ﴿sawā'an﴾ not parsed as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl)?

* Shaykh: It can be a circumstantial accusative, but know that a maṣdar is not parsed as ḥāl except when there is no escape from parsing it as ḥāl. That is, we do not parse a maṣdar as ḥāl except out of necessity. Do you understand? Because the basic nature of ḥāl is that it is derived (mushtaq), while the maṣdar is non-derived (jāmid).

* Student: The saying of Allah, exalted: ﴿And He determined within it its sustenance﴾. Is this the mention of (...)?

* Shaykh: No, it will come to us, Allah willing. The determination is something else. Allah willing, the benefits will come to us.

* Student: Shaykh, which was created first, the earth or the heavens?

* Shaykh: It will come to us, Allah willing.

* Student: Was the creation of the earth with what is in it, the firm mountains and seas, in four days or in two days?

* Shaykh: In four days. He created it in two days like this, then He placed the firm mountains in it and determined the provisions in two other days.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be gracious to you, the saying of Allah, exalted: ﴿Those who do not give zakat, and they are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾ [Fussilat 7]. That is, there are people who are Muslims, some people are Muslims who pray and give zakat, but when you mention to them, for example, the punishment of the grave and the horrors of the Day of Resurrection, they say: Did you see the punishment of the grave? Did you see the horrors of the Day of Resurrection? Have you seen Paradise? What is the ruling on these people?

* Shaykh: If you say to them: This is what Allah and His Messenger said, what do they say?

* Student: I do not know.

* Shaykh: If they say: We only believe what we see, then these are disbelievers, even if they bow in prayer night and day and spend everything in their chests on charity, because they are deniers. This is disbelief in denial.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be gracious to you, in some recitations, the hamza with softening (tashīl), for example in Warsh, some people pronounce it with a hā', for example ﴿a-innakum﴾ they recite as (ahnakum), for example.

* Shaykh: Ahnakum?

* Student: Yes. Is this correct, Shaykh?

* Shaykh: I do not think it is like that.

* Student: I have heard some people say that this is distortion, but it is the apparent recitation, Shaykh.

* Shaykh: No, I do not think a hamza is changed into a hā'?

* Student: Yes, in some places.

* Shaykh: I do not know, by Allah.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: But you are not a proof, you are not a proof.

* Students: For teaching.

* Student: Some of them denied, Shaykh, those who recite Ḥafṣ denied Warsh, but...

* Shaykh: The main point, may Allah bless you: if the recitation with hā' is established, then this is considered substitution (ibdāl), not softening. Changing the hamza into a hā'.

* Student: Is it valid, Shaykh?

* Shaykh: I do not know, by Allah.

* Student: Warsh softens, Shaykh.

* Shaykh: No, softening is not the same as changing. He says: ahnakum, which is not ﴿a-innakum﴾.

* Student: Pronouncing it with softening, some people pronounce it as if it were a hā' (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps this is the reconciliation: some people go to excess in softening until it becomes a hā', and perhaps another goes until it becomes a ḥā'. In truth, some people, may Allah guide us and them, during recitation, and Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, denied this in his fatwas and changed them. He denied this excessive insistence in articulating some recitations. For example, some people in qalqala (the echoing of certain letters) come and echo as if they were echoing a pebble or a stone, meaning they press too much. Yes indeed. The truth is that excessive strictness is not good, and neglect is not good; the best matters are the middle course (...).

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed within it firm mountains above it, and blessed it, and determined within it its sustenance in four days, equally, for those who ask. Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come obedient. Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and revealed in each heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as protection. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [Fussilat 9–12].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come obedient﴾ [Fussilat 11]. His saying ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾: the author said: (in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning obedient or compelled) ﴿They said: We come﴾ with those within us ﴿obedient﴾. There is prevalence of the masculine rational gender here, and they were treated as addressed in that position.

First, we ask: is the saying of Allah, ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth﴾, an emphasized sentence?

* Student: Yes.

* Student: (a-innakum).

* Shaykh: No, without an alif.

* Shaykh: Good, insert an alif between them with realization.

* Student: ﴿aa-innakum﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿aa-innakum﴾, with softening.

* Student: ﴿a-a-innakum﴾.

* Shaykh: Good, may Allah bless you. His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿And He placed firm mountains﴾. This sentence is joined (ʿaṭf) to what?

* Student: ﴿with He who created the earth in two days﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿with He who created﴾ is joined to ﴿created﴾. Did the author, may Allah have mercy on him, follow this view or not?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, on the view that ﴿placed﴾ is joined to ﴿created﴾, he says: it is joined to this.

* Shaykh: That is, he did not join it to ﴿created﴾. Why?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Only? Why did we join it to ﴿created﴾ when he says it is resumptive (isti'nāf)? So why?

* Shaykh: Because of the presence of a foreign separator according to his claim. What is the answer to this reasoning?

* Student: Either it is said that the presence of a separator does not harm at all, or it is said that the separator is connected to the speech.

* Shaykh: Well said. It is connected to the relative clause, so it is not foreign.

His saying, exalted: ﴿equally, for those who ask﴾. First: its i'rab (grammatical analysis)?

* Student: ﴿equally﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

* Shaykh: A circumstantial accusative from whom?

* Shaykh: From the ﴿days﴾? How can it be a circumstantial accusative from ﴿days﴾ when it is a non-derived maṣdar, and a circumstantial accusative must be derived?

* Student: Shaykh, a circumstantial accusative from ﴿four days﴾.

* Shaykh: Good.

* Student: And the maṣdar is not interpreted as a derived word.

* Shaykh: And the estimate?

* Student: Equal.

* Shaykh: Equal ones (feminine plural), good.

* Student: An ism maṣdar.

**The Shaykh:** It is an ism masdar (verbal noun). Meaning: is it in the accusative as a maf'ul mutlaq (absolute object) by estimation (taqdir)?

**Student:** *Istawat sawa'* (It became equal).

**The Shaykh:** *Istawat sawa'.* The phrase ﴿لِلسَّائِلِينَ﴾ (for those who ask) is connected to what?

**The Shaykh:** ﴿جَعَلَ﴾?

**The Shaykh:** You mean *sawa'* for those who ask and for those who do not ask? Does it add or subtract?

**The Shaykh:** Yes, well done. The words of the Most High: ﴿اسْتَوَى إِلَى السَّمَاءِ﴾ (then He turned to the heaven)?

**Student:** (...) ﴿اسْتَوَى إِلَى السَّمَاءِ﴾ here means *qasada* (intended, turned toward).

**The Shaykh:** Well done. It means *qasada* (intended). So the meaning is: then He intended toward the heaven. And how do you parse ﴿وَهِيَ دُخَانٌ﴾ (while it was smoke)?

**Student:** The *waw* is for the circumstantial clause (hal).

**The Shaykh:** The whole sentence.

**Student:** The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

**The Shaykh:** It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal). From where?

**Student:** From ﴿السَّمَاءِ﴾ (the heaven).

**The Shaykh:** From ﴿السَّمَاءِ﴾, correct. The author says: (﴿طَائِعِينَ﴾ contains *taghlib* (prevalence) of the masculine rational, and He treated the two of them as those addressed in the way of their address). What is the meaning of this statement?

**Student:** ﴿طَائِعِينَ﴾ is a sound masculine plural, and the original use of it is for rational beings.

**The Shaykh:** For rational males.

**Student:** For rational males. Here it refers to the heaven and the earth, and they are not rational, but they were placed in the position of rational beings.

**The Shaykh:** What is the evidence that they were placed in that position?

**Student:** Because He reported about them: ﴿قَالَتَا أَتَيْنَا﴾ (they both said, "We have come"), and did not say...

**Another student:** Because He addressed them, so they were placed in the position of rational beings.

**The Shaykh:** Correct. For this reason the author says: (they were placed there because of their being addressed). This is the explanation. If he had said, "they were placed in its position because of their being addressed," it would have been clearer. And his words: (﴿قَالَتَا أَتَيْنَا﴾ with whoever is in them). Why did he estimate his words: (with whoever is in them)? What made him need to say: "with whoever is in them, we have come"?

**Student:** (...).

**Another student:** We did not take it.

**The Shaykh:** Amazing. Alright, let us begin from this point. *Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim, a'udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim.* The Most High said: ﴿فَقَالَ لَهَا وَلِلْأَرْضِ ائْتِيَا طَوْعًا أَوْ كَرْهًا قَالَتَا أَتَيْنَا طَائِعِينَ﴾ (Then He said to it and to the earth, "Come, willingly or by compulsion." They said, "We have come willingly."). The commentator (al-mufassir al-sharih) says: (﴿قَالَتَا أَتَيْنَا﴾ with whoever is in them, ﴿طَائِعِينَ﴾). The author needed to estimate (with whoever is in them) for two reasons. The first reason: ﴿طَائِعِينَ﴾ is plural, while ﴿قَالَتَا﴾ is dual, and there is no agreement between the dual and the plural. If He had intended agreement, He would have said: "qalata: ata'na ta'i'atayn." This is the first reason. The second reason: He used the plural with the masculine, so it was necessary to estimate (with whoever is in them), in order to include the rational beings, and this is from the category of *taghlib*. The words of the author, may Allah have mercy on him: (containing *taghlib* of the masculine rational). We mentioned previously that he gave prevalence to the masculine because of what?

**Students:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** He gave prevalence to the masculine.

**Student:** Because of its nobility.

**The Shaykh:** Because of its nobility.

**Student:** Or because of its greater number.

**The Shaykh:** Or because of its greater number, if we say that rational beings are more numerous. And the words of the author, may Allah have mercy on him: (or they were placed in its position because of their being addressed). That is, the matter contains either *taghlib*, or that the earth and the heaven were placed in the position of rational beings because they were addressed, since generally only a rational being is addressed.

﴿فَقَضَاهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ فِي يَوْمَيْنِ﴾ (Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days). [Fussilat 12] ﴿قَضَاهُنَّ﴾ The author says: (the pronoun refers to the heaven, because it has the meaning of the plural toward which it leads, i.e., He made it ﴿سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ﴾ (seven heavens)). ﴿قَضَاهُنَّ﴾ The author says: (the pronoun refers to the heaven). At this point a problem arises, because ﴿السَّمَاءِ﴾ is singular, while the pronoun in ﴿قَضَاهُنَّ﴾ is plural. How, then, is the matter this way?

He, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (it refers to the heaven, because it has the meaning of the plural toward which it leads). Because this singular ﴿السَّمَاءِ﴾ will eventually become plural. And what is its extent? ﴿سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ﴾ (seven heavens). So it is as if He expressed the heaven in terms of its future state, that it will become ﴿سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ﴾.

And His words ﴿قَضَاهُنَّ﴾ mean: He made them. In this case the pronoun in ﴿قَضَاهُنَّ﴾ is the first object, and ﴿سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ﴾ is the second object. It is also possible that ﴿قَضَاهُنَّ﴾ means: He finished with them. In this case the first pronoun is a direct object, and ﴿سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ﴾ is a circumstantial state, meaning: while they were ﴿سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ﴾. In either case, the heavens were seven.

﴿فِي يَوْمَيْنِ﴾ (in two days). The author said: (on Thursday and Friday; He finished them in the last hour of it, and in it Adam was created. For this reason He did not say here: "equal"). And what is mentioned here corresponds to the verses about the creation of the heavens and the earth in six days. ﴿قَضَاهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ فِي يَوْمَيْنِ﴾. The ﴿فِي﴾ indicates a container, and the container is wider than what it contains. So it is possible that He completed them in two days, from the beginning of the two days to their end. It is also possible that He completed them in two days, meaning within this period, even if the creation or the completion did not fill this whole period. This is what the author adopted, and what is in it will become clear, God willing.

He says: (He finished in the last hour of it, and in it, i.e., in the last hour, He created Adam; for this reason He did not say: "equal"). Whereas about the creation of the earth He said: ﴿فِي أَرْبَعَةِ أَيَّامٍ سَوَاءً﴾ (in four days, equal). Here He did not say "in two days, equal." Why?

Because Adam was created in part of those two days. This is what the author held. But it is clearly problematic, because it implies that Adam was created at the time of the creation of the heavens and the earth, that is, during the six days in which the heavens and the earth were created. This is without doubt an error. Rather, he was created after that, not by millions, but by hundreds of years, since Adam, as you know, was made by Allah the Most High a successor to whom? To people before him, or to the jinn who inhabited the earth before him. For this reason, when He said: ﴿إِنِّي جَاعِلٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ خَلِيفَةً﴾ (Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority), the angels said: ﴿أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَنْ يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسْفِكُ الدِّمَاءَ﴾ (Will You place upon it someone who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?) [Al-Baqarah 30], and so on to the end.

So the claim of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, that Adam was created in the last hour of Friday, the day on which the creation of the heavens and the earth was completed, is not correct. Yes, Adam was created on a Friday, without doubt, as established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.[[Reported by Muslim (854/17) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] But it was not the Friday on which the creation of the heavens and the earth was completed.

So then, He created them in two days. The author says: this corresponds (and what is here corresponds to the verses about the creation of the heavens and the earth in six days). How does it correspond? Because four days were for the creation of the earth, and two days were for the creation of the heaven, so the total is six days. This is an agreed matter among Muslims: that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days. In some verses He says: ﴿وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ (and what is between them) [Al-Furqan 59], because what lies between the heavens and the earth includes great signs deserving to be paired with the creation of the heavens and the earth.

﴿خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ (He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them) [Al-Furqan 59]. We used to say: how can the creation of what is between the heaven and the earth be paired with the creation of the heavens and the earth, when in our view it is worth nothing in comparison to the creation of the heavens and the earth, since we knew only that what lies between the heaven and the earth is clouds and air? We used to say that the moon, the stars, and the sun were in the heaven. We used to say: the moon is in the lowest heaven, the sun is in the fourth heaven, and Saturn is in the seventh heaven. And we used to recite the verse of the poet:

*Zuhal (Saturn) has bought his Mirrikh (Mars) from his Shams (Sun), so the Zuhra (Venus) flourished with 'Utarid (Mercury), and the moons...*

These are the seven planets.

**Student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** Did you not memorize it before? Come on.

**Student:**
*Zuhal shara Mirrikhahu min Shamsihi, fa-tazahharat bi-'Utarid al-aqmar.*

**The Shaykh:** The meaning, moving from the top to the bottom: (Zuhal), this is the highest. (Shara), that is Jupiter (al-Mushtari). (Mirrikhahu), Mars. (Min Shamsihi), the Sun. (Fa-tazaharat), Venus (al-Zuhra). (Bi-'Utarid), Mercury. (Al-aqmar), the Moon is the last. Accordingly, the sun is in the fourth heaven. We used to think that these were set in the sky like a nail set in wood. But it has now become clear that they are in atmospheres between the heaven and the earth, not set within the heavens and the earth, and that the heaven is far above them by a great distance. At that point the wisdom becomes clear in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, making the creation of what is between the heaven and the earth equal to the creation of the heaven and the earth.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: (﴿وَأَوْحَى فِي كُلِّ سَمَاءٍ أَمْرَهَا﴾ (And He revealed in each heaven its affair), namely what He commanded those in it of obedience and worship). ﴿أَوْحَى فِي كُلِّ سَمَاءٍ أَمْرَهَا﴾ means: He ordained by what He revealed in each heaven its affair. Each heaven has its own specific angels, specific acts of worship, and specific atmospheres. Each heaven differs from the other heaven, to the point that some of them, and this is from the Isra'iliyyat (Israelite narratives) which are neither confirmed nor refuted, say that the substance of the lowest heaven differs from the substance of the second, and the second from the third, each one of a material other than the material of the other heaven. And Allah knows best.

His words ﴿أَمْرَهَا﴾ (its affair) is a singular with a possessive, so it covers all matters, everything related to each heaven that Allah has revealed in it.

﴿وَزَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ (And We adorned the lowest heaven). Look at the characteristics of the lowest heaven. (﴿وَزَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِمَصَابِيحَ﴾ with lamps, i.e., stars, ﴿وَحِفْظًا﴾ (and protection). The accusative of ﴿وَحِفْظًا﴾ is governed by its omitted verb, meaning: We protected it from the jinn stealing the hearing by means of shooting stars).

﴿زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ The ﴿الدُّنْيَا﴾ means the nearest, and it is called the lowest because it is close to the earth, so it is the nearest of the heavens. He adorned it with lamps. What are these lamps? They are the stars, and they are called lamps because they are like lanterns hung from the ceiling.

If someone says: the apparent meaning of the verse is that these lamps are set into the heaven, we say: if that is its apparent meaning, the reality is otherwise. There is no obstacle to its being adorned with lamps even if they are not attached to it. Have you not seen that if you hang lamps from a high ceiling and you are beneath these lamps, these lamps are an adornment for the ceiling even though they are not attached to it, rather the side of it, i.e., the side of this ceiling, is adorned with these lamps? So from His words ﴿زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِمَصَابِيحَ﴾ it does not follow that they are set into the heaven. Rather we say: it is adorned with them, even if there is a distance between them and the heaven.

His words ﴿وَحِفْظًا﴾ mean: We protected it with protection. So the heaven is protected, as the Most High said: ﴿وَجَعَلْنَا السَّمَاءَ سَقْفًا مَحْفُوظًا﴾ (And We made the heaven a protected ceiling) [Al-Anbiya 32]. For this reason Jibril could not enter the heavens, although he descended from them, when Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was with him, until he asked permission for him. In the hadith of the Mi'raj: "When Jibril brought the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to the lowest heaven, he asked for it to be opened. It was said: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Jibril.' It was said: 'And who is with you?' He said: 'Muhammad.' It was said to him: 'Has he been sent to him?' or 'Was he given permission?' He said: 'Yes,' and it was opened for him." Why? Because the heaven is protected, and no one can enter it except by Allah's permission. Jibril said: "With me is Muhammad." It was said to him: "And has he been sent for?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Welcome to him, what a good arrival has come!" Then they opened for him, and he entered the lowest heaven,[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3207) and Muslim (164/264) from the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah.]] then the second and the third, and so on. This indicates what? It indicates the perfection of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, in guarding the heavens, and that they are firmly made. Upon them are angels, and none can pass beyond them.

﴿ذَلِكَ تَقْدِيرُ الْعَزِيزِ الْعَلِيمِ﴾ (That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing). [Fussilat 12] ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (That) refers to what preceded it from His words: ﴿أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَكْفُرُونَ بِالَّذِي خَلَقَ الْأَرْضَ﴾ (Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth...) and so on.

His words ﴿ذَلِكَ تَقْدِيرُ الْعَزِيزِ﴾ mean: He who decreed it is the Almighty, the Mighty and Majestic, the All-Knowing. ﴿الْعَزِيزِ﴾ here is appropriate, because the matter needs might and strength. As for might, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿الْعَزِيزِ﴾ in His dominion), meaning: the One who has complete might in His dominion. But so far he has not explained to us what might is.

The scholars said that might is divided into three types: might of rank (*izzat al-qadr*), might of dominance (*izzat al-qahr*), and might of inaccessibility (*izzat al-imtina'*). Three meanings. As for might of rank, its meaning is nobility, meaning that He has a great rank, of supreme greatness. Might of dominance means that He is dominant and cannot be overcome. The third, might of inaccessibility, means that no harm can reach Him, exalted be He, under any circumstances.

To notice this third meaning, we say that it is derived from the expression: *ard 'azaz*, 'azaz meaning firm and solid. We call it in colloquial speech "the land is 'aza" (firm), meaning solid, not soft like sand or a meadow, but firm.

﴿الْعَزِيزِ﴾ So how many meanings does it have? What are they?

**Student:** Dominance, rank, and might.

**The Shaykh:** What?

**Student:** Inaccessibility...

**The Shaykh:** Inaccessibility. What is the meaning of inaccessibility?

**Student:** Inaccessibility from evil; meaning...

**The Shaykh:** Yes, meaning that evil and deficiency cannot reach Him. And dominance means?

**Student:** Dominance is (...), and the dominant one is not (...).

**The Shaykh:** Well done. He is the Victorious who cannot be overcome. And the third, inaccessibility?

**Student:** Inaccessibility, he mentioned it, it was mentioned before.

**The Shaykh:** Inaccessibility, I am saying...

**Student:** He mentioned inaccessibility.

**The Shaykh:** Who mentioned it? What did he say?

**Student:** Deficiency cannot reach Him.

**The Shaykh:** Deficiency cannot reach Him. And might of rank?

**Student:** Might of rank means that Allah is capable of everything.

**The Shaykh:** No. If it were that, we would say "might of power" (*izzat al-qudrah*).

**Student:** Might of rank meaning: strength and dominance.

**The Shaykh:** No, that is might of dominance.

**Student:** (...) the three.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, may Allah reward you with good. The third, might of rank, means?

**Student:** Greatness and nobility, the nobility of things.

**The Shaykh:** Nobility, yes. Might of rank: meaning that He has great rank and great nobility. As for the All-Knowing, He is the possessor of knowledge, and the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, is vast. The Most High said: ﴿لِتَعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ أَحَاطَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عِلْمًا﴾ (So that you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge) [At-Talaq 12]. So His knowledge, exalted be He, is vast and comprehensive of everything. He knows what has occurred, so He does not forget it, and He knows what will occur, so He is not ignorant of it, and He knows how it was and how it will be when it happens, meaning: He does not merely know that this thing will happen, but He knows that it will happen, when it will happen, how it will happen, and where it will happen, from every aspect. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has detailed the fine points of knowledge in His words: ﴿وَعِنْدَهُ مَفَاتِحُ الْغَيْبِ لَا يَعْلَمُهَا إِلَّا هُوَ وَيَعْلَمُ مَا فِي الْبَرِّ وَالْبَحْرِ وَمَا تَسْقُطُ مِنْ وَرَقَةٍ إِلَّا يَعْلَمُهَا وَلَا حَبَّةٍ فِي ظُلُمَاتِ الْأَرْضِ﴾ (And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it, and there is not a grain within the darknesses of the earth), meaning: but He knows it, ﴿وَلَا رَطْبٍ وَلَا يَابِسٍ إِلَّا فِي كِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ (nor anything fresh or dry, but that it is in a clear register) [Al-An'am 59]. And since we know that He is All-Knowing, what does that require in terms of conduct for the servant? If you know that Allah is knowing of everything, what follows from this?

**Student:** We fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in our deeds.

**The Shaykh:** Well done. It follows from this that he fears Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, performs His obedience, and abandons His disobedience, because he knows that Allah, the Most High, knows him, even if it is hidden from people, for you will not be hidden from Allah. Rather, Allah knows from your self what you do not know. You know of yourself only what you can encompass, but Allah knows of your self what you cannot encompass. He knows your future, your outcome, and your state, while you do not know. This requires the believing servant to fear his Lord in secret and in public, so that even if you are in a dark room where no one is with you and you want to do what angers Allah, know that Allah, the Most High, sees you.

**Student:** We said that the words of Allah, the Most High: ﴿وَزَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِمَصَابِيحَ وَحِفْظًا﴾ indicate (...) of Allah, the Most High, of the heavens. What is the meaning of His words, the Most High: ﴿يَا مَعْشَرَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنْسِ إِنِ اسْتَطَعْتُمْ أَنْ تَنْفُذُوا مِنْ أَقْطَارِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ فَانْفُذُوا لَا تَنْفُذُونَ إِلَّا بِسُلْطَانٍ﴾ (O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass; you will not pass except with authority) [Ar-Rahman 33]. What is meant here by "authority" (sultan)?

**The Shaykh (Ibn 'Uthaymin):** ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass beyond them. You will not pass except with authority.﴾ This verse is in the form of a challenge.
