* A student: Shaykh, if we say that the jinn (...) by an action (...) of a kind other than the kind of mankind, and the requirement of wisdom is that..
* The Shaykh: That their legislations be suited to them.
* The student: And it is known that acts of worship are tawqifi (determined by revelation only), so how will they worship Allah, the Exalted, then?
* The Shaykh: No, they worship by a Shari'ah from Allah; the Messenger (peace be upon him) would have taught them, because he met them and taught them what binds them.
* A student: Is it established that Ibn al-Qayyim held that the Fire will come to an end?
* The Shaykh: Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, his discussion in Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah and in Shifa' al-'Alil gives the scent that he leans toward that, because he mentioned both opinions and mentioned the evidences. When he speaks, he may heal and elaborate at length. So his discussion in these two books gives the scent that he inclines to it. But he has another discussion in al-Wabil al-Sayyib indicating that he holds that the Fire is of two kinds: the Fire of the disbelievers, which does not perish, because they abide in it forever; and the Fire of the sinners who are punished according to their sins and then leave it, which perishes, because its people have left it. When they have left it, there is no benefit in its remaining. This division, from the rational standpoint, is a strong division; a person inclines to it from the rational standpoint.

But the question may remain: what is the evidence that there are two fires? That requires evidence. What appears from the evidences is that the Fire is one, and that the sinners are punished with the same Fire with which the disbelievers are punished. But rationally, his detailed discussion, may Allah have mercy on him, is a good discussion. Even if someone says: rationally, reason also indicates that the Fire must be two fires, because it is not possible for a believing sinner to be punished with a fire of intense heat, so that whenever his skin is cooked it is replaced with another skin, as is the case with the fire of the disbelievers — rationally, this agrees completely with reason. If it is correct, it is from Allah; and if it is wrong, Allah pardons it.

* A student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh. What is attributed to Shaykh al-Islam (...) the treatises that came out?
* The Shaykh: By Allah, I have not come across any statement of his on that.
* The student: So they are treatises that came out recently (...) regarding this view?
* The Shaykh: As for me, I have not seen anything about that. But, O brothers, it is absolutely not permissible to know the truth by men; we must know the truth by the evidence. As long as the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are before us, how can we think of preferring one or saying: so-and-so said? If the greatest of people said it, apart from the Messenger (peace be upon him), we would say: no hearing and no obedience, and no acceptance and no belief. The words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are before us, and He is the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, the Knower of everything.

* Student: May Allah reward you well, Shaykh. Are jinn sent messengers from among their own kind?

* Shaykh: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We did not send before you any but men to whom We revealed﴾ [Yusuf 109], ﴿any but men to whom We revealed﴾. The scholars said that the messengers are not from the jinn. However, this reasoning is open to examination, because Allah says in Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn 6]. They said that the other verse, ﴿any but men to whom We revealed from among the people of the towns﴾ [Yusuf 109], ﴿from among the people of the towns﴾, is decisive. It is said in reply: the jinn are also among the people of the towns. Your town is where you are, and the jinn are in it too.

But which of you has a better claim to the earth, mankind or the jinn?

* Student: Mankind.
* Another student: The jinn.
* Shaykh: How could the jinn have a better claim than you do to your house?
* Student: Because, Shaykh, the jinn can live in places where mankind does not live. They are able to do so, and in open spaces.
* Shaykh: And mankind?
* Student: No, mankind cannot.
* Shaykh: Cannot what?
* Student: No, I mean in open spaces. As for...
* Shaykh: Do you not know that now there are artificial satellites up there with people in them for four months, five months?
* Student: Generally speaking...
* Shaykh: In any case, mankind has the better claim without doubt. For this reason, if one of the jinn transgresses and descends upon your house, you have the right to expel him.
* Student: What is the evidence, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: The evidence is this: the Messenger, peace be upon him, made the earth belong to its owner: "Whoever unjustly takes a span of land, Allah will put it around his neck as a collar on the Day of Resurrection, from seven earths" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2452) and Muslim (1610/137), from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd].
* Student: Is this the proof that they have a better claim than the jinn?
* Shaykh: That is it. I can plough the land, plant, build, and do whatever I wish, with no one opposing me. But if they came and transgressed against your house, dug in it, and you woke up to find the roof full of crops and the sitting rooms full of palm trees...
* Student: What if they said: "We have a better claim to the house," the jinn?
* Shaykh: In any case, may Allah reward you with good, you yield to them!
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Is it not permissible that His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Indeed they were losers﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection, in the manner of His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [an-Nahl 1]?
* Shaykh: No. ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ would be taken literally were it not for His saying ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾.

* * *

* Student: (...) ﴿For this Qur'an, and make noise during its recitation, that perhaps you may overcome﴾ [26]. ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieve taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do﴾ [27]. ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the home of eternity, as recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾ [28]. ﴿And those who disbelieved will say: "Our Lord, show us those who misled us of the jinn and mankind; we will put them under our feet so that they will be among the lowest"﴾ [Fussilat 26–29].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted be He, says: ﴿And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them, and the word has come into effect against them, among nations that had passed away before them of the jinn and mankind. Indeed, they were losers﴾.
His saying ﴿qayyadna lahum﴾ [We appointed for them]: what does it mean?
* Student: The commentator said it means "We caused for them." The correct meaning is "We prepared for them."
* Shaykh: Yes. And "al-qurana'" [companions] is the plural of what?
* Student: The plural of "qarin" [companion]. Does it include both mankind and the jinn here?
* Shaykh: Yes. ﴿What is before them﴾?
* Student: ﴿What is before them﴾ is the worldly life.
* Shaykh: ﴿And what is behind them﴾?
* Student: The Hereafter.
* Shaykh: Is the Hereafter behind them or in front of them?
* Student: In front of them. But here "khalf" also comes with the meaning of "amam" [in front], as in His saying: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized every ship by force﴾ [al-Kahf 79].
* Shaykh: So "khalf" and "wara'" may come with the meaning of "front," as in the verse you mentioned.

What is the meaning of making things attractive to them in the worldly life?

* Student: Making things attractive to them in the worldly life takes two forms: either they deny resurrection, or they hold out false hopes to them.
* Shaykh: No. They made attractive to them what was before them in the worldly life.
* Student: Yes, making it attractive in the worldly life is whispering to them about desires.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And making them enjoy desires.
* Shaykh: And raising false hopes, that Allah will forgive them, and similar things.
Now, ﴿and what was behind them﴾: how is the making attractive?
* Student: ﴿And what was behind them﴾ is making attractive in two forms: the first by denying resurrection, and the second by raising hopes that they will have the best reward in the Hereafter.
* Shaykh: Correct. Denying resurrection, by saying: "Do not fear, there is no resurrection."
* Student: This applies to the atheists.
* Shaykh: Or they say: "If you are resurrected, you will have the best reward with Allah." May Allah bless you.

His saying ﴿fi umam﴾ [among nations]: what is its estimated sense? ﴿And the word has come into effect against them, among nations﴾?
* Student: "Among the totality of nations."
* Shaykh: Why did we not say that "fi" indicates location and "umam" is the location?
* Student: Because if we said it indicates location, that would imply the nation is not included in the punishment and torment. If we say "among the totality of nations..."
* Shaykh: Anything other than this?
* Student: If we say "among nations," the meaning is that they share with all the nations, meaning they are a nation...
* Shaykh: And they are a distinct nation. So the meaning is: "among the totality of nations."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat 25], to the end of the verse.

* From the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of the greatness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His saying ﴿qayyadna﴾ [We appointed], because "na" [We] indicates majesty.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the Mu'tazilah [a rationalist sect], who say that a person is independent in his actions and that Allah, exalted be He, has no connection with them. People on this matter are of three categories.
The first category: those who say that a person is compelled in his actions, has no will and no choice, and that his voluntary acts are like his involuntary ones. The one who goes and comes by his own choice is like the one who trembles or walks insanely on the earth. This is the doctrine of whom? The doctrine of the Jabriyyah [determinists]. Their leader is Jahm ibn Safwan, who was a student of al-Ja'd ibn Dirham.
The second extreme: those who say that the servant is independent in his actions and that Allah has no connection with them, so a person is willful and free, and no one has authority over him. This is the doctrine of whom? The Qadariyyah, who are the Mu'tazilah. The Qadariyyah are called the Magians of this Ummah, because they claimed that events have two creators: events that are from Allah's act are from His act, and events that are from the servant's act are from his act, independently. These are the Mu'tazilah and those who resemble them. Their leaders are 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Wasil ibn 'Ata'.
The third view: those who say that the servant has will and choice, but his will and choice follow the will and decree of Allah, exalted be He. These are the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah). They say: the servant is the one who stands, fasts, bows, prostrates, goes and comes; it is the servant, not Allah, who does these. They say these actions are attributed to him, and how often the Qur'an says: ﴿as a recompense for what they used to do﴾ [as-Sajdah 17], "as a recompense for what they used to do." Yet these actions do not occur outside the power and will of Allah, exalted be He; rather they are under Allah's power and will.
The benefit of this: when an act occurs from us, we know that Allah has willed and decreed it, and that we are not independent of Him in it.
Now, this verse ﴿And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them﴾ refutes both groups. ﴿We appointed﴾ refutes the Qadariyyah. ﴿They made attractive﴾ attributes the act to them, and refutes the Jabriyyah.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: caution against the whisperings that Satan casts to the one who commits sin and makes it attractive to him, saying: "This is easy, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, do this and then repent," and similar things. Beware of this, for this is the promise of Satan: ﴿And Satan promises them only delusion﴾ [an-Nisa' 120].
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that those who followed the companions have lost, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, they were losers﴾.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that those who approved of what the companions made attractive to them, the word has come into effect against them. It was previously mentioned that the word according to the author's view is ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [al-A'raf 18], and according to what we have mentioned it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe﴾ [Yunus 96]. It is not far-fetched that both are intended.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the large number of those who were led astray by these companions, by His saying: ﴿And the word has come into effect against them among nations﴾.

And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who disbelieved say﴾ [Fussilat 26] (at the time of the Prophet's ﷺ recitation); meaning: of the Qur'an. He said: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾; meaning: some of them advise others, saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾; that is: do not pay attention to it, do not listen to it, and keep away from it. This is because the Qur'an affects the heart of the one who hears it, to the extent that some of the polytheists among their leaders would come to the Prophet ﷺ and listen to his recitation in secret at night, lest they be seen, because they hear words that captivate the minds and seize the souls. So they advise one another, saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾.

The Qur'an is the speech of Allah. It is on the pattern of (fu'lān), and (fu'lān) is a verbal noun like al-ghufrān (forgiveness) and al-shukrān (gratitude). Is it derived from (qara'a) or from (qara) or from both? We say: it is suitable for all of them. If it is from (qara'a), then it is from recitation (qira'ah), which is recitation (tilawah). If it is from (qara), then it is from qara yaqri, meaning to gather, and from it comes al-qaryah (the town), because it gathers peoples. So the Qur'an is gathering (jami').

Then is it an active or passive participle? We say: if it is from (qara'a), it is passive, because it is a recited Qur'an (maqru'), so it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle. If it is from (qara), it has both active and passive senses; that is, it is shared between active and passive: it is gathering (jami') and gathered (majmu'), because it is written down and its letters are gathered one to another. What is meant by it is what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an and make noise during it﴾. What is meant by the demonstrative here, ﴿this Qur'an﴾? And why did they not say: "Do not listen to the Qur'an"? It is meant to belittle; meaning, this does not deserve anything, so do not listen to it. Something similar in some respects is their saying: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 36], i.e., "Is this the one who mentions your gods?!" – belittling; meaning: who is this one who reviles them?! ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan 41]. This is for belittling, but it is derived from the interrogative. Here, however, it is derived from the demonstrative which indicates belittling.

(﴿And make noise during it﴾: bring about commotion and the like, and shout at the time of its recitation.) ﴿And make noise during it﴾; meaning: when you hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reciting, raise your voices and shout, in order to confuse his recitation and come between him and hearing it. That is, they do this for two reasons: First: to confuse the Prophet ﷺ in his recitation; and second: that no one should hear his recitation because of the din and clamour.

﴿And make noise during it, that perhaps you may prevail﴾. This (la'alla) is for causation. As you know, (la'alla) comes for causation, comes for apprehension, comes for hope, and comes for wishing. All these meanings differ according to context, because context is what determines the meanings of words.

(﴿That perhaps you may prevail﴾, so that he falls silent from the recitation.) Because when he hears the voices, the uproar and the clamour, and his recitation becomes confused, he sees no benefit in reciting, and at that point he falls silent. This is what these polytheists do.

* In this noble verse there are benefits; among them: the fear and alarm of the polytheists at the effect of the Prophet's ﷺ recitation. The evidence for this is that some of them advise others not to listen to this Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strength of the Qur'an's effect on its hearer, and this is the reality, as Allah says: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ [Qaf 37]. However, the Qur'an only affects those who understand the Arabic language and the meanings of its words. As for the non-Arab, in reality or in legal status, he is not affected by it. Secondly: the Qur'an affects, with its full effect, only the one who believes in it. As for the denier who is arrogant, it does not, to the extent that he says: ﴿This is nothing but the tales of the former peoples﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permissible to make noise and clamour while the Qur'an is being recited. Either you listen to it, or you stand up. As for sitting with a Qur'an reciter while raising voices, noise and clamour, the least that can be said of it is that it resembles the conduct of whom? Of the polytheists. That is the least of it. Even if we assume that those people with the noise and clamour do not intend to disturb the reciter, and do not intend that no one should hear his recitation, we say: at the very least, it resembles the actions of the polytheists.

From this follows what some people do in their shops and homes: they play the Qur'an on the recorder and let it recite, and you find them in noise, with foul speech, with lying. This is an insult to the Qur'an. So we say: either you listen to the words of Allah, or you turn it off. As for letting it keep reciting while this one swears, this one curses, this one lies, and this one cheats, this is the utmost humiliation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Even if the person does not intend it, his situation has the appearance of humiliation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that disrupting the one calling to the truth may lead its doer to think that he will prevail and reach his aim, but the matter is not so. The indication of this is that these polytheists did not obtain their desired victory.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.﴾ [Fussilat 27]

﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste﴾: this sentence is emphasized by three emphatics: the implied oath (al-qasam al-muqaddar), which we know from the emphasis of the verb and the lam as well; the second is the lam; and the third is the nun.

﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment﴾; that is, We will surely punish them with a punishment whose pain they will taste. It is a metaphor for the severity of this punishment, which reaches their palate, as though it were a tangible thing they taste with their mouths. ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾: by "those who disbelieved" is meant those mentioned before, who said: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾ [Fussilat 26].

At this point someone may say: why did He not use a pronoun and say: "So We will make them taste"?

We say: here there is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, and an explicit noun in place of a pronoun has benefits:

The first benefit is alerting the listener. How so? Because it is the custom that when the context calls for a pronoun, a pronoun is used. So when an explicit noun comes, it departs from the custom, and the person pauses: why did an explicit noun come in place of a pronoun? Thus there is attention drawn to it. This is one benefit.

The second benefit: passing judgment on the referent of this pronoun by the attribute carried in this explicit noun. In the verse before us, ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, the benefit is therefore to pass judgment on them as disbelievers. And so whenever an explicit noun comes in place of a pronoun, judge by this benefit.

The third benefit: generality. If He had said "So We will make them taste", this threat would have been specific to those who said: "Do not listen to this Qur'an". But when He says ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste﴾, it becomes general to them and to others. Who will repeat these for us?

* A student: First, alerting the listener; second, generality; and third..

* The Shaykh: Passing judgment on the referent of the pronoun by what it entails. This explicit noun, pay attention: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment﴾. Here ﴿a severe punishment﴾ is in the accusative. What put it in the accusative?

* A student: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved﴾, the verb ﴿will make taste﴾.

* The Shaykh: The one that put it in the accusative is ﴿will make taste﴾. Does (nudhīq, "make taste") take one object or two objects?

* The student: It takes one object.

* The Shaykh: One object?

* The student: Two objects.

* The Shaykh: Two objects? How two objects? What is the evidence that it takes two objects? Because we have a rule: if a verb is transitive to one, and the hamza of transitivity is added to it, it becomes transitive to two; and if it is transitive to two and the hamza is added, it becomes transitive to three.

For example: (dhāqa, "to taste"): dhāqa is transitive to how many? One: "Whoever is content with Allah as Lord has tasted the sweetness of faith" [[Narrated by Muslim (34/56) from a hadith of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib.]]. When the hamza is added to it, it becomes transitive to two objects.

And (ra'ā, "to see"): you say: I saw the man standing; it takes two objects. When the hamza is added, it becomes transitive to three: you say: I showed Zayd the man standing.

This is a consistent Arabic rule: if a verb is intransitive and the hamza is added, it becomes transitive to one; if it is transitive to one and the hamza is added, it becomes transitive to two; if it is transitive to two and the hamza is added, it becomes transitive to three.

Good. ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment﴾: ﴿a punishment﴾ means a retribution; ﴿severe﴾ means powerful. ﴿And We will surely recompense them﴾ is conjoined to ﴿We will make taste﴾. ﴿With the worst of what they used to do﴾: ﴿will recompense them﴾ takes two objects; the first is the pronoun (hā'), the second is ﴿the worst﴾.

(﴿The worst of what they used to do﴾ means: the most evil recompense for their deeds.) Look: ﴿the worst of what they used to do﴾, are they recompensed with the worst of what they did, or are they recompensed with their recompense? Yes, they are recompensed with the recompense; the deed is theirs, they are not recompensed with it. They are the ones who did it. So when He says ﴿the worst of what they used to do﴾, the meaning is the worst recompense, not the worst deed, because the deed is the servant's act and the recompense is Allah's act toward him. Here, is the meaning the servant's act or Allah's act toward him? Allah's act toward him, and therefore He said: ﴿We will recompense them﴾.

If someone asks: why did He express their recompense by the word "deed"?

We say: as an indication that the recompense is according to the deed. For this reason the scholars said: the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, but with regard to evil deeds it is justice, and with regard to good deeds it is bounty: a good deed is rewarded tenfold up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples, while an evil deed is repaid with its like.

As for His saying ﴿the worst of what they used to do﴾, the apparent meaning of the verse is that Allah recompenses them with their worst deeds. And what of the non-worst? The non-worst is what is below the worst, meaning the bad. So is the disbeliever recompensed for his worst deeds or for all his deeds? This depends on whether the disbeliever is addressed by the furu' (the secondary rulings of the Shari'ah) or not. Do you know the meaning of this question? For example: is the disbeliever addressed concerning maintaining family ties? Is he addressed concerning truthfulness? Is he addressed concerning prayer? Concerning zakat? And so on.

There is disagreement among the scholars on this, and the correct view is that he is addressed concerning the furu' of the deeds, because if the Muslim is addressed by them, the disbeliever is so all the more. How can we say that the Muslim is recompensed and punished for disobeying his parents, while the disbeliever is not punished? That is impossible. So the correct view is that they are addressed by the furu' of the Shari'ah, but they are not required to perform them. That is, one does not say to a disbelieving man who drinks cigarettes: "Come, do not smoke, it is forbidden for you." Is this appropriate or not? It is not appropriate. A disbelieving man: call him first to Islam, then speak to him.

So "being addressed by the furu' of the Shari'ah" does not mean that he is commanded to perform them, no. Does "being addressed by the furu' of the Shari'ah" mean he must make them up when he becomes Muslim? No, because Allah said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal 38].

So what is the benefit? The scholars said: the benefit of our saying "the disbeliever is addressed by the furu' of the Shari'ah" is the increase of their punishment in the Hereafter, that they will be punished for them. This is true: the People of the Right ask the criminals: ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir 42], that is: what caused you to enter the Fire? ﴿They said: We were not of those who prayed, and we did not feed the needy, and we used to plunge with the plungers, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until certainty came to us﴾ [al-Muddaththir 43-47]. They mentioned prayer and feeding the needy, and both are among the furu' of the Shari'ah. So according to the view that they are not recompensed for the furu' of the Shari'ah, we say: yes, on the Day of Resurrection they are recompensed only for their worst deed, which is disbelief. But according to the preponderant view, that they are addressed by the furu' and punished for them, here ﴿the worst﴾ is mentioned because it is the most severe, and the purpose here is a threat. Is a person threatened with the lighter or the heavier? With the heavier; this is the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best. (﴿What they used to do﴾ means: the worst recompense for their deeds.)

* In this noble verse: a threat to these disbelievers of severe punishment, and this is one of the methods of the Qur'an: that Allah threatens the disbeliever, the criminal, and others who have done evil.

* And in it is evidence that it is not a defect for a person to obey Allah out of fear of Allah's punishment; there is no fault in it, and it is not a defect for a person to avoid disobedience to Allah out of fear of His punishment, contrary to the one who said: worship Allah for Allah's sake alone, neither out of hope for His reward nor out of fear of His punishment.

All the texts refute these people. Indeed Allah the Exalted made the worldly punishment a cause of deterrence from sins. Allah the Exalted said concerning the thief: ﴿Cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, as a deterrent from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 38]. Allah did not legislate the hudud except so that people would fear them and avoid sins. And the town that was destroyed, the town of the Children of Israel, until its people became apes, despised: why? ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what was before it and what was after it﴾ [al-Baqarah 66]. The sum is that there is no fault in a person who abandons sins out of fear of Allah's punishment, worldly or otherwise, and that is not counted as a defect in his conduct and method.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of punishment. Does it occur in this world, in the grave, in the Hereafter, or in all of them? In all of them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will surely make them taste some of the nearer punishment, besides the greater punishment, that perhaps they may return﴾ [as-Sajdah 21]. The nearer punishment is the punishment of this world, and the greater punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter. And it is necessary that the nearer punishment be understood as not the punishment of the grave, as some have said, but the punishment of this world, because the punishment of the grave does not allow for "return" (ruju'). So the nearer punishment is the punishment of this world, and the greater punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter. This is why it came in the hadith of the two who engaged in mutual cursing (al-mutalla'anayn) that the Messenger said: "The punishment of this world is lighter than the punishment of the Hereafter" [[Narrated by Muslim (1493/4) from a hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.]].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of recompense with the worst; because of His saying: ﴿the worst of what they used to do﴾.

* And among its benefits: that recompense is of the same kind as the deed; so good recompense is for good deeds, and evil recompense for evil deeds. And this, glory be to Allah! is even in the recompense of this world. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil like it; but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 40]. So if a person wrongs you with an evil deed, you have the right to repay him with its like; but if you pardon and reconcile, your reward is with Allah.

* A student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. As you have said, many people make the Qur'an a background noise in homes and shops, but when the Qur'an is in a home whose people are not accustomed to idle talk, insults, and cursing, yet they may talk about side matters, such as being in the kitchen, or the like; then the Qur'an on the Qur'an radio sometimes gives a talk and sometimes Qur'an, and they intend by this, that is, they love the Qur'an, take comfort in it, and benefit greatly from it. They say: if we do not put on the Qur'an, anxieties come, and come upon a person..?

* The Shaykh: In any case, this does not need a long explanation. Do they engage in idle talk over it or not?

* The student: But sometimes they do not pay attention.

* The Shaykh: This happens even to the person who reads with the mushaf in front of him; sometimes he does not pay attention, sometimes he reads with his mouth while his heart is not reading.

* The student: The prohibited thing is only idle talk?

* The Shaykh: The prohibited thing is idle talk, yes. What is prohibited is, for example, that people are busy and occupied with their worldly affairs while the Qur'an is being recited. But, for example, a woman who is cooking, or tidying tea, or washing her clothes, and listens to the Qur'an, this does not require being distracted from it.

* A student: Shaykh, can we not derive from His saying ﴿And We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do﴾ that He recompenses them with the worst of this deed of theirs, namely idle talk, by not being guided to its meanings that would guide them to good? So their recompense would be of the same kind as their deed as well?

* The Shaykh: No, because this ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment﴾ is in the Hereafter; the threat here is in the Hereafter.

* A student: May Allah be good to you. Some scholars cited His saying ﴿And We will surely make them taste some of the nearer punishment﴾ [as-Sajdah 21] as evidence for the punishment of the grave. What is the basis of their argument from this verse?

* The Shaykh: Their view that the punishment here is the punishment of the Hereafter, and they said: the punishment of the grave precedes the punishment of the Day of Resurrection.

* The student: ﴿That perhaps they may return﴾, how do they interpret it?

* The Shaykh: They may interpret it; that is, they distort it from its apparent meaning, saying: ﴿that perhaps they may return﴾ means: We informed them of that so that they might return. But this contradicts the apparent sense of the wording.

* A student: If we say this is about the punishment of this world, how do we establish the punishment of the grave from the Qur'an?

* The Shaykh: There is much in the Qur'an. Have you not come across it? There is not only this verse that is problematic for you?

* The student: Only the family of Pharaoh.

* The Shaykh: What about the family of Pharaoh?

* The student: ﴿They are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir 46].

* The Shaykh: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour is established: admit the family of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir 46]. And ﴿If you could see when the angels take the lives of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal 50]. And ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are extending their hands: "Bring out your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, for what you used to say against Allah other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs"﴾ [al-An'am 93].

* A student: Some people cite this verse as evidence for..

* The Shaykh: Which verse?

* The student: ﴿And We will surely make them taste some of the nearer punishment﴾. Some cite it as evidence for the punishment of the grave, saying: the nearer punishment is the punishment of this world, but ﴿min﴾ in the verse is partitive, so some of this punishment remains for them, with which they will be punished in the grave.

* The Shaykh: No, this ﴿min﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah); this is the closer view. It is permissible that it be partitive: "and We will make them taste part of the nearer punishment." But there is no need for that; the affirmation of the punishment of the grave, praise be to Allah, has come in explicit verses, and one need not cite a verse that admits of this and that, when others are more preponderant (...). In this world it has no fruit at all.

* A student: Shaykh, what about someone who plays the Qur'an on a recorder and repeats along with it?

* The Shaykh: You mean for memorization?

* The student: For memorization and to improve pronunciation.

* The Shaykh: There is no harm in it; there is no objection.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding the correct ruling for one who speaks during the recitation of the Qur'an outside al-Fatihah, is listening obligatory or not?

* The Shaykh: In prayer, you mean?

* The student: I mean outside prayer.

* The Shaykh: No, the correct view is that listening is not obligatory, but idle noise is not permitted. For this reason Imam Ahmad said concerning His saying ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy﴾ [al-A'raf 204]: he said: they agreed that this refers to prayer. As for outside prayer, it is not obligatory to listen; for if we said listening is obligatory, we would have to say: if a reciter begins to recite while you are beside him, it is forbidden for you to stand up, because listening is obligatory. And I do not think any scholar says this. What is prohibited is idle talk and noise.

Student: (...) ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. Therein you shall have whatever your souls desire, and therein you shall have whatever you ask for, as a welcome from the Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"?﴾ [Fussilat 31–33].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein will be the abode of eternity, as a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs.﴾ [Fussilat 28].

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, the mufassir, says: (﴿That﴾ refers to the severe punishment, and the worst recompense, ﴿the recompense of the enemies of Allah﴾, with the second hamza made certain and also replaced by a waw (wa'd-a'da'). ) This means that there are two readings in this: the first is to keep the hamza: ﴿jaza'u a'da'i Allah﴾, and the second is to change it into a waw: ﴿jaza'u wa'di Allah﴾ (the word for enemies is read as "wa'di"). This applies consistently to every hamza that follows a waw: it may be kept as a hamza or changed into a waw.

From this is the saying of the muezzin: "Allahu wakbar" (meaning: it is permissible to replace the hamza with a waw, and also to keep it: "Allahu akbar"). This dialect makes easier for us what some muezzins do by changing the hamza into a waw, so you find them saying "Allahu wakbar." Likewise, this dialect also makes easier for us the dialect that puts both parts of the predicate in the accusative after "inna" and its sisters, since some muezzins say: "Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah" (with the second noun in the nominative). The accusative for both parts after "anna" is a established Arabic dialect.

﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah.﴾ Who are the enemies of Allah? The enemies of Allah, exalted is He, are those who take enmity against Him by fighting Him through acts of disobedience. Among them are those who have declared war from Allah and His Messenger: the consumers of usury (riba), according to the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest, if you should be believers. And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah 278, 279]. The point is that the enemy of Allah is one who takes enmity against Him by fighting His disobedience.

And his saying: (﴿The Fire﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to the recompense mentioned about it, ﴿therein for them is the abode of eternity﴾), meaning: the word "the Fire" is an explicative apposition to "the recompense" mentioned about that. This indicates that "dhalika" (that) is the subject (mubtada'), "jaza'u" (recompense) is the predicate, and "al-nar" (the Fire) is an explicative apposition to it: ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah﴾. It seems that the author's grammatical analysis ends here: ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah.﴾

Then he said: ﴿The Fire﴾ is an explicative apposition to this recompense. It is possible that in ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah, the Fire﴾, "dhalika" is the subject, and "jaza'u a'da'i Allah" is an explicative apposition to it. But what the author followed is closer to the rules of grammar.

(﴿The Fire, for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ [Fussilat 28], i.e., a dwelling from which there is no moving away.) ﴿The abode of eternity﴾: he attributed the "abode" to "eternity" by way of the attribution of a qualified noun to its quality, meaning: the abode of eternal life in which there is no moving away. It may also be the attribution of a thing to its type, because abodes are divided into kinds: abodes of transition, and abodes of eternity. The abodes of transition are: the mother's womb, the second is this worldly life, and the third is the barzakh (intermediate state). The abode of eternity is the last one.

It is related that a Bedouin heard a reciter reading ﴿The mutual rivalry in increase diverts you, until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur 1, 2], and said: "By Allah, the visitor does not remain, and indeed there is another abode." Without doubt, this is from the strength of inference and understanding.

(﴿A recompense﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of its implied verb.) It is in the accusative as an absolute object, and an absolute object must have a governing verb. The governing verb sometimes comes from the same root as the verbal noun, and sometimes from its meaning. When you say: "qumtu wuqufan" (I stood standing), the governing verb is from its meaning; when you say: "waqaftu wuqufan" (I stood standing), the governing verb is from its root.

The implied verb is supposed from its root, not from its meaning, because we only resort to supposing the meaning when there is in front of us something that differs in its wording. If we do not find that, it is supposed from its root.

Accordingly, the supposition is: "yujzawna jaza'an" (they will be recompensed with a recompense), ﴿for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾, i.e., because of their denying. On this basis, "ma" here is a verbal (masdariyya) particle and cannot be a relative pronoun. He said: (﴿for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾ — the Qur'an — ﴿they denied﴾), i.e., they used to deny. We supposed "yukadhdhibun" (they deny) only because "jahada" is transitive by itself, so one says "jahadtu al-shay'" (I denied the thing), meaning I rejected it; but when the object is introduced with "bi" (with), the denial is taken to include the sense of rejection, i.e., "bima kanu yukadhdhibuna bi-ayatina" (for what they used to reject Our signs).

* There are benefits in this noble verse. Among them: the recompense of the enemies of Allah is the Fire without fail, and for this He said: ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah, the Fire﴾, clarifying that this recompense is the Fire.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the explanation of the eternity of the people of the Fire therein, from His saying: ﴿the abode of eternity﴾.

Is the eternity everlasting or temporary? What is definitively established is that it is everlasting, since Allah, exalted is He, has stated it in three passages: in al-Nisa', in al-Ahzab, and in al-Jinn. In al-Nisa', Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong, Allah will not forgive them nor guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ [al-Nisa' 168, 169]. In Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing fire, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Ahzab 64, 65]. In Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 23].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's justice, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He punishes no one except for a sin, from His saying: ﴿a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of causes, which is derived from His saying: ﴿for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾, since the "bi" here indicates causation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that denying the signs of Allah is apostasy, because Allah described the deniers as enemies and their recompense as the abode of eternity. This is an agreed matter: whoever denies Allah and His Messenger is an apostate disbeliever who is asked to repent; if he repents and affirms, well and good; otherwise he is put to death.

If someone says: It is well known that whoever denies something of the Qur'an is an apostate, since the Qur'an is established by mass transmission (tawatur). Is it the same for whoever denies something of the Sunnah?

We say: If the Sunnah is authentic and the speaker says, "I know that this is a saying of the Messenger, but it is not authentic," then this person is an apostate, because he acknowledged that it is correctly attributed to the Messenger and then denied it. But if he denies it on the basis of finding it unlikely that it came from the Messenger ﷺ, then he does not become a disbeliever, because he is interpreting; yet it is obligatory for him to examine it again and again until the matter becomes clear to him.

Therefore, whoever denies something of the Qur'an is a disbeliever without detail, because the Qur'an is established by a transmission of a kind that no other book has. And whoever denies something of the Sunnah of the Messenger ﷺ?

* Student: (...) If its attribution to the Prophet ﷺ is authentic and he then denies it, he is a disbeliever; but if he denies it through interpretation and rejects that the Prophet ﷺ said it, then no.

* The Shaykh: We say: if he says, "This is truly the saying of the Messenger, but it is not authentic," then he is a disbeliever, because he denied what he had acknowledged as the saying of the Messenger of Allah. But if he says, "No, I deny it," because it was not established to him, then he does not become a disbeliever, even if it was established to others.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are clear and manifest, so no one can deny them; from His saying: ﴿Our signs﴾. The author's restriction of this to the Qur'an, may Allah have mercy on him, contains some room for consideration; rather, it is said that it is more general.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's greatness, since He used the plural pronoun and did not say "My signs" but said "Our signs." There is no doubt that Allah, exalted is He, possesses absolute greatness in every respect.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 29:**

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who disbelieved will say, "Our Lord, show us those who misled us from among the jinn and mankind"﴾ [Fussilat 29]. ﴿And those who disbelieved will say, "Our Lord, show us"﴾. Disbelieved in whom? They disbelieved in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of the misguidance of the devil, from among the jinn and mankind.

﴿And those who disbelieved will say﴾, that is, the author says: "(in the Fire)". ﴿Our Lord, show us those who misled us﴾. The author's words "(in the Fire)" are a restriction that the Qur'an does not indicate, for it is possible that they say this in the Fire or on the plains of Resurrection; Allah knows best. But they will certainly say this statement.

He said: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who misled us from among the jinn and mankind﴾. ﴿Show us﴾ means: make us see. ﴿Those who misled us from among the jinn and mankind﴾: ﴿those who﴾ (alladhayni) is a dual relative pronoun, and what is meant is the category, not a single individual.

His words ﴿who misled us from among the jinn and mankind﴾ are an explanation of ﴿those who﴾. The author said: "(that is, Iblis and Qabil, who initiated disbelief and killing)." The meaning is that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, took this generality to be specific. He said: ﴿those who misled us﴾ is dual, meaning two: one of them is Iblis, who initiated disbelief, for he was the first to disbelieve; and the second is Qabil, who initiated killing. The first transgressed against the right of Allah, and the second transgressed against the rights of the servants of Allah.

As for Iblis, he was the first to initiate disbelief, because Allah commanded him to prostrate to Adam, but he refused and was arrogant and was among the disbelievers. As for Qabil, he was the first to initiate killing without right, because he killed his brother out of envy and transgression. They offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them and not from the other. How did they know that it was accepted from one and not the other? Allah knows best. Perhaps by a fire that descended and consumed what was accepted, as happened with the spoils in earlier times, or by some other sign. The important point is that it was accepted from one of them, and not from the other. The one from whom it was accepted was Habil, and the other, Qabil, was not accepted, so he envied him and said: "I will surely kill you." Why? Out of envy, because Allah accepted from his brother. His brother Habil said to him: ﴿Indeed, Allah accepts only from the righteous﴾ [al-Ma'idah 27]. It is as if he were saying to him: "Fear Allah, and He will accept from you." ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah 28]. That is, if you intend to kill me (...), I fear Allah. Perhaps this was in the law of those before us.

The one from whom it was accepted was Habil, and the other, Qabil, was not accepted from, so he envied him and said: ﴿I will surely kill you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 27]. Why? Out of envy, because Allah accepted from his brother. His brother Habil said to him: ﴿Indeed, Allah accepts only from the righteous﴾ [al-Ma'idah 27], as if he were saying to him: "Fear Allah, and He will accept from you."

Then he said to him: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah 28]. That is: if you intend that (...), I fear Allah. Perhaps it was in the law of those before us that a person was not permitted to defend himself, or he feared a greater corruption; and it is well known that averting the greater corruption is obligatory.

﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 29]. ﴿So his soul permitted him the murder of his brother﴾ [al-Ma'idah 30], that is, made it easy for him, ﴿and he killed him, and became among the losers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 30]. So Qabil was the first to initiate killing without right, and every soul that is killed without right has some of its burden upon Qabil, and Allah forbid, because he was the first to initiate killing. Whoever initiates an evil practice bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection. But is the matter, as the author said, that it refers to the devil, that is Iblis, who refused and was arrogant regarding prostration to Adam, and Qabil; or is the meaning the category?

The correct view is the second, without doubt, because many disbelievers do not think that they disbelieve by following the devil who refused and was arrogant, and many killers do not imagine that they did so by following Qabil. If the verse indicates generality by its wording, and the meaning requires it, then there is no basis for restricting it to a specific individual.

This is a rule of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) that we must understand: a general expression may not be confined to some of its instances except with evidence. If there is no evidence, then generality is obligatory.

Here we say: generality is obligatory, because the expression is general, and because the meaning requires it, since every disbeliever may not think he is following the devil, that is Iblis, and every person who kills deliberately without right may not think he killed by following Qabil. In that case, neither the wording nor the meaning supports restriction to Iblis and Qabil.

His words ﴿who misled us from among the jinn and mankind﴾ [Fussilat 29]: "the jinn," according to the author's statement, is Iblis, and "mankind" is Qabil.

The correct view is generality.

If someone says: "We know that a person may be misled by other humans; a bad person comes and misleads him. But how can it be from the jinn?"

We say: because the jinn, led by the devil, command the person to indecency, command him to evil, and command him to disbelief, and thereby they mislead him. Have you not seen what happened with Adam and his wife? Did the devil not mislead them? Yes, he did mislead them. Allah forbade them from eating from the tree, but the devil came and lured them with deception, swore to them that he was sincere, and whispered to them until they ate from the tree.

﴿We will make them under our feet﴾ [Fussilat 29]. ("We will make them") is in the jussive mood, as the answer to the imperative in His words ﴿show us﴾ [Fussilat 29]. The meaning: if You show us them, we will make them under our feet in the Fire. There is no doubt that what a person places under his foot has been humiliated to the greatest degree of humiliation. For this reason, among the well-known proverbs is that when a person wants to honor someone he says: "You are upon my head," and when he wants to humiliate him he says: "You are under my foot." So they say: "Show us these two who misled us, that we may place them under our feet."

﴿So that they may be among the lowest﴾ [Fussilat 29] (that is, that they may suffer a greater punishment than us), just as they were above us before. So let us now make them under our feet, so that they may be among the lowest.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the acknowledgment by the disbelievers of the lordship of Allah, and that He is the One who answers supplication, from their saying: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who misled us﴾ [Fussilat 29]. And this is the speech of the disbelievers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person should distance himself, rather, it is obligatory upon him to distance himself from bad companions (qurana' al-su', i.e., bad companions), because of His words ﴿those who misled us from among the jinn and mankind﴾ [Fussilat 29]. The Prophet (ﷺ) warned against the bad companion, saying: "A person is upon the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look at whom he befriends." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (4833) and al-Tirmidhi (2378) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.] That is, upon the religion of his friend and beloved. "So let each of you look at whom he befriends." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of a bad companion is like the bellows-blower: either he will burn your clothes, or you will find from him a foul smell." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5534) and Muslim (2628/146) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.] So beware of the bad companion. Do not associate with him, do not befriend him, and do not entrust him with anything.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the disavowal of the followers from those they followed on the Day of Resurrection. This is supported by His, the Exalted, words: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah 166]. So the ones who were followed in the verse of al-Baqarah disown their followers, just as the followers also disown those they followed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that misguidance comes from the jinn and mankind, because of His words: ﴿who misled us from among the jinn and mankind﴾ [Fussilat 29]. The companionship of a human with a human is clear, and the companionship of a jinn with a human is also derived from His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them﴾ [Fussilat 25].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the intense rage of these misguided ones against those who misled them, because of His words: ﴿We will make them under our feet, so that they may be among the lowest﴾ [Fussilat 29].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verses 30–32 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat 30].

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ [Fussilat 30]: They say it with their tongues and their hearts. Mere utterance by the tongue is not sufficient, because uttering with the tongue is done by both the hypocrite and the sincere believer. Rather, what is meant is saying it with the tongue and the heart together.

﴿They say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾: This saying is not merely a statement on the tongue and a belief in the heart. Rather, it necessarily entails obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. That is why He said: ﴿then remain steadfast﴾, meaning they remained steadfast in obedience to Allah. Faith is in the heart and steadfastness is in the limbs. Allah did not suffice with praising them and mentioning their reward for faith in the heart; rather, steadfastness is necessary. He said: ﴿then remain steadfast﴾. The author said: (upon monotheism and other things that were obligatory upon them). This is correct; that is, they remained steadfast upon monotheism, so there is no association of partners with Allah; they remained steadfast in following the Sunnah, so there is no innovation; they remained steadfast in obedience, so there is no disobedience; they remained steadfast in goodness, so there is no evil, and so on.

Reflect on His saying: ﴿then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat 30]. He used "thumma" (then), which indicates sequence with a delay. That is, their faith was not a fleeting faith that then disappeared. No, it was a settled faith, because they remained steadfast upon the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The Prophet ﷺ was asked: a man said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, tell me a statement about Islam about which I will not ask anyone other than you," meaning a decisive statement. He said to him: "Say: I have believed in Allah, then remain steadfast."[[Recorded by Muslim (38/62) from the hadith of Sufyan ibn 'Abdullah al-Thaqafi.]] This is derived from this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat 30].

His saying: ﴿the angels will descend upon them﴾ [Fussilat 30]. The word "tatanazzalu" (will descend) has a meaning different from "tanazzala" (descended), because "tatanazzalu" contains an addition over "tanazzala." What is the addition? The "ta" (تاء). This addition implies two meanings:

The first meaning: their descent occurs gradually, little by little. "Tatanazzalu" is not a single descent at one time.

The second: the descent or coming down is repeated. ﴿will descend upon them﴾ means that whenever their state calls for the descent of the angels upon them, the angels descend upon them. So the difference now between "tanazzala" and "tatanazzalu" is in two respects. The first respect: "tanazzala" means descent once and at one time, whereas "tatanazzalu" implies repeated descent, and that it occurs gradually.

﴿upon them the angels﴾: The discussion of the mention of the angels has already passed. The author's statement, (at death), is open to question, because Allah, Exalted, did not restrict that. The apparent meaning is that the angels descend upon them whenever the situation calls for descent: at death, in fear, in battles, and in every state that calls for the descent of the angels upon them, because Allah stated it without restriction.

﴿will descend upon them﴾ ﴿that do not fear﴾, i.e., (that do not fear death and what comes after it, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ over what they left behind of family and children, for We will take your place in caring for them).

We say: "Do not fear" for your future, and "do not grieve" over your past. This is because a person in fear either fears the future or grieves over what has passed, saying, "If only I had done such-and-such, it would have been such-and-such," so fear does not arise in him, for example. So the angels descend upon them and say: "Do not fear the future and do not grieve over the past." Fear of the future is mentioned first because it is more important than grief over the past, since a person's future is what makes him move forward or stop. Therefore it was mentioned before grief. If we take it, for example, as one of the things that call for descent at the time of death, then a person at death has a state that calls for him to be strengthened in vigor and energy upon faith and monotheism. So the angels also descend upon them at death and give them this good news.

﴿Do not fear, and do not grieve, and receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat 30]: "Absharu" (receive good news) is from "al-bushra," which is the giving of news.

﴿And receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾: Glad tidings (al-bushra) is the giving of news of what gladdens. It was called "bushra" because when a person is happy, the sign of joy appears on his face and the complexion (bashra) of the face changes. Sometimes "bushra" is used for news of what is displeasing, as a form of mockery (tahakkum). Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nisa' 138], and He said: ﴿So give them good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran 21], even though this is something displeasing; but it is in the manner of mocking them, just as you say to the disobedient person: "Receive good news of a bad end, receive good news of the Fire," and similar things that are said as mockery.

﴿Which you were promised﴾: Paradise is the abode that Allah prepared for His friends, and in it, as in the Noble Qur'an, is ﴿no soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [As-Sajdah 17]. And in it, as is found in the sacred hadith: "That which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that which has not occurred to the heart of a human being."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3244) and Muslim (2824/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

﴿which you were promised﴾: Who promised them with it? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, promised them. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [At-Tawbah 72].

(﴿We are your allies in the worldly life﴾, i.e., We protect you therein, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., We will be with you therein until you enter Paradise, ﴿and for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31], i.e., seek.)

The angels say to them: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Fussilat 31], meaning that the angels take charge of the believers: they urge them toward good and warn them against evil. The Prophet ﷺ informed us that "The angel has an inspiration (lamma) in the heart of the son of Adam, and Satan has an inspiration (lamma)."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2988) and al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (10985) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] So the inspiration of the angel is a promise of good and an urging to obedience, and the inspiration of Satan is the opposite.

His saying: (﴿in the worldly life﴾, i.e., We protect you therein): That is because when the angels are with a person, they guide him, direct him to good, and urge him toward it.

﴿And in the Hereafter﴾: They take charge of them also, for the angels ﴿will receive them: "This is your day which you were promised"﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 103]. In Paradise, the angels enter upon them from every gate: ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home"﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 24]. So they are the allies of the believers in this world and in the Hereafter. May Allah make us and you among them.

﴿And for you therein﴾, i.e., in the Hereafter, ﴿is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31]: Everything a person desires, even if he does not seek it, will be present before him. Likewise, everything he seeks will be present before him. In this world, what a person desires is not always available to him, even if he asks and repeats his request, it may not come to him. But in the Hereafter, as soon as something occurs to a person's heart that he desires, it is present.

Likewise, what they request, what they seek, is present, and there comes to them also what has not occurred to their minds, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35]. That is, there comes to you of bounties what you did not seek and what your soul did not desire, because it had not occurred to your mind.

(﴿An accommodation﴾ [Fussilat 32], a prepared provision, accusative by an implied (ja'ala)). That is: it was made (nuzulan) ﴿from a Forgiving, Merciful One﴾ [Fussilat 32], and He is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because they did not reach Paradise except by His forgiveness and mercy.

* Student: May Allah bless you. Regarding our statement that the restriction of the angels' descent in the Hereafter to death, in the context of the verse, would also apply to His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted life﴾ [Ta-Ha 124], since most exegetes say it refers to the grave, to the Hereafter? Or is the verse general?
* Shaykh: That is so. The verse is general, and its generality is supported by His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [An-Nahl 97]. Its implication is that whoever does not have this characteristic, there is no good life for him.
* Student: What led them to agree that it refers to the Hereafter, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Perhaps they understood that the context indicates this. For example, here: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat 30]. The good news of Paradise in reality occurs at death, so perhaps they thought that the context requires specification.
* Student: Their saying, O Shaykh, may Allah bless you: ﴿Our Lord, show us those two﴾ [Fussilat 29]. Does this not contain an acknowledgment of divinity (uluhiyyah) just as it contains an acknowledgment of lordship (rububiyyah)?
* Shaykh: Does it contain an acknowledgment?
* Student: Of divinity, the tawhid of worship, because supplication is a kind of worship.
* Shaykh: You mean that they called upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic? No. Supplicating to Allah, Exalted, occurs even in this world, but they supplicate to Allah in hardship and forget Him in ease. And there, also in the Hereafter, perhaps they will acknowledge this; that is, they acknowledge that it is true that there is no god but Allah, but this acknowledgment will not benefit them.
* Student: O Shaykh, you mentioned that the Messenger ﷺ informed us that the angel has an inspiration in a person and Satan has an inspiration (...).
* Shaykh: The two inspirations may come at the same moment, so a person desires good, and then Satan turns him away from it. And it may be that the thought of doing good has not occurred to him while Satan has already whispered evil to him.
* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. Is the supplication here specific to the disbelieving humans, or to all disbelievers, both jinn and humans?
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: Their supplication when they said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Our Lord, show us those who misled us, from among the jinn and mankind"﴾ [Fussilat 29]. Is it specific to disbelieving humans, or does it include both disbelieving humans and jinn?
* Shaykh: It includes both, because the disbelieving jinn enter the Fire by consensus.
* Student: O Shaykh, why did the verse use the past tense: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾?
* Shaykh: That is a good question. It asks: has this statement already happened, or will it happen?
The answer: It has not yet occurred, but it is in the manner of narrating a present state, or it may be said that since its occurrence is certain, it has become like the past, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl 1], for the command of Allah has not yet come, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl 1].
* Student: Could it not be said that the statement of the disbelievers, ﴿show us those who misled us﴾, refers to the Fire, as evidenced by His saying afterward: ﴿that we may put them under our feet﴾ [Fussilat 29]?
* Shaykh: Yes, it does not indicate that, because they could put them under their feet while they are in the plains of the Resurrection. It does not necessarily have to be in the Fire.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, is it from all the jinn, or from a specific kind or type?
* Shaykh: It is well known that among the jinn there are the righteous and others below that, and among them there are Muslims and disbelievers. The one who misleads is only the disbeliever. As for the believing jinn, he does not mislead.
* Student: But, O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enable all disbelieving jinn to mislead humans?
* Shaykh: No, it is not like that in every case. But the origin of a human's disbelief comes from Satan and the self. And Satan is of the jinn, without doubt: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾ [Al-Kahf 50].
* Student: Virtuous Shaykh, the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, quoting the first son of Adam: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 28]. You mentioned that this is the law of those before us (shar' man qablana), and that our law has come with something different. Does this apply in our law regarding times of strife, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is strife in it. But the matter of Qabil and Habil did not involve strife. For this reason, the Messenger commanded that during strife a person should be like the better of the two sons of Adam, so he restrains himself, as 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) did when the rebels rose against him, and the Companions wanted to defend him, but he ordered them to hold back.

* * *

Student: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter, and for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request (31). An accommodation from a Forgiving, Merciful One (32). And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteousness, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 31–33].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve"﴾ [Fussilat 30]. When does this descent occur?
* Student: In every state, including at death.
* Shaykh: Yes, in every state they need reinforcement and firmness, and especially at death. The saying of Allah supports this: ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [Al-Anfal 12].

He expressed it with His saying "tatanazzalu" (will descend) rather than "tanazzala" (descended). Why?
* Student: For two reasons: the first is the gradualness of the descent; the second is the repetition and continuity.
* Shaykh: Well done. His saying: ﴿Receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat 30]. What is glad tidings (bushra)?
* Student: Glad tidings is informing people of what is desired.
* Shaykh: The giving of news of what?
* Student: What gladdens.
* Shaykh: And does it come for other than that?
* Student: Yes, it comes with what is displeasing; sometimes it comes with what is displeasing.
* Shaykh: Give an example.
* Student: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nisa' 138].
* Shaykh: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾. Well done. Is this glad tidings in its literal meaning, or is something else intended by it?
* Student: It is intended as punishment for them (...).
* Shaykh: Mockery (tahakkum). It is intended as mockery, like His saying: ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of boiling water (48). Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the honored﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 48–49]. This is said to him in mockery. Yes: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Fussilat 31]. How were they their allies in the worldly life?
* Student: Their allies in the worldly life help them do good deeds and warn them against committing wrongs.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Is there something in the hadith that supports this?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, Satan has an inspiration, and the angel has an inspiration."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2988) and al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (10985) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]
* Shaykh: Well done.

I think we stopped at His saying: ﴿and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31]?

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31], i.e., whatever you seek. So everything the soul desires, even without asking, is attained, and everything they seek is attained, however it may be. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35].

He said: (﴿An accommodation﴾ [Fussilat 32], a prepared provision, accusative by an implied (ja'ala)). That is, according to the author's interpretation, (nuzulan) is the second object of the implied verb (ja'ala), meaning (ja'ala nuzulan), "it was made an accommodation." Its first object is the deputy of the subject, because the deputy of the subject takes the place of the object: an object takes the place of the subject.
