Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verses 30–32 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat 30].

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ [Fussilat 30]: They say it with their tongues and their hearts. Mere utterance by the tongue is not sufficient, because uttering with the tongue is done by both the hypocrite and the sincere believer. Rather, what is meant is saying it with the tongue and the heart together.

﴿They say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾: This saying is not merely a statement on the tongue and a belief in the heart. Rather, it necessarily entails obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. That is why He said: ﴿then remain steadfast﴾, meaning they remained steadfast in obedience to Allah. Faith is in the heart and steadfastness is in the limbs. Allah did not suffice with praising them and mentioning their reward for faith in the heart; rather, steadfastness is necessary. He said: ﴿then remain steadfast﴾. The author said: (upon monotheism and other things that were obligatory upon them). This is correct; that is, they remained steadfast upon monotheism, so there is no association of partners with Allah; they remained steadfast in following the Sunnah, so there is no innovation; they remained steadfast in obedience, so there is no disobedience; they remained steadfast in goodness, so there is no evil, and so on.

Reflect on His saying: ﴿then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat 30]. He used "thumma" (then), which indicates sequence with a delay. That is, their faith was not a fleeting faith that then disappeared. No, it was a settled faith, because they remained steadfast upon the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The Prophet ﷺ was asked: a man said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, tell me a statement about Islam about which I will not ask anyone other than you," meaning a decisive statement. He said to him: "Say: I have believed in Allah, then remain steadfast."[[Recorded by Muslim (38/62) from the hadith of Sufyan ibn 'Abdullah al-Thaqafi.]] This is derived from this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat 30].

His saying: ﴿the angels will descend upon them﴾ [Fussilat 30]. The word "tatanazzalu" (will descend) has a meaning different from "tanazzala" (descended), because "tatanazzalu" contains an addition over "tanazzala." What is the addition? The "ta" (تاء). This addition implies two meanings:

The first meaning: their descent occurs gradually, little by little. "Tatanazzalu" is not a single descent at one time.

The second: the descent or coming down is repeated. ﴿will descend upon them﴾ means that whenever their state calls for the descent of the angels upon them, the angels descend upon them. So the difference now between "tanazzala" and "tatanazzalu" is in two respects. The first respect: "tanazzala" means descent once and at one time, whereas "tatanazzalu" implies repeated descent, and that it occurs gradually.

﴿upon them the angels﴾: The discussion of the mention of the angels has already passed. The author's statement, (at death), is open to question, because Allah, Exalted, did not restrict that. The apparent meaning is that the angels descend upon them whenever the situation calls for descent: at death, in fear, in battles, and in every state that calls for the descent of the angels upon them, because Allah stated it without restriction.

﴿will descend upon them﴾ ﴿that do not fear﴾, i.e., (that do not fear death and what comes after it, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ over what they left behind of family and children, for We will take your place in caring for them).

We say: "Do not fear" for your future, and "do not grieve" over your past. This is because a person in fear either fears the future or grieves over what has passed, saying, "If only I had done such-and-such, it would have been such-and-such," so fear does not arise in him, for example. So the angels descend upon them and say: "Do not fear the future and do not grieve over the past." Fear of the future is mentioned first because it is more important than grief over the past, since a person's future is what makes him move forward or stop. Therefore it was mentioned before grief. If we take it, for example, as one of the things that call for descent at the time of death, then a person at death has a state that calls for him to be strengthened in vigor and energy upon faith and monotheism. So the angels also descend upon them at death and give them this good news.

﴿Do not fear, and do not grieve, and receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat 30]: "Absharu" (receive good news) is from "al-bushra," which is the giving of news.

﴿And receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾: Glad tidings (al-bushra) is the giving of news of what gladdens. It was called "bushra" because when a person is happy, the sign of joy appears on his face and the complexion (bashra) of the face changes. Sometimes "bushra" is used for news of what is displeasing, as a form of mockery (tahakkum). Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nisa' 138], and He said: ﴿So give them good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran 21], even though this is something displeasing; but it is in the manner of mocking them, just as you say to the disobedient person: "Receive good news of a bad end, receive good news of the Fire," and similar things that are said as mockery.

﴿Which you were promised﴾: Paradise is the abode that Allah prepared for His friends, and in it, as in the Noble Qur'an, is ﴿no soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [As-Sajdah 17]. And in it, as is found in the sacred hadith: "That which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that which has not occurred to the heart of a human being."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3244) and Muslim (2824/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

﴿which you were promised﴾: Who promised them with it? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, promised them. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [At-Tawbah 72].

(﴿We are your allies in the worldly life﴾, i.e., We protect you therein, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., We will be with you therein until you enter Paradise, ﴿and for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31], i.e., seek.)

The angels say to them: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Fussilat 31], meaning that the angels take charge of the believers: they urge them toward good and warn them against evil. The Prophet ﷺ informed us that "The angel has an inspiration (lamma) in the heart of the son of Adam, and Satan has an inspiration (lamma)."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2988) and al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (10985) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] So the inspiration of the angel is a promise of good and an urging to obedience, and the inspiration of Satan is the opposite.

His saying: (﴿in the worldly life﴾, i.e., We protect you therein): That is because when the angels are with a person, they guide him, direct him to good, and urge him toward it.

﴿And in the Hereafter﴾: They take charge of them also, for the angels ﴿will receive them: "This is your day which you were promised"﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 103]. In Paradise, the angels enter upon them from every gate: ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home"﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 24]. So they are the allies of the believers in this world and in the Hereafter. May Allah make us and you among them.

﴿And for you therein﴾, i.e., in the Hereafter, ﴿is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31]: Everything a person desires, even if he does not seek it, will be present before him. Likewise, everything he seeks will be present before him. In this world, what a person desires is not always available to him, even if he asks and repeats his request, it may not come to him. But in the Hereafter, as soon as something occurs to a person's heart that he desires, it is present.

Likewise, what they request, what they seek, is present, and there comes to them also what has not occurred to their minds, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35]. That is, there comes to you of bounties what you did not seek and what your soul did not desire, because it had not occurred to your mind.

(﴿An accommodation﴾ [Fussilat 32], a prepared provision, accusative by an implied (ja'ala)). That is: it was made (nuzulan) ﴿from a Forgiving, Merciful One﴾ [Fussilat 32], and He is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because they did not reach Paradise except by His forgiveness and mercy.

* Student: May Allah bless you. Regarding our statement that the restriction of the angels' descent in the Hereafter to death, in the context of the verse, would also apply to His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted life﴾ [Ta-Ha 124], since most exegetes say it refers to the grave, to the Hereafter? Or is the verse general?
* Shaykh: That is so. The verse is general, and its generality is supported by His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [An-Nahl 97]. Its implication is that whoever does not have this characteristic, there is no good life for him.
* Student: What led them to agree that it refers to the Hereafter, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Perhaps they understood that the context indicates this. For example, here: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat 30]. The good news of Paradise in reality occurs at death, so perhaps they thought that the context requires specification.
* Student: Their saying, O Shaykh, may Allah bless you: ﴿Our Lord, show us those two﴾ [Fussilat 29]. Does this not contain an acknowledgment of divinity (uluhiyyah) just as it contains an acknowledgment of lordship (rububiyyah)?
* Shaykh: Does it contain an acknowledgment?
* Student: Of divinity, the tawhid of worship, because supplication is a kind of worship.
* Shaykh: You mean that they called upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic? No. Supplicating to Allah, Exalted, occurs even in this world, but they supplicate to Allah in hardship and forget Him in ease. And there, also in the Hereafter, perhaps they will acknowledge this; that is, they acknowledge that it is true that there is no god but Allah, but this acknowledgment will not benefit them.
* Student: O Shaykh, you mentioned that the Messenger ﷺ informed us that the angel has an inspiration in a person and Satan has an inspiration (...).
* Shaykh: The two inspirations may come at the same moment, so a person desires good, and then Satan turns him away from it. And it may be that the thought of doing good has not occurred to him while Satan has already whispered evil to him.
* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. Is the supplication here specific to the disbelieving humans, or to all disbelievers, both jinn and humans?
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: Their supplication when they said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Our Lord, show us those who misled us, from among the jinn and mankind"﴾ [Fussilat 29]. Is it specific to disbelieving humans, or does it include both disbelieving humans and jinn?
* Shaykh: It includes both, because the disbelieving jinn enter the Fire by consensus.
* Student: O Shaykh, why did the verse use the past tense: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾?
* Shaykh: That is a good question. It asks: has this statement already happened, or will it happen?
The answer: It has not yet occurred, but it is in the manner of narrating a present state, or it may be said that since its occurrence is certain, it has become like the past, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl 1], for the command of Allah has not yet come, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl 1].
* Student: Could it not be said that the statement of the disbelievers, ﴿show us those who misled us﴾, refers to the Fire, as evidenced by His saying afterward: ﴿that we may put them under our feet﴾ [Fussilat 29]?
* Shaykh: Yes, it does not indicate that, because they could put them under their feet while they are in the plains of the Resurrection. It does not necessarily have to be in the Fire.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, is it from all the jinn, or from a specific kind or type?
* Shaykh: It is well known that among the jinn there are the righteous and others below that, and among them there are Muslims and disbelievers. The one who misleads is only the disbeliever. As for the believing jinn, he does not mislead.
* Student: But, O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enable all disbelieving jinn to mislead humans?
* Shaykh: No, it is not like that in every case. But the origin of a human's disbelief comes from Satan and the self. And Satan is of the jinn, without doubt: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾ [Al-Kahf 50].
* Student: Virtuous Shaykh, the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, quoting the first son of Adam: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 28]. You mentioned that this is the law of those before us (shar' man qablana), and that our law has come with something different. Does this apply in our law regarding times of strife, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is strife in it. But the matter of Qabil and Habil did not involve strife. For this reason, the Messenger commanded that during strife a person should be like the better of the two sons of Adam, so he restrains himself, as 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) did when the rebels rose against him, and the Companions wanted to defend him, but he ordered them to hold back.

* * *

Student: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter, and for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request (31). An accommodation from a Forgiving, Merciful One (32). And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteousness, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 31–33].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve"﴾ [Fussilat 30]. When does this descent occur?
* Student: In every state, including at death.
* Shaykh: Yes, in every state they need reinforcement and firmness, and especially at death. The saying of Allah supports this: ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [Al-Anfal 12].

He expressed it with His saying "tatanazzalu" (will descend) rather than "tanazzala" (descended). Why?
* Student: For two reasons: the first is the gradualness of the descent; the second is the repetition and continuity.
* Shaykh: Well done. His saying: ﴿Receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat 30]. What is glad tidings (bushra)?
* Student: Glad tidings is informing people of what is desired.
* Shaykh: The giving of news of what?
* Student: What gladdens.
* Shaykh: And does it come for other than that?
* Student: Yes, it comes with what is displeasing; sometimes it comes with what is displeasing.
* Shaykh: Give an example.
* Student: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nisa' 138].
* Shaykh: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾. Well done. Is this glad tidings in its literal meaning, or is something else intended by it?
* Student: It is intended as punishment for them (...).
* Shaykh: Mockery (tahakkum). It is intended as mockery, like His saying: ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of boiling water (48). Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the honored﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 48–49]. This is said to him in mockery. Yes: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Fussilat 31]. How were they their allies in the worldly life?
* Student: Their allies in the worldly life help them do good deeds and warn them against committing wrongs.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Is there something in the hadith that supports this?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, Satan has an inspiration, and the angel has an inspiration."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2988) and al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (10985) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]
* Shaykh: Well done.

I think we stopped at His saying: ﴿and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31]?

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31], i.e., whatever you seek. So everything the soul desires, even without asking, is attained, and everything they seek is attained, however it may be. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35].

He said: (﴿An accommodation﴾ [Fussilat 32], a prepared provision, accusative by an implied (ja'ala)). That is, according to the author's interpretation, (nuzulan) is the second object of the implied verb (ja'ala), meaning (ja'ala nuzulan), "it was made an accommodation." Its first object is the deputy of the subject, because the deputy of the subject takes the place of the object: an object takes the place of the subject.

* Shaykh: You mean that they called upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic? No. Supplicating to Allah, Exalted, occurs even in this world, but they supplicate to Allah in hardship and forget Him in ease. And there, also in the Hereafter, perhaps they will acknowledge this; that is, they acknowledge that it is true that there is no god but Allah, but this acknowledgment will not benefit them.
* Student: O Shaykh, you mentioned that the Messenger ﷺ informed us that the angel has an inspiration in a person and Satan has an inspiration (...).
* Shaykh: The two inspirations may come at the same moment, so a person desires good, and then Satan turns him away from it. And it may be that the thought of doing good has not occurred to him while Satan has already whispered evil to him.
* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. Is the supplication here specific to the disbelieving humans, or to all disbelievers, both jinn and humans?
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: Their supplication when they said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Our Lord, show us those who misled us, from among the jinn and mankind"﴾ [Fussilat 29]. Is it specific to disbelieving humans, or does it include both disbelieving humans and jinn?
* Shaykh: It includes both, because the disbelieving jinn enter the Fire by consensus.
* Student: O Shaykh, why did the verse use the past tense: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾?
* Shaykh: That is a good question. It asks: has this statement already happened, or will it happen?
The answer: It has not yet occurred, but it is in the manner of narrating a present state, or it may be said that since its occurrence is certain, it has become like the past, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl 1], for the command of Allah has not yet come, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl 1].
* Student: Could it not be said that the statement of the disbelievers, ﴿show us those who misled us﴾, refers to the Fire, as evidenced by His saying afterward: ﴿that we may put them under our feet﴾ [Fussilat 29]?
* Shaykh: Yes, it does not indicate that, because they could put them under their feet while they are in the plains of the Resurrection. It does not necessarily have to be in the Fire.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, is it from all the jinn, or from a specific kind or type?
* Shaykh: It is well known that among the jinn there are the righteous and others below that, and among them there are Muslims and disbelievers. The one who misleads is only the disbeliever. As for the believing jinn, he does not mislead.
* Student: But, O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enable all disbelieving jinn to mislead humans?
* Shaykh: No, it is not like that in every case. But the origin of a human's disbelief comes from Satan and the self. And Satan is of the jinn, without doubt: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾ [Al-Kahf 50].
* Student: Virtuous Shaykh, the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, quoting the first son of Adam: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 28]. You mentioned that this is the law of those before us (shar' man qablana), and that our law has come with something different. Does this apply in our law regarding times of strife, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is strife in it. But the matter of Qabil and Habil did not involve strife. For this reason, the Messenger commanded that during strife a person should be like the better of the two sons of Adam, so he restrains himself, as 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) did when the rebels rose against him, and the Companions wanted to defend him, but he ordered them to hold back.

* * *

Student: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter, and for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request (31). An accommodation from a Forgiving, Merciful One (32). And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteousness, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 31–33].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve"﴾ [Fussilat 30]. When does this descent occur?
* Student: In every state, including at death.
* Shaykh: Yes, in every state they need reinforcement and firmness, and especially at death. The saying of Allah supports this: ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [Al-Anfal 12].

He expressed it with His saying "tatanazzalu" (will descend) rather than "tanazzala" (descended). Why?
* Student: For two reasons: the first is the gradualness of the descent; the second is the repetition and continuity.
* Shaykh: Well done. His saying: ﴿Receive good news of Paradise, which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat 30]. What is glad tidings (bushra)?
* Student: Glad tidings is informing people of what is desired.
* Shaykh: The giving of news of what?
* Student: What gladdens.
* Shaykh: And does it come for other than that?
* Student: Yes, it comes with what is displeasing; sometimes it comes with what is displeasing.
* Shaykh: Give an example.
* Student: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nisa' 138].
* Shaykh: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them is a painful punishment﴾. Well done. Is this glad tidings in its literal meaning, or is something else intended by it?
* Student: It is intended as punishment for them (...).
* Shaykh: Mockery (tahakkum). It is intended as mockery, like His saying: ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of boiling water (48). Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the honored﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 48–49]. This is said to him in mockery. Yes: ﴿We are your allies in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Fussilat 31]. How were they their allies in the worldly life?
* Student: Their allies in the worldly life help them do good deeds and warn them against committing wrongs.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Is there something in the hadith that supports this?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, Satan has an inspiration, and the angel has an inspiration."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2988) and al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (10985) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]
* Shaykh: Well done.

I think we stopped at His saying: ﴿and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31]?

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you request﴾ [Fussilat 31], i.e., whatever you seek. So everything the soul desires, even without asking, is attained, and everything they seek is attained, however it may be. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35].

He said: (﴿An accommodation﴾ [Fussilat 32], a prepared provision, accusative by an implied (ja'ala)). That is, according to the author's interpretation, (nuzulan) is the second object of the implied verb (ja'ala), meaning (ja'ala nuzulan), "it was made an accommodation." Its first object is the deputy of the subject, because the deputy of the subject takes the place of the object: an object takes the place of the subject.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 33–36 (part 1 of 3):

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"?﴾ [Fussilat 33]. These are three attributes; when a person possesses them, none is better in speech than him.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿And who is better in speech﴾, i.e., no one is better in speech). The author's explanation of this clause indicates that (man) is an interrogative particle but carries the meaning of negation: (man ahsan), meaning "no one is better." When an interrogative particle is used, or an interrogative is used with the meaning of negation, it is imbued with the meaning of challenge. Which is more eloquent: to say "No one is better in speech than one who invites to Allah," or to say "Who is better?" The second is more eloquent, because the second includes both negation and challenge, as if it says: "Bring me proof that there is someone better than one who invites to Allah." Every interrogative that comes with the meaning of negation is imbued with the meaning of challenge, because when you say "Who is such-and-such?", its meaning is: "I challenge you to bring me something other than that." Thus "man ahsan" is more emphatic in negation than saying "no one is better," because it is an interrogative sentence imbued with the meaning of challenge.

(Ahsan) here is the predicate of the subject, (man) is the subject, and (qawlan) is a specification (tamyiz), because whenever a noun in the accusative comes after a comparative adjective (ism al-tafdil), it is a tamyiz for it.

﴿Who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah﴾: the author said: (with monotheism). This is undoubtedly good, but the verse is more comprehensive than monotheism: ﴿one who invites to Allah﴾ with monotheism, righteous deeds, and other things (...) to Allah.

And His saying ﴿one who invites to Allah﴾ means to the religion of Allah, and the religion of Allah includes monotheism and righteous deeds.

Secondly, He said: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾. He began with reforming others, then followed with reforming the self, although whoever invites to Allah is also reforming himself.

﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: (righteous) is an adjective of a deleted noun; the estimate is: "and does a righteous deed." A deed is not righteous except with two conditions: sincerity to Allah, and following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

"Righteous": what is its i'rab (grammatical analysis)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, we said it is an adjective of a deleted noun, and the estimate is: "does a deed that is righteous."
When does a deed become righteous?
* Student: When its doer fulfills two conditions: sincerity to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and following His Messenger ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: Well done. Sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Is the deed of one who shows off a righteous deed?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: Because sincerity is lacking.
And is the deed of an innovator righteous? No, because following is lacking. At that point we say to these innovators, who have as much sincerity to Allah as they have: your deed is void. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our matter, it is rejected»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18), the wording is his, from the hadith of 'A'isha.]].
Then we say: the reality of sincerity necessitates that you do not worship Allah except in the manner He has legislated. Do not worship Him according to your whims; for if you worship Allah according to your whims, by innovation, you are not sincere. The sincere person must worship Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in the manner He has legislated. Thus the righteous deed is composed of two things: the first, sincerity; and the second, following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

He said: ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 33]. Is this said with the tongue or with the heart? With both together.

If someone says: his saying "Indeed, I am of the Muslims" is undoubtedly a righteous deed, so what is the benefit of mentioning it?

We say: the benefit is that he proclaims this statement and does not care about whoever opposes him. For among people there is one who does a righteous deed, but you find him concealed, lacking the courage that would make him announce it. As for this one, he proclaims it, saying with his tongue, unconcerned: "Indeed, I am of the Muslims."

The sentence, as you know, (innani) is emphasized with (inna). Some scholars mentioned that what is meant is the muezzin, because the muezzin invites to Allah, saying to people: "Hasten to prayer, hasten to success," and because he is a believer who does righteous deeds; and because he says: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah," proclaiming it, and "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am of the Muslims﴾.

However, the correct view is that the verse is general, including the muezzin and non-muezzin. The preacher on the pulpit enters the verse, does he not? He enters the verse. The teacher in his teaching circle enters it too. Thus the verse is more general than what was mentioned.

But know that some of the early scholars mention a specific meaning for the verse, not wishing to restrict it to that meaning, but intending it as an example. This is a matter that may escape some people. We always look in Ibn Kathir or Ibn Jarir and find that someone said: "So-and-so is such." It is a part of the meaning. They do not intend to confine the general to the specific, for they are too knowledgeable to limit the general to some of its individuals, but they intend an example.

For example, some scholars said regarding: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited by those whom We chose from Our servants; and among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir 32]: the one who wrongs himself is the one who delays the prayer past its time; the moderate one is the one who prays it at the end of its time; the foremost in good deeds is the one who prays it at the beginning of its time. This is undoubtedly a restriction; indeed, undoubtedly a specification of the general. So we say: they intended that as an example.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the varying degrees of deeds, from His saying ﴿and who is better in speech﴾ [Fussilat 33], and (ahsan) is a comparative adjective. Undoubtedly deeds vary in terms of kind, in terms of type, and in terms of form and manner: three considerations: in terms of kind, in terms of type, and in terms of form and manner.

They vary in terms of kind: for example, prayer is better than zakat, zakat is better than fasting, fasting is better than hajj. This is in terms of kind. Then this kind also varies from another aspect: the obligatory act of worship is better than its voluntary form; so the noon prayer, for example, is better than night prayer. This is variation in terms of kind but from another aspect.

The evidence for this: the Prophet ﷺ said, relating from Allah: «My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]].

They vary in terms of type: such as the witr prayer being better than general night prayer, and the regular sunnah prayers being better than general voluntary prayer. This is in terms of type; and if you wish, you may make their variation in terms of obligatory and recommended part of this type.

The third: in terms of form: a prayer in which a person is humble, reflects on what he says and does, and is tranquil, versus another prayer in which he limits himself to the obligatory and without humility of heart, for example. Which is better? The first is better.

The essential point: we believe that deeds vary, and that some are more beloved to Allah than others.

There remains the question: does variation in deeds necessitate variation in the doer? Yes. On this basis the doer also differs and varies. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Do not revile my Companions; for by Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you spent gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673) and Muslim (2541/222), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]. The deed is one, but the doer differs.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿one who invites to Allah﴾ [Fussilat 33].
* And from its benefits: an indication of sincerity in da'wah, which we take from His saying ﴿to Allah﴾; for the caller may invite and stand before people, remind them, admonish them, urge them to good and warn them against evil, yet he wants to be esteemed among them. Is this one calling to Allah, or calling to himself? To himself. Therefore sincerity is necessary.

If someone asks: does sincerity get harmed if one intends by da'wah the reform of people?
The answer: it is not harmed, because the basis of his call is for the reform of people.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of the righteous deed that combines the two matters: sincerity and following; by His saying ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of knowledge. From where do we take it? From His saying ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ [Fussilat 33]; for it is impossible to know whether a deed conforms to the Shari'ah or not except through knowledge, and this is clear. Thus the verse is evidence for the obligation of knowledge; because if the righteous deed is obligatory, you must know it through the Shari'ah, and what an obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that the Muslim should be proud of his religion, proclaim it, say "Indeed, I am of the Muslims," and not be shy when told that he is a Muslim; by His saying ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 33].

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of avoiding self-praise; for He said ﴿of the Muslims﴾ and did not say "and said, I am a Muslim"; because a person may take pride in saying "I am a Muslim" and boast more than he would if he said "I am of the Muslims."

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of brotherhood among Muslims; by His saying ﴿of the Muslims﴾, an indication that "I am like one of these; I do not separate from them."

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is a question that comes up to us often: is seeking knowledge better, or occupying oneself with da'wah?

In reality it is an imprecise question. Firstly, it is possible to combine this and that. We know that the caller does not occupy his time from the dawn prayer until after the night prayer always calling to others. Does anyone among the callers do this? Never. He calls for half an hour here and half an hour there. As for remaining silent from the dawn prayer until the night prayer, that is impossible; there must be intervals. So combining da'wah to Allah with seeking knowledge is not impossible: he seeks knowledge for an hour or two and then calls for half an hour, for example. There is no contradiction. That is one point.

Secondly: it is impossible to call to Allah without knowledge, and calling to Allah in ignorance may cause more harm than not calling. Many callers have zeal and love for good, so you find them forbidding what is permitted or making obligatory what is not obligatory, based on their zeal. Had they possessed knowledge, they would have had steadfastness. It is not hidden from you what 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did at the Treaty of Hudaybiyya: he began to oppose the treaty and came to the Messenger, peace be upon him, wanting to undo the treaty[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2731) from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and in it: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I came to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ and said: Are you not truly the Prophet of Allah? He said: 'Yes.' I said: Are we not upon the truth and our enemy upon falsehood? He said: 'Yes.' I said: Then why should we accept humiliation in our religion? He said: 'I am the Messenger of Allah, and I do not disobey Him, and He is my helper.' I said: Did you not used to tell us that we would come to the House and circumambulate it? He said: 'Yes, but did I inform you that we would come to it this year?' He said: I said: No. He said: 'Then you will come to it and circumambulate it.'"]]. However, steadfastness like that of Abu Bakr is what made the truth manifest. So it is impossible for someone to be a caller to Allah without knowledge.

This is if we mean knowledge of what one calls to; we do not mean that one cannot call to Allah unless he is deeply learned in the sciences. No; if we said that, the saying of the Messenger would not be valid: «Convey from me, even if it is a single verse»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3461) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn 'Amr.]]. Do you understand?

So the answer has two aspects. The first aspect: there is no contradiction between knowledge and da'wah. The second aspect: da'wah is not possible except with knowledge of what one calls to.

There remain the means of da'wah. The means of da'wah are many; da'wah is not restricted to a person standing and speaking. Da'wah occurs through speech, through writing, and through action itself. A person whom you trust, you look at what he does, and you do likewise; this is da'wah, a type of da'wah. Indeed, da'wah through action and deed may be more powerful in influence than da'wah by the tongue.

* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. The student of knowledge who wants to call to Allah, especially in the neighborhoods, because, Shaykh, there are many wrongs in the neighborhoods, including wrongs regarding prayer. And as you know, it has its circumstances. A person is not obliged to leave what concerns him in his religion and worldly life in order to go to people knocking on their doors to command or admonish them. This is not obligatory.
* The student: There is recommendation in it: «Whoever among you sees an evil»[[Narrated by Muslim (49/78) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]].
* The Shaykh: Yes, "whoever sees," but the Messenger ﷺ did not say: seek out the sight of evil. And this one who does not pray, I may admonish him in the market or in the mosque. Therefore we find people now find it burdensome for someone to knock on their door to admonish or command them, and perhaps some reaction results from that, which is called a reactive response.
* Student: Shaykh, how do we reconcile this with the Messenger's hadith: «There will come out of the Fire people who never did a good deed at all»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (806) and Muslim (183/302), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]?
* The Shaykh: Yes, and the creed?
* The student: They have creed; they are monotheists.
* The Shaykh: But this one has now been punished; he was punished, he was not left.
* The student: The creed is that he comes out of the Fire.
* The Shaykh: But has this one been visited by angels? Angels do not descend upon him. Furthermore, this person must have a creed of faith; otherwise we would say the Christians too come out of the Fire by their creed.

* Student: Challenge.

What is meant by this: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah and does righteous deeds﴾ [Fussilat 33]?
* Student: It means everyone who undertakes the call to Allah, whether by word, by deeds, or by speech.
* The Shaykh: That is, general: everyone who calls.
Did someone mention that it is the muezzin?

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: (﴿And the good and the evil are not equal﴾ [Fussilat 34] in their particulars, because some of them are above others).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verses 33–36 (part 2 of 3):

His saying: ﴿And not equal are the good deed and the bad deed﴾. The author (al-Mu'allif, i.e. al-Sa'di) explained it to mean: the good deeds are not equal to one another, and the bad deeds are not equal to one another. On this interpretation, (لَا) (la, "not") is not superfluous; it is original, and the meaning of the verse is the negation of equality among good deeds and the negation of equality among bad deeds. This is a matter without difficulty: some good deeds are better than others, more excellent than others, and more emphatic than others, and likewise some bad deeds are worse than others and more severe. However, there is another interpretation, which is that the meaning is that good and bad deeds are not equal, based on His saying: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ and so on [Fussilat: 34]. Accordingly, (لَا) is superfluous, for emphasis, as it is in His saying: ﴿not [the path] of those who have earned [Your] anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7]. Here (لَا) is superfluous for emphasis, and for this reason, if you said outside the Noble Qur'an, "not [the path] of those who have earned anger and those who are astray," the sentence would be sound.

If someone asks: is there a preference between them?

We say: the author preferred the first meaning, that good deeds are not equal and bad deeds are not equal. Some scholars preferred the second, because He said: ﴿then, [behold], the one between whom and you there was enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend﴾ and so on. If both meanings are taken together, there is no harm, because when a verse can bear two meanings equally, and they are not contradictory, it is interpreted as both of them together. This is a rule in the principles of tafsir (usul al-tafsir).

(Al-hasanah) is that which is praiseworthy to mention, and (al-sayyi'ah) is that which is blameworthy to mention. This is the general explanation of good deed and bad deed.

He said: ﴿Repel﴾ the bad deed ﴿with that which is [better]﴾, i.e., with the characteristic which ﴿is best﴾, and so on.

It is strange that the author's words on ﴿Repel with that which is best﴾ imply that the meaning of the preceding sentence is: the good deed is not equal to the bad deed.

﴿Repel﴾ the bad deed ﴿with that which is [better]﴾, i.e., with the characteristic which ﴿is best﴾. May Allah have mercy on him, he informed us that (الَّتِي, "that which") is an attribute of an omitted noun; that is: with the characteristic which is better than the bad deed.

If someone says: the bad deed has nothing good in it, so how can he say "better than the bad deed"?

We say: the superlative form (ism al-tafdil) may come when there is nothing of it in the other party, as in His saying: ﴿The companions of Paradise, that Day, will have a better dwelling place and a finer resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], although the companions of the Fire have in their dwelling place no good and in their resting place no good.

The meaning of the verse is that, since it is customary for a person not to repel an evil deed with what is better, Allah commanded that one repel with what is better. This is because repelling evil takes three forms:

The first: to repel an evil deed with its like. This is permissible.

The second: to repel an evil deed with a good deed, but there is something better than it. This is also permissible, and it is higher than the first.

The third: to repel an evil deed with that which is better, meaning with the best thing by which it can be repelled. This is superior and purer, and it is what Allah commanded. Thus, the response to an evil deed has three forms:

The first: an evil deed with its like: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The second: with a good deed, but another good deed is better than it.

The third: with that which is better: meaning, if a person wrongs you, do not respond with a wrong, nor even with a good deed; respond with what is better.

The author gives examples: (like anger with patience, ignorance with forbearance, and wrongdoing with pardon). These are examples: (anger with patience) means if a person becomes angry with you, be patient and bear it; (ignorance with forbearance) means if a person behaves ignorantly toward you by wronging you, respond with forbearance.

If someone asks: does ignorance (al-jahl) oppose forbearance (al-hilm), or does it oppose knowledge (al-ilm)?

We say: ignorance in the sense of lack of knowledge is answered with knowledge, but ignorance which is the opposite of forbearance, in the sense that a person is aggressive toward others, is answered with forbearance. An Arab poet said:

Let no one among us act ignorantly, lest we act more ignorantly than the ignorant ones.

Likewise, wrongdoing is answered with pardon: if a person wrongs you, pardon him. It has been mentioned many times before, and we repeat it again and again, that pardon is recommended only when it brings about reform, based on His saying: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

﴿Then, [behold], the one between whom and you there was enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. (Fa-idha): (idha) is the sudden (fuja'iyyah) "idha," and (fa) is conjunctive. That is: when you repel with what is better, this state will suddenly overtake you, which is that the enmity of the person who wronged you turns into a close, devoted friendship, so that he becomes as if he were a close friend, i.e., a near companion. Consider that the answer is introduced by the sudden (idha), so that it becomes clear to you that the transformation of his enmity into devoted friendship does not take long, because the sudden (idha) indicates immediacy.

﴿Then, [behold], the one between whom and you there was enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. If the one informing of this were other than Allah, Glorified and Exalted, a person would hesitate: how can an enemy become a devoted friend so quickly?

We say: who is it that informed of this? It is Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and who is more truthful in speech than Allah? Moreover, the One who informed of this is the One whose control over the hearts of the children of Adam is between two of His fingers; He turns them however He wills. Do not consider this far-fetched. Affairs are in the hand of Allah, and how many an enemy has become a friend, and a friend has become an enemy.

﴿Then, [behold], the one between whom and you there was enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34], meaning: your enemy will become like a close friend in his love, if you do this. So (al-ladhi) is the subject (mubtada'), (ka'annahu) is the predicate (khabar), and (idha) is an adverb (zarf) for the sense of comparison.

﴿Then, [behold], the one between whom and you there was enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. The author parsed it, saying: "(al-ladhi): subject (mubtada')," "﴿between whom and you there was enmity﴾ this is the relative clause (sila al-mawsul)," "(ka'annahu) is the predicate of the subject (al-ladhi)," and "(idha) is an adverb for the sense of comparison." In His saying ﴿Then, [behold], the one﴾, (idha) is an adverb for the sense of comparison which is (ka'annahu), because the comparison includes the meaning of a verb, and therefore it is valid for the adverb to be connected to it.

This is what the author maintained regarding (idha). The correct view is that (idha) is the sudden "idha," which does not require anything to be attached to it.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient; and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35]: ﴿none is granted it﴾, i.e., the characteristic which is best is given, ﴿except those who are patient﴾, and ﴿none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ — reward ﴿great﴾ [Fussilat: 35]).

﴿And none is granted it﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (i.e., the characteristic is given). It was also said that its meaning is: it is not granted success in it. The meanings are close; that is, no one attains this characteristic, which is repelling with what is better, except those who are patient. This sentence contains restriction (hasr) by means of negation and affirmation: ﴿and none is granted it except those who are patient﴾ [Fussilat: 35].

His saying: ﴿except those who are patient﴾ [Fussilat: 35], meaning: they restrain themselves and compel themselves to bear this matter. This is because this matter is difficult, since souls love to take revenge on those who wronged them. But it is said: repel with what is better. For this reason He said: ﴿and none is granted it except those who are patient﴾ [Fussilat: 35]. Every person will suffer great hardship if he takes this path, which is repelling with what is better. He will inevitably face toil and difficulty, so Allah, Exalted, praised those who are patient in this.

Patience does not require us to elaborate at length on it, for they said it has three kinds: patience in obedience to Allah, patience in refraining from His disobedience, and patience in His decrees.

﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient; and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35]. He said: (reward). ﴿One of fortune﴾ means reward. The correct view is that it is said: al-hazz (fortune) is al-nasib (portion), meaning: none is granted it except one who has a great portion, not only of reward but of good character, dignity, deliberateness, and other things; that is, one who has a great portion of reward, good character, dignity, deliberateness, and so on. Therefore one should not restrict it to reward. ﴿And none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35].

When Allah, Exalted, mentioned repelling the enemy among the children of Adam, He mentioned repelling the enemy who is not from the children of Adam, saying: ﴿And if an evocation comes to you from Satan, then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 36]. Look at repelling the enemy who is not from the children of Adam: He did not say "repel with what is better," but said "resort to Allah," because you cannot repel Satan except by resorting to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since Satan is not before you so that you can twist his neck and kill him. Rather, none repels him except Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿And if an evocation comes to you from Satan﴾ [Fussilat: 36].

So the connection between this verse and the one before it is that, when He mentioned repelling the enemy from among the children of Adam, He mentioned repelling the enemy who is not from the children of Adam, saying: ﴿And if an evocation comes to you from Satan, then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 36].

He said: (in) (idha) — there is assimilation (idgham) of the nun of the conditional "in" into the superfluous "ma." The origin of (imma) is (wa-in yanzaghannaka, "and if it should prompt you"), but the superfluous (ma) is frequently added to conditional particles, as in His saying here: (wa-imma yanzaghannaka), and as in His saying: ﴿Whichever [name] you invoke, to Him belong the best names﴾ [al-Isra': 110].

﴿If an evocation comes to you﴾ means: if an evocation comes to you ﴿from Satan﴾, ﴿then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 36] (i.e., if some diverter diverts you from that characteristic or from other good, ﴿then seek refuge in Allah﴾).

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, when we look at his explanation, we find that he restricts this verse to one particular matter, namely, if Satan diverts us from repelling with what is better, then seek refuge in Allah.

The correct view is other than that. The correct view is that the verse is general, which is why He said: ﴿if an evocation comes to you﴾, meaning: if it afflicts you.

﴿from Satan an evocation﴾: (nazgh, "evocation") is indefinite (nakirah) in the context of what?

*Student: Negation.

*Shaykh: Wrong. Read the verse: ﴿And if an evocation comes to you from Satan﴾ [Fussilat: 36]: indefinite in the context of what?

*Student: Indefinite in the context of a condition.

*Shaykh: In the context of a condition. So it is general, whether it concerns repelling with what is better or other matters. Whenever an evocation from Satan afflicts you, seek refuge in Allah. For this reason the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, commanded the one who complained to him of whisperings during prayer to seek refuge in Allah. He said: «Let him spit three times to his left and seek refuge in Allah»[[Narrated by Muslim (2203/68) from the hadith of Uthman ibn Abi al-As.]].

The main point is: whenever an evocation from Satan afflicts you, resort to the One who can repel it, Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But how do I know that Satan has prompted someone? ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268]. Whenever you find that it has been cast into your heart that you should commit a sin, know that it is an evocation from Satan. Whenever it is cast into your heart that you should abandon an act of obedience, that is an evocation from Satan; seek refuge in Allah. Satan is not a tangible thing that a person perceives, sees, or hears; rather, he is recognized by what he casts into the heart.

﴿Then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 36], meaning: hold fast to Him. The author said: (the answer to the condition, and the answer to the command is omitted; that is, He will repel it from you). Where is the command? (seek refuge) — as if someone were saying: "If you seek refuge, what is the result?" The result is that Allah will repel it from you, because Allah, Exalted, did not command you to seek refuge in Him — and seeking refuge, as you know, is seeking protection from what harms — "seek refuge in Allah" and He will repel it from you.

(﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of speech ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ [Fussilat: 36] of deeds): this sentence is causal (ta'lil), explaining His saying ﴿then seek refuge in Allah﴾. That is: when you seek refuge in Him from it, He hears you, and He is All-Knowing of how to repel this Satan who has prompted you. He is All-Hearing of your words when you seek refuge in Him, and All-Knowing of what will repel this Satan from you.

*Among the benefits of the verse: the negation of equality among good deeds with one another, and the negation of equality among bad deeds with one another.

*From this follows a benefit: good deeds differ in rank, and bad deeds differ in rank. Among good deeds are those which are fundamentals of Islam, such as the five pillars, and among them are those which are below that; among them are obligations (fara'id), and among them are supererogatory acts (nawafil).

Among forbidden acts is shirk which expels one from the religion (millah), and there is shirk short of that. The same is said of disbelief (kufr): some of it is grave disbelief, and some is lesser than that. This applies when we say that the meaning is that good deeds are not equal and bad deeds are not equal.

As for when we say: "the good deed and the bad deed are not equal," meaning that the good and bad deed are not alike, this benefits by exhorting to doing good deeds in place of bad deeds. The benefit is not to know that a good deed is not equal to a bad deed, because this is a known matter, and the Qur'an, with its eloquence, would not need to convey it, since it is like saying: "the sky is above us, and the earth is beneath us." Rather, the purpose is to urge that a bad deed be answered with a good deed.

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: guidance to repelling bad deeds.

*Student: "Repel."

*Shaykh: From where is it taken? From His saying: ﴿Repel﴾; it is derived from His saying: ﴿Repel with that which is best﴾ [Fussilat: 34].

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: encouragement to the highest levels in repelling bad deeds, derived from His saying: ﴿best﴾. He did not say "repel with the good," but said: ﴿with that which is best﴾ [Fussilat: 34].

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, Exalted, turns the hearts, so an enemy may become a friend and a friend an enemy, based on His saying: ﴿Then, [behold], the one between whom and you there was enmity﴾ [Fussilat: 34].

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: that pride in sin should not take hold of you so that you say: "It is impossible for me to remain silent before this one who wronged me; I must take my right." We say: if you take your right, that is permissible, but there is a character which is better and more perfect, which is repelling with what is best.

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: that repelling with what is best is burdensome to the soul, based on His saying: ﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient﴾ [Fussilat: 35]. But be patient.

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever takes this path, which is repelling evil with what is better, has a great portion of good character, reward, dignity, manliness, nobility, and other things, based on His saying: ﴿And none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35].

*Among the benefits of the verse that follows: that a person's refuge when fearing what he cannot repel is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying: ﴿And if an evocation comes to you from Satan, then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 36].

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whenever you sense any prompting of Satan, whether by neglecting what is commanded or committing what is forbidden, you must resort to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

If someone says: we find seeking refuge is prescribed in other situations too, such as when reciting the Qur'an, or when entering the lavatory. What is the answer?

The answer: its prescription during recitation of the Qur'an is because Satan dominates a person while he recites the Qur'an, seeking to turn him away from the wise remembrance in it, to turn him away from reflecting upon it, from humility in it, and from a person adhering to its commands and prohibitions and affirming its reports.

The main point is that Satan is keen upon a person when he wishes to recite the Qur'an, so it is fitting that he be commanded to seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Likewise upon entering the lavatory, because the lavatory is a dwelling place of devils. Devils are found in the most vile places, and angels in the purest places. For this reason mosques are the houses of angels, and lavatories are the houses of devils.

*Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Satan and that he has authority over the son of Adam, based on His saying: ﴿from Satan an evocation, then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 36]. And this is so: Allah, Glorified and Exalted, empowered Satan over the children of Adam and strengthened the believers with angels, for when Satan commands immorality, there is another command that opposes it, which is the command of the angel.

Among the benefits of this noble verse is that refuge may be sought only from Allah, as in His words: ﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾ [Fussilat 36]. However, this is restricted to matters that only Allah can accomplish, for refuge from such matters is sought from Allah alone. Likewise, refuge may not be sought from a created being who lacks the power to help. For example, if a person sought refuge in a dead person, that would be shirk (associating partners with Allah), because the dead cannot benefit you. But if he seeks refuge in a living person regarding something that person is able to do, there is no harm in that, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever finds a refuge, let him seek refuge in it."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3601) and Muslim (2886/12), from Abu Hurairah.]] Thus, seeking refuge in a created being regarding what he is able to do is like seeking his help regarding what he is able to do, and like calling upon him for help regarding what he is able to do.

Among the benefits of this noble verse is the affirmation that Allah is As-Sami' (the All-Hearing) and Al-'Alim (the All-Knowing). That is, these are among the Names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It has been mentioned before that belief in a name is not complete except with three elements if the name is transitive (muta'addi), and with two if it is not transitive. As-Sami' is transitive, so one affirms the Name as-Sami', the attribute of hearing (as-sam'), and the effect of it, which is that He hears. The same applies to al-'Alim.

The author's words, may Allah have mercy on him, "(As-Sami' of speech)," are correct, because the object of hearing is speech. His words "(Al-'Alim of action)" are open to objection, because Allah is knowing of action, knowing of speech, and knowing of what is neither action nor speech: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [Qaf 16]. To restrict His knowledge to action is undoubtedly deficient. So it is said: the correct position is that He is Al-'Alim of everything, of speech, action, intentions, the present, the future, and the past.

Among the benefits of the two verses is the eloquence of the Qur'an in mentioning two things close in meaning, even though there is a real difference between them. The reason is that the first verse mentions how to deal with the one who does evil among humankind, namely that you repel him with what is better. The second verse mentions how to deal with the one who does evil from beyond humankind, namely the devil.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 33–36 (part 1 of 3):

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"?﴾ [Fussilat 33]. These are three attributes; when a person possesses them, none is better in speech than him.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿And who is better in speech﴾, i.e., no one is better in speech). The author's explanation of this clause indicates that (man) is an interrogative particle but carries the meaning of negation: (man ahsan), meaning "no one is better." When an interrogative particle is used, or an interrogative is used with the meaning of negation, it is imbued with the meaning of challenge. Which is more eloquent: to say "No one is better in speech than one who invites to Allah," or to say "Who is better?" The second is more eloquent, because the second includes both negation and challenge, as if it says: "Bring me proof that there is someone better than one who invites to Allah." Every interrogative that comes with the meaning of negation is imbued with the meaning of challenge, because when you say "Who is such-and-such?", its meaning is: "I challenge you to bring me something other than that." Thus "man ahsan" is more emphatic in negation than saying "no one is better," because it is an interrogative sentence imbued with the meaning of challenge.

(Ahsan) here is the predicate of the subject, (man) is the subject, and (qawlan) is a specification (tamyiz), because whenever a noun in the accusative comes after a comparative adjective (ism al-tafdil), it is a tamyiz for it.

﴿Who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah﴾: the author said: (with monotheism). This is undoubtedly good, but the verse is more comprehensive than monotheism: ﴿one who invites to Allah﴾ with monotheism, righteous deeds, and other things (...) to Allah.

And His saying ﴿one who invites to Allah﴾ means to the religion of Allah, and the religion of Allah includes monotheism and righteous deeds.

Secondly, He said: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾. He began with reforming others, then followed with reforming the self, although whoever invites to Allah is also reforming himself.

﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: (righteous) is an adjective of a deleted noun; the estimate is: "and does a righteous deed." A deed is not righteous except with two conditions: sincerity to Allah, and following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

"Righteous": what is its i'rab (grammatical analysis)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, we said it is an adjective of a deleted noun, and the estimate is: "does a deed that is righteous."
When does a deed become righteous?
* Student: When its doer fulfills two conditions: sincerity to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and following His Messenger ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: Well done. Sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Is the deed of one who shows off a righteous deed?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: Because sincerity is lacking.
And is the deed of an innovator righteous? No, because following is lacking. At that point we say to these innovators, who have as much sincerity to Allah as they have: your deed is void. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our matter, it is rejected»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18), the wording is his, from the hadith of 'A'isha.]].
Then we say: the reality of sincerity necessitates that you do not worship Allah except in the manner He has legislated. Do not worship Him according to your whims; for if you worship Allah according to your whims, by innovation, you are not sincere. The sincere person must worship Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in the manner He has legislated. Thus the righteous deed is composed of two things: the first, sincerity; and the second, following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

He said: ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 33]. Is this said with the tongue or with the heart? With both together.

If someone says: his saying "Indeed, I am of the Muslims" is undoubtedly a righteous deed, so what is the benefit of mentioning it?

We say: the benefit is that he proclaims this statement and does not care about whoever opposes him. For among people there is one who does a righteous deed, but you find him concealed, lacking the courage that would make him announce it. As for this one, he proclaims it, saying with his tongue, unconcerned: "Indeed, I am of the Muslims."

The sentence, as you know, (innani) is emphasized with (inna). Some scholars mentioned that what is meant is the muezzin, because the muezzin invites to Allah, saying to people: "Hasten to prayer, hasten to success," and because he is a believer who does righteous deeds; and because he says: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah," proclaiming it, and "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am of the Muslims﴾.

However, the correct view is that the verse is general, including the muezzin and non-muezzin. The preacher on the pulpit enters the verse, does he not? He enters the verse. The teacher in his teaching circle enters it too. Thus the verse is more general than what was mentioned.

But know that some of the early scholars mention a specific meaning for the verse, not wishing to restrict it to that meaning, but intending it as an example. This is a matter that may escape some people. We always look in Ibn Kathir or Ibn Jarir and find that someone said: "So-and-so is such." It is a part of the meaning. They do not intend to confine the general to the specific, for they are too knowledgeable to limit the general to some of its individuals, but they intend an example.

For example, some scholars said regarding: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited by those whom We chose from Our servants; and among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir 32]: the one who wrongs himself is the one who delays the prayer past its time; the moderate one is the one who prays it at the end of its time; the foremost in good deeds is the one who prays it at the beginning of its time. This is undoubtedly a restriction; indeed, undoubtedly a specification of the general. So we say: they intended that as an example.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the varying degrees of deeds, from His saying ﴿and who is better in speech﴾ [Fussilat 33], and (ahsan) is a comparative adjective. Undoubtedly deeds vary in terms of kind, in terms of type, and in terms of form and manner: three considerations: in terms of kind, in terms of type, and in terms of form and manner.

They vary in terms of kind: for example, prayer is better than zakat, zakat is better than fasting, fasting is better than hajj. This is in terms of kind. Then this kind also varies from another aspect: the obligatory act of worship is better than its voluntary form; so the noon prayer, for example, is better than night prayer. This is variation in terms of kind but from another aspect.

The evidence for this: the Prophet ﷺ said, relating from Allah: «My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]].

They vary in terms of type: such as the witr prayer being better than general night prayer, and the regular sunnah prayers being better than general voluntary prayer. This is in terms of type; and if you wish, you may make their variation in terms of obligatory and recommended part of this type.

The third: in terms of form: a prayer in which a person is humble, reflects on what he says and does, and is tranquil, versus another prayer in which he limits himself to the obligatory and without humility of heart, for example. Which is better? The first is better.

The essential point: we believe that deeds vary, and that some are more beloved to Allah than others.

There remains the question: does variation in deeds necessitate variation in the doer? Yes. On this basis the doer also differs and varies. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Do not revile my Companions; for by Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you spent gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673) and Muslim (2541/222), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]. The deed is one, but the doer differs.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿one who invites to Allah﴾ [Fussilat 33].
* And from its benefits: an indication of sincerity in da'wah, which we take from His saying ﴿to Allah﴾; for the caller may invite and stand before people, remind them, admonish them, urge them to good and warn them against evil, yet he wants to be esteemed among them. Is this one calling to Allah, or calling to himself? To himself. Therefore sincerity is necessary.

If someone asks: does sincerity get harmed if one intends by da'wah the reform of people?
The answer: it is not harmed, because the basis of his call is for the reform of people.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of the righteous deed that combines the two matters: sincerity and following; by His saying ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of knowledge. From where do we take it? From His saying ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ [Fussilat 33]; for it is impossible to know whether a deed conforms to the Shari'ah or not except through knowledge, and this is clear. Thus the verse is evidence for the obligation of knowledge; because if the righteous deed is obligatory, you must know it through the Shari'ah, and what an obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: that the Muslim should be proud of his religion, proclaim it, say "Indeed, I am of the Muslims," and not be shy when told that he is a Muslim; by His saying ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 33].

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of avoiding self-praise; for He said ﴿of the Muslims﴾ and did not say "and said, I am a Muslim"; because a person may take pride in saying "I am a Muslim" and boast more than he would if he said "I am of the Muslims."

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of brotherhood among Muslims; by His saying ﴿of the Muslims﴾, an indication that "I am like one of these; I do not separate from them."

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is a question that comes up to us often: is seeking knowledge better, or occupying oneself with da'wah?

In reality it is an imprecise question. Firstly, it is possible to combine this and that. We know that the caller does not occupy his time from the dawn prayer until after the night prayer always calling to others. Does anyone among the callers do this? Never. He calls for half an hour here and half an hour there. As for remaining silent from the dawn prayer until the night prayer, that is impossible; there must be intervals. So combining da'wah to Allah with seeking knowledge is not impossible: he seeks knowledge for an hour or two and then calls for half an hour, for example. There is no contradiction. That is one point.

Secondly: it is impossible to call to Allah without knowledge, and calling to Allah in ignorance may cause more harm than not calling. Many callers have zeal and love for good, so you find them forbidding what is permitted or making obligatory what is not obligatory, based on their zeal. Had they possessed knowledge, they would have had steadfastness. It is not hidden from you what 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did at the Treaty of Hudaybiyya: he began to oppose the treaty and came to the Messenger, peace be upon him, wanting to undo the treaty[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2731) from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and in it: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I came to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ and said: Are you not truly the Prophet of Allah? He said: 'Yes.' I said: Are we not upon the truth and our enemy upon falsehood? He said: 'Yes.' I said: Then why should we accept humiliation in our religion? He said: 'I am the Messenger of Allah, and I do not disobey Him, and He is my helper.' I said: Did you not used to tell us that we would come to the House and circumambulate it? He said: 'Yes, but did I inform you that we would come to it this year?' He said: I said: No. He said: 'Then you will come to it and circumambulate it.'"]]. However, steadfastness like that of Abu Bakr is what made the truth manifest. So it is impossible for someone to be a caller to Allah without knowledge.

This is if we mean knowledge of what one calls to; we do not mean that one cannot call to Allah unless he is deeply learned in the sciences. No; if we said that, the saying of the Messenger would not be valid: «Convey from me, even if it is a single verse»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3461) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn 'Amr.]]. Do you understand?

So the answer has two aspects. The first aspect: there is no contradiction between knowledge and da'wah. The second aspect: da'wah is not possible except with knowledge of what one calls to.

There remain the means of da'wah. The means of da'wah are many; da'wah is not restricted to a person standing and speaking. Da'wah occurs through speech, through writing, and through action itself. A person whom you trust, you look at what he does, and you do likewise; this is da'wah, a type of da'wah. Indeed, da'wah through action and deed may be more powerful in influence than da'wah by the tongue.

* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. The student of knowledge who wants to call to Allah, especially in the neighborhoods, because, Shaykh, there are many wrongs in the neighborhoods, including wrongs regarding prayer. He knows that so-and-so and so-and-so neglect the prayer. If he goes walking to them, his time is lost, and some of them say he is not there, and the person falls into embarrassment: either he leaves them or he occupies himself with what he is engaged in, and time is short, and if it is scattered it becomes little. Is the person excused if he thinks that this person is far from responding and far from accepting from him, and he will not find a suitable time for him?
* The Shaykh: This is in reality an admonition or a command. Da'wah is general; but to go to so-and-so and advise him is in reality an admonition; and if you have authority, it is commanding good. And as you know, it has its circumstances. A person is not obliged to leave what concerns him in his religion and worldly life in order to go to people knocking on their doors to command or admonish them. This is not obligatory.
* The student: There is recommendation in it: «Whoever among you sees an evil»[[Narrated by Muslim (49/78) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]].
* The Shaykh: Yes, "whoever sees," but the Messenger ﷺ did not say: seek out the sight of evil. And this one who does not pray, I may admonish him in the market or in the mosque. Therefore we find people now find it burdensome for someone to knock on their door to admonish or command them, and perhaps some reaction results from that, which is called a reactive response.
* Student: Shaykh, how do we reconcile this with the Messenger's hadith: «There will come out of the Fire people who never did a good deed at all»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (806) and Muslim (183/302), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]?
* The Shaykh: Yes, and the creed?
* The student: They have creed; they are monotheists.
* The Shaykh: But this one has now been punished; he was punished, he was not left.
* The student: The creed is that he comes out of the Fire.
* The Shaykh: But has this one been visited by angels? Angels do not descend upon him. Furthermore, this person must have a creed of faith; otherwise we would say the Christians too come out of the Fire by their creed.
