If you blame a person for an act of disobedience he committed, and he then argues by the decree after repenting, I accept from him. This happens often. A person commits a sin, then feels great regret and says: "It is the decree of Allah and He does what He wills. How did this happen to me? How did my soul overcome me?" This is not a problem. We have extended this discussion for you, but excuse us, because we see that a student of knowledge must have, as they say, a background, and I say: what is a background except having knowledge of such matters, so that he may free himself through them from the doubts Satan casts upon him, and free himself from the doubts cast upon him by the allies of Satan.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of Allah's knowledge of everything these people do, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do⁠﴾.
* And from its benefits: restricting the ruling to what is in dispute, even though it is general. That is, even though the ruling is general, we may restrict this ruling to the place of dispute. From where is this derived? From the fronting of the object ﴿of what you do He is Seeing⁠﴾. We do not say that this restriction is literal, that He, the Mighty and Majestic, knows only what they did; rather He knows everything. But since the discussion concerned their deeds, the verse or ruling came in the form of restriction, out of intense warning and to show that they will never escape Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And Allah knows best.

* Student: May Allah reward you well. We said the story of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and his wife Fatimah with the Prophet ﷺ. We said the Messenger ﷺ accepted the reality but disliked the disputation. I did not fully understand...
* Shaykh: He accepted the reality, which is their argument by the decree. The sleeper in reality is not blameworthy: ﴿It is He who takes you in death by night and knows what you have committed by day. Then He resurrects you therein⁠﴾ [al-An'am 60]. From whom? From Allah. So he says: our souls are in the hand of Allah; had He willed us to rise, we would have risen. This is the reality. But as for disputing with the Prophet ﷺ about the decree, this is something that should not be. That is why you sense that he was not pleased; he struck his thigh and said: "And man is more than anything given to disputation." Disputation may sometimes be for the truth and is accepted, even if it involves argument, when it is for the truth.
* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. You gave us a principle: if we find an innovation, we do not counter it with another innovation, but with the Sunnah. Now there is what is called "tamthil" (dramatic representation), which is a degraded representation. If we find what is now called degraded tamthil, and some have called for purposeful tamthil, is this countering innovation with innovation?
* Shaykh: The matter of tamthil is not an innovation in itself. Tamthil is bringing meanings closer through their actual form. Tamthil appears in the authentic hadith in the story of the angel who came to the leper, the bald man and the blind man in his form and said that he was a needy man and a traveller. He was neither needy, nor a traveller, nor a leper, nor bald, nor blind, but this was for approximation. What is wrong is exaggeration in tamthil such that we call people to nothing but it. So we say: calling to Allah has means; anything which presents the reality and warns against it, without including falsehood, imitating animals or the like, or a man imitating a woman and vice versa, there is no harm in it. We do not reject tamthil absolutely, nor do we encourage it, and we reject that it be the means of calling to Allah, because if you accustom people to being called to Allah only by this means, they forget what is more important, which is the admonition of the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
* Student: May Allah increase you. You mentioned in the story of Adam's argument with Musa that he said: "Why do you blame me for something Allah wrote against me before I was created by forty years?" Does this indicate that Adam was created before the pen was created by forty years, while it is known that Allah the Mighty and Majestic...
* Shaykh: No, he says: "It was written against me before I was created." It was written before the creation of Adam.
* Student: That is, when Allah first created the pen, He said: write the decrees...
* Shaykh: Wait, stay with me. I am correcting your question. I understood from your words that this indicates Adam was created before it was written against him? Adam was created after it was written against him, but forty years after. So how do we reconcile his saying "forty years" with Allah having created the pen and said to it: write, fifty thousand years before He created the heavens? It is said: if this wording is sound and preserved, then this is another writing specific to Adam.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah protect you, how do we respond to those who say that injustice may be attributed to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by way of reciprocity? They say that the retaliation of the wrongdoer against the wrongdoer is perfection, and they cite the verse of the pre-Islamic poet:
Let no one ignorant among us act with ignorance toward us, so that we act with ignorance beyond the ignorance of the ignorant.
* Shaykh: I say: this is strange. Where in the Qur'an and Sunnah does Allah the Most High describe Himself with injustice in response to the wrongdoer? Where?
* Student: There is none.
* Shaykh: If there is none, why is Allah named with injustice, when He has negated it from Himself?
* Student: They said that retaliation against the wrongdoer is perfection.

* Shaykh: No, never. Taking revenge on the wrongdoer is perfection, but returning wrong with wrong is not. For this reason the Qur'an and the Sunnah do not say, "When they wronged us, we wronged them." Rather, Allah says: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl 118]. As for mockery, yes; deception, yes; scheming (*makr*) and plotting (*kayd*), this is fine. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned these attributes in response to one who dealt with them in the same way (...).
* * *
* Student: ﴿When it came to them—and indeed it is a Book of might (41). Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation from One who is All-Wise, Praiseworthy (42). Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is the Possessor of forgiveness and of painful punishment﴾ [Fussilat 41–43].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the accursed. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾ [Fussilat 40]. What is the linguistic meaning of *ilhad* (deviation)?
* Student: Inclination (*mayl*).
* Shaykh: *Mayl* is derived from where?
* Student: From *alhada*, meaning "he deviated" and "he inclined."
* Another student: *Al-lahd* is inclination.
* Shaykh: Yes. It is from *lahd al-qabr* (the niche in the grave), because of its inclination to one side of it. Does *ilhad* occur in the names of Allah, and does it occur in the signs of Allah?
* Student: Yes, it occurs in the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: His cosmic signs and His legislative signs.
* Shaykh: It occurs in the names of Allah and it occurs in the signs of Allah. What is the evidence that it occurs in the names of Allah?
* Student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ [al-A'raf 180].
* Shaykh: And regarding the signs?
* Student: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us.﴾ With what does deviation in the names of Allah occur?
* Student: It occurs in the names of Allah (...), describing Allah or naming Allah with what He did not name Himself with, or
* Shaykh: The general rule, or the criterion, is: inclining them away from what is obligatory. Then explain in detail.
* Student: Then what occurs (...) with what He did not name Himself with, or...
* Shaykh: Naming Allah with what He did not name Himself with. Give an example.
* Student: The names of Allah, we have not said them (...), only the legislated ones.
* Shaykh: So, regarding the signs, is the deviation in the signs of Allah?
* Student: (...) three categories. The signs are either legislated signs or cosmic ones, and the legislated signs (...) three types in the cosmic signs...
* Shaykh: Deviation in the cosmic signs:
* Student: That they are attributed to other than Allah.
* Shaykh: That they are attributed to other than Allah.
* Student: Or that one believes in a partner with Allah, or that one takes a helper for Allah.
* Shaykh: Excellent. That one attributes them to other than Allah, such as?
* Student: Such as one saying: "The one who sent down the rain is such-and-such a saint."
* Shaykh: Yes, excellent. That is, one believes that someone created something independently, alone. Partnership?
* Student: Partnership: that one claims that Allah has a helper, that there is someone who shares with Him...
* Shaykh: How "a helper for Allah"? We say "a partner."
* Student: Like some of the Rafidah (Rafidites, a Shi'i sect) who believe that in this universe Allah has a partner...
* Shaykh: That with Allah there is another god who manages the universe, managing it directly. The third?
* Student: The third: that they believe Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has a helper.
* Shaykh: A helper, meaning Allah is the sole creator, but there is someone who assists Him? However, this assistant has no share in creation. By this we know the difference between the helper (*mu'in*) and the partner (*mushārik*). What is the evidence for the negation of these three matters in the Qur'an?
* Student: ﴿Say: "Call upon those you claimed besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth, and they have no partnership in them, and He has no supporter among them"﴾ [Saba' 22].
* Shaykh: Say it, the verse.
* Student: His saying: ﴿Say: "Call upon those you claimed besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth, and they have no partnership in them, and He has no supporter among them"﴾ [Saba' 22].
* Shaykh: Excellent. Deviation in the legislated signs?
* Student: Either by denying them, or by opposing them, or by distorting them.
* Shaykh: Yes, it occurs by denying them and distorting them. The third is opposing them. Excellent.
﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾. We have not spoken about deviation in the names, because it is not in the verse. But for the completeness of the benefit we say: deviation occurs in the names of Allah, and it is inclining them away from what is obligatory. This is, first: naming Allah, exalted is He, with what He did not name Himself with, like the philosophers' naming Him "the efficient cause" (*'illa fa'ila*). They say: "Allah is the efficient cause of this universe." And the Christians' naming Him "Father," they call Him "the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit." Second: denying some of the names, or what they indicate. This is the opposite of the first. The first named Allah with what He did not name Himself with; the second denied what Allah named Himself with, either entirely or partially, or denies what the names include of meanings and attributes. He denies the names, or some of them, or what they indicate of meanings and attributes. For example, those who say that Allah, glorified and exalted, has no names or attributes, like the extreme Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilites, a rationalist theological school) and the Jahmiyyah (followers of Jahm ibn Safwan), these are deviators. And those who say: He has names but they have no meanings, these are also deviators, as is well known from the school of the Mu'tazilah. And those who deny some attributes, like the Ash'ariyyah (followers of al-Ash'ari), are also deviators. They say, for example: Allah has no attributes except seven, which they claim reason indicates, and that the rest are not indicated by reason. We have spoken about this at length, and there is no need to repeat it. How many types is this?
* Student: Two types.
* Shaykh: Two types. The first is what? Naming Allah with what He did not name Himself with. The second is the opposite: denying the names or what they include of meanings and attributes, either all of them or some. The third: deriving from His names names for idols. Among it is the derivation of *Allat* from *al-Ilah* (the God), *al-Uzza* from *al-'Aziz* (the Mighty), and *Manat* from *al-Mannan* (the Bestower). This too is deviation in the names of Allah. All this deviation and other than it concerning the names of Allah, Allah has threatened the one who follows it in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ [al-A'raf 180]. In His saying: ﴿are not hidden from Us﴾, this is a type of attribute. The scholars say: attributes are divided into two kinds. So which kind is His saying: ﴿are not hidden from Us﴾?
* Student: Negative attributes.
* Shaykh: Excellent, negative attributes. May Allah bless you. Our question now: does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, have negative names, meaning pure negation, or not?
* Student: Allah is not described (...) pure.
* Shaykh: By pure negation? Then what is the meaning of the negation by which Allah is sometimes described?
* Student: That it includes affirmation of perfection.
* Shaykh: The affirmation of a perfection opposite to what is negated. Good. For example, ﴿are not hidden from Us﴾ includes the affirmation of the perfection of knowledge. What is meant by this phrase, ﴿are not hidden from Us﴾?
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: No, that is not its meaning. What is meant by it, i.e., what is its purpose?
* Student: Informing about the knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted.
* Shaykh: No, that is not it.
* Student: A warning (*tahdid*).
* Shaykh: A warning. The intended meaning is a warning. In the noble verse, ﴿Is one who will be thrown into the Fire better, or one who will come secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾. Someone may say: this interrogative has no meaning, because everyone knows that one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection is better than one who is thrown into the Fire?
* Student: It is an answer to His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾. So He answered, glorified: ﴿Is one who will be thrown into the Fire...﴾.
* Shaykh: No, I did not mean the connection to what precedes it; you mentioned the connection. But I say: ﴿Is one who will be thrown into the Fire better, or one who will come secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, asks whether this is better or not. I say: how is it asked when it is known?
* Student: A rhetorical question of denial (*istifham inkari*).
* Shaykh: The intended meaning is a rhetorical question of denial, meaning it is in reality a statement. That is one aspect, a good aspect. That the intended meaning is: one who is thrown into the Fire and one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection are not equal. So the interrogative is declarative. What is the second aspect?
* Student: O Shaykh, we say that this kind of expression is intended to silence the opponent (*ifham al-khasm*).
* Shaykh: Yes, that this expression is intended to silence the opponent. Does it have a parallel?
* Student: Yes, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾ [al-Naml 59].
* Shaykh: Yes, it has a parallel: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾. It is known that there is no comparison, let alone a comparison of preference between Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and their gods. But this is from the mode of silencing the opponent, meaning that their gods have no good in them, and likewise the one who is thrown into the Fire has no good in him. What is the guarantee of coming secure on the Day of Resurrection? Who is the one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?
* Student: Allah mentioned them in His Book.
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am 82].
* Shaykh: Allah mentioned them in His saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾.
* Shaykh: Complete it.
* Student: ﴿For them there is security, and they are guided﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿For them there is security, and they are guided﴾ [al-An'am 82]. Security in this world and the Hereafter. May Allah bless you. I think we have stopped at this point?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 41–42 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them—and indeed it is a Book of might (41). Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾ [Fussilat 41, 42].

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them﴾: This is a sentence emphasized with ﴿inna﴾ (indeed). What is meant by ﴿the Reminder﴾ is the Noble Quran, as Allah the Blessed and Exalted says: ﴿And this is a blessed Reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya 50], and He the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [az-Zukhruf 44]. The Quran is called a reminder (dhikr) because it reminds its possessor of what is for the righteous of good and what is for the tyrants of evil; and because it is a remembrance (dhikr) for its possessor, meaning that Allah raises his remembrance by means of it, the remembrance of one who holds fast to it; and for this reason He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. And because it reminds a person of his Lord, for the closest of people, or among the closest of people, to Allah is the one who recites His Book. For this reason we say that the recitation of the Book is the best of remembrance in general, whereas the specific remembrances restricted to a particular thing are subordinate to what they are restricted to.

As for His saying ﴿when it comes to them﴾, it means: at the time it came to them. Know that ﴿lamma﴾ (when/since) comes in the Arabic language in several senses, among them: that it is a temporal adverb, as in this verse, so the meaning of ﴿when it came to them﴾ is: at the time it came to them. Another is that it comes as a negating particle that is jussive, but it is used to indicate the expectation of what follows it, as in His saying the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8]. Here ﴿lamma﴾ means (lam), so it is a negation, but it is only used before something expected. The meaning of ﴿they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ is: they have not tasted it, but they deserve it, and the punishment is near for them. Another is that it comes in the sense of (illa, except), as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [at-Tariq 4], meaning: except that over it is a guardian. Another is that it comes as a conditional particle, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿So when the bearer of good tidings came, he cast it over his face﴾ [Yusuf 96]. ﴿Falaamma an jaa﴾ here is conditional, and you say: "When he visited me, I honoured him." So these are four senses of (lamma): the first: temporal; the second: negating and jussive; the third: in the sense of (illa); the fourth: conditional.

﴿When it came to them﴾, meaning: at the time it came to them. Allah the Exalted did not mention the predicate of (inna) but omitted it so that the mind would wander in estimating it in every direction; that is, a person keeps asking: what will happen to them? You find a person hoping, thinking, this or that or that. For this reason the commentator estimated it by his words: (We will recompense them). So ﴿nujazihim﴾ (We will recompense them), according to the author's interpretation, is the predicate of (inna). It is permissible to estimate other than this; you may say: Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them will be punished, or theirs is the Fire of Hell, or what is similar to that. The point is that its omission is so that the mind goes, what? In every direction in estimating the predicate. But we know with certainty that it cannot be estimated as a pleasant predicate; that is, we cannot say, as an estimate: Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them—for them are the Gardens of Bliss. This is impossible; rather, it is estimated as whatever punishment you estimate. This is from the eloquence of the Quran, that it leaves the matter open for a person to estimate in every way.

He said: (﴿And indeed, it is a Book of might﴾ — mani', unassailable). ﴿And indeed, it is a Book﴾: Allah the Mighty and Majestic has emphasized the might of this Book with two emphatics: (inna) and the lam. In reality, the focus of the benefit is not ﴿Book﴾ alone; the focus of the benefit is His saying ﴿of might﴾; this is what is important. As for ﴿Book﴾, everything is a book; everything written is a book: ﴿She said: O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me. Indeed it is from Sulayman﴾ [an-Naml 29, 30]. But the focus of the benefit is His saying ﴿of might﴾. ﴿And indeed, it is a Book﴾: the pronoun in ﴿indeed it﴾ refers back to the Reminder, which is the Quran, and ﴿Book﴾ here means written, and it is written in the mushafs, in the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels. Do you understand? So it is a book in three places: in the Preserved Tablet; second, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels; third, in the scrolls in our hands. And His saying ﴿of might﴾: the author said: (mani', unassailable). There is no doubt that (mani') is among the meanings of ﴿'aziz﴾, but it is more general than what the author said. ﴿'Aziz﴾: in the sense of mani', meaning that no one can reach it with harm except that Allah exposes him. Second: ﴿'Aziz﴾ in the sense of dominant (ghalib). The Quran undoubtedly dominates everything else, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion﴾ [at-Tawbah 33]. So it is dominant over everything. Thus it is unassailable, so that no one can reach it with harm except that Allah exposes him; and second, it is dominant. For this reason, when the Muslim nation adhered to it, it was dominant; it toppled the thrones of Chosroes and Caesar and other tyrants, and by it the eastern and western parts of the earth were opened. When the Muslim nation turned away from it, it was deprived of this great good, which is might, dominance and subjugation.

﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat 42]: meaning there is no book before it that contradicts it, nor after it. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾: ﴿al-batil﴾ (falsehood) is the opposite of the sound and the opposite of truth. The jurists say: the prayer is invalid (batilah); the prayer is valid (sahihah). So they make invalidity (butlan) the opposite of validity (sihhah). In the Noble Quran: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 62]. So He made falsehood the counterpart of truth. Thus ﴿falsehood cannot approach it﴾ is that which is the opposite of truth. As for His saying ﴿from before it or from behind it﴾, the author explained it with a strange interpretation; he said: (meaning there is no book before it that contradicts it, nor after it). There is clear scrutiny of this, and the correct view is that ﴿falsehood cannot approach it from before it﴾ means in what it reports, and ﴿nor from behind it﴾ means in what it reports about the unseen. Everything it reports is true, and everything it reports as going to happen is true. Also, ﴿falsehood cannot approach it﴾ with respect to rulings: everything it rules is true, and its end is truth. So the meaning is that this Noble Quran contains nothing false, neither in reporting what has passed, which is what is ﴿before it﴾, nor in reporting what is to come, which is His saying ﴿nor from behind it﴾. And if you wish, reverse it and say: what is before it is the future, and what is behind it is the past. Likewise, falsehood cannot approach it with respect to its rulings: all its rulings are justice, with no oppression in them. For this reason you find that the Quran, just as it gives the Lord His right of worship, also gives the created being his right: ﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him﴾: this is the right of Allah; after it: ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ [an-Nisa 36]. So it is true in its rulings and true in its reports. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat 42]. And recite, if you wish, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]: ﴿truth﴾ with regard to reports, ﴿justice﴾ with regard to rulings.

﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾: ﴿tanzil﴾ (revelation) is the predicate of an omitted subject. It may be a second predicate for His saying ﴿And indeed it﴾: a second, or a third? A third. ﴿Book﴾ ... ﴿of might﴾ is an adjective of ﴿Book﴾. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ may also be an adjective of ﴿Book﴾. On this basis ﴿tanzil﴾ is a second predicate. It may also be a second predicate of (inna), meaning: ﴿falsehood cannot approach it﴾ is a second predicate of (inna); on this basis ﴿tanzil﴾ is a third predicate. It may also be that ﴿tanzil﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: it is ﴿a revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾. Perhaps this estimate is preferable, because it indicates that the sentence is a new sentence explaining the greatness of this Quran. He said: ﴿tanzil﴾, meaning: sent down (munazzal) from One Wise, Praiseworthy. When we interpret ﴿tanzil﴾ as "sent down," the verbal noun takes the meaning of what? When we interpret ﴿tanzil﴾ as "sent down" (munazzal), the verbal noun here takes the meaning of what? The verbal noun comes both in the sense of the passive participle and in the sense of the active participle, and what determines this is the context.

﴿A revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾: ﴿Hakim﴾ means possessor of wisdom (hikmah) and possessor of judgment (hukm). Judgment belongs to Allah, and wisdom is in His rulings, the Mighty and Majestic. The Lord the Mighty and Majestic is characterized by judgment that has no one to repel it, by an executed judgment that has no one to prevent it. In the transmitted supplication: "None can withhold what You have given, and none can give what You have withheld."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (844) and Muslim (593/138), from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.]] He is also characterized by wisdom: all His rulings are wisdom. If you look at the decreed rulings, you find them in the utmost wisdom, and if you look at the legislative rulings, you find them likewise in the utmost wisdom. So He the Mighty and Majestic is a Judge and possessor of wisdom. How many a judge has no wisdom? And how many a wise person has no judgment? Many men are wise and sensible, but have no authority; he cannot judge even his own wife. And how many a person is a ruler, powerful with authority, but has no wisdom? As for the Lord the Mighty and Majestic, He is what? A Judge who is Wise. He mentioned the Wise before the Praiseworthy, because praise follows from wisdom, for the wise is praised. The author said: (i.e., Allah, the Praised), meaning: by ﴿Hakim Hamid﴾ is meant Allah. His saying (the Praised) points out that ﴿fa'il﴾ here has the sense of ﴿maf'ul﴾. In Arabic, ﴿fa'il﴾ comes in the sense of active and in the sense of passive: when you say, "so-and-so is jarih" in the sense of "wounded" (majruh), and "so-and-so is sami'" in the sense of "hearing" (sami'), it comes in Arabic in the sense of active and in the sense of passive. Here the author interpreted it as "praised." But is this interpretation deficient? The answer: yes, there is deficiency in it, because ﴿hamid﴾ here has both the sense of active and passive: He is praised, and He is also a praiser. Does not Allah the Exalted praise the believers, the messengers, and whomever He wills of His servants a great deal? This is praise; that is, the description of those created beings whom Allah praised is in reality their praising Him. So will ﴿Hamid﴾ then mean?
* Student: In the sense of active and passive.
* Shaykh: In the sense of active and passive: in the sense of passive, that He is praised; and in the sense of active, that He is a praiser. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, is deficient in his interpretation.

﴿A revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾

* In this noble verse: a warning to those who deny the Quran, by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾; and the predicate is omitted so that the mind may wander in estimating it in every good direction.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that this Quran is a Reminder; Allah named it a reminder for what we mentioned in the commentary.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these people denied the Reminder after it came to them and they had verified and recognized it. It is known that one who denies a thing after it has become certain to him is more sinful and more grievous than one who denies a matter that is doubtful to him. This is taken from His saying ﴿when it came to them﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that this Quran is mighty and dominant; no one can reach it with harm except that Allah exposes him, and no one stands before it except that he is defeated and overcome. Allah the Exalted described the Quran as mighty, glorious, and noble, and with many other attributes, which shows the greatness of this Quran.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever holds fast to the Quran has might. Its basis: if the Quran is mighty, then whoever holds fast to it must attain might, otherwise the Quran would not be mighty. This is indicated by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs might, and to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Noble Quran is truth, free of falsehood in every respect, by His saying ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾. Is this attribute of the Quran one of negation or one of affirmation?
* Students: Negation.
* Shaykh: Yes, negation. So what does it contain in terms of affirmation? We say: when falsehood is removed from it in every respect, from before it and from behind it, it follows that it is truth in what respect? In every respect.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, derived from His saying ﴿A revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾. The reason it is the speech of Allah: the Quran is an attribute, not a separate independent entity. If it is an attribute, and Allah mentioned that it was sent down from Him, it must be His speech. But if the thing Allah said He sent down were a specific thing separate from Allah, this would not indicate that it is one of Allah's attributes. ﴿And He sent down from the sky water﴾ [al-Baqarah 22]: is this water created or one of Allah's attributes?
* Students: Created.
* Shaykh: Created. ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [az-Zumar 6]: created, because it is a thing separate from Allah. ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for the people﴾ [al-Hadid 25]: created. But when sending down or revelation occurs regarding a matter that is an attribute, it cannot be created and separate from Allah; rather it is an attribute of Allah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation (uluw). The proof: He said ﴿a revelation from One Wise﴾, and if it is a revelation from Him, it must be that He is above, and He is so, the Mighty and Majestic. We have mentioned many times, and others have also mentioned, that Allah's elevation is established by all the proofs: the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason, and the natural disposition (fitrah), all of which agree on Allah's elevation.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of these two names for Allah the Mighty and Majestic: (al-Hakim) and (al-Hamid), and the affirmation of the meanings and attributes they include. (Al-Hakim) includes two great attributes. (Al-Hakim) includes two great attributes, which are?
* Student: Hakim (wise) and Hakim (judge).
* Shaykh: That is, Hakim from wisdom (hikmah), and Hakim from judgment (hukm), so He is a judge possessing wisdom. We mentioned in the commentary that among people there is one who is wise but not a judge, and among people there is one who is a judge but not wise, and among people there is one who is neither judge nor wise, and among people there is one who is a wise judge. The divisions are therefore four.
* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: it is not permissible for anyone to legislate a law from himself. From where do you take this?
* Student: His saying ﴿tanzil min﴾.
* Shaykh: Wrong.
* Student: ﴿Hakimin Hamidin﴾?
* Shaykh: No, you do not read the whole verse; it does not work.
* Student: By His saying ﴿Hakim﴾.
* Shaykh: In which of the two meanings: from judge or from wisdom?
* Student: From judge.

Shaykh: "Man hākam" — you did well, because part of judgment is judging between people. Judgment is either judgment over people or judgment between people. It is not permissible for anyone to judge between people except by what God has revealed, because judgment belongs to God, may He be exalted: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾ [al-An'am 57]. Is that clear? But is it permissible for us to exceed God's limit by ruling on someone as a sinner (fāsiq), an innovator (mubtadi'), a disbeliever (kāfir), or a believer, or declaring his creed sound, except with evidence from the Shari'ah? It is not permissible for us except with evidence from the Shari'ah. That is, we have no right to say: "This one is a disbeliever, this one is a sinner, this one is an innovator, this one is a believer, this one has sound creed," unless we present what he holds to the Book and the Sunnah. Otherwise, ﴿if the Truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Mu'minun 71].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that God, exalted is He, is Praiseworthy (Ḥamīd). He is praiseworthy on the basis of what?
* Student: On the basis that it is the subject (fā'il).
* Shaykh: Incorrect (...).
* Student: Clear, O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Clear (...). It was a slip of the tongue. So, on the basis that ﴿Ḥamīd﴾ is a passive participle (ism maf'ūl).
Here we ask: is God praised in every circumstance? In times of ease (sarrā') it is clear that He is praised, because He has done good to you and shown kindness to you. But in times of hardship (ḍarrā'), how is He praised?
* Student: He is praised for what results from it, because (...).
* Shaykh: First: we praise Him because we know He has decreed this only for a wisdom, without doubt. Second: what results from this hardship of great benefits requires that God be praised for it, does it not? When a person is pricked by a thorn and suffers pain from it, what happens to him? His sins are removed. His sin is a heavy, great, shameful burden in the Hereafter, and the thorn is not painful to that extent, nor is it visible to people, and yet he is expiated of his evil deeds by it. For this reason it was said of one of the female worshippers that when her finger was injured, she did not feel pain, was not affected, and did not grieve. She said: "The sweetness of its reward has made me forget the bitterness of its patience." It is a remarkable saying; the Sufis have remarkable sayings about worship and about captivating the heart. "The sweetness of its reward has made me forget the bitterness of its patience," because the reward is greater than the calamity. So even what harm befalls a person, God, exalted is He, is praised for it, because it is for a wisdom, without doubt, and the person is a servant of God, exalted is He, who does with him what He wills, and because the outcome is praiseworthy. Is God praised for the existence of disbelievers?
* Student: No, He is not praised.
* Shaykh: He is not praised? I seek refuge in God, O Shaykh. There is no power and no strength except with God. Ask forgiveness of God. What? Think.
* Student: Yes, Shaykh, He is praised for that, because He prescribed for us fighting them and martyrdom in His way, so we enter Paradise if we die in it.
* Shaykh: Yes. Were it not for the existence of the disbeliever, would the believer be recognized? Would a person know the value of God's blessing upon him if there were no disbeliever? He would not know the value of God's blessing, and would the obligation of jihad be established? And would anyone remain for the Fire? It is necessary. But here is a matter: when something that displeases the Prophet ﷺ befell him, he would not say, for example, "Praise be to God for the hardship," or "for such and such"; he would say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance" [[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3803) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]. This is a matter you should pay attention to. If ease befalls you, say: "Praise be to God by whose blessing good deeds are completed." If hardship befalls you, say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance." Through this we know the error of one who says: "Praise be to God who is not praised for anything disliked except Him." This is wrong, because this phrase indicates emotional distress and dislike of what God has decreed for a person. Moreover, it contains a contradiction: something disliked and praise. This is not sound. Furthermore, it also opposes the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance" [[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3803) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]], and he did not mention the disliked matter nor indicate that he was distressed by it. "Praise be to God in every circumstance." So if you are struck with ease, say: "Praise be to God by whose blessing good deeds are completed." If you wish, specify: "Praise be to God who has granted me a child; praise be to God who has granted me success; praise be to God who has granted me wealth," and the like, because this is good and praising Him for it is clear. But for disliked matters, do you say: "Praise be to God who made me ill"? No. What do you say? "Praise be to God in every circumstance." "Praise be to God who afflicted me with a calamity, the loss of my father or my brother or my uncle"? No. You say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance." And if you wish, say: "Praise be to God for what He has decreed," because this carries the meaning of "in every circumstance."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Lord, exalted is He, is perfect in justice, such that He praises whoever deserves praise, just as He is praised because He is worthy of praise. On the basis of what? On the basis that ﴿Ḥamīd﴾ means "one who praises" (ḥāmid).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that everything in the Qur'an is entirely in accordance with wisdom, whether it is a permission, a prohibition, an obligation, or a release. Why? Its reason is that it was sent down ﴿from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾, and what is sent down from the Wise must necessarily contain wisdom. And God is the Granter of success.
* Student: The statement ﴿Ḥakīm﴾ — do we not take a third attribute from it, which is ihkām (perfection)?
* Shaykh: No. Ihkām is ḥikmah; wisdom is ihkām.
* Student: When the thing sent down is a self-standing entity, like iron and livestock, does "tanzīl" here mean creation (khalq)?
* Shaykh: It means creation, indeed it is more precise than creation, because these things, had God not subjected them, we would not have been able to control them. This indicates a kind of subjugation: He sent them down from on high to below so that they would be subjected to creation.
* Student: Is al-Hādī one of God's names?
* Shaykh: On the interpretation of His saying, ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd 7], if we interpret that the meaning is God, it is correct.
* Student: Our saying, "Praise be to God who afflicted me with this calamity," is without doubt an incorrect phrase. Is it like this with God, the Creator of evil, yet evil is not attributed to God, the Exalted, on account of the Prophet's saying ﷺ: "Evil is not attributed to You" [[Narrated by Muslim (771/201) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. God, exalted is He, is the Creator of everything. For this reason it came in the hadith: "Believe in predestination, its good and its evil" [[Narrated by Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]]. But do not attribute evil to God, because God did not decree this evil except for good. Evil, then, lies in its effect (maf'ūl), not in its act (fi'l). Is that correct? Do you understand this, or not? Do you understand the difference between saying: evil lies in its effect, not in its act? Do you understand this? For example, if God, exalted is He, decrees illness upon people, the evil is not in the illness itself, but in God's decree it is not evil, it is good, because among the greatest benefits of illnesses is the expiation of sins, and among them that people return to God, exalted is He: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may make them taste part of what they have done that perhaps they will return﴾ [al-Rum 41]. And among them that a person recognizes the value of God's blessing upon him through well-being. For example, we now do not know, that is, we do not know the value of the blessing God has bestowed upon us in breath and movement and the like. But if one of us is afflicted with shortness of breath, he will know the value of God's blessing of breath. If one of us is afflicted with fatigue in his limbs so that he struggles to move, he will know the value of God's blessing upon him. Do you understand? For this reason it was said:
...................... ∗∗∗ "And by their opposites things are made clear."
* Student: Please, Shaykh, may God bless you, the Prophet's supplication ﷺ: "To whom will You entrust me, to a distant one who frowns at me, or to a near one whom You have given authority over my affair?" [[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (13/73, no. 181) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib.]] Is it established from the Prophet ﷺ?
* Shaykh: I do not know, by God. I do not know this.
* Student: How valid is naming God the Physician (al-Tabib) and the Clean (al-Nazif)?
* Shaykh: This was reported from Abu Bakr, that he said: "The Physician saw me and said: 'I do what I wish.'" There is no harm in this in the context of narration.
* Student: But by way of naming?
* Shaykh: But naming, no.
* Student: And al-Nazif, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Al-Nazif — a hadith has also been reported regarding this (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 41–42 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them—and indeed it is a Book of might (41). Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾ [Fussilat 41, 42].

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them﴾: This is a sentence emphasized with ﴿inna﴾ (indeed). What is meant by ﴿the Reminder﴾ is the Noble Quran, as Allah the Blessed and Exalted says: ﴿And this is a blessed Reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya 50], and He the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [az-Zukhruf 44]. The Quran is called a reminder (dhikr) because it reminds its possessor of what is for the righteous of good and what is for the tyrants of evil; and because it is a remembrance (dhikr) for its possessor, meaning that Allah raises his remembrance by means of it, the remembrance of one who holds fast to it; and for this reason He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. And because it reminds a person of his Lord, for the closest of people, or among the closest of people, to Allah is the one who recites His Book. For this reason we say that the recitation of the Book is the best of remembrance in general, whereas the specific remembrances restricted to a particular thing are subordinate to what they are restricted to.

As for His saying ﴿when it comes to them﴾, it means: at the time it came to them. Know that ﴿lamma﴾ (when/since) comes in the Arabic language in several senses, among them: that it is a temporal adverb, as in this verse, so the meaning of ﴿when it came to them﴾ is: at the time it came to them. Another is that it comes as a negating particle that is jussive, but it is used to indicate the expectation of what follows it, as in His saying the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8]. Here ﴿lamma﴾ means (lam), so it is a negation, but it is only used before something expected. The meaning of ﴿they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ is: they have not tasted it, but they deserve it, and the punishment is near for them. Another is that it comes in the sense of (illa, except), as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [at-Tariq 4], meaning: except that over it is a guardian. Another is that it comes as a conditional particle, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿So when the bearer of good tidings came, he cast it over his face﴾ [Yusuf 96]. ﴿Falaamma an jaa﴾ here is conditional, and you say: "When he visited me, I honoured him." So these are four senses of (lamma): the first: temporal; the second: negating and jussive; the third: in the sense of (illa); the fourth: conditional.

﴿When it came to them﴾, meaning: at the time it came to them. Allah the Exalted did not mention the predicate of (inna) but omitted it so that the mind would wander in estimating it in every direction; that is, a person keeps asking: what will happen to them? You find a person hoping, thinking, this or that or that. For this reason the commentator estimated it by his words: (We will recompense them). So ﴿nujazihim﴾ (We will recompense them), according to the author's interpretation, is the predicate of (inna). It is permissible to estimate other than this; you may say: Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them will be punished, or theirs is the Fire of Hell, or what is similar to that. The point is that its omission is so that the mind goes, what? In every direction in estimating the predicate. But we know with certainty that it cannot be estimated as a pleasant predicate; that is, we cannot say, as an estimate: Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them—for them are the Gardens of Bliss. This is impossible; rather, it is estimated as whatever punishment you estimate. This is from the eloquence of the Quran, that it leaves the matter open for a person to estimate in every way.

He said: (﴿And indeed, it is a Book of might﴾ — mani', unassailable). ﴿And indeed, it is a Book﴾: Allah the Mighty and Majestic has emphasized the might of this Book with two emphatics: (inna) and the lam. In reality, the focus of the benefit is not ﴿Book﴾ alone; the focus of the benefit is His saying ﴿of might﴾; this is what is important. As for ﴿Book﴾, everything is a book; everything written is a book: ﴿She said: O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me. Indeed it is from Sulayman﴾ [an-Naml 29, 30]. But the focus of the benefit is His saying ﴿of might﴾. ﴿And indeed, it is a Book﴾: the pronoun in ﴿indeed it﴾ refers back to the Reminder, which is the Quran, and ﴿Book﴾ here means written, and it is written in the mushafs, in the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels. Do you understand? So it is a book in three places: in the Preserved Tablet; second, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels; third, in the scrolls in our hands. And His saying ﴿of might﴾: the author said: (mani', unassailable). There is no doubt that (mani') is among the meanings of ﴿'aziz﴾, but it is more general than what the author said. ﴿'Aziz﴾: in the sense of mani', meaning that no one can reach it with harm except that Allah exposes him. Second: ﴿'Aziz﴾ in the sense of dominant (ghalib). The Quran undoubtedly dominates everything else, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion﴾ [at-Tawbah 33]. So it is dominant over everything. Thus it is unassailable, so that no one can reach it with harm except that Allah exposes him; and second, it is dominant. For this reason, when the Muslim nation adhered to it, it was dominant; it toppled the thrones of Chosroes and Caesar and other tyrants, and by it the eastern and western parts of the earth were opened. When the Muslim nation turned away from it, it was deprived of this great good, which is might, dominance and subjugation.

﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat 42]: meaning there is no book before it that contradicts it, nor after it. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾: ﴿al-batil﴾ (falsehood) is the opposite of the sound and the opposite of truth. The jurists say: the prayer is invalid (batilah); the prayer is valid (sahihah). So they make invalidity (butlan) the opposite of validity (sihhah). In the Noble Quran: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 62]. So He made falsehood the counterpart of truth. Thus ﴿falsehood cannot approach it﴾ is that which is the opposite of truth. As for His saying ﴿from before it or from behind it﴾, the author explained it with a strange interpretation; he said: (meaning there is no book before it that contradicts it, nor after it). There is clear scrutiny of this, and the correct view is that ﴿falsehood cannot approach it from before it﴾ means in what it reports, and ﴿nor from behind it﴾ means in what it reports about the unseen. Everything it reports is true, and everything it reports as going to happen is true. Also, ﴿falsehood cannot approach it﴾ with respect to rulings: everything it rules is true, and its end is truth. So the meaning is that this Noble Quran contains nothing false, neither in reporting what has passed, which is what is ﴿before it﴾, nor in reporting what is to come, which is His saying ﴿nor from behind it﴾. And if you wish, reverse it and say: what is before it is the future, and what is behind it is the past. Likewise, falsehood cannot approach it with respect to its rulings: all its rulings are justice, with no oppression in them. For this reason you find that the Quran, just as it gives the Lord His right of worship, also gives the created being his right: ﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him﴾: this is the right of Allah; after it: ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ [an-Nisa 36]. So it is true in its rulings and true in its reports. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat 42]. And recite, if you wish, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]: ﴿truth﴾ with regard to reports, ﴿justice﴾ with regard to rulings.

﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾: ﴿tanzil﴾ (revelation) is the predicate of an omitted subject. It may be a second predicate for His saying ﴿And indeed it﴾: a second, or a third? A third. ﴿Book﴾ ... ﴿of might﴾ is an adjective of ﴿Book﴾. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ may also be an adjective of ﴿Book﴾. On this basis ﴿tanzil﴾ is a second predicate. It may also be a second predicate of (inna), meaning: ﴿falsehood cannot approach it﴾ is a second predicate of (inna); on this basis ﴿tanzil﴾ is a third predicate. It may also be that ﴿tanzil﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: it is ﴿a revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾. Perhaps this estimate is preferable, because it indicates that the sentence is a new sentence explaining the greatness of this Quran. He said: ﴿tanzil﴾, meaning: sent down (munazzal) from One Wise, Praiseworthy. When we interpret ﴿tanzil﴾ as "sent down," the verbal noun takes the meaning of what? When we interpret ﴿tanzil﴾ as "sent down" (munazzal), the verbal noun here takes the meaning of what? The verbal noun comes both in the sense of the passive participle and in the sense of the active participle, and what determines this is the context.

﴿A revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾: ﴿Hakim﴾ means possessor of wisdom (hikmah) and possessor of judgment (hukm). Judgment belongs to Allah, and wisdom is in His rulings, the Mighty and Majestic. The Lord the Mighty and Majestic is characterized by judgment that has no one to repel it, by an executed judgment that has no one to prevent it. In the transmitted supplication: "None can withhold what You have given, and none can give what You have withheld."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (844) and Muslim (593/138), from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.]] He is also characterized by wisdom: all His rulings are wisdom. If you look at the decreed rulings, you find them in the utmost wisdom, and if you look at the legislative rulings, you find them likewise in the utmost wisdom. So He the Mighty and Majestic is a Judge and possessor of wisdom. How many a judge has no wisdom? And how many a wise person has no judgment? Many men are wise and sensible, but have no authority; he cannot judge even his own wife. And how many a person is a ruler, powerful with authority, but has no wisdom? As for the Lord the Mighty and Majestic, He is what? A Judge who is Wise. He mentioned the Wise before the Praiseworthy, because praise follows from wisdom, for the wise is praised. The author said: (i.e., Allah, the Praised), meaning: by ﴿Hakim Hamid﴾ is meant Allah. His saying (the Praised) points out that ﴿fa'il﴾ here has the sense of ﴿maf'ul﴾. In Arabic, ﴿fa'il﴾ comes in the sense of active and in the sense of passive: when you say, "so-and-so is jarih" in the sense of "wounded" (majruh), and "so-and-so is sami'" in the sense of "hearing" (sami'), it comes in Arabic in the sense of active and in the sense of passive. Here the author interpreted it as "praised." But is this interpretation deficient? The answer: yes, there is deficiency in it, because ﴿hamid﴾ here has both the sense of active and passive: He is praised, and He is also a praiser. Does not Allah the Exalted praise the believers, the messengers, and whomever He wills of His servants a great deal? This is praise; that is, the description of those created beings whom Allah praised is in reality their praising Him. So will ﴿Hamid﴾ then mean?
* Student: In the sense of active and passive.
* Shaykh: In the sense of active and passive: in the sense of passive, that He is praised; and in the sense of active, that He is a praiser. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, is deficient in his interpretation.

﴿A revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾

* In this noble verse: a warning to those who deny the Quran, by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾; and the predicate is omitted so that the mind may wander in estimating it in every good direction.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that this Quran is a Reminder; Allah named it a reminder for what we mentioned in the commentary.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these people denied the Reminder after it came to them and they had verified and recognized it. It is known that one who denies a thing after it has become certain to him is more sinful and more grievous than one who denies a matter that is doubtful to him. This is taken from His saying ﴿when it came to them﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that this Quran is mighty and dominant; no one can reach it with harm except that Allah exposes him, and no one stands before it except that he is defeated and overcome. Allah the Exalted described the Quran as mighty, glorious, and noble, and with many other attributes, which shows the greatness of this Quran.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever holds fast to the Quran has might. Its basis: if the Quran is mighty, then whoever holds fast to it must attain might, otherwise the Quran would not be mighty. This is indicated by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs might, and to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Noble Quran is truth, free of falsehood in every respect, by His saying ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾. Is this attribute of the Quran one of negation or one of affirmation?
* Students: Negation.
* Shaykh: Yes, negation. So what does it contain in terms of affirmation? We say: when falsehood is removed from it in every respect, from before it and from behind it, it follows that it is truth in what respect? In every respect.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, derived from His saying ﴿A revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾. The reason it is the speech of Allah: the Quran is an attribute, not a separate independent entity. If it is an attribute, and Allah mentioned that it was sent down from Him, it must be His speech. But if the thing Allah said He sent down were a specific thing separate from Allah, this would not indicate that it is one of Allah's attributes. ﴿And He sent down from the sky water﴾ [al-Baqarah 22]: is this water created or one of Allah's attributes?
* Students: Created.
* Shaykh: Created. ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [az-Zumar 6]: created, because it is a thing separate from Allah. ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for the people﴾ [al-Hadid 25]: created. But when sending down or revelation occurs regarding a matter that is an attribute, it cannot be created and separate from Allah; rather it is an attribute of Allah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation (uluw). The proof: He said ﴿a revelation from One Wise﴾, and if it is a revelation from Him, it must be that He is above, and He is so, the Mighty and Majestic. We have mentioned many times, and others have also mentioned, that Allah's elevation is established by all the proofs: the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason, and the natural disposition (fitrah), all of which agree on Allah's elevation.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of these two names for Allah the Mighty and Majestic: (al-Hakim) and (al-Hamid), and the affirmation of the meanings and attributes they include. (Al-Hakim) includes two great attributes. (Al-Hakim) includes two great attributes, which are?
* Student: Hakim (wise) and Hakim (judge).
* Shaykh: That is, Hakim from wisdom (hikmah), and Hakim from judgment (hukm), so He is a judge possessing wisdom. We mentioned in the commentary that among people there is one who is wise but not a judge, and among people there is one who is a judge but not wise, and among people there is one who is neither judge nor wise, and among people there is one who is a wise judge. The divisions are therefore four.
* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: it is not permissible for anyone to legislate a law from himself. From where do you take this?
* Student: His saying ﴿tanzil min﴾.
* Shaykh: Wrong.
* Student: ﴿Hakimin Hamidin﴾?
* Shaykh: No, you do not read the whole verse; it does not work.
* Student: By His saying ﴿Hakim﴾.
* Shaykh: In which of the two meanings: from judge or from wisdom?
* Student: From judge.

Shaykh: "Man hākam" — you did well, because part of judgment is judging between people. Judgment is either judgment over people or judgment between people. It is not permissible for anyone to judge between people except by what God has revealed, because judgment belongs to God, may He be exalted: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾ [al-An'am 57]. Is that clear? But is it permissible for us to exceed God's limit by ruling on someone as a sinner (fāsiq), an innovator (mubtadi'), a disbeliever (kāfir), or a believer, or declaring his creed sound, except with evidence from the Shari'ah? It is not permissible for us except with evidence from the Shari'ah. That is, we have no right to say: "This one is a disbeliever, this one is a sinner, this one is an innovator, this one is a believer, this one has sound creed," unless we present what he holds to the Book and the Sunnah. Otherwise, ﴿if the Truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Mu'minun 71].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that God, exalted is He, is Praiseworthy (Ḥamīd). He is praiseworthy on the basis of what?
* Student: On the basis that it is the subject (fā'il).
* Shaykh: Incorrect (...).
* Student: Clear, O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Clear (...). It was a slip of the tongue. So, on the basis that ﴿Ḥamīd﴾ is a passive participle (ism maf'ūl).
Here we ask: is God praised in every circumstance? In times of ease (sarrā') it is clear that He is praised, because He has done good to you and shown kindness to you. But in times of hardship (ḍarrā'), how is He praised?
* Student: He is praised for what results from it, because (...).
* Shaykh: First: we praise Him because we know He has decreed this only for a wisdom, without doubt. Second: what results from this hardship of great benefits requires that God be praised for it, does it not? When a person is pricked by a thorn and suffers pain from it, what happens to him? His sins are removed. His sin is a heavy, great, shameful burden in the Hereafter, and the thorn is not painful to that extent, nor is it visible to people, and yet he is expiated of his evil deeds by it. For this reason it was said of one of the female worshippers that when her finger was injured, she did not feel pain, was not affected, and did not grieve. She said: "The sweetness of its reward has made me forget the bitterness of its patience." It is a remarkable saying; the Sufis have remarkable sayings about worship and about captivating the heart. "The sweetness of its reward has made me forget the bitterness of its patience," because the reward is greater than the calamity. So even what harm befalls a person, God, exalted is He, is praised for it, because it is for a wisdom, without doubt, and the person is a servant of God, exalted is He, who does with him what He wills, and because the outcome is praiseworthy. Is God praised for the existence of disbelievers?
* Student: No, He is not praised.
* Shaykh: He is not praised? I seek refuge in God, O Shaykh. There is no power and no strength except with God. Ask forgiveness of God. What? Think.
* Student: Yes, Shaykh, He is praised for that, because He prescribed for us fighting them and martyrdom in His way, so we enter Paradise if we die in it.
* Shaykh: Yes. Were it not for the existence of the disbeliever, would the believer be recognized? Would a person know the value of God's blessing upon him if there were no disbeliever? He would not know the value of God's blessing, and would the obligation of jihad be established? And would anyone remain for the Fire? It is necessary. But here is a matter: when something that displeases the Prophet ﷺ befell him, he would not say, for example, "Praise be to God for the hardship," or "for such and such"; he would say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance" [[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3803) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]. This is a matter you should pay attention to. If ease befalls you, say: "Praise be to God by whose blessing good deeds are completed." If hardship befalls you, say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance." Through this we know the error of one who says: "Praise be to God who is not praised for anything disliked except Him." This is wrong, because this phrase indicates emotional distress and dislike of what God has decreed for a person. Moreover, it contains a contradiction: something disliked and praise. This is not sound. Furthermore, it also opposes the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance" [[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3803) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]], and he did not mention the disliked matter nor indicate that he was distressed by it. "Praise be to God in every circumstance." So if you are struck with ease, say: "Praise be to God by whose blessing good deeds are completed." If you wish, specify: "Praise be to God who has granted me a child; praise be to God who has granted me success; praise be to God who has granted me wealth," and the like, because this is good and praising Him for it is clear. But for disliked matters, do you say: "Praise be to God who made me ill"? No. What do you say? "Praise be to God in every circumstance." "Praise be to God who afflicted me with a calamity, the loss of my father or my brother or my uncle"? No. You say: "Praise be to God in every circumstance." And if you wish, say: "Praise be to God for what He has decreed," because this carries the meaning of "in every circumstance."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Lord, exalted is He, is perfect in justice, such that He praises whoever deserves praise, just as He is praised because He is worthy of praise. On the basis of what? On the basis that ﴿Ḥamīd﴾ means "one who praises" (ḥāmid).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that everything in the Qur'an is entirely in accordance with wisdom, whether it is a permission, a prohibition, an obligation, or a release. Why? Its reason is that it was sent down ﴿from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾, and what is sent down from the Wise must necessarily contain wisdom. And God is the Granter of success.
* Student: The statement ﴿Ḥakīm﴾ — do we not take a third attribute from it, which is ihkām (perfection)?
* Shaykh: No. Ihkām is ḥikmah; wisdom is ihkām.
* Student: When the thing sent down is a self-standing entity, like iron and livestock, does "tanzīl" here mean creation (khalq)?
* Shaykh: It means creation, indeed it is more precise than creation, because these things, had God not subjected them, we would not have been able to control them. This indicates a kind of subjugation: He sent them down from on high to below so that they would be subjected to creation.
* Student: Is al-Hādī one of God's names?
* Shaykh: On the interpretation of His saying, ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd 7], if we interpret that the meaning is God, it is correct.
* Student: Our saying, "Praise be to God who afflicted me with this calamity," is without doubt an incorrect phrase. Is it like this with God, the Creator of evil, yet evil is not attributed to God, the Exalted, on account of the Prophet's saying ﷺ: "Evil is not attributed to You" [[Narrated by Muslim (771/201) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. God, exalted is He, is the Creator of everything. For this reason it came in the hadith: "Believe in predestination, its good and its evil" [[Narrated by Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]]. But do not attribute evil to God, because God did not decree this evil except for good. Evil, then, lies in its effect (maf'ūl), not in its act (fi'l). Is that correct? Do you understand this, or not? Do you understand the difference between saying: evil lies in its effect, not in its act? Do you understand this? For example, if God, exalted is He, decrees illness upon people, the evil is not in the illness itself, but in God's decree it is not evil, it is good, because among the greatest benefits of illnesses is the expiation of sins, and among them that people return to God, exalted is He: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may make them taste part of what they have done that perhaps they will return﴾ [al-Rum 41]. And among them that a person recognizes the value of God's blessing upon him through well-being. For example, we now do not know, that is, we do not know the value of the blessing God has bestowed upon us in breath and movement and the like. But if one of us is afflicted with shortness of breath, he will know the value of God's blessing of breath. If one of us is afflicted with fatigue in his limbs so that he struggles to move, he will know the value of God's blessing upon him. Do you understand? For this reason it was said:
...................... ∗∗∗ "And by their opposites things are made clear."
* Student: Please, Shaykh, may God bless you, the Prophet's supplication ﷺ: "To whom will You entrust me, to a distant one who frowns at me, or to a near one whom You have given authority over my affair?" [[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (13/73, no. 181) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib.]] Is it established from the Prophet ﷺ?
* Shaykh: I do not know, by God. I do not know this.
* Student: How valid is naming God the Physician (al-Tabib) and the Clean (al-Nazif)?
* Shaykh: This was reported from Abu Bakr, that he said: "The Physician saw me and said: 'I do what I wish.'" There is no harm in this in the context of narration.
* Student: But by way of naming?
* Shaykh: But naming, no.
* Student: And al-Nazif, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Al-Nazif — a hadith has also been reported regarding this (...).

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan: "Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is the Possessor of forgiveness and the Possessor of painful punishment. (43) And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, 'Why are its verses not explained in detail? Is it non-Arabic and Arabic?' Say: 'It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And as for those who do not believe, there is deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them. Those are being called from a distant place.' (44) And We certainly gave Musa the Scripture, but it was disputed about. And if not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed they are, concerning it, in disquieting doubt. (45) Whoever does righteousness does so for his own soul, and whoever does evil does so against it. And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants." [Fussilat 43-46].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you," to the end. "Nothing is said to you," the mufassir said: (from denial), meaning and mockery, ridicule, and other things. "Except what was said to the messengers before you." Among it is their saying that he is a sorcerer or a madman, as Allah, the Exalted, said: "Thus did there not come to those before them any messenger except that they said, 'A sorcerer or a madman'" [adh-Dhariyat 52]. This is a statement that everyone says to the Messenger. It may also be that the meaning is: "Nothing is said to you" of revelation "except what was said to the messengers before you," meaning like it. The verses can bear both meanings, and there is no obstacle to intending both. ("Nothing is said to you except" like "what was said to the messengers before you.") His saying: ("except" like) — the author added "like," and it is known that his saying "except what was said" is not equivalent to his saying "except like." The author resorted to this because what was said to the Messenger ﷺ is not, in its wording, identical to what was said to those before him. But the better view is to say: the verse is on its apparent meaning, that what was said to the Messenger has been said to those before him. As I mentioned to you just now: "Thus did there not come to those before them any messenger except that they said, 'A sorcerer or a madman'" [adh-Dhariyat 52]. So it is said: they said the very same statement, but in their own language, not the language of the Arabs.

"Except what was said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is the Possessor of forgiveness and the Possessor of painful punishment." This sentence contains an offer to the deniers to believe; if they do not believe, they have exposed themselves to punishment. It is an offer to believe, by His saying: "Indeed, your Lord is the Possessor of forgiveness." It is as if He is saying: believe, and you will be forgiven. This is like His saying: "Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them" [al-Anfal 38]. "And the Possessor of painful punishment": meaning, if they do not believe, there is in it both encouragement and warning. The encouragement is in His saying "the Possessor of forgiveness," and the warning is "and the Possessor of painful punishment." Punishment ('iqab) is retribution, and "painful" (alim) means "causing pain." The form fa'il frequently comes in the sense of mufil in the Arabic language, as the poet said:

"Is it from Rayhana, the caller, the hearer ∗∗∗ that keeps me awake while my companions sleep?"
"Is it from Rayhana, the caller, the hearer ∗∗∗ ......................"
(al-Sami') means "the one who makes hear."
"......................... ∗∗∗ that keeps me awake while my companions sleep."

* In this noble verse: consolation for the Messenger ﷺ, for when he knows that what was said to the messengers before him has been said to him, the matter becomes easier for him.
* And among its benefits: the sunnah of Allah, the Exalted, is one; the deniers have one saying and one action, due to His saying: "Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you."

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming the attribute of forgiveness for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is the covering of sin and overlooking it.

* And among its benefits: affirming the severity of His punishment, due to His saying: "and the Possessor of painful punishment."

* And among its benefits: the mercy of Allah toward His servants, in that He presents to them what requires repentance so that they do not persist in their disobedience, due to His saying: "Indeed, your Lord is the Possessor of forgiveness."

* And among its benefits: that this Qur'an is "mathani" (oft-repeated); when the aspect of encouragement is mentioned in it, the aspect of warning is mentioned with it, so that the soul does not covet excessively and become secure from the plotting of Allah. Allah the Exalted combines this and that, so that a person does not covet bounty and feel secure from Allah's plan, and so that he does not fear and despair of Allah's mercy. Accordingly, his journey to Allah, the Exalted, is between fear and hope. For this reason Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It is necessary for one traveling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that his fear and his hope be equal; whichever prevails, his companion is destroyed." Some of them said: "Fear and hope should be for a person like the two wings of a bird; if one of them is injured, the bird falls." So hope and fear are equal and balanced: you hope and you fear. For this reason He said: "They call upon their Lord in fear and in hope" [as-Sajdah 16]. Some scholars made a distinction, saying: when a person does good deeds, the side of hope should be weightier for him, because this is good opinion of Allah; its reasoning is that when Allah has enabled you to act, He has promised you reward, and when He has enabled you to supplicate, He has promised you response. So when you do good, favor the side of hope; and if you do evil or intend it, favor the side of fear, so that fear restrains you from persisting in evil or from falling into it. This is one distinction. Another distinction: some took a different path and said: in a state of health, one should favor the side of fear, because a healthy person whom Allah has granted health in body and mind may persist in evil and not care; and when you are ill, favor the side of hope, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "None of you should die except while thinking well of his Lord" [narrated by Muslim (2877/81) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah]. For Allah, the Exalted, is according to His servant's opinion of Him. What should be said is: a person is the physician of his own soul. If he fears for himself persisting in sins and being lax in acts of obedience, let him favor the side of fear; and if he fears for himself pride, arrogance and feeling secure from the plotting of Allah, let him favor the side of fear. A person, in reality, is the physician of his own soul.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 44 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And had We made it an Arabic-less (a non-Arabic) Qur'an, they would have said, "Why have its verses not been made clear?"﴾ [Fussilat 41:44]. ﴿Made it﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. The exegete (al-mufassir, the author of the tafsir) said: "That is, the Reminder (al-dhikr)." He said "dhikr" because its mention (dhikr) came shortly before: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾ [Fussilat 41:41], ﴿and indeed it is a Book﴾. In any case, the meaning is agreed upon: the pronoun in ﴿made it﴾ refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Had We made it an Arabic-less Qur'an﴾, meaning in the language of the non-Arabs ('ajam). And it was revealed to whom? To the Arabs. ﴿They would have said, "Why have its verses not been made clear?"﴾ ﴿They would have said﴾: that is, those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ). (﴿Why not﴾: ﴿hal-la﴾, meaning "would that"; ﴿made clear﴾: explained; ﴿its verses﴾: so that we may understand them.) But God, exalted is He, cut off their argument (proof) and said: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 43:3], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you may reason﴾ [Yusuf 12:2].

As for His words ﴿lawla﴾ meaning "why not" (hal-la): the author, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that "lawla" comes for exhortation (tahdid, urging) and also comes as a conditional particle. In its grammatical analysis (i'rab), it is said: "a particle of prohibition due to the existence of something." Here these particles divide between existence and non-existence. ﴿Law﴾ is a particle of prohibition due to the prohibition (of the consequent). ﴿Lamma﴾ is a particle of existence due to existence. ﴿Lawla﴾ is a particle of prohibition due to existence. You say: "Lamma jaa'ani akramtuhu" (when he came to me, I honored him): here the honoring existed because the coming existed. You say: "Law jaa'a Zayd la-akramtuhu" (if Zayd had come, I would have honored him): here the honoring was prohibited because the coming did not exist. And you say: "Lawla Zaydun la-halaktu" (had it not been for Zayd, I would have perished), or "lawla fa'alta kadhaa wa kadhaa" (had you not done such-and-such): here it is prohibition due to existence. Here, "lawla" is neither of these two.
