Here "lawla" has shifted from the meaning of a conditional to the meaning of exhortation (tahdid), from the rest of their speech. ﴿Is it an Arabic-less Qur'an, and a prophet who is Arab?﴾ is an interrogative of denial from them. That is: if the Qur'an were in the language of the non-Arabs, they would have said: "Why have its verses not been made clear and explained in the Arabic language?" Then they would also have said: ﴿Is it an Arabic-less and an Arab (speech)?﴾, meaning: it is impossible for a Qur'an in the language of the non-Arabs to descend upon an Arab prophet. What they said is an interrogative in reality, meaning that their statement is true: an Arabic-less Qur'an cannot descend upon an Arab prophet. Allah has affirmed this in His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, to make (the message) clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim 14:4]. So their statement is correct, and we accept this statement of theirs. As for their saying ﴿Why have its verses not been made clear?﴾, we say: they are indeed made clear, but it would have been a proof had the Qur'an been non-Arabic. On this basis, their statement would be correct: had the Qur'an been in the non-Arabic language, it would have become a proof for them in their saying ﴿Why have its verses not been made clear?﴾, and it would have been true in their saying ﴿Is it an Arabic-less and an Arab?﴾.

The author said: (with the second hamza made clear). Making the second hamza clear means that you say ﴿a-a'jamiyy﴾ as in the well-known recitation (qira'ah, canonical recitation). He says: (and changing it to an alif), ﴿aa'jamiyy﴾: we changed the second (hamza) into an alif. (With prolongation and without it), ﴿aa'jamiyy﴾, meaning you lengthen the alif with a natural elongation, or you lengthen it beyond that. The natural elongation is his saying: (without it), and the extra elongation is his saying: (with prolongation). On this basis, how many recitations are there in it? Three recitations: ﴿a-a'jamiyy﴾, ﴿aa-a'jamiyy﴾, ﴿aa'jamiyy﴾. Three recitations. And the recitations, as is known, are all a Sunnah (a prophetic practice), all of them a Sunnah, because they were transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). A person who has mastered them and memorized them should recite with this one at times and with that one at other times, just as we say about acts of worship that came in various forms: one should do this at times and that at other times. But should we recite in a way that contradicts the Qur'an that is in the hands of the common people, with another recitation? The answer is no. For this reason, we see that among the lack of wisdom is what some students do: if he knows the recitations, he recites in a recitation that is not in the hands of the common people. This is a great error, because the common person does not grasp these matters, and the status of the Qur'an will decline in his soul and its greatness will diminish in his eyes. Then he may accuse this reciter of having made a mistake and erred. But some people have knowledge without wisdom, and this is a flaw in a servant's balance and conduct: that you have knowledge but not wisdom. If the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, disputed over the recitations, being who they were, then what of the common people of this age?

He says: ﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing."﴾ ﴿Say﴾: that is, say, O Muhammad, in response to them: (﴿It is, for those who believe, guidance﴾ from misguidance, ﴿and healing﴾ from ignorance). ﴿It﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, the Reminder. ﴿For those who believe, guidance﴾: that is, knowledge and light. ﴿And healing﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (from ignorance). This needs review, because "from ignorance" is included in His saying ﴿guidance﴾, since guidance is knowledge and its opposite is ignorance. But ﴿healing﴾ means healing from illness, the illness of hearts, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts﴾ [Yunus 10:57]. So the correct view is that His saying ﴿guidance﴾ means guidance from misguidance, which is ignorance, so it is guidance from ignorance and misguidance, and ﴿healing﴾ means healing from illness, the illness of hearts. Indeed it is also a healing from the illness of bodies, for the Qur'an is sought for healing from illnesses of the heart and is also sought for healing from illnesses of the body. How many a person sick with a bodily illness has been healed by God, exalted is He, through the Qur'an! The story of the one stung by a scorpion is well known among you, or among most of you: the chief of a tribe, upon whom a small company of the Companions descended, and they did not host them. So God caused a large, fierce scorpion to sting their chief. They sought a healer (raqi, one who performs ruqyah) from among the Companions. They said: "We will not perform healing for you unless you give us such-and-such a number of sheep." They gave them the sheep. One of them went and recited al-Fatihah over him until he rose as if released from a tether. But they hesitated about the sheep they had taken; they feared they might not be lawful for them, until they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him. He said: "Take them, and strike for me with you a share."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2276), and Muslim (2201/65), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] He said that not out of need for the meat, but to comfort their hearts and reassure their souls, so that they would know it was lawful and free of doubt. The point is: they informed the Prophet (ﷺ) that they had recited al-Fatihah over this stung man. He said: "And what made you know that it is a ruqyah?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2276), and Muslim (2201/65), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]. Thus it becomes clear that the Qur'an is a healing from illnesses of the heart and diseases of the bodies. But for whom? For those who believe: they believe in the Qur'an, that it is from Allah, and that it is a healing. As for a man who does not believe in it, does not give it any regard, and sees no harm in opposing it, this one does not benefit from it.

He said: ﴿And as for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is upon them blindness﴾ [Fussilat 41:44]. We ask Allah for well-being. ﴿Those who do not believe﴾ is a subject (mubtada'). ﴿In their ears is deafness﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the first subject, which is ﴿those who﴾. That is, it is as if He said: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. As for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness." They do not believe in what? They do not believe in Allah, nor in the messengers, nor in the books. These, ﴿in their ears is deafness﴾: that is, heaviness, because deafness (waqr) means a heavy load. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then the bearers of burdens (wiqran)﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 51:2], meaning the clouds that carry a great deal of water. On this basis, ﴿in their ears is deafness﴾ means heaviness and deafness, so they do not hear, and we seek refuge in Allah. ﴿And it is upon them blindness﴾: so they do not see. Thus the channels of understanding are blocked for those who do not believe: they do not hear and do not see, so the guidance of the Qur'an does not reach their hearts. ﴿And it is upon them blindness. Those are called from a distant place﴾ [Fussilat 41:44]. If someone asks: how can one and the same speech be guidance and healing for one people, and blindness and misguidance for others? We say: this depends on what is in the heart; for God said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff 61:5]. We see that physical food is nourishment and healing for some people, and an illness and affliction for others. For example, some people are prevented from dates, or grapes, or anything lawful that harms them, while others benefit from lawful food, even though the food is the same. But the receptacle differs: the receptacle of these is receptive to it, and the receptacle of those is not.

﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing; and those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is upon them blindness. Those are called from a distant place"﴾ [Fussilat 41:44]. ﴿Those﴾: the ones referred to are those who do not believe. He referred to them with the form of the distant (demonstrative), not to elevate their status, but to show disassociation from them and to distance them.

﴿Those are called from a distant place﴾: that is, they are like one who is called from a distant place. One who is called from a distant place is hindered from responding and accepting by two matters:
The first matter: because of the distance, he may not hear the call.
The second matter: because of the distance, he may see that responding is burdensome for him, so he does not answer.
On this basis, their being called from a distant place is connected to two calamities in their calling. The first: Brother?
* Student: (...) they see the distance as far (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, they see the distance as far, so they become lazy, and they see it as hardship, so they decline to answer the caller. And the second?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That they do not perceive the caller, because they are far from him, so they do not respond in the required manner. (﴿Those are called from a distant place﴾: that is, they are like one called from a distant place who does not hear.)

* In this noble verse there are benefits. Among them: the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in making the revelation sent down upon the Prophet (ﷺ) conform to the language of the people to whom he was sent. This is taken from His saying: ﴿And had We made it an Arabic-less Qur'an, they would have said, "Why have its verses not been made clear?"﴾ [Fussilat 41:44] and so on to the end. And God made it an Arabic Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that proof is not established until a person understands the meaning of this proof, and that mere delivery does not count as an established proof until the one to whom it is delivered understands it. For if you were to speak Arabic in the most eloquent manner to a non-Arab people who do not know your intent at all, would they understand anything? And likewise in reverse: if a non-Arab man came and spoke in the most eloquent Persian (non-Arabic) language, and we did not know his meaning, we would not understand anything from him. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, to make (the message) clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim 14:4].

If someone says: this statement of yours, that understanding is necessary after the proof is delivered, is contradicted by His saying: ﴿That I may warn you thereby, and whoever it reaches﴾ [Al-An'am 6:19]. He did not say: "and whoever it reaches and understands."
We say: this is general, but other verses restrict it, showing that clarification and knowledge are necessary.

Likewise, if someone says: this statement of yours is contradicted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no one from this nation hears of me, be he Jew or Christian, and then does not believe in what I have brought, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire."[[Recorded by Muslim (153/240), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. He said: "hears of me." It is said: yes; because if he hears of him, he is obligated to investigate, even if he does not understand. He is obligated to investigate. As for one who abandons this, he is not excused because of his negligence and laxity. On this basis, the proof must be delivered and must be understood.

In reality, we are not lax in declaring disbelief (takfir) on those whom Allah has declared to be disbelievers, nor do we mind declaring disbelief on those whom Allah has declared to be disbelievers. But we do not dare to declare disbelief on those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has not declared to be disbelievers, because the judgment is not ours. The judgment of declaring disbelief or not declaring it belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; it is not up to us, nor up to our emotions. Had it been up to us or our emotions, we would declare disbelief on whoever is a sinner. Indeed, we might even declare disbelief on one who leaves what is preferable, because a person surely has a zeal by which he hates whoever opposes the Sharia. But our judging him as a disbeliever or not is not up to us; it is up to Allah. The creatures are the servants of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; they are not our servants, so that we judge them by what we see. Rather, we judge them by the implications of the words of Allah and His Messenger. So if the matter is between our saying: "This is a disbeliever, though he claims to be a Muslim," and our saying: "He is not a disbeliever," which is more cautious? That we say: "He is not a disbeliever," because by this we are safe. But if we declare him a disbeliever and then, on the basis of that declaration, we permit his blood and property, because the matter is not easy, and we permit not praying over him and not supplicating for his mercy, then the matter is extremely grave. For this reason, the error of those who rush to declare disbelief is greater than the laxity of one who does not declare them disbelievers; it is greater because of the calamities and trials that follow from declaring disbelief.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that there cannot be a contradiction between the Messenger and the revelation. The evidence is His saying: ﴿And had We made it an Arabic-less Qur'an, they would have said, "Why have its verses not been made clear? Is it an Arabic-less and an Arab?"﴾ And it is impossible for the revelation to contradict the one to whom it was revealed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Qur'an is a mercy for some peoples and a vengeance for others. This is witnessed by his saying (ﷺ): "The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you."[[Recorded by Muslim (223/1), from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari.]]. A mercy for whom? For the believers, and a vengeance upon the disbelievers. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, it is a source of anguish for the disbelievers﴾ [Al-Haqqah 69:50].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that guidance cannot be sought from other than the Qur'an, because of His saying: ﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance."﴾ Whoever seeks guidance from other than the Qur'an, Allah misguides him. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance will not go astray nor suffer. But whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed, for him is a depressed life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:123-124].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 44 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an is a cure for diseases of the hearts and ailments of the body, based on His saying: ﴿It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing﴾. We have understood during the explanation that Surah al-Fatihah is a ruqyah (a spiritual incantation for healing). Likewise, if you wish to perform ruqyah on someone, look along with al-Fatihah for the suitable verses. For example, if you wish to treat him for sorcery, then recite, in addition to al-Fatihah, ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ [al-Falaq 1] and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [an-Nas 1], because they are the two surahs with which the Messenger ﷺ performed ruqyah. Likewise, look at the verses concerning sorcery that nullify sorcery, such as the words of Allah the Exalted about Musa: ﴿What you have brought is sorcery; surely Allah will render it void. Surely Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾ [Yunus 81], and similar verses. If you wish to perform ruqyah for an illness, recite suitable verses such as: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 80]. This is because the correspondence between the verses, which are the medicine, and the illness, which is the disease, must be an important matter that a person takes into account, just as he takes it into account with physical medicines. Hot things are treated with what? With cold. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said regarding fever: «Indeed, fever is from the intensity of the heat of Hell, so cool it with water»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3263) and Muslim (2210 / 81), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]. Physicians now testify that coolness is among the greatest treatments for one afflicted with fever, to the extent that they sometimes place the patient beside air-conditioning fans for coolness, and sometimes place a cloth soaked in water on the feverish patient for the purpose of cooling.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the more a person is strong in faith, the more he is guided and healed. From where do we take this? ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing﴾. We have taken a useful and important principle: every ruling attached to a description, or established upon a description, is strengthened by the strength of that description and weakened by its weakness. Are you with us, brothers? Pay attention to this.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the eloquence of the Qur'an in depicting the intangible in the form of the tangible. Those who do not believe, if you looked at them with a physical glance, you would not find deafness in their ears, because they hear, and they may be stronger in hearing than the believers. Nor would you find that when the Qur'an is recited to them their eyes become blind, as He said: ﴿And it is for them a blindness﴾. Nor would you find that they are called from a far place; rather, the call is presented to them while they are beside the caller. But this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an, that it depicts the intelligible in the form of the perceptible so that it is closer to understanding. Here Allah has depicted the condition of these people as deaf, blind, and far from the caller.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 45 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture, but differences arose concerning it﴾ [Fussilat 45]. ﴿Ataynā﴾ means "We gave." The giving here is both legislative (*shar'ī*) and decreed (*qadarī*). It is legislative because it is attributed to revelation, and decreed because it actually took place. Moses, peace be upon him, is the best of the prophets of the Children of Israel. Relative to the Messengers of Firm Resolve (*ulu al-'azm*), he holds the third rank, because the Messengers of Firm Resolve are five, the best of whom is Muhammad (ﷺ), then Ibrahim, then Moses. Moses, that is, has the most followers among the prophets after the Messenger (ﷺ), based on the hadith that he, peace be upon him, "saw a great black mass that filled the horizon, and it was said: 'This is Moses and his people.'" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5705) and Muslim (220/374), from Ibn 'Abbas.]

(﴿al-Kitāb﴾ means the Torah.) It was called a "Book" (*kitāb*) because it was written. Allah said: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything﴾ [Al-A'raf 145]. So it was revealed in written form.

(﴿But differences arose concerning it﴾ [Fussilat 45], through acceptance and denial, just as with the Qur'an.) ("Differences arose.") Who differed about it? His people, the people of Moses. They differed: some of them affirmed it and some of them denied it. But the people of Moses are well known for their obstinacy, their transgression, their immense arrogance, and their profound ignorance. When they passed by people who worshipped other than Allah, they said: ﴿O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [Al-A'raf 138]. And when they made a calf out of their jewelry, they said: ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses﴾ [Taha 88]. They made the calf that they had fashioned with their own hands into a god. We ask Allah for well-being. The continuation, God willing, follows.

* A student: May Allah be good to you. (...) I am puzzled by his, peace be upon him, saying: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, no Jew or Christian hears of me and then does not believe in me."
* The Shaykh: We have answered that.
* A student: May Allah be good to you. Regarding lawful ruqyah (recitation for healing), some people expand on it and devise methods of their own, indeed (...) ruqyah according to what has come from the early generations (...) they may expand on it.
* The Shaykh: But in the manner, or in the words?
* The student: In the manner; they come up with methods of their own.
* The Shaykh: I see that the best course for the reciter is to limit himself to what has come from the early generations. That is the better course. As for what is other than what has come from the early generations, we might say that it is subject to trial. If it is tried and benefits, then the goal is benefit. If it is not tried, and a person merely guesses, then "some assumptions are sinful."
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. It was mentioned previously in the principles that the basic rule is to keep the unrestricted (*muṭlaq*) as it came. Here, Shaykh, some scholars restrict certain illnesses to specific verses. They say: recite such-and-such verse. So does this contradict the principle, or not?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not contradict the principle. This agrees with wisdom, as we mentioned a little while ago. What did we say?
* The student: We said: recite the appropriate verses.
* The Shaykh: An illness is treated with what suits it.
* The student: Shaykh, how did they come to know this?
* The Shaykh: Through the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We know this from wisdom.
* The student: Shaykh (...), many women, for example, uncover themselves (...).
* Another student: His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, a guidance and healing﴾ [Fussilat 44]. Could it be that "guidance" is from misguidance and "healing" is from error, so that the first is for the disease of doubts and the second is for the disease of desires?
* The Shaykh: We mentioned this, but the wording differs.
* The student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. We said that it is a condition for ruqyah that the one who recites over the patient must be a believer in it, and the patient must be a believer in it.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: And this leader of the people, Shaykh, was he not a Muslim?
* The Shaykh: No, he was a believer. He was not a believer in the Qur'an. We do not know whether he believed in the Qur'an or not, but he believed that their recitation would benefit. This is necessary, because if he does not believe, the soul will not be affected and will not be receptive. The soul cannot be moved to accept this treatment unless he believes that it is beneficial.
* The student: Shaykh, is the disbeliever recited over with the Qur'an? Is a disbeliever treated with the Qur'an?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he is treated with the Qur'an. Its treatment may even be better for him than for the one who believes in it, because if he knows that it is effective, that may be a cause for his becoming Muslim.
* The student: His saying, the Exalted, in Surah Yusuf: ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ [Yusuf 24]. Is this "lawla" conditional or something else? It puzzles me.
* The Shaykh: Read what precedes it: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ [Yusuf 24]. That is, "he would have done it." Its meaning is: had it not been for the proof of his Lord, he would have done it, meaning he would have answered her call. It is not "had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would not have desired." Because if that were the meaning, the speech would be contradictory. Rather, he did desire her, but had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have answered her call.
* The student: Did the desire not occur from him?
* The Shaykh: Yes. That is, had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have acted. So "lawla" is conditional, but its answer is omitted.
* The student: Interrogating the jinn through the Qur'an. Some who perform ruqyah say that they interrogate the jinn, and that the jinn told them such-and-such. Is this possible?
* The Shaykh: By Allah, brother, we do not know about this. They always say what you said: that they interrogate them. And they always treat through imagination (*takhyīl*). The reciter places his hand on the person's head and says: "Close your eyes," and says: "Look, I see such-and-such. Whom do you accuse? I accuse so-and-so." We do not know. These are strange methods, so they need study. That is, the conditions of these reciters need study and knowledge of how they reach this, and from where it came to them.
* The student: May Allah be good to you. If we say that the criterion for establishing proof is understanding?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: What is the answer, Shaykh, to the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their vision is a veil﴾ [Al-Baqarah 7]?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. He sealed them after understanding. A seal may mean a seal that prevents understanding, and it may mean a seal that prevents submission, as in His saying: ﴿No! Rather, what they have been earning has covered their hearts﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 14].

﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture, but differences arose concerning it﴾. When Allah mentioned this Noble Book, and that it is for those who believe a guidance and healing, while for those who do not believe there is deafness in their ears and it is blindness for them, He explained what had happened to earlier nations regarding their scriptures. He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture﴾. ﴿Ataynā﴾ means "We gave." This sentence is emphasized with three emphatics: the oath, the *lām*, and *qad*. The underlying sense is: "By Allah, We had certainly given." This construction occurs frequently in the Noble Book; that is, this form appears often in the Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿We gave Moses the Scripture﴾. This giving is both a cosmic (*kawnī*) and a legislative giving. Allah had indeed sent down the Torah to him, and had indeed given him authority to judge by it. Moses is the son of 'Imran, the best of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and he holds the third rank relative to the Messengers of Firm Resolve, because the Messengers of Firm Resolve are five, the best of whom is Muhammad (ﷺ), then Ibrahim, then Moses.

His saying: ﴿al-Kitāb﴾ means the Torah. Allah called it a "Book" because Allah wrote it with His own hand, as He said: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ [Al-A'raf 145].

He said: (﴿But differences arose concerning it﴾, through acceptance and denial, as with the Qur'an.) ("Differences arose"), that is, the people differed about it. Some affirmed it and some denied it, just as people also did regarding the Qur'an, and likewise all nations regarding what the messengers brought: some affirmed and some denied.

﴿But differences arose concerning it﴾. Likewise, everything the messengers brought is disputed by people, between believer and disbeliever. This is consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. He said: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them﴾. ("Lawla") is a conditional particle. It is, as the grammarians say, a particle of "existence for non-existence": ﴿Had it not been for﴾ is the existing condition, and ﴿it would have been judged﴾ is the non-existing consequence. ("A particle of existence for non-existence.")

His saying: ﴿a word that preceded from your Lord﴾. The commentator says: (the postponement of the reckoning and recompense for creation until the Day of Resurrection). The complete recompense is only on the Day of Resurrection. As for this world, there is indeed a recompense in which the criminals are punished and the believers succeed, but it is not complete recompense in every respect.

(﴿It would have been judged between them﴾ in this world regarding what they differed about.) The meaning of that is complete judgment. This does not contradict what befell the people of Pharaoh of drowning and destruction when they denied Moses, peace be upon him. (﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt about it﴾, that is, those who deny it, "disquieting" meaning causing unease.)

* Among the benefits of this verse: first, emphasizing speech when there is need for it, either because of its importance, or because of doubt in it, or because of denial of it. The scholars of rhetoric (*balāgha*) said: the addressee has three states.

The first state: the state of initiation (*ibtidā'*), which is when the addressee has no knowledge, no hesitation, and no denial. The sentence is addressed to him without emphasis, because there is no need for emphasis, as when one says: "So-and-so arrived today" to a person who had nothing in his heart about his arrival, either affirming or denying it. This sentence is called an initiatory sentence (*ibtidā'iyya*).

The second state: the addressee is hesitant about the matter and doubtful of it, but does not deny it. This requires emphasis, but it is not obligatory, as when you address a man about a matter he finds unlikely but does not deny. Here it is good to emphasize the speech for him, so that doubt and hesitation leave him.

The third state: the addressee is a denier who rejects. Here emphasis of the statement for him is required, because that is more effective in establishing proof against him and persuading him. So the states of the addressee are three: initiation, hesitation, and denial. Each state has its own ruling regarding emphasis.

If someone says: "Your statement is refuted by His saying: ﴿Then indeed, after that, you will surely die. Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be resurrected﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 15-16]. The intended first sentence is ﴿Then indeed, after that, you will surely die﴾. No one denies death, so why is it emphasized for them?"

They answered this by saying that their denial, rejection, arrogance, and defiance make them act like deniers, so they were addressed as deniers. This is undoubtedly a correct answer.

What we have now: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture﴾ is emphasized with three emphatics. Is it for the denial of the addressee, or his hesitation, or what? We said: for the importance of the subject, because the subject is important, so it needs emphasis to console the Messenger, peace be upon him.

* Among the benefits of this verse: affirmation of the prophethood of Moses. From where is this taken? What is the reasoning?
* A student: The reasoning is that a book is only given to a prophet.
* The Shaykh: Well done. The reasoning is that a book is only given to a prophet.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to believe that Allah gave Moses a book, because Allah informed us of it, and His information is true, and because that is part of believing in the books of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that disagreement was not an innovation among nations. Those before this Ummah also differed about their books and messengers, as His saying shows: ﴿but differences arose concerning it﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: consoling the afflicted by mentioning someone who shares his affliction. Why? What is the purpose of the report that Allah gave Moses the Scripture and differences arose concerning it? The purpose is to console the Prophet, peace be upon him. On this basis, it is recommended to console the afflicted. This includes what is called condolence for the bereaved. Whoever is struck by a death, it is part of the Sunnah to offer condolence to him, that is, to strengthen him to endure the calamity.

So, among the benefits of the verse: consoling the afflicted. Is this consolation a sunnah, or is it permissible? We say: it is a sunnah, because it removes the pain of the calamity from your Muslim brother.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in delaying punishment from those who denied the messengers, because Allah has made a measure for everything. So from His wisdom is the delay of punishment from the nations, that perhaps they may return.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the completeness of the authority of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He, may He be exalted, is the one who manages affairs, by raising and by seizing, based on His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the elevated status of the Messenger, peace be upon him, with Allah. Is it taken from this?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, the elevation of his status. Because He said: ﴿from your Lord﴾, attributing lordship to him. This is a special lordship, and it indicates the high rank of the one who is lordship-cherished with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The general and the special lordship are both combined in the saying of the sorcerers from the people of Pharaoh: ﴿They said: We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ [Al-A'raf 121-122]. The first, "Lord of the worlds," is general, and the second is special.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, the Exalted, refers to evil by using the passive voice, when the doer is not named. Based on His saying: ﴿it would have been judged between them﴾, and He did not say: "He would have judged between them." This is the consistent and predominant pattern in the Qur'an. Observe the manners of the jinn, when they said: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [Al-Jinn 10]. This is lofty courtesy. Regarding evil they said: ﴿evil is intended for those on the earth﴾ and did not attribute it to Allah. Regarding guidance they said: ﴿whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾, and they did not say "guidance is intended for them" but rather "their Lord intends for them guidance." This is from the courtesy of the jinn, and the jinn are sometimes more courteous than mankind. ﴿And [mention] when We turned to you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an. When they attended it, they said: Be silent﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 29]. Some of them advised one another to be silent so that they might listen with complete attention. ﴿And when it was concluded﴾, they also did not hesitate or grow lazy, ﴿they went back to their people as warners﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 29]. They hastened to their people as warners. ﴿They said: O our people, indeed we have heard a Book﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 30], and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those who deny the Book of Moses are in disquieting doubt, that is, doubt accompanied by anxiety. The difference between "rayb" and "shakk" (doubt) is close. For this reason some scholars explain "rayb" as "shakk." But Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is a loose explanation, and "rayb" is more specific than general doubt, since it involves anxiety along with the uncertainty. That is because a matter one doubts is either of no importance, so you will find the doubter saying: "It does not matter to me whether it is established or not." Or it is of importance, and then if one doubts it, he will be anxious: will he believe in it or deny it, since it is an important matter? Thus "rayb" generally comes only with important matters. As for mere doubt, such as doubting whether so-and-so has arrived or not, when his arrival or absence is of no importance, this does not require "rayb."

﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt about it﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that faith must not be mixed with doubt, and that if doubt enters the heart, even slightly, provided one does not repel it but inclines to it, this nullifies faith. But if doubt enters the heart and one drives it away and strives against it, this does no harm. That is why the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed that people ask: "Who created such-and-such? Who created such-and-such?" until they say: "Who created Allah?" This is doubt. But the Messenger informed and said: "When one of you reaches that, or a similar word, let him seek refuge in Allah and desist." [Narrated by Muslim (134/212) from Abu Hurayrah.] And the Companions informed him that they find in themselves what they would prefer to be a charred ember rather than speak of. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "That is the clear sign of faith." [Narrated by Muslim (132/209) from Abu Hurayrah.]

So the upshot is this: if a doubt that comes upon the heart is one a person settles into and relies upon, then let him know that he is not a believer, because faith is incompatible with two things: doubt and denial. But if it comes upon the heart and he drives it away and strives against himself to abandon it, does it harm him in this state or not? It does not harm him; rather, this is the clear sign of faith and its pure form. That is because Satan does not cast such matters upon a dead heart. The dead heart is at rest from it; he casts it only upon a living heart, in order to kill it.

When the Jews mentioned to Ibn Mas'ud, or to Ibn 'Abbas, that they did not experience whisperings (waswasah) in their prayer, intending by this to boast over the Muslims, he said: "They have spoken the truth. And what does Satan do with a ruined heart?!" This is a great statement. He means: their hearts are ruined, and what does Satan do with a ruined heart? Does he come to it in order to ruin it? The answer: No. Satan only brings these whisperings to a living heart in order to destroy it or make it sick.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 46 (part 1 of 2):

He says: ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt concerning it.﴾ Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it. And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ [Fussilat 46]. ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul.﴾ This is a conditional sentence. What is its conditional particle and what is its verb of condition?
* Student: "Does" (ʿamila).
* The Shaykh: And what is the response of the condition?
* Student: ﴿it is for his own soul﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿it is for his own soul﴾, correct. This is the conditional sentence: the verb of condition is ﴿does﴾ (ʿamila), and the response of the condition is ﴿it is for his own soul﴾, and it is connected with the fa' (fa), because it is a nominal sentence; the estimated form is: "so his deed is for his own soul." The exegete estimated it with his words: "(so for his own soul is the deed)." But if we estimate it as a nominal sentence, there is no harm.
﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾: ﴿righteousness﴾ (ṣāliḥan) is an adjective of a deleted noun, and the estimate is: "a righteous deed." So what is the righteous deed? The righteous deed is that in which two matters are combined. The first: sincerity (ikhlāṣ) to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The second: following (mutābaʿa) the Sharia of Allah. Pay attention: following the Sharia of Allah. We do not say: following Muhammad (ﷺ), because we are speaking of righteous deeds in this nation and in other nations. So we say: sincerity to Allah and following the Sharia of Allah, so that it encompasses what was in the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was in earlier nations. If sincerity is absent, it is not righteous, because it is shirk, rejected upon its doer. Allah, the Exalted, said in the Hadith Qudsi: "I am the most independent of partners from partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his partnership."[[Recorded by Muslim (2985 / 46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And whoever is sincere but upon other than the Sharia of Allah, his deed is an innovation (bidʿa), rejected, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected."[[Recorded by Muslim (1718 / 18) from the hadith of ʿĀʾisha.]] And in another narration: "Whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not part of it, it is rejected."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718 / 17) from the hadith of ʿĀʾisha.]] So the righteous deed is that in which two conditions are combined.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done, and you know the evidence. He said: ﴿And whoever does evil, it is against it.﴾
His words: ﴿it is for his own soul﴾ mean that the benefit is for himself, for that does not benefit Allah in anything. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said in the Hadith Qudsi narrated by Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah said: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were upon the most pious heart of one man among you, that would not increase My dominion by anything."[[Recorded by Muslim (2577 / 55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] Why? Because Allah, the Exalted, does not benefit from the obedience of the obedient, nor is He harmed by the disobedience of the disobedient. The deed is for one's own self.
(﴿And whoever does evil, it is against it﴾, meaning: the harm of his evil falls upon himself.) If we said the estimate is "so his evil is against it," that would suffice. ﴿Whoever does evil﴾, meaning: he does a deed that is not righteous. What shows us that the meaning of evil here is a deed that is not righteous? Because it is contrasted with what preceded it: "whoever does righteousness." This is one of the methods by which the Quran is explained, and indeed other speech as well: when a thing is mentioned, and then what follows it is mentioned in contrast, the latter is explained in the opposite sense of the former. Among examples is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So go forth in groups or go forth all together﴾ [an-Nisa' 71]. If you reflect on the meaning of ﴿in groups (thubat)﴾, does it mean: "go forth steadfast in jihad"? No. What explains it is what follows it, ﴿or go forth all together﴾, so the meaning of ﴿thubat﴾ is: individually, or all together.
﴿And whoever does evil, it is against it.﴾ So evil occurs either through associating partners with Allah, such as showing off (riyaʾ) for example, or through innovation (bidʿa), such as the innovations of the Sufis and others among the adherents of the orders who are sincere to Allah and wish to draw near to Allah, but by other than what Allah has legislated, so they are astray, just like the Christians entirely.
(﴿And whoever does evil, it is against it, and your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾, meaning: not one who is unjust.) ﴿And your Lord﴾: this is like His saying earlier: ﴿what has preceded from your Lord﴾. ﴿And your Lord﴾: to whom is the address? To the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. And is the (mā) here Tamimi or Hijazi? Everything in the Quran is Hijazi, because it is in the dialect of Quraysh. Accordingly, whenever (mā) comes, it is Hijazi. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿This is not a human﴾ [Yusuf 31]. Had it been Tamimi, He would have said "mā hādhā bashar" without the accusative; but He said ﴿mā hādhā basharan﴾. So whenever (mā) comes that is ambiguous between Hijazi and Tamimi, make it Hijazi. Here we say: (mā) is Hijazi, (rabb) is its noun, and (ẓallām) is its predicate, but it is put in the genitive by the superfluous preposition.
And as for His saying ﴿And your Lord﴾: is the address to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or is it general? The context of the verse shows that it is specific to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. However, the fact that a address is directed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) does not mean that the ruling is specific to him; rather it is for him and for the Ummah. For this reason we say: the address directed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, divides into three categories:
The first: what evidence shows is specific to him, such as His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [ash-Sharh 1]. Is this specific or general? Specific to the Messenger.
The second: what evidence shows is general, such as His saying, ﴿O Prophet﴾, which is an address to the Messenger, ﴿when you divorce women, divorce them﴾ [at-Talaq 1]. This is general, because He said: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce﴾. And among it is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [at-Tahrim 1, 2]. So the first part of the verse is specific and the second is general.
The third category: what has no evidence for either of these, so it is specific to the Messenger, but we too have an example in it. It has also been said that it is for the Ummah, but the Messenger was addressed with it because he is its leader, peace and blessings be upon him.
﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾. The author said: "(i.e., not one who is unjust)," indicating, may Allah have mercy on him, that ẓallām is a form of attribution (nisba), not an intensive form (mubālagha), because faʿʿāl comes for attribution, like najjār, haddād, khashshāb, and similar, and it comes for intensity. So here, is ẓallām intensive or attributive? It must be attributive, because if you made it intensive, the negation would be of intensity in injustice and not of injustice itself, whereas it is known that Allah, the Exalted, is free of injustice in its essence and of intensity in it.
So it must be said that ẓallām is a form of attribution, not an intensive form, and for this reason he explained it with the words: "(i.e., not one who is unjust)," and he cited in support of this the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ [an-Nisa' 40]. ﴿He does not wrong the weight of an atom﴾: whoever is free of injustice even to the weight of an atom cannot have injustice in more, nor in the weight of an atom either, nor less than it.
If someone says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the weight of an atom﴾ implies that what is less than it is possible.
We say: No, because ﴿the weight of an atom﴾ is brought as an intensifier, not as a restriction. And what is a restriction for intensity has no implicit meaning (mafhūm). Have you seen the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, it will be hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection"?[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2452) and Muslim (1610 / 137) from the hadith of Saʿid ibn Zayd.]] Do we say: whoever seizes half a span is not punished for it? No, but it was mentioned as an intensifier.
﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ (i.e., not one who is unjust). And His saying: ﴿to the servants﴾: do the servants mean by legislation (sharʿan) or by existence (kawnan)? By existence (kawnan): to the servants by existence; that is, He will not wrong anyone, even the disbeliever. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not wrong him.
If someone says: Allah, the Exalted, far be it, wrongs the disbeliever. The disbeliever is given enjoyment in this world, and even if he lives a thousand years in disbelief, [and ʿAbd Allah al-Afghani, I think, is thinking about this], he will be eternal in the Fire for how long? For ages upon ages, millions of years, although he only disbelieved for a thousand years. So the punishment exceeds the deed, and this is injustice. Would someone say this?
We say: No, by Allah. Allah, the Exalted, has given this man an excuse by sending messengers, sending down books, and giving him intellect, and He said: "If you do such and such, I will punish you forever and ever." So he went forward by his own choice. And if one does what necessitates this punishment by his own choice, and then is punished with it, is it said that he is wronged? Never is it said that he is wronged. Had he been ignorant of the punishment, we would say: yes, it is obligatory that he not be punished except in proportion to his sin in quantity and quality. But we say: this man knew, and an excuse was given to him by the sending of messengers and the explanation of what he would be punished with, and yet he persisted, as if he were saying: "I do not care if I am punished forever and ever." At that point it is he who has brought harm upon himself and done what necessitates this everlasting punishment.
﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾
* Among the benefits of this verse: the encouragement to righteous deeds, from His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul﴾, because when you know that your deed is for yourself, you will strive in it. So there is in it encouragement to righteous deeds.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: every deed without sincerity is a harm to its doer and not for him, because we explained the righteous deed as that which combines two conditions: sincerity and following.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever does an innovated deed, his deed is against him and not for him, because it does not enter into the righteous deed. My brothers, many of those who practice these innovations, you find them weeping and humbling themselves, and their hearts are softened, and they have more weeping than the sincere, following ones. So what do we say? Answer? We say: ﴿Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing good work﴾ [al-Kahf 103, 104]. So do not let what they do deceive you, because this is from the Shaytan's seduction of them and his deception of them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the reward of a righteous deed cannot reach another person, from His saying: ﴿for his own soul﴾. Most scholars have taken this view and said: the deceased benefits only from the deed of his child, but not from anyone else. That is, if you performed ʿumrah on behalf of a deceased or living friend of yours who cannot perform ʿumrah, that does not benefit him. Why? Because whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self and does not extend to others. What the Sunnah has brought, such as a woman fasting a month's vow on behalf of her mother,[[Recorded by Muslim (1148 / 156) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]] or performing Hajj on behalf of her father who cannot sit upon the mount, this only occurred from the child, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the best of what you eat is from your earnings, and indeed your children are from your earnings."[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (3528) and al-Tirmidhi (1358) from the hadith of ʿĀʾisha.]] So the deed is from the earnings of the father and mother, and the child is part of his father, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fatimah is a part of me; what troubles her troubles me."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5230) and Muslim (2449 / 93) from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah.]] He said this from the pulpit. In this long hadith, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also censured ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and praised Abu al-ʿAs ibn al-Rabiʿ, the husband of his daughter Zaynab, and said: "He spoke to me and told the truth, and promised me and fulfilled his promise to me." He criticized ʿAli because it was said that he wanted to marry the daughter of Abu Jahl. The Messenger stood, gave a sermon to the people, and said: "Fatimah is a part of me; what troubles her troubles me."
He spoke in harsh terms, but ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, gave up the matter when he saw the Prophet (ﷺ) so affected, and that it was not possible to combine the daughter of the Prophet of Allah with the daughter of the enemy of Allah, because this would become a topic for people.
In any case, we say: some scholars took what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates, and said: a deed one intends for anyone is not beneficial except from a child. But many scholars said: rather, what the deceased benefits from his child, there is no objection to his benefiting from it from others. It may be cited as evidence for this the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man saying: "Labbayka on behalf of Shubrumah." He said: "Who is Shubrumah?" He said: "A brother of mine or a relative of mine." He said: "A brother or a relative, and you are in ihram on his behalf." They said: this indicates that it is permissible for a person to act as a proxy for another, so it is said: this is proxy for another, and Hajj is also accepted from him. But what appears to me is that there is no difference between the child and others, or between Hajj and other acts. What we criticize, however, is the extravagance of people now in deeds for the dead. You find someone who memorizes the Quran several times in Ramadan and says: "The first time is for my mother, the second for my parents, the third for my grandmother, the fourth for my grandfather, the fifth for my brother, the sixth for my sister, the seventh for my paternal uncle, the eighth for my paternal aunt," and Ramadan ends with him having no reward, all of it given to the people. This is an error, excessive, and not the guidance of the righteous predecessors.
Likewise, some people are extravagant and oppose the Sunnah in their extravagance. You find him going to perform ʿumrah: his first ʿumrah, and at the same time, while in Makkah, a second ʿumrah for his mother, and a third ʿumrah for his father, an ʿumrah every day. If we suppose he has ten days left and ten relatives, that is ten ʿumrahs. This is an error; it is not the guidance of the predecessors, and the Sharia is not according to taste, inclination, or whim. The Sharia is defined. Was it reported from the predecessors that they repeated ʿumrah? No, neither for themselves nor for others. Nothing of the kind was reported at all. Therefore the basic principle of repeating ʿumrah within a single journey is that it is not legislated. For this reason ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, the scholar of Makkah in his time, said: "I do not know whether those who go out to al-Tanʿim, will they sin or be safe?" meaning that they have no reward, because it was not reported from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, nor from the Companions. Therefore it is obligatory upon you, students of knowledge, to clarify to the people even if they criticize you. We always warn against this in the Haram, and we say: this is an error, and it is not legislated. Then they come and go to some people, who say: "No, it does not contradict. On your first day, for you; on your second day, for your mother; on your third day, for your father; it does not contradict."
(...) Every scholar: one ʿumrah each. Even if your relatives are many and your days in Makkah are few, there is no harm in taking two ʿumrahs in one day; there is no objection. If they are even more and the days fewer, make two ʿumrahs in the day and two at night. There is no god but Allah! Who said this?! But the problem is that some scholars are lax in these matters and do not ease the lives of Allah's servants. You find a poor man during the Hajj season, bearing an enormous burden in crowding and hardship, and yet he insists on performing an ʿumrah for his father and mother, though this is not the guidance of the predecessors, and he constricts the people, and people constrict one another. We ask Allah for guidance.
So in any case, His saying ﴿for his own soul﴾ has been cited by some scholars as proof that a righteous deed does not extend to others, that is, does not extend beyond its doer. We say: what the Sunnah has brought specifies this, and the Sunnah explains and clarifies the Quran. Then can it be analogized? This is open to consideration, and in my view there is no harm in analogizing from it, because what was reported are specific cases; when they are specific cases, we may say: and we analogize from these particular cases to what resembles them. But what is condemned is extravagance and excess.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: whoever does evil, it is against himself that he does evil, and he does not harm Allah in any way. But if someone says: Did not the Prophet (ﷺ) inform us that, «Whoever establishes a bad practice in Islam, he bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection»?[[Reported by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah.]] So then this person's wrongdoing becomes a burden upon him, while Allah says: ﴿and whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾, meaning against himself alone. It is said in reply: his establishing this evil practice is his own deed, which the people followed him in. Had he not done what he did, the people would not have done it; they only did it by following him. So in reality it is from his own doing, because he is the one who established this bad practice. For this reason, «No soul is slain unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its guilt»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6867) and Muslim (1677) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]].

Who was the first of the sons of Adam to kill? It was Qabil (Cain), who killed Habil (Abel). He killed Habil out of envy, without any wrong done to him. They both offered an offering, and Allah accepted it from Habil and did not accept it from Qabil. So he said to him: "I will surely kill you." Why? Out of envy, because Allah accepted from his companion and did not accept from him. So his brother advised him what would make acceptance possible, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah accepts only from the righteous﴾ [al-Ma'idah 27]. The meaning of the verse is an exhortation to him to be God-fearing; it does not mean that he was praising himself, saying that he was righteous and so it was accepted. Rather, he was urging piety, as if he were saying: fear Allah, and He will accept from you.

Then he said to him: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah 28]. Perhaps defending oneself was not permitted in their time, because in our law, if someone wants to kill you, you must defend yourself; even if you kill him, he is in the Fire, and if he kills you, you are a martyr. But perhaps in their time that was not permitted, and it is one of the burdens that Allah imposed on those before us, from which Allah has freed us. ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds. Indeed, I want you to bear my sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah 28-29], and so on to the end. The point in any case is that we say: whoever establishes a bad practice, its establishment is from his deed, so the burden of whoever acts upon it falls on him, because he is the one who established it.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the negation of injustice from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿and your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾. Is this among the attributes of negation or the attributes of affirmation? It is among the attributes of negation. The attributes of Allah, exalted is He, are of two kinds: attributes of affirmation and attributes of negation. The attributes of affirmation are very numerous, and the attributes of negation are fewer. Yet the attributes of negation are in reality attributes of affirmation, because what is meant by negation is the affirmation of the opposite of that. For example, ﴿and your Lord is not unjust﴾ means the affirmation of His perfect justice, and that His justice contains no injustice in any way whatsoever.

So take this as a broad principle: pure negation does not occur in the attributes of Allah at all. Every negation in the attributes of Allah is an affirmation. An affirmation of what? Is it an affirmation of the negation, or an affirmation of its opposite? It is an affirmation of its opposite. So it is as if He, Mighty and Majestic, is saying: He is the most just of judges, and there is no injustice in His judgment at all. Is that clear?

﴿And your Lord was not ever forgetful﴾ [Maryam 64]. Is this among the attributes of negation or affirmation? It is among the attributes of negation, but it affirms the perfection of His knowledge, and because of the perfection of His knowledge, forgetfulness never reaches Him at all. Our knowledge, by contrast, is subject to forgetfulness, and it is also acquired after prior ignorance: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [al-Nahl 78]. So our knowledge is defective in several respects. It is in two respects, and then in three:
The first respect: it is preceded by ignorance.
The second: it is followed by forgetfulness.
The third: it is not comprehensive or all-encompassing.

In any case, we say: this negation regarding the attribute of Allah is not meant as pure negation; rather it is in reality an affirmation. For what is it meant? 
* Student: The affirmation of the perfection of its opposite.
* The Shaykh: The affirmation of the perfection of its opposite. ﴿and your Lord is not unjust﴾ means He is just, and there is no injustice in His justice at all.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the affirmation of justice at its highest level. How? Because He said: ﴿to the servants﴾, meaning to His servants. This is more eloquent than if I said to you: you do not wrong your servants, which is more eloquent than if I said: you do not wrong people. Why? Because your not wronging people is because you have no power over them. But if you do not wrong your servants, this is more eloquent in affirming justice.

If you do not wrong one over whom you have authority, then by a fortiori you do not wrong one over whom you have no authority. So compare ﴿and your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ with the saying of someone: so-and-so does not wrong people. Which is more eloquent? The first. Because if he does not wrong his servants, though they are his servants and he may do with them as he wishes, then he will not wrong others. But this is by way of supposition; otherwise, everyone in the heavens and the earth comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (the determinist sect). The Jabriyyah say: injustice with regard to Allah is impossible, and the negation of what is impossible is not praise. I tell you now: the negation of what is impossible is not praise.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, why? Because the impossible cannot exist in its own essence, and even if a person wanted it, it would not come into being, because it is impossible. But the negation of what is possible, when the negation is praiseworthy, is praise. Here, ﴿and your Lord is not unjust﴾: does the verse indicate that injustice with regard to Him is possible? Yes, it indicates that it is possible, but because of His perfect justice it cannot occur. So injustice is not impossible in its essence with regard to Allah; rather it is impossible because of Allah's perfect justice. Do you understand, or not? And thus praise is realized: the praise of Allah, exalted is He, by the negation of injustice from Him. As for something that is impossible and cannot occur, what is impossible is not praised.

﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾. Shall we proceed, or has the time ended?
* Student: (...) those who do (...).
* The Shaykh: It will be in their hearts.
* Student: (...) and we took as evidence His saying, exalted is He: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Say: Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?﴾
* Student: (...) although this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers (...).
* The Shaykh: Everyone who does evil while thinking he is doing good is included in the verse. Although this verse ﴿those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in His meeting﴾ [al-Kahf 105] is about them, it also includes others.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We follow this. Now we judge by this that what has been established as ugly through a specific deed is shared by whatever agrees with it in the cause.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding matters that a person speaks to himself about, other than shirk, such as sins, if he inclines toward them but does not act upon them, are they included in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, Allah..."?
* The Shaykh: «Indeed, Allah has overlooked for my Ummah what its souls whisper about, so long as it does not act upon it or speak of it»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5269) and Muslim (127/202) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Student: Provided it is not shirk and he inclines toward it, like sins?
* The Shaykh: That is, he wanted it?
* Student: And he did not do it..
* The Shaykh: I am asking you: did he want it or not?
* Student: I am not saying he wanted it; because if he wanted it...
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of this?
* Student: That is, he thought about it.
* The Shaykh: He thought about it, but he did not resolve upon it. There is nothing on him for that. But safety is safer. Therefore we say: whoever wants a sin and does not commit it has three states:

The first state: he is unable to do it, and he takes the means by which he intends to reach it, but he is unable. Like a thief who resolved to steal and placed a ladder against the wall to climb up, and while he was in the midst of climbing, a man passed by in the street, so he descended and fled. This is recorded for him as though he had committed the bad deed completely, even though he did not commit it. We say: because he wanted it and worked toward it, but was unable. The evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire.» They said: O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, so what about the killed? He said: «Because he was eager to kill his companion»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (31) and Muslim (2888/14) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]]. So whoever resolves upon an evil deed and works toward it, but is unable to complete it, its full burden is recorded for him.

The second: one who resolves upon it and desires it, but is unable to do it without actually doing its deed. For this there is the burden of intention. The evidence for this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) reported about a man whom Allah had given wealth, and he began to spend it recklessly. The poor man said: If only I had wealth like so-and-so's, I would act as so-and-so acts. He said: «He is by his intention, and the two of them are equal in the burden»[[Reported by al-Tirmidhi (2325) and Ibn Majah (4228) from the hadith of Abu Kabshah al-Ansari.]]. Is it the burden of action or the burden of will? It is the burden of will, because this one did not act.

The third: one who resolved upon the evil and determined upon it, but then remembered the fear of Allah and abandoned it out of fear of Allah. For this, it is recorded for him as a complete good deed.

There is a fourth category, but it does not fall within our division: one to whom the sin never occurred, it never crossed his mind. For such a person nothing is recorded for him or against him, like an upright person to whom theft, adultery, or drinking wine never comes to mind. This is neither for him nor against him. But this is not included in the division of intention; we are speaking of the division of intention, that is, one who wills evil.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. Here there are two forms for one who intends to act on behalf of another:
The first form: he forms the intention for the other from the beginning of the act, from the moment he intends to say the takbir, he intends that it is for his father or mother. This is valid and there is no problem with it, because it is like one who performs Hajj intending it on behalf of his father or mother from the outset.
The second: he performs the act, and then after finishing it, he intends it for his father or mother. Scholars differ regarding this, even those who hold that it is permissible to gift acts of worship (ihda' al-qurab) differ on whether this is valid or not.

The difference between this and the previous one is that in the previous one, he began the intention from the start of the action; he acts, moves, and speaks while feeling that he is performing it on behalf of another. As for this one, he prayed and finished his prayer intending it for himself, so the reward was established for him. When the reward is established for him, it is not his right to dispose of the reward; he can dispose of the deed, but not of the reward. So these people say: if he gifts the deed after performing it, it does not reach the one to whom it is gifted. Why? Because the deed was established for himself and the act and intention ended for himself. If he gifts it to another, he has disposed of the reward, and disposing of the reward is not up to him; it is up to whom? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is not a financial matter. You say: By Allah, I give so-and-so ten dirhams, a hundred dirhams; this is a reward with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it was recorded for you, and the matter is finished. This distinction is a good distinction and has a subtle meaning. Do you understand?
* Student: Two types: the first (...).
* The Shaykh: From the beginning, yes.
* Student: And the second, if he acts (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, some scholars say: this is not valid. The second: because he disposed of the reward, and the reward was completed when he finished the worship, and it was completed for whom? For this worshipper himself.
* Student: And disposing of the reward belongs to Allah.
* The Shaykh: Yes, no... good, may Allah bless you, that is correct. What is it with you sitting opposite me entirely?
I say: there is no doubt that this is a good meaning, the distinction between performing the deed from its beginning for your companion and performing it for yourself and then afterward gifting its reward to your companion. It is said: now the deed has been recorded for you, and the reward has been recorded for you, so you cannot dispose of it; the disposing of the reward belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And Allah knows best. Is that so?
* Student: The second opinion: (...) The first opinion: that it is not valid.
* The Shaykh: Did we not say the first? We said: there is no harm; scholars do not distinguish. But the second is the one in which there is disagreement.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What? The emphasis is for what?
* Student: For emphasis.
* The Shaykh: For emphasis?
* Student: The emphasis (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, the form of a declarative statement? Is it emphasized or not emphasized?
* Student: We say: the emphasis (...) in the sense of a declarative statement.
* The Shaykh: That is, do you mean that a declarative sentence is emphasized to show concern for the matter? Yes, what about it?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: In the three states, for what?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, the concern with it, even if the addressee is affirming it. That is, emphasizing a statement for concern with it, even when the addressee already accepts it. The condition of the addressee does not require emphasis, since he accepts it, but concern with the matter requires emphasis. For example, ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah 1]: if we address it to a believer, it is for emphasis only, for emphasis and concern with the matter. If we address it to a denier, it becomes a rejection of denial.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

We begin the morning summer study session in the Grand Mosque in 'Unayzah this day, Saturday, the first of Rabi' al-Awwal. We ask Allah, blessed and exalted, to grant us and you beneficial knowledge, righteous and accepted deeds, and abundant good provision. As for the schedule that will be before you, God willing, we will follow it by Allah's leave; we ask Allah for success. We now begin the tafsir. Who is the reader? Who among you is the best in recitation and voice?

Begin with the name of Allah: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾.

* The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour, and no fruits come out of their coverings﴾.

* The Shaykh: It is better to stop.

* The student: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour, and no fruits come out of their coverings, and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?" They will say, "We have informed You that none of us bears witness."﴾ (47) ﴿And lost from them is what they used to invoke before, and they will be certain that there is for them no place of escape.﴾ (48) ﴿Man does not tire of supplication for good, but if evil touches him, he is hopeless and despairing.﴾ (49) ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "This is for me, and I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]." But We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment.﴾ [Fussilat 47–50].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾. This is the lesson of tafsir, meaning the explanation of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It should be known that the most important thing to be concerned with in understanding its meaning is the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because it is the most truthful of books, the most wise, and the most beneficial for the heart and the limbs; "and because this has been the practice of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, for they did not go beyond ten verses until they had learned them and what they contained of knowledge and action, so they learned the Qur'an together with knowledge and action."[[Narrated by al-Tahawi in al-Mushkil (1452) from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami.]]

The best method of tafsir is that the Qur'an be explained by the Qur'an, because explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an is an explanation from the One who revealed it, blessed and exalted, and He is the most knowing of His intended meaning. So the Qur'an is explained by the Qur'an. If that is not possible, then by the Sunnah. If that is not possible, then by the sayings of the Companions, especially those well known for tafsir, such as Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both. If that is not possible, do we refer to the sayings of the Successors (tabi'un) on this or not? As for one who is known for taking from the Companions, there is no doubt that his saying is preferred over others, but it is not binding. Then after this, the tafsir of the Qur'an is taken from the tafsir of the Imams who are attested to for knowledge and faith. People have dealt with the tafsir of the Qur'an: some explained it by what we have mentioned, and some explained it by their own opinion, bending the verses to what they believe from a misguided doctrine, and such a person deserves the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family: "Whoever speaks about the Qur'an by his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2950) from a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] Therefore, it is obligatory upon you to ponder the meaning of the Qur'an before you judge, so that the Qur'an does not become subordinate to your judgment.

Then, a person should first reflect on the meaning of the verse himself, ponder and contemplate. When a meaning occurs to his mind, then he should return to the words of the scholars, lest he has erred, and he should not be an imitator who consults and says what the people say. He must first ponder; when a meaning occurs to his mind, then he should return to the words of the scholars, lest he be astray in this understanding.

As for one whose only concern is to consult the books of tafsir, his knowledge of the Qur'an must be deficient. We have spoken about what we have spoken about of the tafsir of the Qur'an, until we reached the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself; and whoever does evil, it is against himself. And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants. To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Fussilat 46, 47].

﴿To Him﴾ means to Allah alone. We said "alone" because of the fronting of the complement (al-ma'mul), and the fronting of the complement conveys restriction (hasr). That is because the complement's place is after the governing word (al-'amil); when it is placed before, it falls under the category of fronting what should be delayed, and the linguistic-rhetorical rule is: "fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction." Accordingly, for His saying ﴿To Him is referred﴾ we say: the meaning is: to Him and not to other than Him. And from where do we derive this negation ("not to other than Him")? From the fronting of the complement, because the complement's place is after the governing word; when it is fronted, this falls under fronting what should be delayed, and fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction. This is a linguistic-rhetorical rule.

﴿is referred﴾ means "is returned." ﴿the knowledge of the Hour﴾: the commentator said, "when it will occur," then he said, "none knows it but Him." He derived this restriction, "none knows it but Him," from the fronting of the complement, which is ﴿To Him﴾.

There is no doubt that none knows when the Hour will be established except Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. For this reason Allah said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time? Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal its time except Him."﴾ [al-A'raf 187], meaning: its knowledge is only with my Lord. And the Prophet ﷺ, when Jibril asked him, "Tell me, when is the Hour?" said: "The one asked about it is no more knowing than the one asking,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from Abu Hurayrah.]] meaning: I have no knowledge of it, just as you have no knowledge. Accordingly, whoever claims knowledge of the Hour is undoubtedly a liar, and moreover he is a disbeliever, because he denies the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour, and no fruits come out of their coverings﴾. As for His saying ﴿and no fruits come out﴾, it may appear to a person that "ma" is a relative pronoun, meaning: "and to Him is referred the knowledge of what fruits come out of their coverings." But this is a mistake, and accordingly we say: "ma" is a negation particle.

(﴿﴿And no fruit comes out﴾﴾ and in a reading ﴿fruits﴾): the author explained according to the reading ﴿fruit﴾ in the singular, while the reading in our Mushaf is ﴿fruits﴾ in the plural. Know that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, has a convention: when he says "and in a reading," it is one of the seven canonical readings; and when he says "and it was read," it is a irregular reading not among the seven. This is the convention of the two Jalals, may Allah have mercy on them both.

So (in a reading: ﴿fruits﴾), this reading is canonical; that is, it is established, and it is permissible to recite with it in prayer, and it serves as evidence in legal rulings and in factual reports. As for the plural form, it is clear: ﴿fruits﴾ means all fruits.
