As for the singular form, it also conveys generality, because "thamarah" is an indefinite noun in a negative context, emphasized by the extra "min," so it encompasses all fruits. Accordingly, there is no difference in meaning between "thamarat" and "thamarah."

(﴿﴿And no fruit comes out of its coverings﴾﴾ and in a reading ﴿fruits﴾, ﴿of their coverings﴾: their containers.) "Akmam" means containers; he says: (plural of "kimm," with a kasra on the kaf) "from their coverings" means the sheaths of the spathe. This is well known in palm trees, and likewise well known in flowers: you find the blossom has a sheath called "kimm." So no fruit comes out of its sheath except by the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; whatever fruit is small or large, edible or inedible, it is by the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The reason it is by His knowledge is that these fruits are created by Allah, and everything created by Allah is known to Him, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14]. So whenever you affirm that Allah is the Creator of these, it necessarily follows from your affirmation that Allah knows them, because it is impossible for Him to create them while not knowing. For this reason Allah established this by a rational proof: ﴿Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14].

﴿And no fruits come out of their coverings, and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fussilat 47]: "and no female conceives," meaning any female, of the children of Adam or of animals; no female conceives or gives birth except by the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So the beginning of pregnancy is known to Allah, and its delivery is likewise known to Allah, blessed and exalted. We return to His saying ﴿from a female﴾ and to His saying ﴿from fruit﴾.

Grammatical analysis: ﴿min﴾ is a prepositional particle, an extra (za'id) one in terms of grammatical function, but not extra in terms of meaning, because it conveys a meaning, namely emphasis. Accordingly, we say: ﴿from fruit﴾: ﴿min﴾ is an extra prepositional particle, and ﴿fruit﴾ is a subject in the nominative case marked by a presumed damma at its end, prevented from appearing by the movement of the extra preposition's place. Likewise it is said: ﴿min unthā﴾: ﴿min﴾ is an extra preposition, and ﴿unthā﴾ is a subject in the nominative case marked by a presumed damma at its end, prevented from appearing by the impossibility (ta'adhdhur) of pronouncing it, and it is in the genitive position verbally because ﴿min﴾ precedes it.

As for His saying ﴿except with His knowledge﴾: is it His knowledge prior, or knowledge that arises at the moment the thing exists? The answer: prior, because Allah's knowledge encompasses everything eternally and everlastingly; so He knows what fruits come out of their coverings until the Day of Resurrection, and likewise what a female conceives and does not deliver.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Fussilat 47]. ﴿The day﴾ is an adverbial complement of time, and an adverb requires something it relates to, since it is an object of time; and if it is an adverbial object, there must be a verb that governs it. Where is the governing word? The governing word here is implied, and the estimate is: "Remember the day He calls to them." Such an expression is frequent in the Qur'an. The estimate, as I mentioned, is that the governing word is omitted: "Remember the day He calls to them, 'Where are My partners?'" etc. Allah commanded His Prophet to mention it only to frighten these deniers and to console the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

His saying ﴿He calls to them﴾ means He summons them with a raised voice, because calling (nida') is with a raised voice, whereas secret conversation (munajah) is with a lower voice. The subject of ﴿calls to them﴾ is Allah, as is shown by His saying ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, meaning that Allah, blessed and exalted, calls these polytheists, saying: "Where are My partners?" This interrogation is both for rebuke and for reproach; it combines two meanings: rebuke (ta'jiz), and second, reproach (tawbikh). That is: where are those you associated with Me? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿They will say, "We have informed You"﴾ [Fussilat 47], that is, we now inform You, ﴿that none of us bears witness﴾ [Fussilat 47]. ("Adhana" means "a'lama," "informed") as in His saying: ﴿And a declaration from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 3], meaning an announcement from Allah and His Messenger; so "adhana" means "a'lama." And from this is what is in the hadith, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the women who washed his daughter: "When you finish, inform me" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1253) and Muslim (939/36) from Umm 'Atiyyah al-Ansariyyah.]], meaning: inform me.

﴿We have informed You﴾: the author says, "we have informed You now." By his saying "now" the author indicates that the past verb ﴿adhannaka﴾ carries the sense of the present; so it is a declarative clause of the present state, meaning: "now we inform You." "None of us is a witness." And it was said that "adhannaka" is a past verb in its original sense, and thus is a report about a past matter.

So there are two views: is the informing here on the Day of Resurrection, as the author said, "we have informed You now," or is it a prior informing in this world? If we look at the apparent wording, we would prefer that it is an informing in this world, meaning: "We informed You in this world," and it would be on its apparent sense. But this explanation is problematic, because the reality of their condition does not indicate this, since they are in fact polytheists; how would they inform Him that none of them bears witness to that? Those who hold this view answered that the meaning is: "we informed You according to the fitrah and what is in our hearts," because "no child is born except upon the fitrah." Pay attention now to the meaning.

﴿adhannaka﴾: its form is a past verb, which requires that this informing preceded the time of address; this is one point.

﴿adhannaka﴾ is a past verb but is intended to report on the present state, so it means: "we now inform You." This explanation contradicts the apparent wording but agrees with the reality of their condition. The first explanation agrees with the wording but contradicts the apparent reality of their condition, since they do not inform Him of that, being in fact polytheists. Those who say "adhannaka" refers to this world answered that they informed Him according to the fitrah with which they were created, because "no child is born except upon the fitrah."

﴿They said, "We have informed You; none of us is a witness"﴾ [Fussilat 47] (that is, a witness that You have a partner). ﴿mā﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿minnā﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate preceding the subject. ﴿min﴾ is an extra preposition grammatically. ﴿shahīd﴾ is a subject in the nominative case marked by a presumed damma at its end, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the movement of the extra preposition. The meaning is: we have now acknowledged that none of us bears witness that You have a partner, and they say this now, but it does not benefit them, because it is an acknowledgment after seeing the punishment, and acknowledgment after seeing the punishment does not benefit. For this reason Pharaoh, when he was drowned, acknowledged that ﴿there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed﴾ [Yunus 90], but it did not benefit him, and it was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus 91].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 47–48 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those they used to invoke before will vanish from them﴾ [Fussilat 48]. That is: (ghaaba), ﴿vanish from them, what they used to invoke before﴾. ﴿What﴾ (ma) is a relative noun, the subject, meaning: "that which". ﴿Vanish from them what they used to invoke﴾. The author said: (they worshipped) ﴿before﴾ (in the world, of the idols), their idols to which they clung and which they worshipped, supposing that they would bring them near to Allah in rank, on that day when they are most in need of them. They will vanish from them and will not benefit them. Therefore He said: ﴿vanished from them﴾, that is, was lost and disappeared, ﴿what they used to invoke﴾, that is, worship before, meaning by this the idols which they worshipped in the world. For example, the Christians worship 'Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary); the Quraysh worshipped al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat and Hubal; some worship fire, like the Magians; some worship the sun, some worship the moon, and so on. These idols that are worshipped besides Allah: will they benefit them on the Day of Resurrection? No. Therefore He said: ﴿vanished from them what they used to invoke before﴾. Perhaps from His saying ﴿vanished from them﴾ we may understand that they went looking for them, searching for them, but they were lost and disappeared, and this will be a greater grief in their souls, that they sought them at the time of need but did not find them.

﴿And they were certain﴾ — he said: (they became certain) ﴿that there was for them no escape﴾ (zanna) here means "to be certain" (ayqana). Does the word zann come in the sense of certainty? The answer: Yes, it comes often. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are going to fall into it, and will not find from it any way of turning away﴾ [al-Kahf 53]. So "zannu" means "ayqanu" (they were certain).

Allah the Blessed and Exalted also said: ﴿those who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 46]. The meaning of ﴿yazunnun﴾ is: they are certain that they will meet their Lord. Had zann meant a probable thing, they would not have been believers; rather, yazunnun means yuqinun (they are certain). So zann in the Arabic language comes in the sense of certainty. Here, ﴿zannu ma lahum min mahis﴾ means they became certain. Did it become for them a probable matter? No, they became certain.

As for His saying ﴿ma lahum min mahis﴾, there is in it inversion and emphasis. The inversion is that the predicate was placed first and the subject was placed last. Where is the predicate? ﴿lahum﴾. Where is the subject? ﴿mahis﴾. There is also emphasis in it, namely the extra ﴿min﴾; because ﴿mahis﴾ is a postponed subject, and the extra ﴿min﴾ entered upon it for emphasis. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is that it is a subject in the nominative case by virtue of beginning, and the sign of its nominative case is a presumed damma on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the harmonizing vowel.

His saying: (﴿mahis﴾: a place of escape from the punishment) means they became certain that there is no escape for them from the punishment, and no refuge for them from it, and that it will inevitably befall them.

Then the author said: (And the negation in both places is suspended from operating, and the negative clause took the place of the two objects.) Where are the two places? ﴿They said: "We have told You, there is none of us who can bear witness"﴾ [Fussilat 47]. This "ma" is a negation suspending the operation, because "adhannaka" means "We have informed You". (a'lama) governs three objects. You say, for example: "I informed Zayd 'Amran qa'iman" (I made Zayd know that 'Amr was standing). How many objects did it govern here? Three: Zayd, 'Amr and standing. Here, in ﴿adhannaka﴾, the first object is present, which is the kaf (You). The second and third objects are suspended, and the interrogative clause ﴿ma minna min shahid﴾ has stood in for them.

On this basis, the whole clause ﴿ma minna min shahid﴾ is in the place of accusative standing in for the two objects of (adhana). I say: the first and second? No, I say: the second and third.

﴿And they were certain: ma lahum min mahis﴾ — this is the second. ﴿Zannu﴾ — this (zanna) governs how many objects? It governs two objects. Here there are no two objects; where are they? They were suspended from operating by the negative clause, which is His saying ﴿ma lahum min mahis﴾. On this basis, ﴿ma lahum min mahis﴾ is a clause in the place of accusative standing in for the two objects of (zanna). This is an i'rab that in reality only one who has knowledge of objects grasps; but we have now explained it, so whoever understands it, that is the goal, and whoever does not understand it, it does not harm him, because it has no connection with us; its relevance is only to i'rab.

Returning to deriving rulings from the verses, Allah said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Fussilat 47], etc.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that knowledge of the Hour is with Allah alone. From where is this taken, brother?
* Student: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾.
* The Shaykh: How did you take from it that it is with Allah alone?
* The student: Because what should be postponed was placed first, so it indicates restriction.
* The Shaykh: Because he placed first what should be postponed, namely the object, and this conveys restriction.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever claims knowledge of the Hour is a disbeliever. The reason: he contradicts Allah, and contradicting Allah is disbelief; and whoever believes him is also a disbeliever, because he has affirmed what contradicts the noble Qur'an, and whoever affirms what contradicts the noble Qur'an is without doubt a disbeliever.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, then he is despairing and hopeless. And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine, and I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best." But We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment. And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself, but when evil touches him, he is one of long supplication﴾ [Fussilat 49–51].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾. ﴿Does not tire﴾ means does not grow weary. He constantly asks for good: wealth, richness, status and other things.

Now let us take the benefits. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit emerges from its sheath, and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fussilat 47].

* Among its benefits: knowledge of the Hour is with Allah the Mighty and Majestic; none knows it but Him. We have mentioned evidence for this in the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), when he asked Jibril about the Hour to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to him: "The one asked is no more knowing than the asker."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* Among its benefits: whoever claims knowledge of the Hour is a disbeliever, because he denies Allah and His Messenger, and denying Allah and His Messenger is among the causes of apostasy, since apostasy revolves around two things: either denial or arrogance. Every apostasy for which scholars pass judgment does not go beyond these two matters: either denial or arrogance.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of Allah the Mighty and Majestic's knowledge, by His saying ﴿and no fruit emerges from its sheath﴾ [Fussilat 47], etc.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the rebuke of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, by His saying ﴿and on the day He will call to them: "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Fussilat 47]. Rebuke in that place is among the greatest rebukes, because it is the witnessed day which Allah, His angels and all His creation witness.
* Among its benefits: the acknowledgment by these deniers of resurrection, on that day, that Allah the Mighty and Majestic has no partner, by His saying ﴿They said: "We have told You, none of us can bear witness"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the following verse: that what is worshipped besides Allah is destruction and error, and will not avail its worshippers at all, by His saying ﴿And those they used to invoke before will vanish from them﴾ [Fussilat 48].
* Among its benefits: that these deniers will be certain on that day that there is no escape for them from the punishment of Allah, because there is no one there who can repel Allah's punishment from them, so they become certain that there is no refuge for them from it.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

We begin the morning summer study session in the Grand Mosque in 'Unayzah this day, Saturday, the first of Rabi' al-Awwal. We ask Allah, blessed and exalted, to grant us and you beneficial knowledge, righteous and accepted deeds, and abundant good provision. As for the schedule that will be before you, God willing, we will follow it by Allah's leave; we ask Allah for success. We now begin the tafsir. Who is the reader? Who among you is the best in recitation and voice?

Begin with the name of Allah: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾.

* The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour, and no fruits come out of their coverings﴾.

* The Shaykh: It is better to stop.

* The student: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour, and no fruits come out of their coverings, and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?" They will say, "We have informed You that none of us bears witness."﴾ (47) ﴿And lost from them is what they used to invoke before, and they will be certain that there is for them no place of escape.﴾ (48) ﴿Man does not tire of supplication for good, but if evil touches him, he is hopeless and despairing.﴾ (49) ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "This is for me, and I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]." But We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment.﴾ [Fussilat 47–50].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾. This is the lesson of tafsir, meaning the explanation of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It should be known that the most important thing to be concerned with in understanding its meaning is the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because it is the most truthful of books, the most wise, and the most beneficial for the heart and the limbs; "and because this has been the practice of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, for they did not go beyond ten verses until they had learned them and what they contained of knowledge and action, so they learned the Qur'an together with knowledge and action."[[Narrated by al-Tahawi in al-Mushkil (1452) from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami.]]

The best method of tafsir is that the Qur'an be explained by the Qur'an, because explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an is an explanation from the One who revealed it, blessed and exalted, and He is the most knowing of His intended meaning. So the Qur'an is explained by the Qur'an. If that is not possible, then by the Sunnah. If that is not possible, then by the sayings of the Companions, especially those well known for tafsir, such as Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both. If that is not possible, do we refer to the sayings of the Successors (tabi'un) on this or not? As for one who is known for taking from the Companions, there is no doubt that his saying is preferred over others, but it is not binding. Then after this, the tafsir of the Qur'an is taken from the tafsir of the Imams who are attested to for knowledge and faith. People have dealt with the tafsir of the Qur'an: some explained it by what we have mentioned, and some explained it by their own opinion, bending the verses to what they believe from a misguided doctrine, and such a person deserves the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family: "Whoever speaks about the Qur'an by his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2950) from a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] Therefore, it is obligatory upon you to ponder the meaning of the Qur'an before you judge, so that the Qur'an does not become subordinate to your judgment.

Then, a person should first reflect on the meaning of the verse himself, ponder and contemplate. When a meaning occurs to his mind, then he should return to the words of the scholars, lest he has erred, and he should not be an imitator who consults and says what the people say. He must first ponder; when a meaning occurs to his mind, then he should return to the words of the scholars, lest he be astray in this understanding.

As for one whose only concern is to consult the books of tafsir, his knowledge of the Qur'an must be deficient. We have spoken about what we have spoken about of the tafsir of the Qur'an, until we reached the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself; and whoever does evil, it is against himself. And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants. To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Fussilat 46, 47].

﴿To Him﴾ means to Allah alone. We said "alone" because of the fronting of the complement (al-ma'mul), and the fronting of the complement conveys restriction (hasr). That is because the complement's place is after the governing word (al-'amil); when it is placed before, it falls under the category of fronting what should be delayed, and the linguistic-rhetorical rule is: "fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction." Accordingly, for His saying ﴿To Him is referred﴾ we say: the meaning is: to Him and not to other than Him. And from where do we derive this negation ("not to other than Him")? From the fronting of the complement, because the complement's place is after the governing word; when it is fronted, this falls under fronting what should be delayed, and fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction. This is a linguistic-rhetorical rule.

﴿is referred﴾ means "is returned." ﴿the knowledge of the Hour﴾: the commentator said, "when it will occur," then he said, "none knows it but Him." He derived this restriction, "none knows it but Him," from the fronting of the complement, which is ﴿To Him﴾.

There is no doubt that none knows when the Hour will be established except Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. For this reason Allah said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time? Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal its time except Him."﴾ [al-A'raf 187], meaning: its knowledge is only with my Lord. And the Prophet ﷺ, when Jibril asked him, "Tell me, when is the Hour?" said: "The one asked about it is no more knowing than the one asking,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from Abu Hurayrah.]] meaning: I have no knowledge of it, just as you have no knowledge. Accordingly, whoever claims knowledge of the Hour is undoubtedly a liar, and moreover he is a disbeliever, because he denies the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour, and no fruits come out of their coverings﴾. As for His saying ﴿and no fruits come out﴾, it may appear to a person that "ma" is a relative pronoun, meaning: "and to Him is referred the knowledge of what fruits come out of their coverings." But this is a mistake, and accordingly we say: "ma" is a negation particle.

(﴿﴿And no fruit comes out﴾﴾ and in a reading ﴿fruits﴾): the author explained according to the reading ﴿fruit﴾ in the singular, while the reading in our Mushaf is ﴿fruits﴾ in the plural. Know that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, has a convention: when he says "and in a reading," it is one of the seven canonical readings; and when he says "and it was read," it is a irregular reading not among the seven. This is the convention of the two Jalals, may Allah have mercy on them both.

So (in a reading: ﴿fruits﴾), this reading is canonical; that is, it is established, and it is permissible to recite with it in prayer, and it serves as evidence in legal rulings and in factual reports. As for the plural form, it is clear: ﴿fruits﴾ means all fruits. As for the singular form, it also conveys generality, because "thamarah" is an indefinite noun in a negative context, emphasized by the extra "min," so it encompasses all fruits. Accordingly, there is no difference in meaning between "thamarat" and "thamarah."

(﴿﴿And no fruit comes out of its coverings﴾﴾ and in a reading ﴿fruits﴾, ﴿of their coverings﴾: their containers.) "Akmam" means containers; he says: (plural of "kimm," with a kasra on the kaf) "from their coverings" means the sheaths of the spathe. This is well known in palm trees, and likewise well known in flowers: you find the blossom has a sheath called "kimm." So no fruit comes out of its sheath except by the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; whatever fruit is small or large, edible or inedible, it is by the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The reason it is by His knowledge is that these fruits are created by Allah, and everything created by Allah is known to Him, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14]. So whenever you affirm that Allah is the Creator of these, it necessarily follows from your affirmation that Allah knows them, because it is impossible for Him to create them while not knowing. For this reason Allah established this by a rational proof: ﴿Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14].

﴿And no fruits come out of their coverings, and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fussilat 47]: "and no female conceives," meaning any female, of the children of Adam or of animals; no female conceives or gives birth except by the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So the beginning of pregnancy is known to Allah, and its delivery is likewise known to Allah, blessed and exalted. We return to His saying ﴿from a female﴾ and to His saying ﴿from fruit﴾.

Grammatical analysis: ﴿min﴾ is a prepositional particle, an extra (za'id) one in terms of grammatical function, but not extra in terms of meaning, because it conveys a meaning, namely emphasis. Accordingly, we say: ﴿from fruit﴾: ﴿min﴾ is an extra prepositional particle, and ﴿fruit﴾ is a subject in the nominative case marked by a presumed damma at its end, prevented from appearing by the movement of the extra preposition's place. Likewise it is said: ﴿min unthā﴾: ﴿min﴾ is an extra preposition, and ﴿unthā﴾ is a subject in the nominative case marked by a presumed damma at its end, prevented from appearing by the impossibility (ta'adhdhur) of pronouncing it, and it is in the genitive position verbally because ﴿min﴾ precedes it.

As for His saying ﴿except with His knowledge﴾: is it His knowledge prior, or knowledge that arises at the moment the thing exists? The answer: prior, because Allah's knowledge encompasses everything eternally and everlastingly; so He knows what fruits come out of their coverings until the Day of Resurrection, and likewise what a female conceives and does not deliver.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Fussilat 47]. ﴿The day﴾ is an adverbial complement of time, and an adverb requires something it relates to, since it is an object of time; and if it is an adverbial object, there must be a verb that governs it. Where is the governing word? The governing word here is implied, and the estimate is: "Remember the day He calls to them." Such an expression is frequent in the Qur'an. The estimate, as I mentioned, is that the governing word is omitted: "Remember the day He calls to them, 'Where are My partners?'" etc. Allah commanded His Prophet to mention it only to frighten these deniers and to console the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

His saying ﴿He calls to them﴾ means He summons them with a raised voice, because calling (nida') is with a raised voice, whereas secret conversation (munajah) is with a lower voice. The subject of ﴿calls to them﴾ is Allah, as is shown by His saying ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, meaning that Allah, blessed and exalted, calls these polytheists, saying: "Where are My partners?" This interrogation is both for rebuke and for reproach; it combines two meanings: rebuke (ta'jiz), and second, reproach (tawbikh). That is: where are those you associated with Me? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿They will say, "We have informed You"﴾ [Fussilat 47], that is, we now inform You, ﴿that none of us bears witness﴾ [Fussilat 47]. ("Adhana" means "a'lama," "informed") as in His saying: ﴿And a declaration from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 3], meaning an announcement from Allah and His Messenger; so "adhana" means "a'lama." And from this is what is in the hadith, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the women who washed his daughter: "When you finish, inform me" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1253) and Muslim (939/36) from Umm 'Atiyyah al-Ansariyyah.]], meaning: inform me.

﴿We have informed You﴾: the author says, "we have informed You now." By his saying "now" the author indicates that the past verb ﴿adhannaka﴾ carries the sense of the present; so it is a declarative clause of the present state, meaning: "now we inform You." "None of us is a witness." And it was said that "adhannaka" is a past verb in its original sense, and thus is a report about a past matter.

So there are two views: is the informing here on the Day of Resurrection, as the author said, "we have informed You now," or is it a prior informing in this world? If we look at the apparent wording, we would prefer that it is an informing in this world, meaning: "We informed You in this world," and it would be on its apparent sense. But this explanation is problematic, because the reality of their condition does not indicate this, since they are in fact polytheists; how would they inform Him that none of them bears witness to that? Those who hold this view answered that the meaning is: "we informed You according to the fitrah and what is in our hearts," because "no child is born except upon the fitrah." Pay attention now to the meaning.

﴿adhannaka﴾: its form is a past verb, which requires that this informing preceded the time of address; this is one point.

﴿adhannaka﴾ is a past verb but is intended to report on the present state, so it means: "we now inform You." This explanation contradicts the apparent wording but agrees with the reality of their condition. The first explanation agrees with the wording but contradicts the apparent reality of their condition, since they do not inform Him of that, being in fact polytheists. Those who say "adhannaka" refers to this world answered that they informed Him according to the fitrah with which they were created, because "no child is born except upon the fitrah."

﴿They said, "We have informed You; none of us is a witness"﴾ [Fussilat 47] (that is, a witness that You have a partner). ﴿mā﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿minnā﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate preceding the subject. ﴿min﴾ is an extra preposition grammatically. ﴿shahīd﴾ is a subject in the nominative case marked by a presumed damma at its end, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the movement of the extra preposition. The meaning is: we have now acknowledged that none of us bears witness that You have a partner, and they say this now, but it does not benefit them, because it is an acknowledgment after seeing the punishment, and acknowledgment after seeing the punishment does not benefit. For this reason Pharaoh, when he was drowned, acknowledged that ﴿there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed﴾ [Yunus 90], but it did not benefit him, and it was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus 91].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 47–48 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those they used to invoke before will vanish from them﴾ [Fussilat 48]. That is: (ghaaba), ﴿vanish from them, what they used to invoke before﴾. ﴿What﴾ (ma) is a relative noun, the subject, meaning: "that which". ﴿Vanish from them what they used to invoke﴾. The author said: (they worshipped) ﴿before﴾ (in the world, of the idols), their idols to which they clung and which they worshipped, supposing that they would bring them near to Allah in rank, on that day when they are most in need of them. They will vanish from them and will not benefit them. Therefore He said: ﴿vanished from them﴾, that is, was lost and disappeared, ﴿what they used to invoke﴾, that is, worship before, meaning by this the idols which they worshipped in the world. For example, the Christians worship 'Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary); the Quraysh worshipped al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat and Hubal; some worship fire, like the Magians; some worship the sun, some worship the moon, and so on. These idols that are worshipped besides Allah: will they benefit them on the Day of Resurrection? No. Therefore He said: ﴿vanished from them what they used to invoke before﴾. Perhaps from His saying ﴿vanished from them﴾ we may understand that they went looking for them, searching for them, but they were lost and disappeared, and this will be a greater grief in their souls, that they sought them at the time of need but did not find them.

﴿And they were certain﴾ — he said: (they became certain) ﴿that there was for them no escape﴾ (zanna) here means "to be certain" (ayqana). Does the word zann come in the sense of certainty? The answer: Yes, it comes often. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are going to fall into it, and will not find from it any way of turning away﴾ [al-Kahf 53]. So "zannu" means "ayqanu" (they were certain).

Allah the Blessed and Exalted also said: ﴿those who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 46]. The meaning of ﴿yazunnun﴾ is: they are certain that they will meet their Lord. Had zann meant a probable thing, they would not have been believers; rather, yazunnun means yuqinun (they are certain). So zann in the Arabic language comes in the sense of certainty. Here, ﴿zannu ma lahum min mahis﴾ means they became certain. Did it become for them a probable matter? No, they became certain.

As for His saying ﴿ma lahum min mahis﴾, there is in it inversion and emphasis. The inversion is that the predicate was placed first and the subject was placed last. Where is the predicate? ﴿lahum﴾. Where is the subject? ﴿mahis﴾. There is also emphasis in it, namely the extra ﴿min﴾; because ﴿mahis﴾ is a postponed subject, and the extra ﴿min﴾ entered upon it for emphasis. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is that it is a subject in the nominative case by virtue of beginning, and the sign of its nominative case is a presumed damma on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the harmonizing vowel.

His saying: (﴿mahis﴾: a place of escape from the punishment) means they became certain that there is no escape for them from the punishment, and no refuge for them from it, and that it will inevitably befall them.

Then the author said: (And the negation in both places is suspended from operating, and the negative clause took the place of the two objects.) Where are the two places? ﴿They said: "We have told You, there is none of us who can bear witness"﴾ [Fussilat 47]. This "ma" is a negation suspending the operation, because "adhannaka" means "We have informed You". (a'lama) governs three objects. You say, for example: "I informed Zayd 'Amran qa'iman" (I made Zayd know that 'Amr was standing). How many objects did it govern here? Three: Zayd, 'Amr and standing. Here, in ﴿adhannaka﴾, the first object is present, which is the kaf (You). The second and third objects are suspended, and the interrogative clause ﴿ma minna min shahid﴾ has stood in for them.

On this basis, the whole clause ﴿ma minna min shahid﴾ is in the place of accusative standing in for the two objects of (adhana). I say: the first and second? No, I say: the second and third.

﴿And they were certain: ma lahum min mahis﴾ — this is the second. ﴿Zannu﴾ — this (zanna) governs how many objects? It governs two objects. Here there are no two objects; where are they? They were suspended from operating by the negative clause, which is His saying ﴿ma lahum min mahis﴾. On this basis, ﴿ma lahum min mahis﴾ is a clause in the place of accusative standing in for the two objects of (zanna). This is an i'rab that in reality only one who has knowledge of objects grasps; but we have now explained it, so whoever understands it, that is the goal, and whoever does not understand it, it does not harm him, because it has no connection with us; its relevance is only to i'rab.

Returning to deriving rulings from the verses, Allah said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Fussilat 47], etc.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that knowledge of the Hour is with Allah alone. From where is this taken, brother?
* Student: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾.
* The Shaykh: How did you take from it that it is with Allah alone?
* The student: Because what should be postponed was placed first, so it indicates restriction.
* The Shaykh: Because he placed first what should be postponed, namely the object, and this conveys restriction.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever claims knowledge of the Hour is a disbeliever. The reason: he contradicts Allah, and contradicting Allah is disbelief; and whoever believes him is also a disbeliever, because he has affirmed what contradicts the noble Qur'an, and whoever affirms what contradicts the noble Qur'an is without doubt a disbeliever.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, then he is despairing and hopeless. And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine, and I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best." But We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment. And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself, but when evil touches him, he is one of long supplication﴾ [Fussilat 49–51].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾. ﴿Does not tire﴾ means does not grow weary. He constantly asks for good: wealth, richness, status and other things.

Now let us take the benefits. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit emerges from its sheath, and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fussilat 47].

* Among its benefits: knowledge of the Hour is with Allah the Mighty and Majestic; none knows it but Him. We have mentioned evidence for this in the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), when he asked Jibril about the Hour to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to him: "The one asked is no more knowing than the asker."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* Among its benefits: whoever claims knowledge of the Hour is a disbeliever, because he denies Allah and His Messenger, and denying Allah and His Messenger is among the causes of apostasy, since apostasy revolves around two things: either denial or arrogance. Every apostasy for which scholars pass judgment does not go beyond these two matters: either denial or arrogance.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of Allah the Mighty and Majestic's knowledge, by His saying ﴿and no fruit emerges from its sheath﴾ [Fussilat 47], etc.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the rebuke of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, by His saying ﴿and on the day He will call to them: "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Fussilat 47]. Rebuke in that place is among the greatest rebukes, because it is the witnessed day which Allah, His angels and all His creation witness.
* Among its benefits: the acknowledgment by these deniers of resurrection, on that day, that Allah the Mighty and Majestic has no partner, by His saying ﴿They said: "We have told You, none of us can bear witness"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the following verse: that what is worshipped besides Allah is destruction and error, and will not avail its worshippers at all, by His saying ﴿And those they used to invoke before will vanish from them﴾ [Fussilat 48].
* Among its benefits: that these deniers will be certain on that day that there is no escape for them from the punishment of Allah, because there is no one there who can repel Allah's punishment from them, so they become certain that there is no refuge for them from it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 49–50 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Most High said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good.﴾ His saying, ﴿does not tire﴾, means he does not become weary; rather, he never ceases to ask. And ﴿man﴾ here may refer to the disbeliever, or it may refer to the species, i.e., mankind, whether believing or disbelieving, and then the states are applied to what suits each.

﴿Man does not tire of asking for good.﴾ ﴿Asking﴾ is in construct form, and ﴿good﴾ is the genitive complement. It is of the type of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. This (i.e., "good") is also the object of ﴿asking﴾. The one asked is Allah, the Most High. So we have: the one who asks (du'a, lit. caller), the one asked, and the thing asked for, i.e., the sought-after good. The one who asks is man, the one asked is Allah, and the thing asked for is good.

The author said: (i.e., he never ceases to ask his Lord for wealth, health and other things) such as children, wives, status, honor, and other things that a person asks for out of desire for them.

﴿But if evil touches him﴾ (poverty and hardship). Restricting "evil" to poverty and hardship is not meant as an exclusive limitation but as an example, since it includes poverty and hardship, loss of children, loss of status, harm from people, and many other things. So the author's restriction of it to poverty and hardship is by way of illustration.

﴿But if evil touches him, then he is despairing, despondent.﴾ The fa' is connective for the response, and the response is (in), and (despairing) is the predicate of an omitted subject; that is, he is: despairing, despondent. The author said: (from the mercy of Allah, the Exalted; this and what follows is about the disbelievers). (Despairing) and (despondent).

Is there a difference between yas (despair) and qunut (despondency)?
Answer: Yes. Yas is the cessation of hope such that a person's hope is cut off, and qunut is the intensest form of despair. Accordingly, his saying "despairing" is the beginning of despondency, and "despondent" is its end.

As for His saying ﴿despairing, despondent﴾: we parsed "despairing" as the predicate of an omitted subject. How do we parse ﴿despondent﴾? We parse it as a second predicate. Multiple predicates are permissible, occur in the Arabic language, and occur in the Qur'an. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Lord of the Throne, the Glorious, Accomplisher of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj 14–16]. All of these are multiple predicates. The second cannot be an attribute of the first, because they all refer to one subject; therefore we say ﴿despondent﴾ is a second predicate of the omitted subject, and it cannot be an adjective of (despairing), because (despairing) itself is an adjective.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (and this and what follows is about the disbelievers). This indicated thing, despair and despondency, and (what follows) he will mention (about the disbelievers). The author said this because the believer does not despair or despond. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf 87], and He said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?﴾ [al-Hijr 56]. So it is not possible for a believer to despair, and therefore this description applies to the disbelievers.

﴿And if We let him taste﴾ [Fussilat 50] (We gave him). His saying ﴿And if﴾: he says (the lam of oath), meaning the lam, and in (in) is conditional. ﴿We let him taste﴾ (We gave him) ﴿mercy﴾ (wealth and health) ﴿from Us, after adversity﴾ ﴿from Us﴾ means from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿After adversity﴾ (hardship and affliction) ﴿has touched him﴾ meaning it befell him. ﴿He will surely say, "This is mine"﴾ (i.e., by my own effort).

Look at this man's state. We begin first with the grammar, because there is some difficulty in it: His saying ﴿And if We let him taste﴾ up to His saying ﴿he will surely say﴾. In the first clause, ﴿If We let him taste﴾ — (in) is a conditional particle, and a condition requires a response, but in the context of the verse we do not find a response to the condition. So where is it? The response of the condition in this verse is omitted, because an oath and a condition have come together, and when an oath and a condition come together, the response of the latter of the two is omitted. Here an oath and a condition have come together: the oath is in the lam, and the condition is (in). Which of them is later?
* Student: The condition.
* The Shaykh: The condition. So the response of the condition is omitted; that is why the response of the oath came in His saying ﴿he will surely say﴾. Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the Alfiyya:
"Omit upon the coming together of a condition and an oath / the response of whichever is placed later; that omission is obligatory."
The response of whichever you postponed — that omission is obligatory.

The Most High said: ﴿And if We let him taste﴾ (We gave him). But He expressed giving by "letting taste," because whoever tastes something has benefited from it, whereas giving may or may not be benefited from. For instance, if I give you a loaf of bread, you may benefit from it or not — that is, you may eat it or not. But if you taste it, you have eaten it or benefited from it. Therefore He expressed bestowal as tasting, because it is more emphatic in contact and in benefit.

His saying ﴿mercy from Us﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, explained mercy as wealth and health. This is an example, not an exclusive limitation; mercy includes everything a person seeks, such as wealth and health, status, property, children, and other things.

His saying ﴿from Us﴾ is a clear indication that this mercy is not from his own earning, but is a bounty from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Wealth came to him from where he did not reckon, health came to him from where he did not reckon, and children and others are from Allah; it is clear that they are from Allah and not from his earning.

His saying ﴿mercy from Us after adversity has touched him﴾ [Fussilat 50] means that it makes the harm certain, then mercy came from whom? From Allah. This is more emphatic in blessing: that it comes after harm, because a lasting blessing is not felt, but a blessing that arrives after harm is what is felt. Therefore whoever has not tasted the bitterness of illness does not savor the sweetness of health, even in religious matters. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Only one who does not know jahiliyya will undo Islam" [cited by Ibn al-Qayyim in al-Da' wa al-Dawa' p. 214], or words to that effect, meaning that one who does not know disbelief does not know the worth of faith. Likewise, mercy when it is constant and continuous is not felt by a person, but when it comes after harm he feels it and tastes its flavor. Let me give you an example now with breath: breath is one of the greatest blessings; a person does not feel it as long as the blessing is continuous, but if he is afflicted with choking and obstruction, then is relieved, he will find in this breath a great blessing and a great effect. Likewise illness: a healthy person continuously in health does not know its worth, but if he falls ill and then is cured, the worth of the blessing becomes clear to him. The mercy that Allah mentions here, mercy after hardship, has an effect far greater than if the mercy were continuous.

When Allah lets him taste mercy from Him after hardship, ﴿he will surely say, "This is mine"﴾ [Fussilat 50]: this is the response of the oath, meaning: he says, "This is mine." What is the meaning of "this is mine"? It is said: the meaning is "this is by my effort," so the lam is in the sense of (min, from); that is, "this is from me and not from Allah." It is also said: the lam denotes entitlement; that is, I deserve it, so there is no favor of Allah upon me in it, because I am worthy of it and deserving of it.

The author followed the first view, that the lam means (min): i.e., "he will surely say, 'this is from me,' and I am the one who acquired it, I am the one who traded, I acquired it," and the like.

The second view says: this is from Allah, but He has no favor upon me in it, because I deserve it. The verse allows both of these, and the principle in tafsir is that if a verse admits of two meanings, neither of which negates the other, it is interpreted as both together when there is no preponderant evidence for one of them.

﴿He will surely say, "This is mine," and I do not think the Hour will be established﴾ [Fussilat 50]. We ask Allah for well-being. That is, he thought he would live forever when this mercy came to him, and said: "Then there is no resurrection and no recompense": ﴿and I do not think the Hour will be established﴾. Then He said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat 50], meaning: supposing the Hour is established and I am brought back to Allah, then He who bestowed blessings on me in this world will bestow them on me in the Hereafter. Therefore He said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat 50], i.e., (Paradise).

Regarding ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, the grammar is as we said for ﴿And if We let him taste﴾, because an oath and a condition have come together, and the condition is later, so its response is omitted, and the response of the oath remains in His saying ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾. You find this man, from his delusion — may Allah protect us — stressed with an oath. (In) and the lam: the oath is in His saying ﴿And if﴾; (in) is in His saying ﴿indeed I have﴾; and the lam is in His saying ﴿the best﴾. So he affirmed emphatically that, supposing he returns to Allah, he will find the best, which is Paradise, as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said. The author took this interpretation from the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of the Most High's saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and extra﴾ [Yunus 26], where he said: the best is Paradise, and the extra is looking at the Face of Allah.

So this man is deluded to the utmost delusion. First: he attributed the blessing that came to him in this world to himself, either directly, that he obtained it without Allah, or because he deserves it, so there is no favor of Allah upon him in it. The second delusion: he denied resurrection, by His saying ﴿I do not think the Hour will be established﴾. The third delusion: supposing the Hour is established, he will find with Allah what is better: ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾.

The Most High said: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50]. ﴿We will surely inform﴾ means We will tell them. The fa' is conjunctive, and the lam is preparatory for the omitted oath; the sense is: "By Allah, We will surely inform." So the sentence is emphasized with three emphases: ﴿Then We will surely inform﴾ — the first emphasis is the oath, the second is the lam, and the third is the energetic nun in (la-nunabbi'anna). The pronoun in (la-nunabbi'anna) refers to Allah the Most High, and it returns to Him in the plural form out of glorification; otherwise Allah is one God.

﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, i.e., of what they had done. We will inform them of that on the Day of Resurrection. The manner of this is that Allah, glorified and exalted, will account for their deeds on the Day of Resurrection, and will call out against them before all witnesses, since Allah has disgraced them: ﴿Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 18].

Then He says: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, meaning after We inform them and they acknowledge it, We will make them taste a severe punishment, i.e., (harsh). He said: (the lam in both verbs is the lam of oath). Where are the two verbs? (la-nunabbi'anna) and (la-nudhiqanna).

* In this verse and the one before it: a statement of the state of the disbelieving human being, in his ingratitude for Allah's blessing and his self-conceit; His saying ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine"﴾ [Fussilat 50]. This indicates his severe disbelief, his admiration of himself, and his self-conceit.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, the Most High, shows mercy to the disbeliever, as in His saying ﴿And if We let him taste mercy﴾. Based on this, if someone asks: does Allah show mercy to the disbeliever? The answer is yes, He shows him mercy, and the proof is this verse. But know that the mercy of Allah, blessed and exalted, is of two kinds: special mercy and general mercy. What sustains the body is general mercy, and what sustains the religion is special mercy. General mercy is for the body, since it includes the believer and disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, humans and animals. Special mercy is what sustains religion, and it is specific to the believers. The difference between them is that general mercy is nourishment for the body only and ends with its ending, while special mercy is nourishment for the soul and remains as long as the soul remains. The souls, since Allah created them, do not perish; souls are among the things created for permanence, unlike bodies. Allah said of bodies: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman 26], but the soul does not perish, like the young boys and the dark-eyed maidens in Paradise, who were created for permanence.
So we say: the difference between general and special mercy is that general mercy is nourishment for bodies only and ends with the death of the body, while special mercy is nourishment for souls and remains forever in this world and the Hereafter.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's favor upon the disbeliever, since the mercy that reached the disbeliever came from Allah; by His saying ﴿from Us﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the disbeliever's admiration of himself, in that he attributes this mercy, which is from Allah, to himself; by His saying ﴿This is mine﴾, or he attributes it to his own entitlement to it, as if Allah had no favor upon him. On the second view, the meaning of His saying ﴿This is mine﴾ is "this is what I deserve."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the disbeliever's arrogance, in that he denies what the legal, rational and sensory proofs have established, in His saying ﴿and I do not think the Hour will be established﴾ [Fussilat 50].
The legal proofs for the establishment of the Hour are too numerous to count. The rational proof is that it is not wise for Allah to create this creation, command and forbid it, and set some of it upon others with the sword, so that the believer fights the disbeliever, and then the end is nothing. That would be folly, and Allah alluded to this in His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 115]; that is, what benefit is there in creating something that exists, is commanded and forbidden, and has some of it set upon others in deliberate killing, and then the end is nothing? There is no benefit in this, and the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted, refuses that such a thing should come from Allah. This is a clear rational proof, a proof that requires that people be resurrected to be recompensed for their deeds.

As for the sensory proof of the establishment of resurrection, its possibility and its permissibility, Allah the Most High repeats it in the Qur'an: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾ [Fussilat 39], meaning barren, with no vegetation; ﴿but when We send down upon it water﴾ [Fussilat 39], ﴿water﴾ meaning rain; ﴿it quivers and grows⁠﴾ [Fussilat 39], so it becomes alive after it was dead. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, He who has brought it to life is the Giver of life to the dead. Indeed, He is over all things competent﴾. So the revival of the earth after its death, while people witness it, is a proof of the possibility of reviving the dead and resurrecting them. This is a clear sensory proof — is it sensory or rational? Sensory, observed. Likewise, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made us witness the revival of the dead in this world. Let us review this in the Qur'an:

The first scene: of whom? The Children of Israel said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. The thunderbolt seized them and they died, then they were resurrected. This is in this world.

The second scene: the slain man over whom the two tribes disputed. Allah commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike the slain man with part of it. They did so, the slain man came back to life and said: the one who killed him was so-and-so. Revival after death.

The third scene: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death?﴾ [al-Baqarah 243]. They feared death and left their homes, so Allah said to them: die; they died, then He revived them. He caused them to die so that they would know there is no escape from the decree of Allah, then He revived them to fulfill a specified term. How many scenes is this?

The fourth scene: the man who passed by a town fallen upon its roofs, and said: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾ So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then resurrected him ﴿[al-Baqarah 259]﴾.

The fifth scene: Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. Allah commanded him to slaughter four birds, place a portion of each on every mountain, and call them. He did so, and they came to him swiftly, either flying or walking quickly. These five scenes mentioned in al-Baqarah all indicate the possibility of revival after death.

The story of Jesus is likewise. Jesus, upon him be peace, would bring the dead to life by the permission of Allah. He would stand over the dead and say: "O so-and-so, arise!" and he would arise. Indeed, he would stand at the grave, while the dead person is buried, and command him to come out alive, and he would come out, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you brought forth the dead by My permission﴾ [al-Ma'idah 110]. And regarding the Dajjal, the Prophet, upon him be peace, informed us that he will cut a man into two pieces, and pass between them, then he will stand and command him to come back, and this dead man will command the two pieces to come together, and they will join instantly and he will rise while the people look on. This too is a tangible witness. The point is that resurrection is indicated by revelation, reason, and the senses. This disbeliever says: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever be established﴾ [al-Kahf 36].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: this disbeliever had such conceit and self-confidence, though he had nothing to rely upon, that he could say: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have with Him the best﴾ [Fussilat 50].

* And among the benefits of the verse: acknowledging Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah) does not admit a person into Islam, because this denier does acknowledge Lordship. From where do we take this? ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾. And the polytheists used to acknowledge Lordship: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 9]. But acknowledging Lordship does not avail a person anything. Some ignorant people have boasted that one of the astronauts testified that this universe has a Creator, when he went up into space and saw the earth and the signs around him, and testified that it has a Creator. So some ignorant people have begun to loudly trumpet the affirmation that the universe has a Creator on the testimony of this disbelieving man. In truth, this indicates the weakness of their faith, because the report of Allah and His Messenger on this matter is more truthful and more binding for faith. Yes, if we were debating a person who denies and does not believe in religions, we might say to him: "Your companion who is like you acknowledged that the universe has a Creator," which may be beneficial, and this would be a way of establishing the proof against him. But to make this an absolute proof is open to question.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: emphasis that these disbelievers will be informed of what they did, as His saying indicates: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾ [Fussilat 50]. When? It will be on the Day of Resurrection.
If someone says: Does this restriction have an implication, or is it merely to describe the reality: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved﴾?
The answer: It is to describe the reality and has no implication, because if you were to give it an implication, the believers would not be informed of what they did, even though they will be informed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [az-Zalzalah 7]. And it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that Allah will privately converse with His believing servant and make him acknowledge his sins: "You did such and such on such and such a day" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4685), and Muslim (2768/52) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar]. So the restriction of the informing to the disbeliever is to describe the reality, meaning: those who denied, their reality is that they will be informed of what they did.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that every deed is recorded and preserved for a person. We take this from His saying: ﴿of what they did﴾ [Fussilat 50], as "mā" is a relative pronoun that conveys generality. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an observer, ready﴾ [Qaf 18], meaning: every word you utter, there is with you a ready, present observer, meaning one present who writes down what you say.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of these disbelievers will be harsh (ghaliz), meaning severe, because ghilaz means harshness, and it is according to its context. The harshness of character is not like the thickness of clay, dough, or the like. The harshness of punishment is not like the thickness of clay and dough, and the harshness of speech and the like; each harshness is according to what it refers to.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of punishment in the Hereafter: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50]. Is there punishment before the Hereafter? The answer: Yes, a person is punished in his grave before he is resurrected, and this is established in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Listen to it in the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the overwhelming agonies of death, and the angels are extending their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation"﴾ [al-An'am 93].
His saying "Discharge your souls" indicates that they are stingy with their souls, not wanting them to leave; this is why it is said to them, "Discharge your souls," as a rebuke. Then it is said to them: "Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation" [al-An'am 93]. When is "today"? On the day of your death you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, and this is an explicit text affirming the punishment of the grave.
And Allah, blessed and exalted, said concerning the family of Pharaoh: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening; and on the Day the Hour is established, "Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment"﴾ [Ghafir 46].
As for the Sunnah, it overflows with this and is abundant, and among it is what the Muslims have agreed upon: all Muslims say in prayer, "I seek refuge in Allah from the punishment of Hell and from the punishment of the grave." Can it be imagined that anyone seeks refuge from something without believing in its existence? Answer me!
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: It cannot be imagined. So the punishment of the grave is established by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and consensus. Accordingly, the punishment mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50] is the punishment of the Hereafter, which is more severe than the punishment of the grave. May Allah protect us and you from it.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. No, it is not appropriate. Attributing a deed to oneself is permissible, indeed the Messenger, upon him be peace, said about his uncle Abu Talib: "Were it not for me, he would be in the lowest level of the Fire" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883), and Muslim (209/357) from the hadith of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib]. But a person attributes it to himself in the sense that this disbeliever said: ﴿This is mine﴾, meaning "this is by my deed," or "it came to me from Allah because I deserve it." This is what is prohibited.
* * *
* Student: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself, and when evil touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication. Say: "Have you considered: if this is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one in extreme dissension?" We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness? Unquestionably, they are in doubt about meeting their Lord. Unquestionably, He is, of all things, encompassing﴾ [Fussilat 51–54].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself﴾. ﴿When We bestow favor upon man﴾ means: We give him a blessing. Blessing revolves around two things: the attainment of what is sought, and deliverance from what is feared. So whoever falls into the sea and then Allah provides someone to rescue him from drowning, that is a blessing. Likewise, whoever Allah grants wealth and children, that is a blessing. Thus blessing is either the removal of a calamity or the attainment of something beloved to a person.
As for His saying: ﴿upon man﴾, the author says: the intended meaning is (the species), meaning it is not only the believer nor only the disbeliever; this attribute can be found in a believer and also in a disbeliever. You have said now that there remain benefits for us: which verses?
Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, he is hopeless and despairing﴾ [Fussilat 49].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that man is stingy and eager for good, stingy in giving up what is asked of him.
* And among its benefits: that man always loves good, as His saying indicates: ﴿does not tire﴾ ﴿of asking for good﴾. This is by human nature: he loves good, which suits his self and his aim.
* And among its benefits: that a person who has no faith, when evil touches him, despairs and loses hope in the mercy of Allah.
* And among its benefits: the censure of people of despair and hopelessness regarding the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah the Exalted related this in the manner of censure.
* And among the benefits of the verse: a person should not give dominance to the side of despair and hopelessness, just as he should not give dominance to the side of mercy alone; because if he gives dominance to the side of hope and mercy, he enters among those who do not feel secure from the plotting of Allah, and if he gives dominance to the side of despair and hopelessness, he enters among the people of despair and hopelessness.
And which should a person give dominance to: hope or fear? The wayfarers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, have differed on this. Some said: one should give dominance to the side of fear, so as to beware of sins and avoid them, because when the side of fear dominates, one fears and guards against sins.
Others said: one should give dominance to the side of hope, because Allah, the Exalted, is according to His servant's good opinion of Him, and when hope dominates, one keeps away from despair and hopelessness.
Others said: one should not give dominance to one over the other, but make one's fear and hope equal. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: one's fear and hope should be equal; whichever prevails, its companion is destroyed.
Some said: a person should be between fear and hope like a bird between its two wings; if one drops, it falls. Some scholars said: the side of hope should be given dominance when performing an act of obedience, hoping for acceptance and reward, and the side of fear should be given dominance when intending a sin, so that one does not disobey Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Some scholars say: one gives dominance to the side of hope during sickness, so that when one dies one meets Allah having a good opinion of Him; and in a state of health one gives dominance to the side of fear, because a state of health calls a person to insolence and arrogance; rather, one gives dominance to the side of fear.
All these opinions, which reach six or seven, in reality all look to the state of the servant. This is why we see, in this matter, that a person should look to his own state: if he has done righteous deeds and striven in what pleases Allah, then let him give dominance to the side of hope; whenever he performs an act of obedience, let the side of hope dominate, that Allah, glorified and exalted, has overlooked it for him, that Allah has accepted it and will reward him. And if he sees in himself arrogance and self-magnification, then let him give dominance to the side of fear, until he travels to Allah, exalted, in a good manner.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse, which is His saying: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say: this is mine﴾ [Fussilat 50]: among its benefits: that some of Allah's servants do not thank Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, nor acknowledge His favor; so when mercy comes to them after adversity, they claim that this is by their deed, and that they are entitled to it and deserving of it; because of His, blessed and exalted, saying: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him﴾ and so on to the end [Fussilat 50].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that mercy is only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; a person cannot bring himself benefit, nor ward off harm from himself, but that is up to Allah. However, Allah has made a cause for everything: mercy has causes, and punishment has causes.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: clarification of the condition of this person who, when mercy and good befall him, says: ﴿This is mine﴾, then makes another claim, that if he were to return to Allah he would find with Him better than that, although he denies the establishment of the Hour.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that acknowledging Lordship is not enough for a person's tawhid and faith, because this man acknowledged Lordship in his saying: ﴿returned to my Lord﴾ [Fussilat 50].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to one in this condition that Allah, glorified and exalted, will surely make him account for his sins and make him taste the harsh punishment; because of His saying: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved﴾ [Fussilat 50].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, where the pronoun would have been in its place, is better than the pronoun. That is: when it is a matter of choosing between bringing the pronoun of the one spoken about, or an explicit noun, the default is to bring the pronoun; but when there is a benefit in the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, it is more preferable and better. The explicit noun in place of the pronoun is in His saying: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved﴾; had it used a pronoun it would have said "Then We will surely inform him." But it used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun. We mentioned that there are three benefits in this. Who will memorize them?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The statement of the attribute for which he deserves to be punished with this punishment. The second?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, its meaning is recording against them disbelief, recording disbelief against one in this condition.
* The student: Indicating generality.
* The Shaykh: Yes, indicating generality; meaning that this threat is not for this man alone, but for every disbeliever. This is with respect to the verse before us; in the use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun there are these benefits. There is also a fourth benefit: alerting the addressee, because when speech follows one pattern in its pronouns and explicit nouns, a person does not pay attention; but when something comes that takes the speech out of its context, one must pay attention.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of resurrection, by His saying: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50].
* And among its benefits: the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since one who informs of deeds must necessarily have knowledge of them.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted, in that He attributes the pronouns to Himself in the plural form, and the plural used for the singular is intended to express magnification.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 49–50 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Most High said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good.﴾ His saying, ﴿does not tire﴾, means he does not become weary; rather, he never ceases to ask. And ﴿man﴾ here may refer to the disbeliever, or it may refer to the species, i.e., mankind, whether believing or disbelieving, and then the states are applied to what suits each.

﴿Man does not tire of asking for good.﴾ ﴿Asking﴾ is in construct form, and ﴿good﴾ is the genitive complement. It is of the type of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. This (i.e., "good") is also the object of ﴿asking﴾. The one asked is Allah, the Most High. So we have: the one who asks (du'a, lit. caller), the one asked, and the thing asked for, i.e., the sought-after good. The one who asks is man, the one asked is Allah, and the thing asked for is good.

The author said: (i.e., he never ceases to ask his Lord for wealth, health and other things) such as children, wives, status, honor, and other things that a person asks for out of desire for them.

﴿But if evil touches him﴾ (poverty and hardship). Restricting "evil" to poverty and hardship is not meant as an exclusive limitation but as an example, since it includes poverty and hardship, loss of children, loss of status, harm from people, and many other things. So the author's restriction of it to poverty and hardship is by way of illustration.

﴿But if evil touches him, then he is despairing, despondent.﴾ The fa' is connective for the response, and the response is (in), and (despairing) is the predicate of an omitted subject; that is, he is: despairing, despondent. The author said: (from the mercy of Allah, the Exalted; this and what follows is about the disbelievers). (Despairing) and (despondent).

Is there a difference between yas (despair) and qunut (despondency)?
Answer: Yes. Yas is the cessation of hope such that a person's hope is cut off, and qunut is the intensest form of despair. Accordingly, his saying "despairing" is the beginning of despondency, and "despondent" is its end.

As for His saying ﴿despairing, despondent﴾: we parsed "despairing" as the predicate of an omitted subject. How do we parse ﴿despondent﴾? We parse it as a second predicate. Multiple predicates are permissible, occur in the Arabic language, and occur in the Qur'an. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Lord of the Throne, the Glorious, Accomplisher of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj 14–16]. All of these are multiple predicates. The second cannot be an attribute of the first, because they all refer to one subject; therefore we say ﴿despondent﴾ is a second predicate of the omitted subject, and it cannot be an adjective of (despairing), because (despairing) itself is an adjective.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (and this and what follows is about the disbelievers). This indicated thing, despair and despondency, and (what follows) he will mention (about the disbelievers). The author said this because the believer does not despair or despond. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf 87], and He said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?﴾ [al-Hijr 56]. So it is not possible for a believer to despair, and therefore this description applies to the disbelievers.

﴿And if We let him taste﴾ [Fussilat 50] (We gave him). His saying ﴿And if﴾: he says (the lam of oath), meaning the lam, and in (in) is conditional. ﴿We let him taste﴾ (We gave him) ﴿mercy﴾ (wealth and health) ﴿from Us, after adversity﴾ ﴿from Us﴾ means from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿After adversity﴾ (hardship and affliction) ﴿has touched him﴾ meaning it befell him. ﴿He will surely say, "This is mine"﴾ (i.e., by my own effort).

Look at this man's state. We begin first with the grammar, because there is some difficulty in it: His saying ﴿And if We let him taste﴾ up to His saying ﴿he will surely say﴾.
