In the first clause, ﴿If We let him taste﴾ — (in) is a conditional particle, and a condition requires a response, but in the context of the verse we do not find a response to the condition. So where is it? The response of the condition in this verse is omitted, because an oath and a condition have come together, and when an oath and a condition come together, the response of the latter of the two is omitted. Here an oath and a condition have come together: the oath is in the lam, and the condition is (in). Which of them is later?
* Student: The condition.
* The Shaykh: The condition. So the response of the condition is omitted; that is why the response of the oath came in His saying ﴿he will surely say﴾. Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the Alfiyya:
"Omit upon the coming together of a condition and an oath / the response of whichever is placed later; that omission is obligatory."
The response of whichever you postponed — that omission is obligatory.

The Most High said: ﴿And if We let him taste﴾ (We gave him). But He expressed giving by "letting taste," because whoever tastes something has benefited from it, whereas giving may or may not be benefited from. For instance, if I give you a loaf of bread, you may benefit from it or not — that is, you may eat it or not. But if you taste it, you have eaten it or benefited from it. Therefore He expressed bestowal as tasting, because it is more emphatic in contact and in benefit.

His saying ﴿mercy from Us﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, explained mercy as wealth and health. This is an example, not an exclusive limitation; mercy includes everything a person seeks, such as wealth and health, status, property, children, and other things.

His saying ﴿from Us﴾ is a clear indication that this mercy is not from his own earning, but is a bounty from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Wealth came to him from where he did not reckon, health came to him from where he did not reckon, and children and others are from Allah; it is clear that they are from Allah and not from his earning.

His saying ﴿mercy from Us after adversity has touched him﴾ [Fussilat 50] means that it makes the harm certain, then mercy came from whom? From Allah. This is more emphatic in blessing: that it comes after harm, because a lasting blessing is not felt, but a blessing that arrives after harm is what is felt. Therefore whoever has not tasted the bitterness of illness does not savor the sweetness of health, even in religious matters. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Only one who does not know jahiliyya will undo Islam" [cited by Ibn al-Qayyim in al-Da' wa al-Dawa' p. 214], or words to that effect, meaning that one who does not know disbelief does not know the worth of faith. Likewise, mercy when it is constant and continuous is not felt by a person, but when it comes after harm he feels it and tastes its flavor. Let me give you an example now with breath: breath is one of the greatest blessings; a person does not feel it as long as the blessing is continuous, but if he is afflicted with choking and obstruction, then is relieved, he will find in this breath a great blessing and a great effect. Likewise illness: a healthy person continuously in health does not know its worth, but if he falls ill and then is cured, the worth of the blessing becomes clear to him. The mercy that Allah mentions here, mercy after hardship, has an effect far greater than if the mercy were continuous.

When Allah lets him taste mercy from Him after hardship, ﴿he will surely say, "This is mine"﴾ [Fussilat 50]: this is the response of the oath, meaning: he says, "This is mine." What is the meaning of "this is mine"? It is said: the meaning is "this is by my effort," so the lam is in the sense of (min, from); that is, "this is from me and not from Allah." It is also said: the lam denotes entitlement; that is, I deserve it, so there is no favor of Allah upon me in it, because I am worthy of it and deserving of it.

The author followed the first view, that the lam means (min): i.e., "he will surely say, 'this is from me,' and I am the one who acquired it, I am the one who traded, I acquired it," and the like.

The second view says: this is from Allah, but He has no favor upon me in it, because I deserve it. The verse allows both of these, and the principle in tafsir is that if a verse admits of two meanings, neither of which negates the other, it is interpreted as both together when there is no preponderant evidence for one of them.

﴿He will surely say, "This is mine," and I do not think the Hour will be established﴾ [Fussilat 50]. We ask Allah for well-being. That is, he thought he would live forever when this mercy came to him, and said: "Then there is no resurrection and no recompense": ﴿and I do not think the Hour will be established﴾. Then He said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat 50], meaning: supposing the Hour is established and I am brought back to Allah, then He who bestowed blessings on me in this world will bestow them on me in the Hereafter. Therefore He said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat 50], i.e., (Paradise).

Regarding ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, the grammar is as we said for ﴿And if We let him taste﴾, because an oath and a condition have come together, and the condition is later, so its response is omitted, and the response of the oath remains in His saying ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾. You find this man, from his delusion — may Allah protect us — stressed with an oath. (In) and the lam: the oath is in His saying ﴿And if﴾; (in) is in His saying ﴿indeed I have﴾; and the lam is in His saying ﴿the best﴾. So he affirmed emphatically that, supposing he returns to Allah, he will find the best, which is Paradise, as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said. The author took this interpretation from the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of the Most High's saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and extra﴾ [Yunus 26], where he said: the best is Paradise, and the extra is looking at the Face of Allah.

So this man is deluded to the utmost delusion. First: he attributed the blessing that came to him in this world to himself, either directly, that he obtained it without Allah, or because he deserves it, so there is no favor of Allah upon him in it. The second delusion: he denied resurrection, by His saying ﴿I do not think the Hour will be established﴾. The third delusion: supposing the Hour is established, he will find with Allah what is better: ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾.

The Most High said: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50]. ﴿We will surely inform﴾ means We will tell them. The fa' is conjunctive, and the lam is preparatory for the omitted oath; the sense is: "By Allah, We will surely inform." So the sentence is emphasized with three emphases: ﴿Then We will surely inform﴾ — the first emphasis is the oath, the second is the lam, and the third is the energetic nun in (la-nunabbi'anna). The pronoun in (la-nunabbi'anna) refers to Allah the Most High, and it returns to Him in the plural form out of glorification; otherwise Allah is one God.

﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, i.e., of what they had done. We will inform them of that on the Day of Resurrection. The manner of this is that Allah, glorified and exalted, will account for their deeds on the Day of Resurrection, and will call out against them before all witnesses, since Allah has disgraced them: ﴿Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 18].

Then He says: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, meaning after We inform them and they acknowledge it, We will make them taste a severe punishment, i.e., (harsh). He said: (the lam in both verbs is the lam of oath). Where are the two verbs? (la-nunabbi'anna) and (la-nudhiqanna).

* In this verse and the one before it: a statement of the state of the disbelieving human being, in his ingratitude for Allah's blessing and his self-conceit; His saying ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine"﴾ [Fussilat 50]. This indicates his severe disbelief, his admiration of himself, and his self-conceit.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, the Most High, shows mercy to the disbeliever, as in His saying ﴿And if We let him taste mercy﴾. Based on this, if someone asks: does Allah show mercy to the disbeliever? The answer is yes, He shows him mercy, and the proof is this verse. But know that the mercy of Allah, blessed and exalted, is of two kinds: special mercy and general mercy. What sustains the body is general mercy, and what sustains the religion is special mercy. General mercy is for the body, since it includes the believer and disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, humans and animals. Special mercy is what sustains religion, and it is specific to the believers. The difference between them is that general mercy is nourishment for the body only and ends with its ending, while special mercy is nourishment for the soul and remains as long as the soul remains. The souls, since Allah created them, do not perish; souls are among the things created for permanence, unlike bodies. Allah said of bodies: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman 26], but the soul does not perish, like the young boys and the dark-eyed maidens in Paradise, who were created for permanence.
So we say: the difference between general and special mercy is that general mercy is nourishment for bodies only and ends with the death of the body, while special mercy is nourishment for souls and remains forever in this world and the Hereafter.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's favor upon the disbeliever, since the mercy that reached the disbeliever came from Allah; by His saying ﴿from Us﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the disbeliever's admiration of himself, in that he attributes this mercy, which is from Allah, to himself; by His saying ﴿This is mine﴾, or he attributes it to his own entitlement to it, as if Allah had no favor upon him. On the second view, the meaning of His saying ﴿This is mine﴾ is "this is what I deserve."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the disbeliever's arrogance, in that he denies what the legal, rational and sensory proofs have established, in His saying ﴿and I do not think the Hour will be established﴾ [Fussilat 50].
The legal proofs for the establishment of the Hour are too numerous to count. The rational proof is that it is not wise for Allah to create this creation, command and forbid it, and set some of it upon others with the sword, so that the believer fights the disbeliever, and then the end is nothing. That would be folly, and Allah alluded to this in His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 115]; that is, what benefit is there in creating something that exists, is commanded and forbidden, and has some of it set upon others in deliberate killing, and then the end is nothing? There is no benefit in this, and the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted, refuses that such a thing should come from Allah. This is a clear rational proof, a proof that requires that people be resurrected to be recompensed for their deeds.

As for the sensory proof of the establishment of resurrection, its possibility and its permissibility, Allah the Most High repeats it in the Qur'an: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾ [Fussilat 39], meaning barren, with no vegetation; ﴿but when We send down upon it water﴾ [Fussilat 39], ﴿water﴾ meaning rain; ﴿it quivers and grows⁠﴾ [Fussilat 39], so it becomes alive after it was dead. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, He who has brought it to life is the Giver of life to the dead. Indeed, He is over all things competent﴾. So the revival of the earth after its death, while people witness it, is a proof of the possibility of reviving the dead and resurrecting them. This is a clear sensory proof — is it sensory or rational? Sensory, observed. Likewise, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made us witness the revival of the dead in this world. Let us review this in the Qur'an:

The first scene: of whom? The Children of Israel said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. The thunderbolt seized them and they died, then they were resurrected. This is in this world.

The second scene: the slain man over whom the two tribes disputed. Allah commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike the slain man with part of it. They did so, the slain man came back to life and said: the one who killed him was so-and-so. Revival after death.

The third scene: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death?﴾ [al-Baqarah 243]. They feared death and left their homes, so Allah said to them: die; they died, then He revived them. He caused them to die so that they would know there is no escape from the decree of Allah, then He revived them to fulfill a specified term. How many scenes is this?

The fourth scene: the man who passed by a town fallen upon its roofs, and said: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾ So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then resurrected him ﴿[al-Baqarah 259]﴾.

The fifth scene: Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. Allah commanded him to slaughter four birds, place a portion of each on every mountain, and call them. He did so, and they came to him swiftly, either flying or walking quickly. These five scenes mentioned in al-Baqarah all indicate the possibility of revival after death.

The story of Jesus is likewise. Jesus, upon him be peace, would bring the dead to life by the permission of Allah. He would stand over the dead and say: "O so-and-so, arise!" and he would arise. Indeed, he would stand at the grave, while the dead person is buried, and command him to come out alive, and he would come out, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you brought forth the dead by My permission﴾ [al-Ma'idah 110]. And regarding the Dajjal, the Prophet, upon him be peace, informed us that he will cut a man into two pieces, and pass between them, then he will stand and command him to come back, and this dead man will command the two pieces to come together, and they will join instantly and he will rise while the people look on. This too is a tangible witness. The point is that resurrection is indicated by revelation, reason, and the senses. This disbeliever says: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever be established﴾ [al-Kahf 36].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: this disbeliever had such conceit and self-confidence, though he had nothing to rely upon, that he could say: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have with Him the best﴾ [Fussilat 50].

* And among the benefits of the verse: acknowledging Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah) does not admit a person into Islam, because this denier does acknowledge Lordship. From where do we take this? ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾. And the polytheists used to acknowledge Lordship: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 9]. But acknowledging Lordship does not avail a person anything. Some ignorant people have boasted that one of the astronauts testified that this universe has a Creator, when he went up into space and saw the earth and the signs around him, and testified that it has a Creator. So some ignorant people have begun to loudly trumpet the affirmation that the universe has a Creator on the testimony of this disbelieving man. In truth, this indicates the weakness of their faith, because the report of Allah and His Messenger on this matter is more truthful and more binding for faith. Yes, if we were debating a person who denies and does not believe in religions, we might say to him: "Your companion who is like you acknowledged that the universe has a Creator," which may be beneficial, and this would be a way of establishing the proof against him. But to make this an absolute proof is open to question.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: emphasis that these disbelievers will be informed of what they did, as His saying indicates: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾ [Fussilat 50]. When? It will be on the Day of Resurrection.
If someone says: Does this restriction have an implication, or is it merely to describe the reality: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved﴾?
The answer: It is to describe the reality and has no implication, because if you were to give it an implication, the believers would not be informed of what they did, even though they will be informed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [az-Zalzalah 7]. And it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that Allah will privately converse with His believing servant and make him acknowledge his sins: "You did such and such on such and such a day" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4685), and Muslim (2768/52) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar]. So the restriction of the informing to the disbeliever is to describe the reality, meaning: those who denied, their reality is that they will be informed of what they did.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that every deed is recorded and preserved for a person. We take this from His saying: ﴿of what they did﴾ [Fussilat 50], as "mā" is a relative pronoun that conveys generality. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an observer, ready﴾ [Qaf 18], meaning: every word you utter, there is with you a ready, present observer, meaning one present who writes down what you say.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of these disbelievers will be harsh (ghaliz), meaning severe, because ghilaz means harshness, and it is according to its context. The harshness of character is not like the thickness of clay, dough, or the like. The harshness of punishment is not like the thickness of clay and dough, and the harshness of speech and the like; each harshness is according to what it refers to.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of punishment in the Hereafter: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50]. Is there punishment before the Hereafter? The answer: Yes, a person is punished in his grave before he is resurrected, and this is established in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Listen to it in the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the overwhelming agonies of death, and the angels are extending their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation"﴾ [al-An'am 93].
His saying "Discharge your souls" indicates that they are stingy with their souls, not wanting them to leave; this is why it is said to them, "Discharge your souls," as a rebuke. Then it is said to them: "Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation" [al-An'am 93]. When is "today"? On the day of your death you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, and this is an explicit text affirming the punishment of the grave.
And Allah, blessed and exalted, said concerning the family of Pharaoh: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening; and on the Day the Hour is established, "Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment"﴾ [Ghafir 46].
As for the Sunnah, it overflows with this and is abundant, and among it is what the Muslims have agreed upon: all Muslims say in prayer, "I seek refuge in Allah from the punishment of Hell and from the punishment of the grave." Can it be imagined that anyone seeks refuge from something without believing in its existence? Answer me!
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: It cannot be imagined. So the punishment of the grave is established by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and consensus. Accordingly, the punishment mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50] is the punishment of the Hereafter, which is more severe than the punishment of the grave. May Allah protect us and you from it.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. No, it is not appropriate. Attributing a deed to oneself is permissible, indeed the Messenger, upon him be peace, said about his uncle Abu Talib: "Were it not for me, he would be in the lowest level of the Fire" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883), and Muslim (209/357) from the hadith of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib]. But a person attributes it to himself in the sense that this disbeliever said: ﴿This is mine﴾, meaning "this is by my deed," or "it came to me from Allah because I deserve it." This is what is prohibited.
* * *
* Student: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself, and when evil touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication. Say: "Have you considered: if this is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one in extreme dissension?" We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness? Unquestionably, they are in doubt about meeting their Lord. Unquestionably, He is, of all things, encompassing﴾ [Fussilat 51–54].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself﴾. ﴿When We bestow favor upon man﴾ means: We give him a blessing. Blessing revolves around two things: the attainment of what is sought, and deliverance from what is feared. So whoever falls into the sea and then Allah provides someone to rescue him from drowning, that is a blessing. Likewise, whoever Allah grants wealth and children, that is a blessing. Thus blessing is either the removal of a calamity or the attainment of something beloved to a person.
As for His saying: ﴿upon man﴾, the author says: the intended meaning is (the species), meaning it is not only the believer nor only the disbeliever; this attribute can be found in a believer and also in a disbeliever. You have said now that there remain benefits for us: which verses?
Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, he is hopeless and despairing﴾ [Fussilat 49].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that man is stingy and eager for good, stingy in giving up what is asked of him.
* And among its benefits: that man always loves good, as His saying indicates: ﴿does not tire﴾ ﴿of asking for good﴾. This is by human nature: he loves good, which suits his self and his aim.
* And among its benefits: that a person who has no faith, when evil touches him, despairs and loses hope in the mercy of Allah.
* And among its benefits: the censure of people of despair and hopelessness regarding the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah the Exalted related this in the manner of censure.
* And among the benefits of the verse: a person should not give dominance to the side of despair and hopelessness, just as he should not give dominance to the side of mercy alone; because if he gives dominance to the side of hope and mercy, he enters among those who do not feel secure from the plotting of Allah, and if he gives dominance to the side of despair and hopelessness, he enters among the people of despair and hopelessness.
And which should a person give dominance to: hope or fear? The wayfarers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, have differed on this. Some said: one should give dominance to the side of fear, so as to beware of sins and avoid them, because when the side of fear dominates, one fears and guards against sins.
Others said: one should give dominance to the side of hope, because Allah, the Exalted, is according to His servant's good opinion of Him, and when hope dominates, one keeps away from despair and hopelessness.
Others said: one should not give dominance to one over the other, but make one's fear and hope equal. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: one's fear and hope should be equal; whichever prevails, its companion is destroyed.
Some said: a person should be between fear and hope like a bird between its two wings; if one drops, it falls. Some scholars said: the side of hope should be given dominance when performing an act of obedience, hoping for acceptance and reward, and the side of fear should be given dominance when intending a sin, so that one does not disobey Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Some scholars say: one gives dominance to the side of hope during sickness, so that when one dies one meets Allah having a good opinion of Him; and in a state of health one gives dominance to the side of fear, because a state of health calls a person to insolence and arrogance; rather, one gives dominance to the side of fear.
All these opinions, which reach six or seven, in reality all look to the state of the servant. This is why we see, in this matter, that a person should look to his own state: if he has done righteous deeds and striven in what pleases Allah, then let him give dominance to the side of hope; whenever he performs an act of obedience, let the side of hope dominate, that Allah, glorified and exalted, has overlooked it for him, that Allah has accepted it and will reward him. And if he sees in himself arrogance and self-magnification, then let him give dominance to the side of fear, until he travels to Allah, exalted, in a good manner.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse, which is His saying: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say: this is mine﴾ [Fussilat 50]: among its benefits: that some of Allah's servants do not thank Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, nor acknowledge His favor; so when mercy comes to them after adversity, they claim that this is by their deed, and that they are entitled to it and deserving of it; because of His, blessed and exalted, saying: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him﴾ and so on to the end [Fussilat 50].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that mercy is only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; a person cannot bring himself benefit, nor ward off harm from himself, but that is up to Allah. However, Allah has made a cause for everything: mercy has causes, and punishment has causes.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: clarification of the condition of this person who, when mercy and good befall him, says: ﴿This is mine﴾, then makes another claim, that if he were to return to Allah he would find with Him better than that, although he denies the establishment of the Hour.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that acknowledging Lordship is not enough for a person's tawhid and faith, because this man acknowledged Lordship in his saying: ﴿returned to my Lord﴾ [Fussilat 50].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to one in this condition that Allah, glorified and exalted, will surely make him account for his sins and make him taste the harsh punishment; because of His saying: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved﴾ [Fussilat 50].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, where the pronoun would have been in its place, is better than the pronoun. That is: when it is a matter of choosing between bringing the pronoun of the one spoken about, or an explicit noun, the default is to bring the pronoun; but when there is a benefit in the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, it is more preferable and better. The explicit noun in place of the pronoun is in His saying: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved﴾; had it used a pronoun it would have said "Then We will surely inform him." But it used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun. We mentioned that there are three benefits in this. Who will memorize them?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The statement of the attribute for which he deserves to be punished with this punishment. The second?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, its meaning is recording against them disbelief, recording disbelief against one in this condition.
* The student: Indicating generality.
* The Shaykh: Yes, indicating generality; meaning that this threat is not for this man alone, but for every disbeliever. This is with respect to the verse before us; in the use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun there are these benefits. There is also a fourth benefit: alerting the addressee, because when speech follows one pattern in its pronouns and explicit nouns, a person does not pay attention; but when something comes that takes the speech out of its context, one must pay attention.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of resurrection, by His saying: ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ [Fussilat 50].
* And among its benefits: the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since one who informs of deeds must necessarily have knowledge of them.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted, in that He attributes the pronouns to Himself in the plural form, and the plural used for the singular is intended to express magnification.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 51:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself (with his side)﴾ [Fussilat 51]. What is meant by "man" here is the genus, as the author (al-Mu'allif) said; that is, the human species, considered merely as human, is in this state: when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away from gratitude. And what is gratitude? Gratitude in reality is obedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic; this is gratitude, and it is by the heart, by the tongue, and by the limbs.

That gratitude is obedience to Allah is shown by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the Messengers, so Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾, and He said to the believers: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and give thanks to Allah﴾." [Narrated by Muslim (1015/65) from Abu Hurairah.] So the Prophet (ﷺ) made thanks to Allah to be righteous deeds; that is, performing obedience to Allah. Gratitude, then, is the performance of obedience to Allah, and it is by the heart, by the tongue, and by the limbs. As for the heart, it is a person's sense that this blessing is from Allah the Exalted, and that were it not for Allah's grace he would not have obtained it; so he acknowledges with his heart and confesses that it is from Allah and not by his own power and strength. As for the tongue, gratitude by the tongue is speaking of Allah's blessing, acknowledging His favour, not boasting over His creation, by saying: "Praise be to Allah, Allah has provided me with wealth, children, knowledge, standing and the like." Among gratitude by the tongue are all verbal acts of obedience, for they are gratitude by the tongue. So, the recitation of the Qur'an: brother, is it part of gratitude or not?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: It is part of gratitude, because every act of obedience by the tongue is part of thanking Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Gratitude by the limbs is action, such as bowing, prostration, standing, sitting, charity, and what is similar to these. On this the poet says:

"Three blessings have been bestowed upon you by me: ∗∗∗ my hand, my tongue, and the concealed conscience."

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself (with his side)﴾ [Fussilat 51]. The author, in explaining ﴿distances himself﴾, says (that is, he bends his side, strutting). That is, he turns away with his body and his heart, boasting and being arrogant. This concerns his state; as for what is required of him in gratitude: he turns away and does not thank Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This is the state of many of the children of Adam; therefore Allah generalised it, saying: ﴿When We bestow favour upon man﴾, because most of the children of Adam are in this state.

As for His saying ﴿nā'a﴾ [distanced], I have here ﴿nā'a bi-janibihi﴾ (and in another reading with the hamza placed first), a reading of the Seven. Know that the terminology of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is that when he says "and in a reading" it is of the Seven, that is, one of the seven readings; and when he says "and it was recited" it is one of the irregular (shādhdh) readings. So "nā'a" and "na'ā" have the same meaning, like "ays" and "yi's" with the hamza placed before and after, and they have the same meaning: "ayisa min kadhā" and "ya'isa min kadhā" have the same meaning; "nā'a bi-kadhā" or "na'ā bi-kadhā" have the same meaning. The intended meaning, as the author said, is: he bent his side and turned away strutting and arrogant.

﴿And when harm touches him﴾ [Fussilat 51], he turns to ﴿supplication, prolonged﴾ (that is, abundant). When harm touches him, he resorts to Allah and prolongs and increases his supplication. Consider what Allah the Exalted related about the polytheists when they were at sea and the sea was rough: ﴿they called upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: "If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful"﴾ [Yunus 22], but they deceive and lie; when He delivers them they return to disbelief, and we seek refuge in Allah.

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself﴾.

* Benefits derived from this noble verse: that man, as man, is insolent when blessed with ease, but attentive when afflicted; by His saying: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself﴾.

* Among its benefits: that whatever bliss a person enjoys is from Allah; by His saying: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾.

* Among its benefits: a warning against this state. If a person sees in himself that when he has a blessing he rejoices, grows insolent, and neglects what Allah has made obligatory upon him, let him know that he falls within this blameworthy "man".

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person recognises in himself weakness when harm befalls him, and turns to Allah; even the disbeliever recognises his own weakness and turns to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the disbelievers believe in Allah, and that He is the Remover of harm; by His saying: ﴿so he is one of abundant supplication﴾ [Fussilat 51]. The "turning away" in His saying ﴿when We bestow favour upon man﴾ is a conditional clause, so where is the response (jawāb)? Brother, you? ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself﴾. You raised your left hand, and this is not proper etiquette; therefore your punishment will be deprivation of being answered.

* Student: "He turns away and distances himself with his side."

* Shaykh: ﴿He turns away﴾ is the response. ﴿And distances himself with his side﴾ is conjoined to it; this is correct. And where is the response in His saying ﴿And when harm touches him﴾?

* Student: ﴿so he is one of abundant supplication﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿so he is one of abundant supplication﴾. ﴿So he is one of abundant supplication﴾: where is its governing element?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Implied? Say it with the implication?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Then he is one of abundant supplication. Why was the fā' joined to the response of the conditional?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Because the response of the conditional is a nominal sentence, and when the response of the conditional is a nominal sentence it must be joined with the fā', and it is dropped only rarely. What are the sentences which, when they occur as the response of the conditional, are joined with the fā'?

* Student: (...) nominal, imperative.

* Shaykh: They are gathered in the words of the versifier:

"Nominal, imperative, with a non-inflecting (jāmid) verb, and with lan, qad, and the future particles (sa/sawfa)."

Yes, when the response of the conditional is one of these seven sentences, it must be joined with the fā', and it is omitted only rarely, like the saying of the poet:

"Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them..."

The original: "Whoever does good deeds, then Allah rewards them." But it was dropped, either out of the necessity of poetry or because of its rarity; for it is dropped even in prose, but that is rare.

The point now, understand: whenever the response clause is one of these sentences, it must be joined with the fā'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verse 52:

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Say: Have you considered: if it is from Allah,﴾ [Fussilat 52] as the Prophet ﷺ said, ﴿and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾ [Fussilat 52] "Have you considered" (ara'aytum) means: inform me.

His saying: ﴿if it is from Allah﴾ means: (the Quran) is from Allah, and you disbelieved in it and denied that it is from Allah. ﴿Who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾ [Fussilat 52] The original structure of the sentence is: "Who is more astray among you?" "Have you considered: if it is from Allah, and it has become clear to you that it is from Allah, and then you disbelieved in it, [who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition]." The original is: "Who is more astray among you?" but it has been expressed explicitly in place of the pronoun, for a benefit that we will mention, Allah willing.

His saying: ﴿if it is from Allah﴾ means: that is, the Quran, and that became clear to you and manifest. ﴿Then you disbelieved in it﴾ [Fussilat 52]: He used "then" (thumma), which indicates sequence and delay, as an indication that these people denied and disbelieved after deliberation, and after the period in which whoever wishes to believe would believe. ﴿Then you disbelieved in it.﴾

His saying: ﴿in it﴾: the pronoun refers to the Quran, and it is permissible that it refers back to the Messenger ﷺ, since he is the one to whom the Quran was revealed.

﴿Who is more astray﴾: The author said: (that is, no one is more astray), as an indication that the interrogative here carries the meaning of negation. Know that the interrogative often comes with the meaning of negation, and its occurrence in the place of negation is stronger than plain negation; for when the interrogative occurs in the place of negation, it takes on the sense of challenge, as if he said: "Show me anyone more astray." There is no doubt that this includes both negation and challenge.

He said: ﴿Who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾ ﴿Who⟩ here is the subject, an interrogative noun in the position of the subject, and ﴿more astray⟩ (aḍall) is its predicate. ﴿Than one who is⟩ means: than the one who is ﴿in opposition⟩ (khilaf) ﴿extreme⟩. Rather, shiqaq (extreme opposition) is more specific than khilaf (disagreement); for one may oppose you without being in shiqaq with you, but these people opposed and were in shiqaq.

His saying: ﴿extreme⟩ means: (far from the truth). This was placed in the position of "from you," as an explanation of their state. ("This was placed") refers to ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition⟩ (placed in the position of "from you"), meaning: in the position of the pronoun. So it is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun, to clarify their state; that is, to clarify that they are more astray than anyone, and that their state is extreme opposition. In it there is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun. Abdullah, will you explain to us the benefit of the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun? Go on.

* Student: It was mentioned a little while ago.

* Shaykh: Do not say "it was mentioned a little while ago," meaning that you repeated what was said.

* Student: (...) the explicit noun in place of the pronoun?

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. What is its benefit?

* Student: Its benefit is: clarifying the attribute deserved by the one spoken about, like (...) upon these people (...).

* Shaykh: Perfect.

* Student: And among its benefits also: clarifying generality, meaning that everyone who does this, this description applies to him...

* Shaykh: Applies to him. Yes, well done. Three?

* Student: And among its benefits also.

* Shaykh: Now we will hold you to your own words: "it was mentioned a little while ago."

* Student: Alerting.

* Shaykh: Good. Alerting the addressee, since the context has turned contrary to what was expected, and this leads to his attention being awakened.

﴿Who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition﴾: In this verse there are benefits:

* First: The challenge to these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ who disbelieve in the Quran, and that after they knew the truth, they disbelieved in it.

* Among its benefits: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿Have you considered: if it is from Allah﴾. The reasoning for this: the Quran is an attribute, and an attribute must subsist in a described entity. If it is from Allah, then the one it subsists in must be Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Pay attention, brother. Now this verse contains evidence that the Quran is the speech of Allah. The reasoning: the Quran is an attribute, because it is speech, and an attribute must subsist in something described by it. If it is from Allah, then in whom does it subsist? In Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is what we believe, and what the Salaf, the People of the Sunnah and the Community believe: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, He truly spoke it with its letters, Jibril heard it from Him, and he conveyed it to the heart of the Prophet ﷺ.

The people of ta'til (negation of divine attributes) hold that the Quran is the speech of Allah but it is created, not an attribute of His attributes, but a created thing among His creations. This is the view of the Jahmiyyah and the Mu'tazilah. This view nullifies the command and prohibition and nullifies the entire Sharia, because if that is the case, it becomes mere sounds or mere letters with no meaning, like the sound of thunder for example, from which we benefit nothing; it is only something heard and has no meaning, or letters created in this manner, as if they were carvings on a wall or a door, engravings with no meaning. For this reason this view is considered among the gravest forms of atheism, because the Sharia is entirely nullified by it. For example, (qul, "say"): if we say it is created, and you write it on a paper, it becomes merely the form of a word, as if it were a carving, because it is not speech. And if you utter it, the sound is created. Indeed, when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, spoke it and revealed it to Jibril, it would be considered a created sound with no meaning, because it is a created thing among creations.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, distinguished between creation and command, saying: ﴿Surely to Him belong the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf 54], and He said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura 52]. Is it "from Our creation"? No, "from Our command." So those who say the Quran is the speech of Allah but it is created have entirely nullified the laws, since there is then no command and no prohibition.

There is another view of the Ash'arites, who say: the Quran is the speech of Allah, but speech itself—that is, the speech—is the meaning subsisting in His essence. As for what Jibril heard, it is created. So the Quran, in their view, is the speech of Allah, but the speech of Allah is the meaning subsisting in the self. And what is heard from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, such as His communing with Musa, and His speech by revelation to Jibril, is created, an expression of the meaning subsisting in the soul. This view is more severe and more wicked than the view of the Mu'tazilah. Why? Because the Mu'tazilah say: what we read in the mushafs is truly the speech of Allah. The Ash'arites say: it is an expression of the speech of Allah, and not the speech of Allah. All agree that what we read in the mushafs is created, but the Mu'tazilah say it is the speech of Allah, while the Ash'arites say it is an expression of the speech of Allah. Thus in this respect they became more wicked and more evil than the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah. As for us, we believe that what is written in the mushafs and preserved in hearts is the speech of Allah, and it is uncreated.

If someone says: Have you considered a reciter who recites, whose voice we hear in recitation: is this voice created or uncreated?

We say: it is created, because a person's voice is one of his attributes, so it is created like its source. But the thing uttered and the thing vocalized is uncreated. There is a difference between the voice and the utterance, and between the thing vocalized and the thing uttered. Is that not so?

If I read a book composed by a scholar, I am reading it. The voice is my voice, but the thing read is that of the scholar who wrote the book. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the creed al-Wasitiyyah: "Speech is attributed in truth to the one who said it originally, not to the one who conveys and relays it." So if a person wants to inquire whether the wording of a person's recitation of the Quran is created or not, what do we say?

We say: his wording, which is his articulation, is created, because it is the movements of his tongue, lips, and voice. As for the thing uttered, it is the uncreated speech of Allah. Evidence for this is that Allah, the Most High, said in the Noble Quran: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, [19] Possessed of power, with the Owner of the Throne, secure⟩ [al-Takwir 19, 20]. Who is the messenger here? Jibril. And He said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, [40] And it is not the word of a poet⟩ [al-Haqqah 40, 41]. Who is the messenger here? Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. It is impossible for one speech to be the speech of two speakers, but He attributed it to both because they are two messengers conveying from Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿the word of a messenger﴾ in both verses. So be alert to this and understand it.

It is reported from Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him: whoever says "my utterance of the Quran is created" is a Jahmi, and whoever says "it is uncreated" is an innovator. This is how it was transmitted from him.

In another narration: whoever says "my utterance of the Quran is created," meaning the Quran, is a Jahmi, and whoever says "it is uncreated" is an innovator. The second narration from him explains the first; that is, whoever says "my utterance of the Quran is created," meaning the Quran which is the thing uttered. If someone asks: can "utterance" (lafz) be meant as the thing uttered?

We say: yes, because lafz is a verbal noun (masdar), and a verbal noun sometimes comes with the meaning of the passive participle, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected» [narrated by Muslim (1718/18) from 'Aishah], where radd means "mardud" (rejected). And as in the words of Allah, the Most High: ﴿And if they are pregnant⟩ [al-Talaq 6], that is: "possessors of a burden," so al-hamal is a verbal noun and is meant as the passive participle.

In any case, we say about the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: it is speech heard with letters and sound, it is uncreated, and it is one of His attributes.

That is: whoever says "my utterance of the Quran is created," meaning the Quran which is the thing uttered.

If someone asks: can "utterance" (lafz) be meant as the thing uttered? We say: yes, because lafz is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun sometimes comes with the meaning of the passive participle, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18), the wording being Muslim's, from 'Aishah], "radd" meaning "mardud"; and as in the words of Allah, the Most High: ﴿And if they are pregnant⟩ [al-Talaq 6], that is: "possessors of a burden," and al-hamal is a verbal noun meant as the passive participle.

In any case, we say about the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: it is speech heard with letter and sound, it is uncreated, and it is an attribute of His attributes. But is it among the essential attributes or the active attributes?

We say: as regards its origin, and that He, the Exalted, has never ceased and will never cease to be speaking, it is among the essential attributes. As regards its individual instances, it is among the active attributes, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is⟩ [Ya-Sin 82]. When did "Be" come about? After the will. This is evidence that the speech of Allah, in terms of its individual instances and particulars, is among the active attributes.

* Student: Does the saying of the Ash'arites make them disbelievers by this statement?

* Shaykh: You must know an important principle: a mujtahid from this Ummah, even if he errs, is forgiven. They intend by this that Allah is exalted above having events subsist in Him, because they believe, with their feeble minds, that events subsist only in an event. They know that speech is an event: each letter occurs after the letter before it. But because of their feeble minds, they thought that whatever an event subsists in is itself an event, and this is an error. We do not declare them disbelievers for this. Yes, if a person's truth has become clear to him and he says he does not want the truth but follows his desires, then he may be declared a disbeliever. Yes.

* Student: The saying of Allah, the Most High: (...). Is this an indication that the context concerns disbelievers, or that whoever does these attributes has disbelieved and apostatized?

* Shaykh: Some scholars say: this concerns the disbeliever; the human, that is, the disbeliever, and the indicator is what you mentioned. Others say it concerns both the disbeliever and the believer, but Allah specified the disbeliever, by His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment⟩ [Fussilat 50].

* * *

* Student: ﴿Unquestionably, He is all-encompassing of all things⟩ [Fussilat 54].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself⟩. We have taken its benefits.

﴿And when adversity touches him, he is one of abundant supplication⟩ [Fussilat 51]. What is meant by "man" in His saying: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man⟩? (...) According to the first, the believer is excluded from His saying: ﴿And when adversity touches him, he is one of abundant supplication⟩, or what?

* Student: ﴿And when adversity touches him, he is one of abundant supplication⟩: the believer is excluded by His saying: ﴿And when adversity touches him, he is one of abundant supplication⟩.

* Shaykh: That is, its meaning is that even the believer, when adversity touches him, calls upon his Lord.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Say: Have you considered: if it is from Allah﴾ [Fussilat 52]. ("Have you considered," ara'aytum) means: inform me.

His saying: ﴿if it is from Allah﴾ (that is, the Quran) ﴿from Allah﴾.

His saying: ﴿and you disbelieve in it; who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition﴾ [Fussilat 52]. We have mentioned that this is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun, and the original is: "No one is more astray than you," but it was expressed explicitly in place of the pronoun. We have mentioned that the explicit noun in place of the pronoun has benefits, among them: alerting the addressee; second: clarifying the attribute by which the one referred to deserves this description.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: That is, generality? Good, generality. There is a fourth, but it is not in every place: observing the rhyme of the verses. Yes.

Then Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat 53] to the end. ﴿We will show them⟩: the sin is for future tense.

* Student: (...) The people of ta'til hold that the Quran is the speech of Allah, but it is a created, uttered thing.

* Shaykh: No, these are not among the benefits. Then let us start again.

First: that the Quran is the speech of Allah. The evidence is His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾. Furthermore, the evidence is that it is from Allah, and that speech is an attribute and not a self-standing entity, such that we could say it is created, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord are not too proud to worship Him; they exalt Him and to Him they prostrate﴾ [al-A'raf 206]. But speech is an attribute subsisting in a described entity, so this is evidence that it is from Allah.

* Thus it is derived: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, from His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾. The reasoning is that speech is an attribute that cannot subsist by itself, so it must be the speech of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that disbelief after clarity is more ugly than disbelief with ignorance, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿then you disbelieved in it﴾, for "then" (thumma) indicates sequence and delay, and their disbelief came after the matter had been made clear.

* Among its benefits: that no one is more astray than those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, since they are in extreme opposition, by His saying: ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete eloquence of the Quran, in that it chooses in each construction what suits the situation, by His saying: ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the occurrence of the interrogative in the place of negation, and that placing the interrogative in the place of negation is a correct Arabic style. What is its benefit? When it is in the form of an interrogative, it carries the sense of challenge, so His saying: ﴿who is more astray﴾ is more eloquent than saying "no one is more astray."

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾. The sīn (السين) is for the near future, and it indicates proximity and certainty. Sawfa (سوف) is for the distant future, and it indicates certainty with distance. For this reason we must distinguish between sawfa and sīn: if the matter will happen soon, say sayakūn (سيكون), and if it is distant, say sawfa yakūn (سوف يكون). This is why you find Allah's saying: ﴿No! You will come to know. Then, no! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur 3–4], because it has not yet come, and it is distant with respect to the time of this world.

﴿We will show them﴾ means: soon, a showing that is certain. ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾ means: We will make them manifest to them, so that they see them with their eyes, or so that they see them with their insight.

﴿Our signs﴾: āyāt (الآيات) is the plural of āyah (آية), which in the language means a sign or indicator. The meaning of Allah's signs is His indicators that point to the perfection of His knowledge, His wisdom, His power, and other requirements of His lordship.

Know that Allah's signs are of two types: legislative signs (āyāt shar'iyyah), which are what the messengers brought, among them this noble Qur'an; and cosmic signs (āyāt kawniyyah), which point to the perfection of Allah, blessed and exalted, in knowledge and creation, and in everything related to His lordship, and which human beings cannot match. All of mankind is unable to create an earth, a sky, stars, a sun, or a moon. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat 37]. These are cosmic signs, because no human can match them. Legislative signs are like His saying: ﴿When Our signs are recited to him, he says, "Fables of the ancients"﴾ [al-Qalam 15].

(﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾: the regions of the heavens and the earth, of luminous bodies, plants and trees.)

His saying: ﴿in the horizons﴾. The word āfāq (آفاق) is the plural of ufuq (أفق), which means a direction or region. The word here is plural, which indicates that these signs will be in every direction of the heavens and the earth. In the heavens there are stars, in the heavens there is the sun, in the heavens there is the moon, and in them there are rising points and setting points. All of these are among Allah's signs. Who can create the like of the sun? No one. Who can keep it running with this wondrous regularity since Allah created it until Allah permits the ruin of the world? No one can. Who can shift it from its eastern-northern risings to its eastern-southern risings? No one. And so on. This is in the horizons of the heavens.

Among the horizons of the heavens are the abundant or light rains, thunder, lightning, and other things. The point is that the horizons of the heavens are everything that is high; everything that is high is included in the horizons of the heavens.

Likewise, the horizons of the earth: the horizons of the earth contain, among the signs of Allah, what points to the perfection of His knowledge, power, wisdom and mercy: mountains, rivers, seas, deserts, valleys, hills, and so on; various plants, so that you see a plant like a patterned piece of cloth, this one green, that one violet, and that one white; their flowers differ, their fruits differ, they are watered with one water, yet Allah favours some of them over others in their produce.

Likewise, included in His saying ﴿in the horizons﴾ is what occurs in the horizons of war and peace, of security and fear, of hardship and ease. All of this is among Allah's signs in the horizons. Likewise what occurs of victory and defeat, and other things. So Allah promised that He would show His servants His signs in the horizons. Have you understood now?

Thus everything in the upper and lower horizons that creation cannot bring the like of is among Allah's signs.

﴿And in themselves﴾, meaning: and We will show them Our signs in themselves, and that is in several respects. First: in terms of creation. How Allah, glorified and exalted, created the human being in this wondrous, strange form, which no animal possesses in the like of its beautiful stature, its excellent management and its intellect, and other things.

Likewise, in themselves: tallness and shortness, whiteness and blackness, good character and bad character. Likewise, in themselves: the changing of states, and the fact that a person sometimes wants this and sometimes wants that, and sometimes wants a thing and resolves upon it, and then he is turned away from it. He is turned away. These are among Allah's signs. For this reason it was said to a Bedouin: "By what did you know your Lord?" He said: "By the turning of resolves and the overturning of hearts." You find a person, for example, intending to go north, and then he turns south without any apparent cause, but by the decree of Allah, glorified and exalted.

Likewise, among Allah's signs in the human being is the composition of this wondrous, amazing body. Ask the people of anatomy about this and you will find marvels upon marvels. If you come to the head and what is in it of brain and what is in it of instruments, and if you come to the intestines, the stomach, the liver, the glands and others, you will find marvels upon marvels. It is in reality a state unto itself; every part of it has its own special function. Who can compose this? Allah, mighty and majestic.

Likewise, among the signs in themselves is what happened to Quraysh at Badr, when Quraysh went out to Badr as Allah, mighty and majestic, described: ﴿insolently and to be seen by people, and barring from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Anfal 47]. One of them said: "By Allah, we will not return until we reach Badr, and remain there three days: we will slaughter camels, give wine to drink, have singing girls play for us, and the Arabs will hear of us, and so they will continue to fear us forever"[[Dala'il al-Nubuwwah of al-Bayhaqi (948), from the narration of 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr.]].

That is what they said, but the matter turned out the opposite, praise be to Allah: the Arabs have been speaking of their defeat until Allah wills the duration of the world. This is among the signs.

Likewise, among Allah's signs in the human being is that people differ greatly in understanding, memorization and action. You find this one choosing this work, and another saying: "How can this man endure this work?" Is that not so? And another the opposite. This is among the signs of Allah, blessed and exalted.

Likewise, people differ in understanding: among people, when you read a statement to one of them he understands it the first time, and among people, when you read it to one of them he does not understand it the first time. Among people, when you recite a statement to one of them he memorizes it the first time, and among people he is not like that. All of this is among the signs of Allah. Otherwise, the blood is one, the nerves are one, the bones are one, the skin is one, and everything is one; yet people differ with this great difference. All of this is included in His saying: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves﴾.

Let us look at the commentator: (﴿and in themselves﴾: from the subtle craftsmanship and wondrous wisdom).

﴿until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾. ﴿Becomes clear﴾ means: becomes evident. ﴿To them﴾ means: to these deniers. ﴿That it﴾: the author says: (i.e., the Qur'an), and it may be intended to refer to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it may be that both meanings are intended. (﴿That it is the truth﴾: the truth sent down from Allah, blessed and exalted, concerning resurrection, reckoning and punishment, so they will be punished for their disbelief in it and in the one who brought it.)

﴿That it is the truth﴾: truth (al-haqq, الحق) originally means a thing that is established and will certainly occur, and from it is His saying: ﴿The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah 1–2], meaning: the established thing. It is applied to several meanings, among them that it is truthfulness: truthfulness is truth, and its opposite, falsehood, is falsehood. Among them is justice: justice is truth, and its opposite, injustice, is falsehood. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truthfulness and justice; none can alter His words﴾ [al-An'am 115].

Among its meanings also is that it is a thing that is established and that no one can shake, and its opposite is a thing that does not stand firm and is not settled, and which everyone refutes. Now you find that however much the disputant argues to repel the Qur'an, his argument is false, and no one can overcome the Qur'an; rather, the Qur'an prevails.

But know, brothers, that the Qur'an's prevailing depends on its bearer. For this reason you find that a sharp sword in the hand of a coward is of no benefit. The Qur'an must be in accordance with its bearer; otherwise the Qur'an itself can never be overcome, but it may be overcome through its bearer, and this is no defect in the Qur'an, but a defect in the one who bears it.

﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ (sent down from Allah with resurrection and reckoning). This specification by the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is by way of example; otherwise it becomes clear that it is the truth in everything: in that it prevails and is not overcome, in that its rulings are just, its reports are true, and so on.

He said: (so they will be punished for their disbelief in it). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, has informed us that what is meant by "becoming clear" here is its necessary consequence, which is punishment; for if what was meant were merely becoming clear, without punishment for opposing it after it has become clear, there would be no benefit.

Among the same usage, where clarification or knowledge is mentioned and what is meant is its necessary consequence, is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿On that Day people will depart in scattered groups to be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah 6]. Now, will they be shown them only, or be shown them and be recompensed for them? The second: that is, they will be shown them and be recompensed for them. This too is an instance of "becoming clear": (they will be punished for their disbelief in it and in the one who brought it). Who is the one who brought it? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Allah said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾ When Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that He would display the signs until it becomes clear that this Qur'an is true, and that Muhammad is true, He mentioned something greater as evidence that the Qur'an is true and that the Messenger ﷺ is true: who is it? Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾

The answer: yes, that suffices. For when Allah sees this man calling people to what he calls them to, fighting them with it, Allah giving him victory over them, establishing him in the earth, people following him, could Allah approve of that while it is false? It is impossible, absolutely impossible. That Allah establishes His Messenger ﷺ in the earth, draws the hearts of people to him, gives him victory over his enemies, and opens the East and the West through his religion, all of this is evidence of what? That it is true.

The witnessing of Allah, glorified and exalted, to His Messenger is of two kinds: verbal witness and practical witness. The proof of the verbal witness is His saying: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness﴾ [an-Nisa' 166]. This is a witness from Allah. ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness, and sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾.

As for the practical witness, it is Allah's establishing of Muhammad ﷺ in the earth, His support for him, and the triumph of his religion over all other religions.

As for His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord﴾, the author said: (the subject of yakfi), and the bā' (ب) in it is extra, to beautify the wording. Its parallel is: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾, meaning: and Allah suffices as a witness. Accordingly, we say in its grammatical analysis: the bā' is an extra (zā'id) preposition, grammatically superfluous, its purpose being the beautification of the expression, and rabb (رب) is the subject of yakfi (يكف), marked with a presumed ḍammah on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the extra preposition.

As for His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord﴾, He attributed lordship (rubūbiyyah) to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Is this for specification, or for honour and dignity? The second. Why? Because He is the Lord of all things. Consider His saying: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾ [an-Naml 91], and after it He said: ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾, lest the one who thinks it might suppose that His lordship is limited to this city. Likewise, attributing lordship to the Messenger is by way of honour and dignity, and an indication that He will give him victory over his enemy, because Allah's lordship over the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is a special lordship.

(﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord that He is a witness over all things﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it.) A substitute of what? A substitute for His saying: ﴿your Lord﴾. The scholars define the badal as: that which, if you drop the replaced noun (mubdal minhu), the sentence remains sound. The badal is that which, if you delete the replaced noun, the sentence is correct. You say: "Zayd's character pleased me," this is a badal; drop "Zayd": "The character of Zayd pleased me," do you understand? "I ate the loaf, its third," drop "the loaf": does the sentence remain sound or not? This is the rule for the badal.

Here we say: ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord﴾; drop ﴿your Lord﴾, and you say: "Is it not sufficient that Allah is a witness over all things?" It holds together. But there is no doubt that the noble Qur'an cannot have a substitute and a replaced noun except for a great benefit. So ﴿Is it not sufficient for your Lord﴾ is a witnessing, a support, a strengthening, and the like.

Then He said: ﴿that He is a witness over all things﴾. This is part of the requirement of His lordship, glorified and exalted: ﴿that He is a witness over all things﴾. He said: (a substitute of it), meaning: Has it not sufficed them, regarding your truthfulness, that your Lord nothing escapes from Him? This is clear. And the witnessing here is what kind?

* Student: Verbal and practical.
* The Shaykh: The witnessing here is practical. That is: Has it not sufficed, with your Lord, that Allah is a witness over all things, and that He has established you in the earth, strengthened you, and given you victory over them and over every enemy of yours? The answer: Yes, by Allah, this is indeed sufficient. This is like His saying: ﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner"﴾ [al-'Ankabut 50]. After it: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 51]. So the Book is the greatest sign; Allah's witness to the truthfulness of His Messenger is the greatest sign.

Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾. ﴿Unquestionably﴾ (ألا) is an opening particle that conveys two things: the first is emphasis, and the second is alerting. Is it compounded of the hamzah and lā, or is it not compounded? The answer: it is not compounded, but is a single word.

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt﴾: in suspicion, ﴿about the meeting with their Lord﴾, because of their denial of resurrection. So they are, may Allah protect us, in doubt about meeting Allah. Had they hoped to meet Allah, they would have gone straight and feared Him. Every person who believes that he will meet his Lord will surely go straight in the command of Allah, because he knows that the Lord, mighty and majestic, will call him to account for this.

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Unquestionably﴾: another opening particle conveying alerting and emphasis. (﴿Unquestionably, He﴾ — exalted is He — ﴿encompasses all things﴾ in knowledge and power, so He will recompense them for their disbelief.) They are in doubt about meeting Allah, but Allah, mighty and majestic, will inform them of what they did, because He encompasses all things. Accordingly, the connection of His saying ﴿Unquestionably, He encompasses all things﴾ with what precedes it indicates that He will recompense them.

* Among the benefits of these verses: that Allah, exalted, will manifest what shows the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, ﴿in the horizons and in themselves﴾. From where do we take it? From His saying: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves﴾.
* Among them: that this showing is near and certain. From where is it taken? From ﴿We will show them﴾, because it is introduced with the sīn, which indicates certainty and proximity.
* Among them: that a person should reflect upon Allah's signs in the horizons and in himself, because that is a path to the truth becoming clear to him. From where do we take it? ﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ So the more you contemplate and reflect upon Allah's signs of the horizons and the signs within yourself, the more without doubt your faith increases, and the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, becomes clear to you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 41, verses 53–54 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the lessons of these noble verses is that a human being's knowledge is gravely deficient. The reason is that God shows them His signs within themselves, and a person has no knowledge of their own self except what God teaches them. That is why, brothers, your own self, which is the substance of your life, is something you do not truly know. Do you know what the soul (nafs) is? No, we do not know it.

For this reason the scholars of speculative theology (al-nuzzar, al-mutakallimun) and the philosophers and others have disagreed about it. Some said: the soul is the blood. Some said: the soul is a part of the body. Some said: the soul is an accident (ʿaraḍ) in the body. Some said: the soul cannot be described as anything, neither inside the world nor outside it, neither connected nor separate, and so on with what they say in absolute negation. Others said: the soul is a created thing among God's creations, that it has a physical substance, and that it enters the body and moves through it as a coal moves through charcoal, or water through clay.

What supports this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that when a person dies, his soul is taken. The angels take it and place it in a shroud and embalming perfume.[[Narrated by Aḥmad (18534) from the hadith of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib.]] He also said that when a person dies, the gaze follows it.[[Narrated by Muslim (920/7) from the hadith of Umm Salama.]] This indicates that it is a created thing that has a body and substance. Yet, despite that, we know only a little of it. That is why, when they asked about the spirit (rūḥ), God said: ﴿Say, "The spirit is by the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little."﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 85]

* Among the lessons of these verses is that the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ) are true, because of His saying: ﴿until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾.

* Among their lessons: the signs that indicate this are signs that lead to certainty, because of His saying: ﴿until it becomes clear (yatabayyana)﴾. Tabayyun means clarity and manifestness. From it is God's saying: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ [al-Baqara 187]. So if you know that you have not reached certainty, then blame yourself. You must treat this grave and dangerous disease until you reach certainty, until you arrive at what the Messenger's saying indicates: "That you worship God as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (50) and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abū Hurayra.]]

* Among the lessons of the noble verse: God's sufficiency over everything through His testimony, because of His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient regarding your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?﴾

* Among the lessons of the noble verse: deducing causes from their effects (al-istidlāl bil-āthār ʿalā muʾaththirātihā). The basis of this is that God argued, through His enabling of the Messenger, that he is true. So a person deduces from effects their causes. That is why it was said: "The dropping indicates the camel." This was the answer of a Bedouin who was asked, "How did you know your Lord?" He answered at once: "The dropping indicates the camel." He chose this because he was a Bedouin who knew only camels. The dropping indicates the camel, and the track indicates the traveler. Is that correct? If you see, for example, the imprint of a foot on the ground, you know that someone has walked this way. So, "a sky with constellations, an earth with wide paths, and seas with waves, do they not indicate the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing?" The answer is yes. This Bedouin deduced from the signs of the horizons the existence of God and His power.

* Among the lessons of these verses: caution against opposition. This is an educational lesson. From where is it taken? ﴿Is it not sufficient regarding your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?﴾ When you know that God is a Witness over everything, over yourself, your deeds, your words, all your conduct, you will watch over God, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever is not admonished by a verse like this will not be admonished. If you know that God is a Witness over you in your private moments, in your solitude, in your sitting with your family, in your sitting with your companions, you will watch over God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is the meaning of the Messenger's (ﷺ) saying: "That you worship God as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (50) and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abū Hurayra.]]

* Among the lessons of the noble verse: clarification of the state of these deniers, and that the cause of their denial is that they are in doubt about meeting God. It is known that whoever is in doubt about meeting God will not act for God. That is why you find God always linking belief in Him with the Last Day, because whoever's faith in the Last Day is deficient, his deeds will be deficient, and whoever's faith in the Last Day is complete, his deeds will be complete, because he hopes to be happy on that day.

When you bow or prostrate, keep in mind that this bowing and prostration will benefit you when? On the Day of Resurrection. It benefits you now too, because prayer forbids indecency and evil. But the tangible fruit is on the Day of Resurrection, which appears to everyone. In this world, the believer experiences the complete benefit of acts of obedience, as Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya (may God have mercy on him) said: "What can my enemies do to me? My paradise is in my breast; my imprisonment is seclusion; my exile is wandering; my killing is martyrdom." May God have mercy on him. So the believer finds this in himself before the Day of Resurrection. On the Day of Resurrection, the full manifestation occurs, and everything is uncovered.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of God's encompassing of everything, in knowledge, power, authority, governance, and other things. He encompasses everything, His acts and the acts of the servants. The Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿That you may know that God is over all things competent, and that God has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 12].

* Also among the lessons of this noble verse: the realization of watchfulness over God. Because when you believe that God encompasses everything, then you will, what? You will watch Him with complete watchfulness, so that He does not find you where He commanded you, and does not see you where He forbade you. And God knows best.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Ḥā Mīm. ʿAyn Sīn Qāf.
